                  Transcription note 
                  
                

The main steps and every boxed result are transcribed; some intermediate algebra lines are abbreviated — see the original pages above.


Final version of HW 5.
Problem 1
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial u^2}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial uv}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}\;;\qquad (x, y, t) \Longleftrightarrow (\xi, \eta, \tau)
(a) Coordinate transformations (using t = \tau & \tau \neq f(x, y)), as in the draft, give the chain-rule conservation-law form:
\boxed{\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \xi_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)u}_{\text{term 1}} + \underbrace{\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)u^2}_{\text{term 2}} + \underbrace{\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)uv}_{\text{term 3}} = \underbrace{\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)}_{\text{term 4}}}
(b) To maintain conservation, convert to the strong conservation-law form: (1) J\times (PDE from above); (2) move the J term inside via the chain rule. Terms 1–3 are as in the draft (\frac{\partial(Ju)}{\partial\tau}, and the u^2 and uv flux terms, each leaving a geometric conservation law = 0). Term 4, with a = \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}:
J\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) = J\xi_y\frac{\partial a}{\partial\xi} + J\eta_y\frac{\partial a}{\partial\eta} = \frac{\partial(J\xi_ya)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_ya)}{\partial\eta} - a\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_y)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y)}{\partial\eta}\right)}_{=0\text{ (geometric cons. law)}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)
Therefore, the final strong conservative form:
\frac{\partial(Ju)}{\partial\tau} + \left[\frac{\partial(J\xi_xu^2)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_xu^2)}{\partial\eta}\right] + \left[\frac{\partial(J\xi_yuv)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_yuv)}{\partial\eta}\right] = \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)
\boxed{\frac{\partial(Ju)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(J\xi_xu^2 + J\xi_yuv - J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(J\eta_xu^2 + J\eta_yuv - J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right) = 0}
Transcriber’s note: the \eta-flux carries J\xi_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} where J\eta_y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} is expected; as written.
(c) The highlighted terms in blue show the 4 geometric conservation laws (in the expressions above).
Problem 2
Incompressible potential flow: \nabla^2\underbrace{\psi}_{\text{stream function}} = 0.
(a) Describe the problem (typed)
Potential flow is used to model irrotational where the viscosity effects are assumed to be negligible - typically externally flow over solid surfaces or flow at high Reynolds number. In such cases, the thickness of the boundary layer is assumed to be much smaller than the dimen sions of the object.
The given equation is the Laplace equation using stream function. Stream function (\psi) can be defined for any 2D flow such that the stream function is constant along a streamline. Additionally, change in stream function between a pair of streamlines equals the volummetric flowrate between the two streamlines. Finally, lines of constant streamlines are perpendicular to the lines of constant velocity potential (\Phi).
(b) Governing equations
(sketch: the converging–diverging nozzle — inlet height h_1 with u = u_{in}, outlet height h_2, \psi = 0 on the lower wall (curve 1) and \psi = u_{in}h_1 on the upper wall (curve 2).)
2D, axisymmetric flow; \psi = stream function (constant along a streamline):
u = \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\;;\quad v = -\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\;\therefore\;\boxed{\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} = 0}\;\downarrow\;\frac{\partial(-v)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0\;;\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 0
BCs: (inflow) u_{in} = \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\big|_{x=0}; (outflow) \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\big|_{x=C} = 0; (walls) \psi = 0 (@ curve 1), \psi = u_{in}h_1 (@ curve 2).
We also use Bernoulli’s principle to relate pressure & fluid velocity @ steady state:
P_{inlet} + \frac{1}{2}\rho u_{in}^2 = \text{constant}\;;\qquad @\;x = 0,\;P_{inlet} = P_{atm} = 100{,}000\text{ Pa}
(c) Two-boundary method to generate a 2D grid
\int_{(y-h_1)}^{(y+h_1)}u_{in}\,dy = \int_{\psi=0}^{\psi(y)}\partial\psi \;\Rightarrow\; \psi(y) = u_{in}\left((y + h_1) - (y - h_1)\right) = u_{in}(2h_1)
X_1(\xi, \tau) = x(\xi, \eta = 0, \tau)\;;\quad Y_1(\xi, \tau) = y(\xi, \eta = 0, \tau)\;;\qquad X_2(\xi, \tau) = x(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)\;;\quad Y_2(\xi, \tau) = y(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)
\vec{r}_1 = X_1\hat{i} + Y_1\hat{j}\;;\qquad \vec{r}_2 = X_2\hat{i} + Y_2\hat{j}
Hermite interpolation:
x(\xi, \eta, \tau) = X_1(\xi, \tau)h_1(\eta) + X_2(\xi, \tau)h_2(\eta) + \frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 0, \tau)}{\partial\eta}h_3(\eta) + \frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta}h_4(\eta)\;;\qquad y(\xi, \eta, \tau) = Y_1(\xi, \tau)h_1(\eta) + Y_2(\xi, \tau)h_2(\eta)\cdots
h_1(\eta) = 2\eta^3 - 3\eta^2 + 1\;;\quad h_2(\eta) = -2\eta^3 + 3\eta^2\;;\quad h_3(\eta) = \eta^3 - 2\eta^2 + \eta\;;\quad h_4(\eta) = \eta^3 - \eta^2
(sketch: curves 1 and 2 with a line of constant \xi between them; at curve 2 the tangent \vec{e}_\xi and the normal \vec{e}_\eta, with \vec{e}_\xi\cdot\vec{e}_\eta = 0.)
\vec{e}_\xi = \frac{\partial X_2(\xi, \tau)}{\partial\xi}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial Y_2(\xi, \tau)}{\partial\xi}\hat{j}\;;\qquad \vec{e}_\eta = \frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta}\hat{i} + \frac{\partial y(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta}\hat{j}
\frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta} = -K_2(\xi, \tau)\frac{\partial Y_2(\xi, \tau)}{\partial\xi}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial y(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta} = +K_2(\xi, \tau)\frac{\partial X_2(\xi, \tau)}{\partial\xi}\quad\}\;K\text{-factors}
Parametrize the boundaries: x = \xi, y = f(x) = f(\xi); \vec{r} = \xi\hat{i} + f(\xi)\hat{j}. We are given:
\text{Curve 1, }f_1(x):\;\begin{cases}x \in [A, B]: & Y_1 = (D - a_1) - a_1\cos\left[\frac{\pi(x - A)}{(B - A)}\right] \\ x \in (B, C]: & Y_1 = (D - a_2) + a_2\cos\left[\frac{\pi(x - B)}{(C - B)}\right]\end{cases}
\text{Curve 2, }f_2(x):\;\begin{cases}x \in [A, B]: & Y_2 = (E + a_1) + a_1\cos\left[\frac{\pi(x - A)}{(B - A)}\right] \\ x \in (B, C]: & Y_2 = (E + a_2) - a_2\cos\left(\frac{\pi(x - B)}{(C - B)}\right)\end{cases}
(d) Transform (x, y) to (\xi, \eta)
\nabla^2\psi = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; J\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\right)}_{f} + J\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\right)}_{g} = 0\quad(\text{strong conservative form, times by }J^2)
\Rightarrow\frac{\partial(J\xi_xf)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(\eta_xJf)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_yg)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_yg)}{\partial\eta} - f\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_x)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_x)}{\partial\eta}\right)}_{0} - g\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_y)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y)}{\partial\eta}\right)}_{0} = 0
\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(J\xi_x\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x} + J\xi_y\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(J\eta_x\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x} + J\eta_y\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\right) = 0}
with J\xi_x\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)\psi = \xi_x\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_x\psi)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y\psi)}{\partial\eta}\right), ∴
\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(\xi_x\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_x\psi)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y\psi)}{\partial\eta}\right) + \xi_y\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_y\psi)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y\psi)}{\partial\eta}\right)\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(\eta_x\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_x\psi)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_x\psi)}{\partial\eta}\right) + \eta_y\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_y\psi)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y\psi)}{\partial\eta}\right)\right) = 0
(e), (f) FDEs/FVEs for the governing equations + algorithm
(J^2\xi_x)\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\right) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left[(J^2\xi_x^2)\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\right] - \left(\xi_x\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\right)\frac{\partial(J^2\xi_x)}{\partial\xi}
with the first term \approx \frac{(J^2\xi_x^2)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\right)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j} - (J^2\xi_x^2)_{i-\frac{1}{2},j}\left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\right)_{i-\frac{1}{2},j}}{\Delta\xi}, \left(\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\right)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j} = \frac{\psi_{i+1,j} - \psi_{i,j}}{\Delta\xi}, and the second \to \xi_x\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial\xi}\left[J\frac{\partial(J\xi_x)}{\partial\xi} + \xi_xJ\frac{\partial J}{\partial\xi}\right].
\frac{\partial(J\xi_x\psi)}{\partial\xi} = \left[(J\xi_x)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j+\frac{1}{2}}\psi_{i+\frac{1}{2},j+\frac{1}{2}} - (J\eta)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j-\frac{1}{2}}\psi_{i+\frac{1}{2},j-\frac{1}{2}}\right]/\Delta\xi\;;\qquad \psi_{i+\frac{1}{2},j+\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{1}{4}\left(\psi_{i+1,j} + \psi_{i,j} + \psi_{i+1,j+1} + \psi_{i,j+1}\right)
\vec{A}_\xi = (J\xi_x)\hat{i} + (J\xi_y)\hat{j}
Metric coefficients & Jacobian:
J = x_\xi y_\eta - y_\xi x_\eta\;;\quad \xi_x = \frac{y_\eta}{J}\;;\quad \xi_y = -\frac{x_\eta}{J}\;;\quad \eta_x = -\frac{y_\xi}{J}\;;\quad \eta_y = \frac{x_\xi}{J}
(\xi_x)_{ij} = \frac{y_{i,j+1} - y_{i,j-1}}{2\Delta\eta J_{ij}}\;;\quad (\xi_y)_{ij} = -\frac{x_{i,j+1} - x_{i,j-1}}{2\Delta\eta J_{ij}}\;;\quad (\eta_x)_{ij} = -\frac{y_{i+1,j} - y_{i-1,j}}{2\Delta\xi J_{ij}}\;;\quad (\eta_y)_{ij} = \frac{x_{i+1,j} - x_{i-1,j}}{2\Delta\xi J_{ij}}
J_{ij} = \left(\frac{x_{i+1,j} - x_{i-1,j}}{2\Delta\xi}\right)\left(\frac{y_{i,j+1} - y_{i,j-1}}{2\Delta\eta}\right) - \left(\frac{y_{i+1,j} - y_{i-1,j}}{2\Delta\xi}\right)\left(\frac{x_{i,j+1} - x_{i,j-1}}{2\Delta\eta}\right)
Algorithm:

Generate the grid via the two-boundary method.

↳ Use IL, JL = 41 (from lecture) → step sizes of \Delta\xi = \frac{1}{(IL - 1)}; \Delta\eta = \frac{1}{(JL - 1)}.
↳ Use Hermite interpolation → (parameterized curves, computed basis functions, using a K factor of 0.08) → gives the grid for x, y.


Set initial conditions (u_{in}, P_{in}, \rho).
Compute the Jacobian & metric coefficients for the transformation.
Finite difference loops for solving for \psi in the transformed domain.
Inverse transform & use the u & v relation to obtain the velocity in the physical domain.
Plotting the contour plot.

(g), (h) Code + solutions for velocity = 100 m/s; P = 100,000 Pa; ρ = 1000 kg/m³
See the attached document for the code (debugging via LLM software). The two-boundary method code was borrowed from the Fortran code that was shown in lecture 16, slide 35.
(plot: “Velocity Magnitude in Converging-Diverging Nozzle” — a contour plot over x from 0 to 6 m; the velocity is low through the inlet and throat and shows large, irregular high-velocity lobes in the diverging section near the exit.)
(i) Discuss the accuracy of results (typed)
There seems to be a bug in the code which prohibited a physical solution that can be analyzed; however, we can still discuss about the results we expect from a solution to the converging-diverging nozzle
Due the converging geometry, we expect that the velocity will be the highest in the constriction of the nozzle (i.e. for this geometry it should be at x=2); as the fluid moves past the constriction into the diverging part of the nozzle. Since we are assuming incompressible potential flow, the diverging section would decelerate the flow (as the area increases, and velocity decreases). However, this contradicts real compressible flows where you could have supersonic acceleration.
Extra credit: Changing the geometry of the nozzle
Moving the value of B to a higher value of x i.e. B = 4, should simulate the nozzle contraction moving to a later value and hence the expected velocity peak also changes around this constriction. Changing the C parameter will just extend the diverging part of the nozzle which will pretty much make the flow to be converted to flow in a tube (i.e. the peak velocities should decelerate pretty quickly - my code does not show this effect accurately sorry)
Something that would have been also interesting to look at (if my code would have worked) is changing the geometry angles which is known to minimize flow separation and have smooth acceleration to the throat. The throat length can also be varied to stabilize flow before divergence.
(plots: “Varying the B parameter” — the throat moved downstream, with the high-velocity lobes concentrated near the exit; “Changing the E parameter” — a longer, gentler nozzle with the high-velocity region again near the exit.)

Working draft of HW 5; the submitted version is HW 5 final.
Problem 1
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial u^2}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial uv}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}\;;\qquad (x, y, t) \Longleftrightarrow (\xi, \eta, \tau)
(a) We can use coordinate transformations (using t = \tau & \tau \neq f(x, y)):
\frac{\partial}{\partial x} = \xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial y} = \xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \xi_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}
\therefore\;\boxed{\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \xi_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)u}_{\text{term 1}} + \underbrace{\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)u^2}_{\text{term 2}} + \underbrace{\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)uv}_{\text{term 3}} = \underbrace{\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)^2u}_{\text{term 4}}}
↑ Chain-rule conservation-law form.
(b) To maintain conservation, have to convert to the strong conservation-law form:

J\times (PDE from above).
Move the J term inside via the chain rule.

Term 1:
J\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \xi_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)u = \frac{\partial(Ju)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_tu)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_tu)}{\partial\eta} - \underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial J}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_t)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_t)}{\partial\eta}\right)}_{0\text{ (geometric conservation law)}}u = \frac{\partial(Ju)}{\partial\tau}
(with \xi_t = \eta_t = 0.) Similar manipulation of term 2 & term 3 (first-order spatial derivatives):
J\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)u^2 = \frac{\partial(J\xi_xu^2)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_xu^2)}{\partial\eta} - u^2\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_x)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_x)}{\partial\eta}\right)}_{=0\text{ (geometric conservation law)}}
J\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)uv = \frac{\partial(J\xi_yuv)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_yuv)}{\partial\eta} - uv\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial(J\xi_y)}{\partial\xi} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_y)}{\partial\eta}\right)}_{=0\text{ (geometric cons. law)}}
Term 4:
J\cdot\frac{J}{J}\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)^2u = \frac{1}{J}\left(J\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + J\eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)^2u = \frac{1}{J}\left(J^2\xi_y^2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\xi^2} + J^2\eta_y^2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\eta^2} + 2J^2\xi_y\eta_y\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}\right)u
= \frac{1}{J}\left[\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y^2u)}{\partial\xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2(J^2\eta_y^2u)}{\partial\eta^2} + 2\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y\eta_yu)}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}\right] - \frac{u}{J}\underbrace{\left(\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y^2)}{\partial\xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2(J^2\eta_y^2)}{\partial\eta^2} + 2\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y\eta_y)}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}\right)}_{0\text{ (= geometric conservation law)}}
Therefore, the final strong conservative form:
\boxed{\frac{\partial(Ju)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(J\xi_xu^2 + J\xi_yuv\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(J\eta_xu^2 + J\eta_yuv\right) = \frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y^2u)}{\partial\xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2(J^2\eta_y^2u)}{\partial\eta^2} + \frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y\eta_yu)}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}}
Transcriber’s note: the \frac{1}{J} factor and the 2 on the mixed derivative from term 4 are dropped in the final form; as written.
(c) The highlighted terms in blue show the 4 geometric conservation laws (in the expressions above).
Problem 2
Incompressible potential flow: \nabla^2\underbrace{\psi}_{\text{stream function}} = 0.
(a) Describe the problem (left blank in this draft).
(b) Governing equations
(sketch: a converging–diverging nozzle with inlet half-height h_1 at x = 0 where u = u_{in}, outlet height h_2; streamline \psi = 0 on the lower wall and \psi = u_{in}h_1 on the upper wall; a sample streamline drawn between.)
2D, axisymmetric flow; \psi = stream function (constant along a streamline):
u = \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\;;\quad v = -\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\;\therefore\;\boxed{\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} = 0}\;\downarrow\;\frac{\partial(-v)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0\;;\quad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 0
BCs:

(Inflow) u_{in} = \dfrac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\Big|_{x=0}
(Outflow) \dfrac{\partial\psi}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=C} = 0
(Walls) \psi = 0 (@ curve 1); \psi = u_{in}h_1 (@ curve 2)

\int_{(y-h_1)}^{(y+h_1)}u_{in}\,dy = \int_{\psi=0}^{\psi(y)}\partial\psi \;\Rightarrow\; \psi(y) = u_{in}\left((y + h_1) - (y - h_1)\right) = u_{in}(2h_1)
(c) Two-boundary method to generate a 2D grid (sketch: the same nozzle with u = u_{in} at the inlet of height h_1, \psi = 0 on the lower wall and \psi = u_{in}h_1 on the upper.)
u_{in} = \frac{\partial\psi}{\partial y}\Big|_{x=0}\;;\qquad \int_{-h_1}^{h_1}u_{in}\,dy = \int_{\psi=0}^{\psi(y)}\partial\psi
(d) Transform (x, y) to (\xi, \eta):
\nabla^2\psi = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial y^2} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; J^2\left(\xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)^2\psi + J^2\left(\xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\right)^2\psi = 0\quad(\text{strong conservative})
\Rightarrow\left[\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_x^2\psi)}{\partial\xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2(J^2\eta_x^2\psi)}{\partial\eta^2} + 2\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_x\eta_x\psi)}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}\right] + \left[\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y^2\psi)}{\partial\xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2(J^2\eta_y^2\psi)}{\partial\eta^2} + 2\frac{\partial^2(J^2\xi_y\eta_y\psi)}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}\right] - \psi\underbrace{\left[\cdots\right]}_{=0\,?}
\Rightarrow\;\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\xi^2}\underbrace{\left(J^2\xi_x^2\psi + J^2\xi_y^2\psi\right)}_{\tilde{f}} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\eta^2}\left(J^2\eta_x^2\psi + J^2\eta_y^2\psi\right) + 2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\xi\partial\eta}\left(J^2\xi_x\eta_x + J^2\xi_y\eta_y\right) = 0
(margin, in red: J^2\xi_x^2 \to y_\eta^2, with y_\eta = \xi_x\cdot J; and \psi_{i+1} - 2\psi + \psi_{i-1}.)
(e), (f) FDEs/FVEs for the governing equations + algorithm:
\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial\xi^2} = \frac{\psi_{i+1,j} - 2\psi_{i,j} + \psi_{i-1,j}}{\Delta\xi^2}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial\eta^2} = \frac{\psi_{i,j+1} - 2\psi_{i,j} + \psi_{i,j-1}}{\Delta\eta^2}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial\xi\partial\eta} = \frac{\psi_{i+1,j+1} - \psi_{i+1,j-1} - \psi_{i-1,j+1} + \psi_{i-1,j-1}}{4\Delta\xi\Delta\eta}
with \xi_x = \frac{\partial\xi}{\partial x} = \frac{y_\eta}{J}.
(g), (h) Code + solutions for velocity = 100 m/s (not filled in).
(i) Discuss the accuracy of results (not filled in).

The main steps and every boxed result are transcribed; some intermediate algebra lines are abbreviated — see the original pages above.


Problem 1
(i) Derive the difference operator for \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL} w/ O(\Delta x^2) accuracy

No. of terms to be kept in the Taylor series: N = order of derivative + order of accuracy = 1 + 2 = 3.
Stencil: (sketch: points i-2, i-1, i, with arrows from i-2 and i-1 to i.)
N - 1 truncated Taylor series about T_{IL}:

T_{IL-1} = T_{IL} - \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\Delta x + \left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_{IL}\frac{\Delta x^2}{2!} - O(\Delta x^3)\;;\qquad T_{IL-2} = T_{IL} - \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}(2\Delta x) + \left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_{IL}\frac{(2\Delta x)^2}{2!} - O(\Delta x^3)

Solving the coupled linear equations. Subtracting the two terms:

T_{IL-1} - T_{IL-2} = \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\Delta x - \left(\frac{3}{2}\Delta x^2\right)\left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_{IL}\;\Rightarrow\;\left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_{IL} = \left[(-T_{IL-1} + T_{IL-2}) + \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\Delta x\right]\frac{2}{3(\Delta x^2)}
Substituting here:
T_{IL-1} = T_{IL} - \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\Delta x + \frac{1}{3}(-T_{IL-1} + T_{IL-2}) + \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\left(\frac{1}{3}\Delta x\right)
\left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\left(\Delta x - \frac{1}{3}\Delta x\right) = T_{IL} - T_{IL-1} - \frac{1}{3}T_{IL-1} + \frac{1}{3}T_{IL-2}\;\Rightarrow\;\left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL}\left(\frac{2}{3}\Delta x\right) = T_{IL} - \frac{4}{3}T_{IL-1} + \frac{1}{3}T_{IL-2}
\boxed{\left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_{IL} = \frac{3T_{IL} - 4T_{IL-1} + T_{IL-2}}{2\Delta x} + O(\Delta x^2)}
(ii) Following a similar strategy for the difference operator for \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1

N = 3.
(sketch: points i, i+1, i+2 with arrows back to i.)
T_2 = T_1 + \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1\Delta x + \left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_1\frac{(\Delta x)^2}{2} + O(\Delta x^3); T_3 = T_1 + \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_12\Delta x + \left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_1\frac{(2\Delta x)^2}{2} + O(\Delta x^3).
Subtracting the equations: T_2 - T_3 = -\left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1\Delta x - \left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_1\left(\frac{3}{2}\Delta x^2\right) ⇒ \left(\frac{d^2T}{dx^2}\right)_1 = \left[(T_3 - T_2) - \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1\Delta x\right]\frac{2}{3\Delta x^2}.

Substituting:
T_2 = T_1 + \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1\Delta x + \left[(T_3 - T_2) - \left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1\Delta x\right]\frac{\Delta x^2}{2}\cdot\frac{2}{3\Delta x^2}\;\Rightarrow\;\left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1\left(-\frac{2\Delta x}{3}\right) = T_1 - T_2 + \frac{T_3}{3} - \frac{T_2}{3} = \left[\frac{3T_1 - 4T_2 + T_3}{3}\right]
\boxed{\left(\frac{dT}{dx}\right)_1 = \frac{-3T_1 + 4T_2 - T_3}{2\Delta x} + O(\Delta x^2)}
Problem 2 — 4th-order compact operators
c\frac{\partial U}{\partial x} = \nu\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial x^2}\;;\qquad @\;x = 0:\;U = 1\;;\qquad @\;x = L = 10:\;\frac{dU}{dx} = 2\;;\qquad \frac{cL}{\nu} = 2
↓ cF_i - \nu S_i = 0, with F_i = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\right)_i and S_i = \left(\frac{\partial^2U}{\partial x^2}\right)_i.
Compact differencing yields (derived via the operator approach):
F_{i+1} + 4F_i + F_{i-1} = \frac{3}{\Delta x}(U_{i+1} - U_{i-1})\quad\cdots(1)
S_{i+1} + 10S_i + S_{i-1} = \frac{12}{\Delta x^2}(U_{i+1} - 2U_i + U_{i-1})\quad\cdots(2)
We know cF_i = \nu S_i, so S_i = \frac{c}{\nu}F_i → substituting in the above equation:
\therefore\;\frac{c}{\nu}F_{i+1} + 10\frac{c}{\nu}F_i + \frac{c}{\nu}F_{i-1} = \frac{12}{\Delta x^2}(U_{i+1} - 2U_i + U_{i-1})\quad\cdots(3)
Similarly, F_i = \frac{\nu}{c}S_i:
\frac{\nu}{c}S_{i+1} + 4S_i + S_{i-1} = \frac{3}{\Delta x}(U_{i+1} - U_{i-1})\quad\cdots(4)
Transcriber’s note: in (4) only the first term carries the \frac{\nu}{c} factor; as written.
We can combine (1) and (3) in matrix form. From (1):
F_{i+1} + 4F_i + F_{i-1} - \frac{3}{\Delta x}(U_{i+1} - U_{i-1}) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \left[F_{i+1} - \frac{3}{\Delta x}U_{i+1}\right] + 4F_i + \left[\frac{3}{\Delta x}U_{i-1} + F_{i-1}\right] = 0
From (3):
\left[\frac{c}{\nu}F_{i+1} - \frac{12}{\Delta x^2}U_{i+1}\right] + \left[10\frac{c}{\nu}F_i + \frac{24}{\Delta x^2}U_i\right] + \left[\frac{c}{\nu}F_{i-1} - \frac{12}{\Delta x^2}U_{i-1}\right] = 0
Combining the above expressions in matrix form:
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{3}{\Delta x} & 1 \\ -\frac{12}{\Delta x^2} & \frac{c}{\nu}\end{bmatrix}}_{L_i}\begin{bmatrix}U_{i+1} \\ F_{i+1}\end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 \\ \frac{24}{\Delta x^2} & 10\frac{c}{\nu}\end{bmatrix}}_{M_i}\begin{bmatrix}U_i \\ F_i\end{bmatrix} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\frac{3}{\Delta x} & 1 \\ -\frac{12}{\Delta x^2} & \frac{c}{\nu}\end{bmatrix}}_{N_i}\begin{bmatrix}U_{i-1} \\ F_{i-1}\end{bmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{d_i}
If we define V_i = \begin{bmatrix}U_i \\ F_i\end{bmatrix}, where V_{i-1} = \begin{bmatrix}U_{i-1} \\ F_{i-1}\end{bmatrix}, we obtain:
\boxed{L_iV_{i-1} + M_iV_i + N_iV_{i+1} = d_i}\quad\cdots(5)
Transcriber’s note: L_i multiplies V_{i+1} in the matrix form but V_{i-1} in (5); as written.
↳ Solving this system of equations will yield an O(\Delta x^4) accurate solution.

Interior points: L_iV_{i-1} + M_iV_i + N_iV_{i+1} = d_i.
Apply boundary conditions ↳ one-sided differencing that relates \frac{dU}{dx} at the boundary to two neighbouring points.

@ x = 0 (i = 1), U = 1: V_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ F_1\end{bmatrix}; L_2V_1 + M_2V_2 + N_2V_3 = d_1.
@ x = L, \frac{dU}{dx} = F = 2: V_{IL} = \begin{bmatrix}U_{IL} \\ 2\end{bmatrix}; L_{IL-1}V_{IL-2} + M_{IL-1}V_{IL-1} + N_{IL-1}V_{IL} = d.



Overall algorithm

Discretize the domain (x_i = (i - 1)\Delta x; i = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, m, m+1) ↳ the grid is initialized for a given \Delta x.
Use compact differencing to discretize the ODE (arriving at eq. (5) from above).
Apply the given boundary conditions & solve for the interior points → iterate using a for loop.
Plot and analyze results.

Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 78-83)

The main steps and every boxed result are transcribed; some intermediate algebra lines are abbreviated — see the original pages above.


Problem 1
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial u^2}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(x + y)u}{\partial y} = \nu\left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y}\right) + au^2\;;\qquad 0 \leq x \leq L_x\;,\;0 \leq y \leq L_y
(a) FDE for interior points
Domain discretized as x_i = (i - 1)\Delta x, i = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, IL; y_j = (j - 1)\Delta y, j = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, JL. Let u_{i,j}^n represent the value of u at the (i, j) spatial point & n time step.
(i) Self-starting second-order implicit for time differencing ↳ Crank–Nicolson scheme: \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} \approx \frac{u_{i,j}^{n+1} - u_{i,j}^n}{\Delta t} with \theta = \frac{1}{2}.
(ii) Second-order central differencing for spatial derivatives:
\frac{\partial u^2}{\partial x} = \frac{(u_{i+1,j}^n)^2 - (u_{i-1,j}^n)^2}{2\Delta x}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial(x + y)u}{\partial y} = \frac{(x_i + y_{j+1})u_{i,j+1}^n - (x_i + y_{j-1})u_{i,j-1}^n}{2\Delta y}
\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} = \frac{u_{i+1,j}^n - 2u_{i,j}^n + u_{i-1,j}^n}{(\Delta x)^2}\;;\quad \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2} = \frac{u_{i,j+1}^n - 2u_{i,j}^n + u_{i,j-1}^n}{(\Delta y)^2}\;;\quad \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y} = \frac{u_{i+1,j+1}^n - u_{i+1,j-1}^n - u_{i-1,j+1}^n + u_{i-1,j-1}^n}{4\Delta x\Delta y}
(iii)
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \nu\left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y}\right) + au^2 - \frac{\partial u^2}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial(x + y)u}{\partial y}
\frac{u_{i,j}^{n+1} - u_{i,j}^n}{\Delta t} = \left[\nu\left(D_x^2 + D_y^2 + D_xD_y\right)u_{i,j} + \underbrace{a(u_{i,j})^2}_{\text{source term}} - D_x(u_{i,j})^2 - D_y(x_i + y_j)u_{i,j}\right]^{n+1}
⇒ Linearizing and writing in operator form:
(u_{i,j}^2)^{n+1} \approx (u_{i,j}^2)^n + 2u_{i,j}\underbrace{(u^{n+1} - u^n)}_{\Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1}} + O(\Delta t^2)\;;\qquad u_{i,j}^{n+1} = (u^{n+1} - u^n) + u^n = \Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1} + u_{i,j}^n
\therefore\;\frac{\Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1}}{\Delta t} = \left[\nu(D_x^2 + D_y^2 + D_xD_y)u_{i,j}^{n+1} + a\left((u_{i,j}^2)^n + 2u_{i,j}^n\Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1}\right) - D_x\left((u_{i,j}^2)^n + 2u_{i,j}^n\Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1}\right) - D_y(x_i + y_j)u_{i,j}^{n+1}\right]
In operator form:
\Delta u^{n+1} - \Delta t\left[\nu(D_x^2 + D_y^2 + D_xD_y)\Delta u^{n+1} - a(2u^n\Delta u^{n+1}) + D_x(2u^n\Delta u^{n+1}) + D_y(x + y)\Delta u^{n+1}\right] = \left[\nu(D_x^2 + D_y^2 + D_x^2)u^n + a(u^2)^n - D_x(u^2)^n - D_y(x + y)u^n\right]\Delta t
We can treat the cross-derivative term explicitly (while maintaining second-order accuracy) ↳ D_xD_y\Delta u^{n+1} \approx D_xD_y(u^n) → this term is then moved to the RHS:
\left\{1 - \Delta t\left[\nu(D_x^2 + D_y^2) - a(2u^n) + D_x(2u^n) + D_y(x + y)\right]\right\}\Delta u^{n+1} = \underbrace{\left[\nu(D_x^2 + D_y^2 + D_x^2)u^n + a(u^2)^n - D_x(u^2)^n - D_y(x + y)u^n - D_xD_yu^n\right]\Delta t}_{\text{RHS}}
Transcriber’s note: D_x^2 appears twice in the RHS operator where D_xD_y is presumably meant; as written.
Now we can factor approximately (2 spatial dimensions), split the x & y factors & then apply the split operators at grid points i, j & replace spatial derivatives by difference operators (here the source term is put in w/ the x factor) — although this is not the best method:
\left\{1 - \Delta t\left[\nu D_x^2 - a2u^n + D_x(2u^n)\right]\right\}\underbrace{\left\{1 + \Delta t\left(\nu D_y^2 + D_y(x + y)\right)\right\}\Delta u^{n+1}}_{\Delta u^*} = \text{RHS}
\Rightarrow\;\Delta u_{i,j}^* + \Delta t\left(\frac{\Delta u_{i+1,j}^* - 2\Delta u_{i,j}^* + \Delta u_{i-1,j}^*}{\Delta x^2}\right) - \Delta ta2\left[u^n\Delta u^*\right]_{i,j} + \Delta t\left(\frac{(2u^n\Delta u^*)_{i+1,j} - (2u^n\Delta u^*)_{i-1,j}}{2\Delta x}\right) = \text{RHS}_{i,j}
L_{i,j}^*\Delta u_{i-1,j}^* + M_{i,j}^*\Delta u_{i,j}^* + N_{i,j}^*\Delta u_{i+1,j}^* = \text{RHS}_{i,j}\quad\to\text{Eq. (1)}
with L_{i,j}^* = \left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x^2} - \frac{2u_{i-1,j}^n\Delta t}{2\Delta x}\right), M_{i,j}^* = \left(1 - \frac{2\Delta t}{\Delta x^2} - \Delta ta2u_{i,j}^n\right), N_{i,j}^* = \left(\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x^2} + \frac{\Delta t\,2u_{i+1,j}^n}{2\Delta x}\right), j = 1, 2, 3, \ldots, JL-1.
Therefore, our tridiagonal matrix for interior points:
\begin{bmatrix}M_{2,j}^* & N_{2,j}^* & & & \\ L_{3,j}^* & M_{3,j}^* & N_{3,j}^* & & \\ & & \ddots & & \\ & & L_{IL-2,j}^* & M_{IL-2,j}^* & \\ & & & & M_{IL-1,j}^*\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta u_{2,j}^* \\ \Delta u_{3,j}^* \\ \vdots \\ \Delta u_{IL-1,j}^*\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\text{RHS}_{2,j} \\ \text{RHS}_{3,j} \\ \vdots \\ \text{RHS}_{IL-1,j}\end{bmatrix}
↳ Boundary conditions need to be handled separately (the above solution is only for interior points).
Similarly,
\Delta u^* = \left\{1 + \Delta t\left(\nu D_y^2 + D_y(x + y)\right)\right\}\Delta u^{n+1} = \left\{1 + \Delta t\nu\left(\frac{\Delta u_{i,j+1}^{n+1} - 2\Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1} + \Delta u_{i,j-1}^{n+1}}{\Delta y^2}\right)\right\} + \Delta t\left(\frac{(x_i + y_j)\Delta u_{i,j+1}^{n+1} - (x_i + y_j)\Delta u_{i,j-1}^{n+1}}{2\Delta y}\right)
\Delta u^* = L_{i,j}\Delta u_{i,j-1}^{n+1} + M_{i,j}\Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1} + N_{i,j}\Delta u_{i,j+1}^{n+1}\quad\to\text{Eq. (2)}
with L_{i,j} = \left(\frac{\Delta t\nu}{\Delta y^2} - \frac{(x_i + y_j)\Delta t}{2\Delta y}\right), M_{i,j} = \left(1 - \frac{2\Delta t\nu}{\Delta y^2}\right), N_{i,j} = \left(\frac{\Delta t\nu}{\Delta y^2} + \frac{\Delta t(x_i + y_j)}{2\Delta y}\right).
A similar tridiagonal matrix can be constructed for Eq. (2) for i = 2, 3, \ldots, IL-1, which are the interior points:
\begin{bmatrix}M_{i,2} & & & \\ L_{i,3} & M_{i,3} & N_{i,3} & \\ & \ddots & & \\ & L_{i,JL-2} & M_{i,JL-2} & N_{i,JL-2} \\ & & & M_{i,JL-1}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\Delta u_{i,2}^{n+1} \\ \Delta u_{i,3}^{n+1} \\ \vdots \\ \Delta u_{i,JL-1}^{n+1}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\Delta u_{i,2}^* \\ \Delta u_{i,3}^* \\ \vdots \\ \Delta u_{i,JL-1}^*\end{bmatrix}
(b) Solution algorithm

Use Eq. (1) to solve for \Delta u_{i,j}^* from j = 2, 3, \ldots, JL-1 via the Thomas algorithm.
Use Eq. (2) to solve for \Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1} (using the constructed tridiagonal matrix) from i = 2, 3, \ldots, IL-1 using the Thomas algorithm.
Calculate u_{i,j}^{n+1} = u_{i,j}^n + \Delta u_{i,j}^{n+1}.

↳ Repeat the above steps until convergence or the duration of interest.
Problem 2
Compressible, inviscid flow; ideal gas; 2D converging–diverging nozzle:
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G}{\partial y} = 0
(a) Describe the problem; given where the Mach number and the static temperature at the duct inlet are 0.2 and 300 K, respectively and the pressure at the duct exit is 1 atm. (typed)
The given governing equation is the continuity equation for inviscid flow, where variables U, F, G are related to the flow quantities such as mass/density, velocity, pressure and energy. The 2D converging-diverging nozzle has only one inlet (left boundary) and outlet (right boundary), with no flow through the top and bottom walls
The Mach number represents the ratio of the flow velocity to the speed of sound in the medium. Since the Mach number at the inlet is 0.2, the flow is subsonic at the inlet.
(b) Formulate the governing equations for the problem by using the Euler equations with appropriate boundary conditions at the walls and the inflow and outflow boundaries.
The Euler equations for compressible, inviscid flow are given by:

Continuity eq.: \dfrac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial(\rho u)}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial(\rho v)}{\partial y} = 0
Momentum eq.: \dfrac{\partial(\rho u)}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\rho u^2 + P) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\rho uv) = 0; \dfrac{\partial(\rho v)}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\rho uv) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\rho v^2 + P) = 0
Energy equation: \dfrac{\partial e}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(u(e + P)\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(v(e + P)\right) = 0

} Combining these equations yields the given expression \frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G}{\partial y} = 0, where P = (\gamma - 1)\left(e - \frac{m^2 + n^2}{2\rho}\right) ↓ is given by Bernoulli’s principle.
Boundary conditions:

@ walls: u = v = 0
@ outflow: P = 1 atm
@ inflow: M = 0.2, T = 300 K

For an ideal gas, the \{P, V, T\} relationship is an additional equation that defines the variables.
(sketch: the converging–diverging nozzle, inlet height h_1 at the dashed inflow line and outlet height h_2 at the dashed outflow line.)
(c) Generate a boundary-fitted grid for the 2-D nozzle geometry by using the two-boundary method, where grid lines should intersect boundary curves orthogonally.
As in HW 5: X_{1,2}(\xi, \tau) = x(\xi, \eta = 0/1, \tau), Y_{1,2}(\xi, \tau) = y(\xi, \eta = 0/1, \tau), \vec{r}_{1,2} = X_{1,2}\hat{i} + Y_{1,2}\hat{j}, with Hermite interpolation
x(\xi, \eta, \tau) = X_1h_1(\eta) + X_2h_2(\eta) + \frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 0, \tau)}{\partial\eta}h_3(\eta) + \frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta}h_4(\eta)\;;\qquad y(\xi, \eta, \tau) = Y_1h_1(\eta) + Y_2h_2(\eta)
h_1 = 2\eta^3 - 3\eta^2 + 1, h_2 = -2\eta^3 + 3\eta^2, h_3 = \eta^3 - 2\eta^2 + \eta, h_4 = \eta^3 - \eta^2; \vec{e}_\xi\cdot\vec{e}_\eta = 0; K-factors:
\frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta} = -K_2(\xi, \tau)\frac{\partial Y_2(\xi, \tau)}{\partial\xi}\;;\quad \frac{\partial x(\xi, \eta = 0, \tau)}{\partial\eta} = +K_2(\xi, \tau)\frac{\partial Y_1(\xi, \tau)}{\partial\xi}\;;\quad \frac{\partial y(\xi, \eta = 1, \tau)}{\partial\eta} = \frac{\partial X_2}{\partial\xi} = \frac{C}{IL}\;;\quad \frac{\partial y(\xi, \eta = 0, \tau)}{\partial\eta} = \frac{\partial X_1}{\partial\xi} = \frac{C}{IL}
Parametrize the boundaries (x = \xi, y = f(\xi)), with curves 1 and 2 given piecewise by the same cosine profiles as HW 5, and
y(\xi, \eta) = Y_1(x(\xi)) + \eta\left(Y_2(x(\xi)) - Y_1(x(\xi))\right)
(d) Transform the governing equations and boundary conditions to boundary-fitted generalized coordinates.
(t, x, y) \to (\tau, \xi, \eta); \tau = \tau(t, x, y), \eta = \eta(t, x, y), \xi = \xi(t, x, y):
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial\tau}{\partial t}}_{\tau_t}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial t}}_{\eta_t}\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial t}}_{\xi_t}\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\;;\quad \frac{\partial}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\tau}{\partial x}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial\eta}{\partial x}\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial\xi}{\partial x}\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\;;\quad \frac{\partial}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial\tau}{\partial y}\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial\eta}{\partial y}\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial\xi}{\partial y}\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}
\left(\tau_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \eta_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta} + \xi_t\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\right)U + \left(\tau_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \eta_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta} + \xi_x\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\right)F + \left(\tau_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\tau} + \eta_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\eta} + \xi_y\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\right)G = 0
↳ Transforming and converting to strong conservation form (multiply by J), each term becomes \frac{\partial(J\tau_tU)}{\partial\tau} - U\frac{\partial(J\tau_t)}{\partial\tau} + \cdots; grouping:
\left[\frac{\partial(J\tau_tU)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_tU)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_tU)}{\partial\xi}\right] + \left[\frac{\partial(J\tau_xF)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_xF)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_xF)}{\partial\xi}\right] + \left[\frac{\partial(\tau_yGJ)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(\eta_yJG)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(\xi_yJG)}{\partial\xi}\right]
- U\left[\frac{\partial(J\tau_t)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_t)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_t)}{\partial\xi}\right] - F\left[\frac{\partial(J\tau_x)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(J\eta_x)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(J\xi_x)}{\partial\xi}\right] - G\left[\frac{\partial(J\tau_y)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial(\eta_yJ)}{\partial\eta} + \frac{\partial(\xi_yJ)}{\partial\xi}\right] = 0
If we assume t = \tau & \tau \neq f(x, y) & use the geometric conservation laws ↳ then our transformed governing equation (in strong conservative form) becomes:
\boxed{\therefore\;\frac{\partial(J\tau_tU)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(J\xi_xF + J\xi_yG\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}\left(J\eta_xF + J\eta_yG\right) = 0}
with contravariant velocities \tilde{U} = \xi_xu + \xi_yv, \tilde{V} = \eta_xu + \eta_yv.
Transforming the boundary conditions:

Inlet wall: \xi = 0 plane
Outlet wall: \xi = 1 plane
Bottom wall: \eta = 0 } zero mass flux through walls: \tilde{U}\eta_x - \tilde{V}\xi_x = 0
Top wall: \eta = 1 }

(e) Derive the FDE/FVEs for the governing equations by using the implicit Euler method with first-order upwinding using flux-vector splitting (any variation) that maintains the conservative property.
Flux-splitting scheme. The flux Jacobians \frac{\partial F}{\partial U} and \frac{\partial G}{\partial U} are 4\times4 matrices of \frac{\partial F_k}{\partial(\rho, m, e, n)}, with
F = \begin{bmatrix}m \\ \frac{m^2}{\rho} + \gamma e - e - \frac{\gamma}{2\rho}(m^2 + n^2) + \frac{(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho} \\ \frac{mn}{\rho} \\ \frac{em}{\rho} + \frac{m}{\rho}\gamma e - \frac{me}{\rho} - \frac{m\gamma(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho^2} + \frac{m(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho^2}\end{bmatrix}\;;\qquad G = \begin{bmatrix}n \\ \frac{mn}{\rho} \\ \frac{n^2}{\rho} + \gamma e - e - \gamma\frac{(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho} + \frac{(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho} \\ \frac{en}{\rho} + \frac{n}{\rho}\gamma e - \frac{ne}{\rho} - \frac{\gamma n(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho^2} + \frac{n(m^2 + n^2)}{2\rho^2}\end{bmatrix}
(the entries of A = \frac{\partial F}{\partial U} and B = \frac{\partial G}{\partial U} are written out in full on the original page.)
F = AU = (A^+ + A^-)U = F^+ + F^-
(A^+ → positive eigenvalues; A^- → negative eigenvalues.)
Flux splitting in the non-transformed domain:
\therefore\;\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(F^+ + F^-) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(G^+ + G^-) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial F^+}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F^-}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G^+}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G^-}{\partial y} = 0
\frac{U_{ij}^{n+1} - U_{ij}^n}{\Delta t} + \frac{F_{ij}^+ - F_{i-1,j}^+}{\Delta x} + \frac{F_{i+1,j}^- - F_{ij}^-}{\Delta x} + \frac{G_{ij}^+ - G_{i,j-1}^+}{\Delta y} + \frac{G_{i,j+1}^- - G_{ij}^-}{\Delta y} = 0
For Euler implicit, F^+, F^-, G^+ & G^- are all at time level n+1.
↳ Similar logic applied on the transformed equations — central differencing outside derivatives:
\frac{\partial(J\tau_tU)}{\partial\tau} + \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}(J\xi_xF + J\xi_yG) + \frac{\partial}{\partial\eta}(J\eta_xF + J\eta_yG) = 0
\frac{\partial(J\tau_tU)}{\partial\tau} \to \frac{(J\tau_tU)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j}^n - (J\tau_tU)_{i-\frac{1}{2},j}^n}{\Delta\tau}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}(J\xi_xF + J\xi_yG) \to \frac{(J\xi_xF + J\xi_yG)_{i+\frac{1}{2},j}^n - (J\xi_xF + J\xi_yG)_{i-\frac{1}{2},j}^n}{\Delta\xi}
↳ We can apply this on the transformed equation.
(f) Develop an algorithm to generate solutions to the FDE/FVEs that uses approximate factorization.
Algorithm:

Discretize the domain: \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta t ↳ choose IL, JL ↳ set \Delta\eta = \Delta\xi = 1.
Solve for Y_1, Y_2, X_1, X_2, \frac{dY_1}{d\xi}, \frac{dY_2}{d\xi} & h coefficients.
Euler implicit time-differencing + linearization:

\frac{U_{i,j}^{n+1} - U_{i,j}^n}{\Delta t} = -\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G}{\partial y}\right)_{ij}^{n+1}\;;\qquad \left[I + \Delta t(D_xA + D_yB)\right]\Delta U_{ij}^{n+1} = \text{RHS}_{ij}\;,\quad \text{RHS} = -\Delta t\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G}{\partial y}\right)_{ij}^n
(A, B from the above transformed equations.)

Approximate factorization in the spatial direction:

\left\{I + \Delta t\left[D_x(A^+ + A^-) + D_y(B^+ + B^-)\right]\right\}\Delta U_{ij}^{n+1} = \text{RHS}_{ij}\;;\qquad \left[I + \Delta t(L + K)\right]\Delta U_{ij}^{n+1} = \text{RHS}_{ij}
L = \delta_x^bA^+ + \delta_y^bB^+\;;\qquad K = \delta_x^fA^- + \delta_y^fB^-
\delta^b & \delta^f are backward & forward difference operators.

The equations are solved by splitting the operator yields (similar to Problem 1).

(g) Write a computer program for the algorithm. (typed)
I have tried to program the above algorithm in my code (used LLM for debugging and help) - find attached.
(h) Obtain the steady-state solution
For steady-state solutions, the LHS can be 1st-order accurate but the RHS is second-order accurate.
(typed) The steady state solution is when there is not time dependence i.e. the solution is time invariant and the governing equations become just \frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G}{\partial y} = 0
(plot: “Nozzle Flow Velocity Magnitude (Euler Equations)” — x from 0 to 6 m; the core of the nozzle is near zero velocity, with high velocities (~90 m/s) confined to thin bands along the upper wall near the inlet and the exit.)
(i) Discuss accuracy of results with a grid sensitivity study. (typed)
There seems to be a bug in the code that I was not able to resolve due to time constraint so my analysis is only limited to the results I obtained. Here are some expected outcomes/analysis based on the physics of converging-diverging nozzle: we expect that the maximum velocity should reach asymptotic value with grid refinement and finer grids should show decreasing differences in the parameters.
Further refining the grid did not change the contour plot solution. Therefore, the observed solution convergence across grid refinements indicates that discretization errors from mesh resolution were negligible. Hence, the remaining numerical errors most likely are from the accuracy of finite difference formulation (assuming no bugs in the code).

Thomas algorithm

Residuals ↳ but a small residual only makes sense if the matrix is ill-conditioned. Always do relative error!

\kappa(A) \geq 1\;;\qquad \kappa(A) = \|A^{-1}\|\,\|A\|\quad(\text{expensive to calculate})
\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x + \delta x\|} \leq \kappa(A)\frac{\|\delta A\|}{\|A\|}

PDEs

↳ Second-order PDE classification

                  Potential flow problem (typed note)
                  
                

Potential flow is used to model irrotational where the viscosity effects are assumed to be negligible - typically externally flow over solid surfaces or flow at high Reynolds number. In such cases, the thickness of the boundary layer is assumed to be much smaller than the dimensions of the object.
The given equation is the Laplace equation using stream function. Stream function (\psi) can be defined for any 2D flow such that the stream function is constant along a streamline. Additionally, change in stream function between a pair of streamlines equals the volummetric flowrate between the two streamlines. Finally, lines of constant streamlines are perpendicular to the lines of constant velocity potential (\Phi).

\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha\frac{\partial^2T}{\partial x^2}\quad[\text{unsteady, 1D, conduction}]

Discretize the time & space domain: T_i^n = T(x_i, t^n).

(sketch: a grid with spatial nodes 1, \ldots, i-1, i, i+1, \ldots, m+1 from x = 0 to x = L and time levels 0, \ldots, n-1, n, n+1; \Delta t = t^n/n, \Delta x = L/m.) Need m equations to solve for the value of T at every grid point.
Transforming the PDE to FDEs (finite difference equations): we use the Taylor expansion.
f(x + \Delta x, y) = f(x, y) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Delta x + \frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x^2}\frac{\Delta x^2}{2!} + \frac{\partial^3f}{\partial x^3}\frac{\Delta x^3}{3!} + \cdots
f(x - \Delta x, y) = f(x, y) - \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\Delta x + \frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x^2}\frac{\Delta x^2}{2!} - \frac{\partial^3f}{\partial x^3}\frac{\Delta x^3}{3!} + \cdots
\therefore\;\underbrace{\frac{f(x + \Delta x) - f(x - \Delta x)}{2\Delta x}}_{\text{difference operator}} = \underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}}_{\text{derivative}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2\Delta x}\left[\frac{2\Delta x^3}{3!}\frac{\partial^3f}{\partial x^3} + \frac{2\Delta x^5}{5!}\frac{\partial^5f}{\partial x^5} + \cdots\right]}_{\text{truncation error (TE)}}
TE is O(\Delta x^2) ↳ second order in mesh spacing. Thus the difference operator is second-order accurate.

→ If f is single-valued, finite and cont., the Taylor series for f is convergent ↳ this means that as \Delta x \to \infty, the TE for a higher-order approx. will be smaller than that of a lower-order TE.
→ Similarly, from the Taylor expansion we get the “central difference”:

\frac{f(x + \Delta x, y) - 2f(x, y) + f(x - \Delta x, y)}{\Delta x^2} \approx \frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x^2}\;;\qquad TE = O(\Delta x^2) = \frac{2\Delta x^2}{4!}\frac{\partial^4f}{\partial x^4} + \frac{2\Delta x^4}{6!}\cdots
Transcriber’s note: “as \Delta x \to \infty” is as written; presumably \Delta x \to 0.
Explicit method
Finding the value for n+1, when the solution @ n is assumed to be known (this is the given initial cond. T(x, t = 0) = T_0) ↓ this just becomes an algebraic expression. I.e. FDEs which use no information at the new time level give uncoupled ODEs:
\frac{T_i^{n+1} - T_i^n}{\Delta t} = \alpha\left(\frac{T_{i+1}^n - 2T_i^n + T_{i-1}^n}{\Delta x^2}\right)
Implicit method
→ Coupled m equations where spatial information about the new time level is needed (but we only know the solution at time level n) ↓ therefore all eqs need to be solved simultaneously → A\vec{x} = \vec{b}.
We could also use a generalized approach of both explicit & implicit → this gives second-order accurate in both space & time.
Now based on the PDE → there are general requirements for BCs in order to get a solution:

↳ Hyperbolic, 1st order → need BC only at points where characteristic base curves enter the domain.
↳ Parabolic/elliptical → BC at every point on the boundary of the spatial domain.

Consistency, stability & convergence

Discretization error → replacing PDEs w/ FDEs.
Stability error → round-off errors (finite digits used in computations).
Truncation error → O(\Delta t, \Delta x^2), error due to approximation.

1) Consistency
\lim_{\substack{\Delta x \to 0 \\ \Delta t \to 0}}(\text{FDE} - \text{PDE})_i^n = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0}(TE)_i^n = 0
How well does the FDE locally approx. the PDE. (sketch: a wavy curve matching a parabola only near its minimum — “consistent here (locally)”.)
How to check?
\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \alpha\left(\frac{\partial^2T}{\partial x^2}\right)\;;\qquad \frac{T_i^{n+1} - T_i^n}{\Delta t} = \alpha\left(\frac{T_{i+1}^n - 2T_i^n + T_{i-1}^n}{\Delta x^2}\right)
Expand all terms via Taylor series & then substitute:
T_{i+1}^n = T_i^n + \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right)_n^i\Delta x + \cdots\;;\quad T_{i-1}^n = T_i^n - \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right)_n^i\Delta x + \cdots\;;\quad T_i^{n+1} = T_i^n + \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial t}\right)_i^n\Delta t + \cdots
↓ Let \Delta t \to 0, \Delta x \to 0 → if the same as the PDE, then consistent.

↳ Unconditional vs. conditional consistency: unconditional ↓ no dependence on the rates of \Delta x & \Delta t; conditional ↳ depends on the relative rates of \Delta x & \Delta t \to 0.
↳ Since \Delta x & \Delta t are finite computationally → consistency alone does not guarantee accuracy; thus a consistent soln. still behaves diff. than the PDE.

2) (Numerical) stability

When the time domain is involved (i.e. accumulation or growth of errors) (parabolic & hyperbolic PDEs).
Depends solely on the FDE; can be bounded (i.e. don’t grow). (sketch: an oscillation decaying under a bounding envelope — “bounded”.)
The computational domain must include all of the analytical domain.

\underbrace{\phi}_{\text{dimensionless parameter}} = \frac{\alpha\Delta t}{\Delta x^2} \leq \frac{1}{2}\;\rightarrow\;\text{conditionally stable}
Any chosen \Delta t, \Delta x → unconditionally stable (most implicit methods).
How to check?

Discrete perturbation → perturbation \varepsilon @ i & n:

\left|\frac{\Delta T}{\varepsilon}\right| \leq 1 → perturbations cannot grow, & \frac{\Delta T}{\varepsilon} \geq 0 → decay must be monotonic } hence need to do for only one time step.


Fourier method → disturbance \varepsilon at every grid point at an arbitrary time n:

Obtain an evolution eq., i.e. w/ \varepsilon as f(\Delta x, \Delta t).
Use a Fourier series expansion: \varepsilon_i^n = \sum_{-N}^{N}\underbrace{A_j^ne^{Ik_jx_i}}_{\text{Fourier component}} (amplitude A_j^n, wave no. = k_j).
Analyze the error in the components: A_j^{n+1} = \underbrace{G_j}_{\text{amplification factor}}A_j^n.
Accounts well for periodic BC (but other BCs may be an issue).
} Assume the distribution of errors along the x-axis is given by a Fourier series in x & the time-wise variation is exponential in t ↓ \varepsilon(x, t) = e^{at}\sum_me^{ik_mx}.
G = \left|\dfrac{\varepsilon_i^{n+1}}{\varepsilon_i^n}\right| \leq 1 [errors should not be growing].

↳ For \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} ↓ \frac{\Delta t}{(\Delta x)^2} \leq \frac{1}{2} [stability requirement].
For \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + c\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = 0: \underbrace{C}_{\text{Courant number}} = c\frac{\Delta t}{\Delta x} \leq 1 (from von Neumann stability analysis) [called the CFL condition].




Matrix method → FDEs at every interior & boundary grid point are written in matrix form: T^{n+1} = AT^n + b.

Introduce a disturbance to get \varepsilon^{n+1} = A^{(n+1)}\varepsilon^0.
If A is a convergent matrix, \varepsilon^{n+1} will approach zero in the limit as n \to \infty ↓ \|A\| \leq 1; \rho(A) \leq 1 (smallest norm = spectral radius).


Modified equation method

Lax–Wendroff method to derive an FDE } ↳ express the time derivative in terms of spatial derivatives; ↳ use a Taylor series for each point.
Courant no. \left[C_0 = \frac{c\Delta t}{\Delta x}\right]. If C_0 = 1, then the truncation error is zero.



3) Convergence
If the total error (discretization + stability) → 0 as \Delta x \to 0, \Delta t \to 0.

If the FDE is convergent, then a numerical soln. of any accuracy can be obtained by changing the grid spacing & time step.
The FDE must give the same solution as the PDE in some limiting cases.

Example: modified equation
u_t = Ku_{xx}\;,\quad K > 0\;;\quad u(t, x)
\frac{u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n}{\Delta t}\;\text{can also be written as}\; = \frac{u_i^n(t + \Delta t, x) - u_i^n(t, x)}{\Delta t} = \frac{\left[u_i^n + \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\right)_i^n\Delta t + \left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2}\right)_i^n\Delta t^2\right] - u_i^n}{\Delta t}
Taylor series: f(x)\big|_{x=a} = f(a) + \frac{f'(a)}{1!}(x - a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2!}(x - a)^2\cdots = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x - a)^n.
\therefore\;u_t = \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\right)_i^n + \left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2}\right)_i^n\frac{\Delta t}{2} + O(\Delta t^2)
Similarly, with u_{i+1}^n = u(t, x + \Delta x) and u_{i-1}^n = u(t, x - \Delta x):
Ku_{xx} = \frac{1}{\Delta x^2}\left(u_{i+1}^n - 2u_i^n + u_{i-1}^n\right) = \frac{1}{\Delta x^2}\left[\left(u_i^n + \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_i^n\Delta x + \left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}\right)_i^n\frac{\Delta x^2}{2} + \cdots\right) - 2u_i^n + \left(u_i^n - \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_i^n\Delta x + \left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}\right)_i^n\frac{\Delta x^2}{2}\right)\right]
= \frac{1}{\Delta x^2}\left[\left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}\right)_i^n\Delta x^2 + \left(\frac{\partial^4u}{\partial x^4}\right)_i^n\frac{\Delta x^4\cdot2}{4!} + \cdots\right] = \left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}\right)_i^n + \left(\frac{\partial^4u}{\partial x^4}\right)_i^n\frac{\Delta x^2}{12} + O(\Delta x^4)
∴ Modified equation of u_t - Ku_{xx} = 0:
\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}\right)_i^n + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\left(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2}\right)_i^n + O(\Delta t^2) = K\left[u_{xx} + \frac{\Delta x^2}{12}u_{xxxx} + O(\Delta x^4)\right]
Neglecting higher-order terms:
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} - K\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} = K\frac{\Delta x^2}{12}\frac{\partial^4u}{\partial x^4} - \underbrace{\frac{\Delta t}{2}\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2}}_{\text{this makes it hyperbolic}}
tt, t, xx, xxxx.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 22) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Error analysis
Hard to show convergence ↗ need FDEs to model physical properties/parameters.
Conservation principle → In − out + gen = Acc. for a CV (“conservative property”).
For fluid flow, a disturbance at any location in the flow field can spread to other locations by three transport mechanisms:

Convection (due to fluid motion)
Diffusion → spreads in every direction by random molecular motion ↓ but the disturbance is smoothed over by a process called dissipation.
Pressure waves

} FDEs have the transportive property.
Dispersion → solutions (= waves w/ Fourier transform) that have different wavelengths travel at different speeds } speed ∝ f(wavelength) ↓ error if waves are not travelling at the same speed.

All fluids are modelled as non-dispersive.
↳ The presence of an odd-order space derivative in the TE is responsible for dispersion.

When there is a \frac{\partial}{\partial t} term (first order) →

even derivatives = diffusion error (dissipation)
odd derivatives = dispersion error



                  
                  "Even likes to 'diss'" 
                  
                

If \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (1st order in time), then even-order spatial derivatives are dissipation (\mu\nabla^2u, \mu\nabla^2v), i.e. truncation error w/ leading even-order space derivatives are termed dissipative terms.


Given a PDE, we can define multiple FDEs.

↳ Now of the FDEs we can write modified equations (Taylor expansion).
↳ The order of dissipation of an FDE is the lowest even-order spatial derivative of the modified equation.

↳ For ex.: pg. 65, book.
↳ A 4th-order dissipation means there will be less dissipation error than that of a first order.



↓ ∴ The coefficients of the FDE should be the same as the PDE for even to model properly ↓ if not then dissipative error.

Grid generation
Physical grid → computational grid (uniform)
(sketch: left — a body-fitted grid around an airfoil in the (x, y, t) plane, with curvilinear coordinates \xi wrapping around the body and \eta pointing away from it; right — the uniform computational grid in (\xi, \eta, \tau) with spacings \Delta\xi and \Delta\eta.)
\xi = \xi(x, y, t)\;;\qquad \eta = \eta(x, y, t)\;;\qquad \tau = \tau(t)
\text{Jacobian matrix }(J) = \frac{\partial(x, y)}{\partial(\xi, \eta)} = \begin{vmatrix}\dfrac{\partial x}{\partial\xi} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial\xi} \\[2mm] \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial\eta} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial\eta}\end{vmatrix}

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 29-30) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Conservative & non-conservative
Conservative ↓ equations obtained from directly applying fundamental physical principles to a finite control volume ↓ i.e. eq. in integral form (that are then applied to obtain PDEs).
Entire system of governing equations in conservation form } continuity, momentum & energy:
\boxed{\underbrace{\frac{\partial U}{\partial t}}_{\text{unsteady (solution vector)}} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial F}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial H}{\partial z}}_{\text{flux terms}} = \underbrace{J}_{\text{source term}}}
“Shock” → sharp, discontinuous changes in the primitive flow-field variables (p, \rho, u, T).

↳ The conservation form of equations should be used to get smooth + stable (or else you get wiggles).
↳ Because the conservation form in fact uses (\rho u) & products of dependent variables, ↳ which are generally conserved in a shock! (i.e. changes in flux are either zero or small across a shock wave).

Office hours

Two-boundary method for grid generation ↓ Jacobian → area in 2D ↳ volume in 3D. (sketch: a grid with one cell outlined and its neighbours dashed.)
↳ Local thermodynamic equilibrium ↓ when can you assume it? If it is changing …

→ Equations of state (PV = nRT)
→ Connect measurable/non-measurable variables (T, P ↳ energy)


↳ Gaussian elimination (accuracy)

Condition no.
Residual
Iterative refinement


↳ Modified equation & phase angles — \phi, the phase angle, relates to odd-derivative terms.
↳ Implicit vs. explicit ✓
↳ FDEs
↳ Error

Types of PDEs & their significance
u = u(x, y)\;;\quad v = v(x, y)\;;\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial x},\;\frac{\partial u}{\partial y},\;\frac{\partial v}{\partial x},\;\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}
du = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}dy\;;\qquad dv = \frac{\partial v}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial v}{\partial y}dy
} Characteristic lines ↓ derivatives of u & v are indeterminate (i.e. the derivative of the solution does not have a unique solution) ↓ PDEs simplify to ODEs.
Making a matrix & checking the determinant/eigenvalues → gives the type of PDE. For first order (quasilinear): hyperbolic, parabolic, elliptic:

Hyperbolic → information at a given point P influences only those regions b/w advancing characteristics. E.g. \dfrac{\partial(\rho u)}{\partial t} + \dfrac{\partial(\rho u^2 + p)}{\partial x} = 0.
Parabolic → information at point P in the xy-plane influences the entire region of the plane to one side of P.
Elliptic → info at P influences all other regions of the domain ↓ the entire boundary must be defined.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 15-17) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Linear algebra
A\vec{x} = \vec{b}

Unique solution exists if A is non-singular (i.e. if \det(A) \neq 0).

Eigenvalues of an N×N matrix: \det(A - \lambda I) = 0; A\underbrace{x_i}_{\text{eigenvector}} = \lambda_ix_i.

There are N eigenvalues; depending on A they might be real or complex (i.e. rank N + symmetric (a_{ij} = a_{ji} & square) will have N real eigenvalues & all eigenvectors are orthogonal).



                  
                  Tip
                  
                

Eigenvalues tell us how a system behaves, evolves and transforms ↓ i.e. they provide deep insights into the matrix’s properties and behavior. E.g.:

→ how a linear transformation will stretch or compress vectors
→ dynamical stability
→ observable quantities such as energy levels etc.




Positive definite: A is positive definite if \vec{x}^TA\vec{x} > 0, x \neq 0 ↳ all eigenvalues are positive.
Spectral radius: of a square matrix, \rho(A) is the largest absolute value of its eigenvalues ↳ \rho(A) \leq \|A\|.

Methods of solving Ax = b
Direct methods

Diagonal matrix
Triangular matrix → forward/backward sub.
Cramer’s rule — O(N^4)
Gaussian elimination — \left(\frac{N^3}{3} + O(N^2)\right) arithmetic operations

→ Gauss–Jordan \left(\frac{N^3}{2} + O(N^2)\right)
→ LU decomposition
→ Thomas algorithm (for tridiagonal matrix)



} Require pivoting & equilibration (unless banded or positive definite). Banded = diagonally dominant [?] (sketch: a diagonal band).
Iterative methods

Jacobi iteration [A = D + L' + U']
Gauss–Seidel iteration [A = D(L' + I + U')] — convergence guaranteed if A is banded or positive definite.

Error/accuracy
All computations have round-off errors → hence you get approximate solutions ↓ need to assess accuracy by comparing the magnitude/size of different solutions ↓ norms (works for scalars, vectors, tensors):
L_p(x) = \|x\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}|x_i|^p\right)^{1/p}\;(\text{unweighted})\;;\qquad L_p(x) = \|x\|_{p,w} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_i|x_i|^p\right)^{1/p}\;(\text{weighted})
a = approx., e = exact:
A_a = A_e + \delta A\;;\qquad x_a = x_e + \delta x\;;\qquad A_ax_a = b_e
\text{Relative error} = \frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x_e + \delta x\|} \leq \kappa(A)\frac{\|\delta A\|}{\|A_e\|}
\kappa(A) → spectral condition number \left(= \frac{\lambda_{max}}{\lambda_{min}}\right) (measure of how sensitive the solution of a linear system Ax = b is to small changes in b).

\kappa(A) \approx 1 (well-conditioned)
If \kappa(A) \gg 1 (ill-conditioned)

↳ Iterative refinement: improving the accuracy of the solution.

Calculate the residual (using twice precision) \vec{r}.
Calculate the error making this residual: LU\,\vec{\delta x} = \vec{r}.
Subtract the error from the original solution: x_a = x_a - \delta x.
Check \left\|\frac{\delta x}{x_a}\right\| < \varepsilon [relative error].
End loop.

Partial differential equations
Phenomena where changes occur over multiple variables → very real-world applicable.
F(x, y, \ldots, U_x, U_y, \ldots, U_{xx}, U_{yy}, U_{xy}\ldots) = 0

F → functional relationship among the independent vars, dependent vars & the partial derivatives; U_x = \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}, U_{xx} = \frac{\partial^2U}{\partial x^2}.
U → dependent var; x, y → independent vars.
Order → determined by the highest-order PD in the entire expression.


Linear → F is a linear function of the dependent variable & its partial derivatives: xU_x + xyU_y + \underbrace{U_{xy}}_{\text{2nd order}} = 0.
Almost linear → small or mild non-linearities.
Quasi-linear → F is linear in the highest-order partial derivative, but non-linear in the dependent variable and/or lower-order derivatives: \underbrace{UU_x}_{\text{non-linearity}} + U_y = xy, but U_x & U_y are linear (i.e. no U_x^2 or \sin(U_x)).
Non-linear → F is non-linear in any or all of the highest-order partial derivatives appearing in the equation: UU_x + U_y^2 = xy.

E.g.:

↳ U^2U_{xx} + U_y = xy^2 → quasi-linear
↳ U_xU_{xy} = \sin(xy) → non-linear ↳ this (\sin(xy)) doesn’t matter since U & its derivatives are what we check for.

Solving
First-order linear + quasi-linear
↳ Characteristic curves (by converting to a system of ODEs, where a family of curves in the x_i–U space) ↓ along the curves, the PDE is converted to an ODE requiring one BC/IC.
E.g.: U_t + cU_x = 0 → x = c_0 + ct.
(sketch: three panels — (1) parallel characteristic lines in the x–t plane; (2) the initial profile U_0(x), a bump; (3) the same bump translating unchanged along x as t increases.)
Weak vs. strong solutions
System of ODEs: U_t + AU_x = 0 (eigenvalues of A):

→ Elliptic
→ Hyperbolic
→ Mixed

Second-order linear & quasi-linear PDEs
Real or complex characteristic curves; may have two curves passing through each point.
a_{ij}U_{x_ix_j} + b = 0
a_{ij} & b are functions only of x_i, U and U_x → quasi-linear.
↳ Quasi-linear are further defined (A = a_{ij}):

Problems w/ evolutionary character:

→ Ultrahyperbolic (all eigenvalues are non-zero & at least two positive & two negative)
→ Hyperbolic (all eigenvalues are non-zero & all but one have the same sign)
→ Parabolic (at least one eigenvalue is zero)


Equilibrium problems:

→ Elliptic (all eigenvalues of A have the same sign)


→ Mixed

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: AAE 512: Computational aerodynamics
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Handwritten class notes from AAE 512 (Spring 2025), exported from OneNote and transcribed into Markdown and LaTeX. Each note shows the typed version first. The original handwritten pages are in a collapsible box at the top, with a link to open just those pages as a PDF.

All original pages (PDF, 19 MB)

Lectures

Lecture 01-24 · 2025-01-24 — Direct methods for Ax = b (Cramer, Gaussian elimination, Gauss–Jordan, LU, pivoting, equilibration), the Thomas algorithm, Jacobi/Gauss–Seidel/SOR iteration, and error analysis with the condition number and iterative refinement.
Lecture 01-29 · 2025-01-29 — Review of root finding (bisection, Newton–Raphson) and Ax = b (pivoting, equilibration, checking solutions), then an introduction to PDE classification and conservative vs. non-conservative forms, with a characteristics sketch showing a shock.
Lecture 01-31 · 2025-01-31 — Shock speed for the inviscid Burgers equation in conservative form, solutions through characteristic lines, explicit vs. implicit discretizations, the second-order PDE types, and continuum, equilibrium and energy assumptions.
Lecture 02-05 · 2025-02-05 — Finite differences vs. finite volumes, exact/discrete/numerical solutions and the split of error into discretization and round-off, consistency vs. convergence vs. stability, and the main stability-analysis methods (discrete perturbation, von Neumann, matrix, modified equation).
Lecture 02-07 · 2025-02-07 — Stability analysis continued — the matrix method, error growth through powers of the iteration matrix, the spectral-radius criterion for a convergent matrix, and the Gershgorin circle theorem for bounding eigenvalues.
Lecture 02-12 · 2025-02-12 — The linear advection and advection–diffusion equations and their discretization, what even- and odd-order derivatives represent, the modified-equation method, the Courant number and CFL condition, and linearizing a non-linear diffusion term.
Lecture 02-17 · 2025-02-17 — Stability of the physics vs. the discretization; consistency, convergence and stability; and checking the engineering through finite volumes, transportive error, dissipation error (Lax–Wendroff) and dispersion.
Lecture 02-24 · 2025-02-24 — FD vs. FV methods, the method of lines, convergence and the Lax equivalence theorem, conservation of errors in finite volumes, sources of error (scanning, truncation, resolution), and monotonicity and positivity.
Lecture 03-05 · 2025-03-05 — Midterm logistics, then the finite volume method — integrating the Euler equation over a control volume with the divergence theorem, cell- vs. vertex-centred cells, face area vectors and cell volume, converting FDM to FVM, and a typed note on potential flow.
Lecture 03-26 · 2025-03-26 — What conservative form means, transforming derivatives to generalized coordinates by the chain rule, strong conservative form and the geometric conservation laws, and metric coefficients times the Jacobian as physical face areas and cell volumes.
Lecture 03-31 · 2025-03-31 — Strong vs. weak conservation form under a coordinate mapping, and the method of lines (space and time discretized separately).
Lecture 04-14 · 2025-04-14 — Flux-differencing schemes and their dissipative errors — the Godunov scheme and the Riemann problem, approximate Riemann solvers (Osher, Roe and the mean value theorem), and the first-order accuracy of Riemann solvers.
Lecture 04-21 · 2025-04-21 — Exam 2 logistics, the main drawbacks of explicit and implicit methods, time-split methods, accelerating convergence (residual smoothing, local time stepping, multigrid), and inflow/outflow BCs for compressible flow.
Lecture 04-23 · 2025-04-23 — Wall and inflow boundary conditions and incompressible flow, then the last class — flux vector splitting with local eigenvalues, upwind vs. central differencing, linearizing implicit schemes, conservative diffusion differencing, and Dirichlet/Neumann BCs in a tridiagonal system.

Homework

HW · 2025-02-05 — Title page for the AAE 512 homework section (5 February 2025); the page itself is blank.
HW 01 · 2025-02-05 — HW 1 — Heun’s method (2nd-order Runge–Kutta) for a second-order ODE, the implicit 2nd-order Adams–Moulton (trapezoidal) method solved with Newton–Raphson, and steady conduction in a flat plate with variable conductivity and heat generation set up as a tridiagonal system.
HW 01 (2) · 2025-02-05 — Revised HW 1 — the same Heun and Adams–Moulton results, plus the full Newton–Raphson Jacobian for the non-linear flat-plate conduction problem, the boundary-condition derivatives, the Thomas-algorithm update loop and the grid-independence plots.
HW 02 · 2025-02-17 — HW 2 — classifying PDEs by order and linearity, the inviscid Burgers equation in non-conservative and conservative upwind form with exact characteristic solutions, weak solutions, shock speed and the entropy condition, and classifying second-order PDEs by eigenvalues and canonical form.
HW 03 · 2025-03-04 — HW 3/4 — consistency and von Neumann stability of the θ-scheme for the linear Burgers equation, the Lax equivalence theorem, dissipation and dispersion errors of the Crank–Nicolson (θ = 1/2) scheme with plots, and typed answers to conceptual questions on FD/FV methods and numerical errors.
HW 05 · 2025-03-24 — HW 5 (draft) — transforming a 2D Burgers-type equation to generalized coordinates in chain-rule and strong conservation-law form with the geometric conservation laws, and setting up incompressible potential flow through a nozzle with a stream function, two-boundary grid generation and FDEs.
HW 05 final · 2025-03-24 — HW 5 (final) — strong conservation-law form of a 2D Burgers-type equation in generalized coordinates, and incompressible potential flow through a converging–diverging nozzle: two-boundary grid generation with Hermite interpolation, metric coefficients, FDEs, the algorithm, velocity contours and geometry variations.
HW 06 · 2025-04-08 — HW 6 — deriving second-order one-sided boundary difference operators from Taylor series, and fourth-order compact (Padé) operators for the steady advection–diffusion equation assembled into a block-tridiagonal system with boundary conditions and an overall algorithm.
HW 07 · 2025-04-23 — HW 7 — a linearized Crank–Nicolson scheme for a 2D non-linear advection–diffusion equation with approximate factorization into tridiagonal sweeps, and compressible Euler flow in a converging–diverging nozzle: governing equations, two-boundary grid, transformation to generalized coordinates, flux-vector splitting, approximate factorization and the steady-state result.

Other notes

Review · 2025-02-17 — Midterm review — linear algebra (eigenvalues, positive definiteness, spectral radius), direct and iterative methods for Ax = b, norms, condition number and iterative refinement, and the classification of PDEs and solution by characteristics.
Review 2.0 · 2025-03-04 — Review of finite-difference discretization of the 1D unsteady heat equation — Taylor-series difference operators and truncation error, explicit vs. implicit methods, BC requirements, and consistency, stability (discrete perturbation, von Neumann, matrix, modified equation) and convergence.
Review 3.0 · 2025-03-04 — Review of error analysis — the conservative and transportive properties of FDEs, dissipation (even-order spatial derivatives) vs. dispersion (odd-order) errors, and the order of dissipation from the modified equation.
Review 4.0 · 2025-03-22 — Review of grid generation — mapping a body-fitted physical grid (x, y, t) to a uniform computational grid (ξ, η, τ) and the Jacobian matrix of the transformation.
Review 5.0 · 2025-04-08 — Review — conservative vs. non-conservative forms and why conservation form handles shocks, office-hour notes (two-boundary grid generation, local thermodynamic equilibrium, Gaussian elimination accuracy), and the types of PDEs and their domains of influence.

Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 85-89) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF





                  
                  Transcription note 
                  
                

The pasted spreadsheet tables are summarized below (band totals); the full per-state tables (n, K, \cos K, k, energy) are in the original pages above.


Question 1
As shown in class, for a periodic Dirac comb with periodicity n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \dots: for 0 < x < a, V(x) = 0, so the TISE is -\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\dfrac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} = E\psi, giving \psi(x) = A\sin(kx) + B\cos(kx), k = \sqrt{2mE/\hbar^2}.
Applying Bloch’s theorem for -a < x < 0: \psi(x + a) = e^{iKa}\big[A\sin(k(x+a)) + B\cos(k(x+a))\big], K = \dfrac{2\pi n}{Pa}.
Plugging in the conditions at x = 0 — \psi_{0^-} = \psi_{0^+} (continuity) and \left.\frac{d\psi}{dx}\right|_{0^+} - \left.\frac{d\psi}{dx}\right|_{0^-} = \frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\psi(0) (the “cusp”) — and eliminating A and B:
\cos(Ka) = \cos(ka) + \frac{m\alpha a}{\hbar^2}\frac{\sin(ka)}{ka}\qquad\text{(Eq. 1)}
Equation 1 can be solved numerically with m = \alpha = a = \hbar = 1:
\cos(K) = \cos(k) + \frac{\sin(k)}{k}\;;\qquad K = \frac{2\pi n}{P}\;;\qquad k = \sqrt{2E}
(a) Solving for the specific k values given the K values for the first band (n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \pm3, \pm4, \pm5 — P + 1 non-interacting fermions). A band is defined when we fill all discrete energy levels between 1 > \cos(K) > -1.

P = 10: n = P + 1 = 11 particles → discrete band energy 33.4 (levels from 0.854 at K = 0 to 4.935 at K = \pm\pi).
P = 20: n = P + 1 = 21 particles → discrete band energy 53.2.

(b) P = 10, with the first two bands occupied (total N = 21): band 1 = 33.4, band 2 = 171.5 (levels 8.205 → 19.739).
(c) P = 10, with the first three bands occupied (total N = 31): band 1 = 33.4, band 2 = 171.5, band 3 = 517.0 (levels 24.964 → 44.413).
(d) As seen from the tables, the integral method (a trapezoid numerical integration) gives larger energies than the discrete energy summation:









































CaseBandDiscrete band energyIntegral band energyP = 10133.436.8P = 102171.5174.9P = 103517.0520.3P = 20153.255.7P = 202316.1318.5
(e) DFT energy per unit cell for all cases. For the Dirac comb, the DFT energy functional is
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_{-na}^{na}\rho^3\,dx + \int_{-na}^{na}V_{ext}(x)\,\rho\,dx\;;\qquad \frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho} = 0 \rightarrow \rho_{min}(x) = \left(\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\big(\mu - V_{ext}(x)\big)\right)^{1/2}
\therefore solving for the ground-state energy (m = a = \hbar = 1, \alpha = 1, N_{cell} = N/P):
\frac{E_{GS}}{P} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6ma^2}N_{cell}^3 + \frac{\alpha}{a}N_{cell} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}N_{cell}^3 + N_{cell}
DFT values compared with the integral method:















































CaseDiscreteIntegralDFT ground state% differenceP = 10, band 133.436.832.92.0%P = 10, band 2171.5174.9173.31.9%P = 10, band 3517.0520.3521.00.1%P = 20, band 153.255.759.14.5% [?]P = 20, band 2316.1318.5153.5 [?]0.7%
(values for P = 20 are as recorded in the pasted table; some cells are hard to read.)
The DFT values fall in between the discrete and integral calculations, and the difference from the integral band values decreases from P = 10 to P = 20 (i.e. DFT becomes more accurate).
Question 2
Sine-wave potential: V(x) = \alpha\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{a}\right). We know
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_{-na}^{na}\rho^3\,dx + \int_{-na}^{na}V(x)\,\rho\,dx\;;\qquad F[\rho] = E[\rho] - \mu\left(\int_{-na}^{na}\rho\,dx - N\right)
For \alpha = 5: V(x) = 5\sin(2\pi x/1) → a period of 1.
F[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2}{6}\int_0^1\rho^3\,dx + \int_0^15\sin(2\pi x)\,\rho\,dx - \mu\left(\int_0^1\rho\,dx - N\right)
Solving this, \rho_{min}(x) = \left(\dfrac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\big(\mu - 5\sin(2\pi x)\big)\right)^{1/2}, with the constraint \int_0^1\rho_{min}(x)\,dx = N:
\therefore\quad \int_0^1\frac{2}{\pi^2}\big(\mu - 5\sin(2\pi x)\big) = N
— solved numerically for \mu for each N value. These \mu values are then used to find \rho_{min}, which is used to find E[\rho_{min}] by evaluating the integral numerically.
Plots (in the original): \rho_{min}(x) for N = 1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 over 0 < x < 1 — the densities show the periodic nature of the potential (a sine-curve shape, with the minimum near x = 0.25 and maximum near x = 0.75). A log–log plot of E vs N (from N = 1 to 100) is linear → i.e. power-law behaviour between E and N.
