Question 1
Ab-initio phase diagram for H adsorption on Pt(111) (surface and sub-surface layers):
E_{ads} = \underbrace{\left(E_{DFT}^{nH} - E_{DFT}^{Pt(111)} - \frac{n}{2}E_{DFT}^{H_2}\right)}_{\text{excess surface energy}}\frac{1}{n}

Excess surface energy: \big(E_{DFT} - E_{DFT}^{clean}\big) → instead of (\mu_{Pt}\cdot N_{Pt}).
Excess surface entropy = 0 ↳ one way to better approximate this would be to calculate the configurational entropy, i.e. counting all possible arrangements of the H adsorbate.
Plot: \Omega vs \mu (x-axis: \mu - E_{gas}).
Plot: T, P scale.
ZPEs on the surface → assume each H atom has harmonic vibrational frequencies of 450, 450 and 900 cm⁻¹.
Assume the surface is in equilibrium with bulk phases [\mu_i = \mu_i^{gas}, \mu_i = \mu_i^{bulk\ metal}]:

\gamma = \big(U - \cancel{TS}^{\,0} - \textstyle\sum\mu_iN_i\big)\frac{1}{A} = \big(U - \mu_Hn_H - \mu_{Pt}N_{Pt}\big)\frac{1}{A}
U \approx (n_H\cdot E_{ads}) + \text{ZPE}\;;\qquad \text{ZPE} = \sum\tfrac{1}{2}h\nu_i
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\gamma A = \big(E_{ads} + \text{ZPE} - \mu_Hn_H\big) = \Omega
Varying \mu_H will give values of \Omega.
Plots (in the original): \Omega - \Omega_{clean} vs \mu - E_{gas} for configurations fcc, hcp, 4×fcc, 4×hcp, 4×oct, 4×tet, 4×fcc-tet, 4×fcc-2×tet, 4×fcc,4×hcp, 4×hcp-4×oct, 4×fcc-4×tet. This phase diagram shows that certain plane and subsurface structures are thermodynamically stable, and adsorption on these surfaces will be preferred. ↳ The lowest (\Omega - \Omega_{clean}) values can be extracted and plotted as the lower envelope (second plot).
T, P relations (ideal gas):
\mu_H = U_{tot}^H + k_BT - TS_{tot}^H
U_{tot}^H = U_{vib} + U_{rot} + U_{trans} = \sum\Bigg(\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}h\nu_i}_{\text{ZPE}} + \underbrace{\frac{h\nu_i}{e^{\beta h\nu_i} - 1}}_{\text{thermal excitation}}\Bigg) + \underbrace{k_BT}_{\text{linear}} + \frac{3}{2}k_BT\;;\qquad \beta = \frac{1}{k_BT}
S_{tot}^H = S_{vib} + S_{rot} + S_{trans} = \sum_i\left(-\frac{h\nu_i}{2T} - k_B\ln\big(1 - e^{-h\nu_i\beta}\big)\right) + \frac{1}{T}\sum_i\left(\frac{1}{2}h\nu_i + \frac{h\nu_i}{e^{\beta h\nu_i} - 1}\right) + \left[k_B\ln\left[\left(\frac{m}{2\pi\beta\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}\frac{k_BT}{P}\right] + \frac{5}{2}k_B\right]n_H + k_B\ln\left(\frac{I}{\sigma\beta\hbar^2}\right) + k_B
Given a T and P array, \mu_H can be calculated, and this value can be associated with the lowest (\Omega - \Omega_{clean}) value and then the corresponding H coverage (ML). ↳ This can be used to create a heat map (log(pressure) vs temperature, colored by coverage, 0–2 ML).

Question 1
Mechanism (from class): \mathrm{A(g) + * \rightleftharpoons A^*} (1), \mathrm{A^* \rightleftharpoons B^*} (2), \mathrm{B(g) + * \rightleftharpoons B^*} (3).
Approach 1
Fully quasi-steady state (Case IV derived in class):
r_1 = r_2 \Rightarrow k_1P_A'\theta_* - k_{-1}\theta_A = k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B
\qquad
r_2 = -r_3 \Rightarrow k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B = k_{-3}\theta_B - k_3P_B'\theta_*
\qquad
\theta_A + \theta_B + \theta_* = 1
QE for steps 1 and 3: (k_2 \sim k_{-2}) \ll (k_1 \sim k_{-1}) \sim (k_3 \sim k_{-3}).
Dividing the first equation by k_1 (the k_2/k_1 and k_{-2}/k_1 terms → 0):
P_A'\theta_* - \frac{k_{-1}}{k_1}\theta_A = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\theta_A = \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_*}
Similarly, for the second equation:
0 = k_{-3}\theta_B - k_3P_B'\theta_* \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\theta_B = \frac{k_3}{k_{-3}}P_B'\theta_*}
The obtained \theta_A and \theta_B expressions are equal to those obtained when steps 1 and 3 are at QE ↓ this must mean that r_1, r_3 are QE, as shown in Case 1 in class.
Approach 2
(a) Dimensional rate expressions as above; dividing by k_{-1} gives the non-dimensional equations:
r_1 = r_2:\;\; \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_* - \theta_A = \frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\theta_A - \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_B\quad\text{(1)}
\qquad
r_2 = -r_3:\;\; \frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\theta_A - \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_B = \frac{k_{-3}}{k_{-1}}\theta_B - \frac{k_3}{k_{-1}}P_B'\theta_*\quad\text{(2)}
(b) Expand: \theta_A = \theta_{A1} + \theta_{A2}, \theta_B = \theta_{B1} + \theta_{B2}, \theta_* = \theta_{*1} + \theta_{*2}, with \theta_{A2} \ll \theta_{A1}, \theta_{B2} \ll \theta_{B1}, \theta_{*2} \ll \theta_{*1}. Plugging into the non-dimensional equations and grouping orders:
\text{(1)}\;\; \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*1} + \theta_{A1}\left(-1 - \frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\right) + \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B1} = \theta_{A2}\left(1 + \frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\right) - \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*2} - \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B2}
\text{(2)}\;\; \frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\theta_{A1} - \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B1} + \frac{k_{-3}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B1} + \frac{k_3}{k_{-1}}P_B'\theta_{*1} = -\frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\theta_{A2} + \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B2} - \frac{k_{-3}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B2} - \frac{k_3}{k_{-1}}\theta_{*2}P_B'
\text{(3)}\;\; \big(\theta_{A1} + \theta_{B1} + \theta_{*1}\big) + \big(\theta_{A2} + \theta_{B2} + \theta_{*2}\big) = 1
(c) From Approach 1, (k_2 \sim k_{-2}) \ll (k_1 \sim k_{-1}) \sim (k_3 \sim k_{-3}):

① For order 1: \dfrac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*1} - \theta_{A1} = 0 \Rightarrow \theta_{A1} = \dfrac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*1}
② For order 1: \dfrac{k_3}{k_{-1}}P_B'\theta_{*1} = -\dfrac{k_{-3}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B1} [sign as written]
③ Site balance: (\theta_{A1} + \theta_{B1} + \theta_{*1}) = 1 and (\theta_{A2} + \theta_{B2} + \theta_{*2}) = 0

\therefore for first order: \dfrac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*1} + \dfrac{k_3}{k_{-3}}P_B'\theta_{*1} + \theta_{*1} = 1
\boxed{\theta_{*1} = \frac{1}{\left(\frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A' + \frac{k_3}{k_{-3}}P_B' + 1\right)}} \qquad \text{— the first-order approximation}
For the second-order expression we cannot make the simplification assumptions → we have to solve the earlier equations:
\begin{aligned}
1)&\;\; 0 = \theta_{A2}\left(1 + \frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\right) - \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*2} - \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B2}P_B' \;\Rightarrow\; \theta_{B2} = \frac{\theta_{A2}(k_{-1} + k_2) + k_1P_A'\theta_{*2}}{P_B'k_{-2}} \\
2)&\;\; 0 = -\frac{k_2}{k_{-1}}\theta_{A2} + \frac{k_{-2}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B2} - \frac{k_{-3}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B2} - \frac{k_3}{k_{-1}}\theta_{*2} \;\Rightarrow\; \theta_{A2}\underbrace{\left(-k_2 + \frac{(k_{-2} - k_{-3})(k_{-1} + k_2)}{P_B'k_2}\right)}_{A_1} + \theta_{*2}\underbrace{\left[(k_{-2} - k_{-3})\frac{k_1}{k_{-2}}P_A' - k_3\right]}_{A_2} = 0 \\
3)&\;\; \theta_{A2} + \theta_{B2} + \theta_{*2} = 0
\end{aligned}
so \theta_{A2} = -\theta_{*2}\dfrac{[A_2]}{[A_1]}. Plugging everything back into expression ③:
-\theta_{*2}\frac{[A_2]}{[A_1]} - \frac{(k_{-1} + k_2)}{k_{-2}}\frac{[A_2]}{[A_1]}\theta_{*2} + \frac{k_1P_A'}{k_{-2}}\theta_{*2} + \theta_{*2} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\theta_{*2} = 0}
\therefore\quad \theta_{A2} = -\theta_{*2}\frac{\left[(k_{-2} - k_{-3})\frac{k_1}{k_{-2}}P_A' - k_3\right]}{\left[-k_2 + \frac{(k_{-2} - k_{-3})(k_{-1} + k_2)}{P_B'k_2}\right]}\;;\qquad \theta_{B2} = \frac{\theta_{A2}(k_{-1} + k_2) + k_1P_A'\theta_{*2}}{P_B'k_{-2}}
Plugging in \theta_{A2} will give \theta_{B2} = f(\theta_{*2}) only!
(d) r_1 = r_2 = -r_3, with r_2 = k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B. For first order:
r_2^{(1)} = k_2\theta_{A1} - k_{-2}\theta_{B1}\;;\qquad \theta_{A1} = \frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*1}\;;\qquad \frac{k_3}{k_{-1}}P_B'\theta_{*1} = -\frac{k_{-3}}{k_{-1}}\theta_{B1}
r_2^{(1)} = \frac{k_2k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A'\theta_{*1} - k_{-2}\frac{k_3}{k_{-3}}P_B'\theta_{*1} = \Big[k_2K_1P_A' - k_{-2}K_3P_B'\Big]\theta_{*1}\;;\qquad \theta_{*1} = \frac{1}{\left(\frac{k_1}{k_{-1}}P_A' + \frac{k_3}{k_{-3}}P_B' + 1\right)}
This first-order approximation matches the QE expressions obtained in Approach 1 → the exact solution.
(e) The first-order solution represents steps 1 and 3 as QE.

↳ This means that their forward and reverse rates are much faster than those of step 2, so it “appears” that steps 1 and 3 are at equilibrium (sketch: long r_1/r_{-1} and r_3/r_{-3} arrows vs short r_2/r_{-2} arrows; r_{net} is their small difference).
↳ The first-order perturbation represents that exact QE solution.
↳ Given this analysis, the net rate should be first order (since the second-order solution gives the trivial case).

Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 1-6) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF





                  
                  Announcements 
                  
                


Term projects
Tutorial session in 2 weeks (need laptop)



Many particles in a box
Time-independent Schrödinger equation (TISE), no particle interaction. For N particles:
H = -\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i^2}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
-\sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x_i^2} = E\psi,
\qquad
\int\!\cdots\!\int \psi^*\psi \, dx_1\, dx_2 \cdots dx_N = 1
Example: 2 particles
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x_1^2} - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x_2^2} = E\psi
Solving for \psi by separation of variables, \psi(x_1,x_2) = \phi_1(x_1)\,\phi_2(x_2):
\begin{aligned}
&-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\phi_1''\phi_2 - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\phi_1\phi_2'' = E\,\phi_1\phi_2 \\
\Rightarrow\; &\underbrace{-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\phi_1''}{\phi_1}}_{f(x_1)} \underbrace{-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\phi_2''}{\phi_2}}_{f(x_2)} = E = \text{constant}, \qquad \text{separation constant } \lambda^2 \;(\lambda \text{ real})
\end{aligned}
\therefore\quad -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\phi_1}{dx_1^2} = (E-\lambda^2)\,\phi_1 \;; \qquad -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\phi_2}{dx_2^2} = \lambda^2\phi_2
BCs: (1) \psi(0,x_2) = 0, (2) \psi(L,x_2) = 0 = \psi(x_1,0) = \psi(x_1,L)
\;\hookrightarrow\; \phi_1(0) = \phi_1(L) = 0\,;\quad \phi_2(0) = \phi_2(L) = 0
\begin{aligned}
\therefore\quad \phi_1(x_1) &= A_1 \sin\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2m(E-\lambda^2)}{\hbar^2}}\,x_1\right) + \cancel{\cos(\cdots)}^{\,0} \\
\phi_2(x_2) &= A_2 \sin\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2m\lambda^2}{\hbar^2}}\,x_2\right) + \cancel{\cos(\cdots)}^{\,0}
\end{aligned}
\sqrt{\frac{2m(E-\lambda^2)}{\hbar^2}}\,L = n_1\pi, \qquad \sqrt{\frac{2m\lambda^2}{\hbar^2}}\,L = n_2\pi, \qquad n_1, n_2 = 1,2,3,\dots
E - \lambda^2 = \frac{n_1^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\;;\qquad \lambda^2 = \frac{n_2^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{E = \frac{(n_1^2+n_2^2)\,\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}}, \quad n_1,n_2 = 1,2,3,\dots
\psi(x_1,x_2) = \phi_1(x_1)\,\phi_2(x_2) = A_1A_2 \sin\!\left(\frac{n_1\pi x_1}{L}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{n_2\pi x_2}{L}\right)
Normalization: A_1A_2 = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{L}}\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{L}}
\boxed{\psi_{n_1 n_2}(x_1,x_2) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sin\!\left(\frac{n_1\pi x_1}{L}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sin\!\left(\frac{n_2\pi x_2}{L}\right)}


                  
                  Any linear combination of the \psi_{n_1n_2}'s is also a valid solution. The subscripts (e.g. \psi_{1,1}) are the quantum numbers.
                  
                

Lowest-energy state of many particles
Q: What is the lowest energy state for a system of multiple particles (e.g. e^-)?
Naive answer: n_1 = n_2 = 1 \Rightarrow E_{GS} = \dfrac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{mL^2}, \;\psi_{1,1} = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{L}}\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi x_1}{L}\right)\sqrt{\tfrac{2}{L}}\sin\!\left(\tfrac{\pi x_2}{L}\right)

This analysis is correct for bosons (integer spin).
From relativistic QM, we know that fermions (half-integer spin), such as e^-, satisfy \psi(x_1,x_2) = -\psi(x_2,x_1) (note: \psi^*\psi(x_1,x_2) = \psi^*\psi(x_2,x_1)).
If we take \psi_{GS}(x_1,x_2) = \phi_{1,1}(x_1)\,\phi_{1,1}(x_2), then \phi_{1,1}(x_1)\,\phi_{1,1}(x_2) = \phi_{1,1}(x_2)\,\phi_{1,1}(x_1) (the same, because \phi_1 = \phi_2 = \phi = \sqrt{2/L}\,\sin(\pi x/L)). Not true for fermions.
For fermions without spin, we cannot have more than one particle in the lowest energy state.

\Rightarrow We can use Slater determinants to make sure the linear combination of \phi_{n_1}(x_1) and \phi_{n_2}(x_2) is antisymmetric. We know:
\begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = -\begin{vmatrix} c & d \\ a & b \end{vmatrix}
So:
\psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{vmatrix} \phi_1(x_1) & \phi_2(x_1) \\ \phi_1(x_2) & \phi_2(x_2) \end{vmatrix}
= -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{vmatrix} \phi_1(x_2) & \phi_2(x_2) \\ \phi_1(x_1) & \phi_2(x_1) \end{vmatrix}
\qquad (\text{columns: } n_1,\ n_2)
Thus, the GS for two fermions is:
\psi(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Big[\phi_1(x_1)\,\phi_2(x_2) - \phi_1(x_2)\,\phi_2(x_1)\Big], \qquad n_1 = 1,\; n_2 = 2


                  
                  In HW: show that, with \psi antisymmetric,
                  
                

E = \frac{\int_0^L\!\int_0^L \psi^* H \psi\, dx_1\,dx_2}{\iint \psi^*\psi\, dx_1\,dx_2} = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2
where \varepsilon_i are energy levels. The interpretation is one particle in \varepsilon_1 and one particle in \varepsilon_2 (sketch: one particle on each of the two lowest levels) — a simplified Pauli exclusion principle.


Density functional theory: the idea
For many-particle systems, we can make more progress with DFT.
Idea: the total ground-state e^- density of atoms or molecules uniquely determines all electronic-structure properties (i.e. energies, positions, wave functions).
TISE: H\psi = E\psi
H = \underbrace{\sum_{i,\,e^-} -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e}\nabla_i^2}_{\text{(1) electron kinetic energy}}
+ \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}^{N}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,|r_i - r_j|}}_{\text{(2) Coulomb repulsion}}
+ \underbrace{\sum_{i,\,e^-}\sum_{\alpha,\,\text{nuclei}}\frac{Z_\alpha e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,|r_i - R_\alpha|}}_{\text{(3) electron–nuclei interaction}}
Born–Oppenheimer approximation: assumes nuclear motion is separated (since the nucleus is much heavier).
Since \psi gives all knowable properties of the system, if we know H, then we know all properties of the system. If H is completely determined by the total \rho (e^- density), then \rho determines all properties.
Total electron density is defined as:
n(\underline{x}) = \rho(\underline{x}) \equiv N \int\!\cdots\!\int \psi^*\psi \; dx_2\,dx_3\cdots dx_N
i.e. the probability that any of the e^-‘s will be found in a box (dx\,dy\,dz).
\therefore\quad \int \rho(\underline{x})\,dx\,dy\,dz = N
and thus \rho determines terms ① and ② of H.
Hohenberg–Kohn 1st theorem (1964)
States that \rho(\underline{x}) also determines term ③ (i.e. it determines H for any potential external to the e^-).
\hookrightarrow H is completely determined by \rho(\underline{x}). In principle, \rho(\underline{x}) determines E_n and \psi_n (not just the GS).


                  
                  Functionals 
                  
                

A functional gives out a number given a function as input, e.g. F[y(x)] = \int_a^b y(x)\,dx.
F[\rho] = \int f\big(\underline{r}, \rho(\underline{r}), \nabla\rho(\underline{r})\big)\, d\underline{r}
The functional derivative is
\frac{\delta F}{\delta \rho(\underline{r})} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \rho} - \nabla\cdot\frac{\partial f}{\partial \nabla\rho}
and this can be used to find the ground state when the functional derivative is set to zero.


Hohenberg–Kohn 2nd theorem
States that there is a unique functional of \rho(\underline{x}) that, when minimized with respect to \rho(\underline{x}), gives the GS energy and \rho(\underline{x}) of the system:
\min_{\rho(\underline{x})}\Big\{E\big[\rho(\underline{x})\big]\Big\} = E_{GS}
A simple functional for 1D problems
Non-interacting fermions, N = total number of particles:
E_{GS} = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 + \dots + \varepsilon_N
For a particle in a box (PIB), ignoring spin: \varepsilon_{n_i} = \dfrac{n_i^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}
E = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\,n_i^2 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N} n_i^2, \qquad n_i = 1,2,3,\dots,N
The sum can be evaluated analytically:
E = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\left(\frac{1}{3}N^3 + \frac{1}{2}N^2 + \frac{1}{6}N\right) \approx \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}\,\frac{N^3}{3}
(the N^3 term is dominant for large N). For large N, \rho(x) becomes approximately uniform in space (sketch: density profiles across the box from 0 to L flattening as N grows).
Thus if \rho = constant, N = \int_0^L \rho(x)\,dx \approx \rho\int_0^L dx = \rho L \;\therefore\; \rho = N/L. So:
\boxed{\frac{E}{N} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6mL^2}N^2 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\,\rho^2}
\rightarrow kinetic energy per particle for non-interacting fermions, e_{kin}(\rho).

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 7-12) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Simple kinetic-energy functional
For non-interacting fermions in a box:
\frac{E}{N} = e_{kin}(\rho) = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\rho^2 \qquad (\text{energy per particle})

\rho(x)\,dx is the number of particles in length dx
e_{kin}(\rho)\,(\rho\,dx) is the KE in length dx
Total energy is E_{KE}[\rho(x)] = \int e_{kin}(\rho)\,\rho\,dx over all space — the general KE expression

If there is potential energy or interactions: E[\rho(x)] = \int e_{tot}(\rho)\,\rho\,dx
Example 1: reproduce the PIB energies for N particles
E[\rho] = \int_0^L \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\rho^3\,dx \;; \qquad \text{constraint: } \int_0^L \rho(x)\,dx = N \;\; (\text{to avoid the trivial solution})
Use Lagrange multipliers. Define
F[\rho] \equiv E[\rho] - \mu\left(\int_0^L \rho(x)\,dx - N\right), \qquad \mu = \text{Lagrange multiplier}


                  
                  Note 
                  
                

\dfrac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\displaystyle\int F(\rho,\nabla\rho)\,dr = \frac{\partial f}{\partial\rho} - \frac{\partial f}{\partial\nabla\rho}, where F is a function of \rho and \nabla\rho.


Then minimize:
\frac{\partial F(\rho)}{\partial\rho} = 0 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2 - \mu\Big(\underbrace{\tfrac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\textstyle\int\rho\,dx}_{1} - \underbrace{\tfrac{\partial N}{\partial\rho}}_{0}\Big)
\quad\therefore\quad \mu = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2
\int_0^L \sqrt{\frac{2m\mu}{\pi^2\hbar^2}}\,dx = N \;\Rightarrow\; \sqrt{\frac{2m\mu}{\pi^2\hbar^2}} = \frac{N}{L}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \boxed{\rho_{min} = \frac{N}{L}}
\therefore\quad \boxed{E_{min} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\frac{N^3}{L^3}L}
This approximation improves for large N (energies in units of \pi^2\hbar^2/2mL^2):





























NE_{exact}E_{DFT}DFT / exact111/30.3343064/30.712028708000/30.93


                  
                  Principle 
                  
                

DFT gives more accurate results for systems that are similar to the systems for which the functional was derived. However, results are surprisingly good for different system types as well.


Example 2: delta-function spike
Sketch: V(x) in a box from 0 to L with a sharp spike at L/2.
Properties of \delta:

\int_0^\infty \delta(x)\,dx = 1 (thin and tall)
\int_0^L f(x)\,\delta\!\left(x-\tfrac{L}{2}\right)dx = f\!\left(\tfrac{L}{2}\right)\int_0^L \delta\!\left(x - \tfrac{L}{2}\right)dx = f\!\left(\tfrac{L}{2}\right)

New functional:
E[\rho] = \int_0^L \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\rho^3\,dx + \underbrace{\alpha\int\delta\!\left(x-\tfrac{L}{2}\right)\rho\,dx}_{\text{external PE}}
Lagrange functional:
F[\rho] \equiv E[\rho] - \mu\left(\int_0^L \rho\,dx - N\right)
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\rho} = -\mu + \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2 + \underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho}\Big(\rho\big(\tfrac{L}{2}\big)\,\alpha\Big)}_{\to\,0}
\qquad\therefore\quad \rho_{min} = \sqrt{\frac{2m\mu}{\pi^2\hbar^2}} = \frac{N}{L} \;\;(\text{constant})
\delta does not affect the density.
E_{min} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\left(\frac{N}{L}\right)^3 L + \frac{\alpha N}{L}\underbrace{\int_0^L \delta\!\left(x - \tfrac{L}{2}\right)dx}_{1}
\quad\therefore\quad E_{min} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\left(\frac{N}{L}\right)^3 L + \frac{\alpha N}{L}
\delta does add \alpha/L per particle (\alpha = constant) → physically, an obstacle (or nucleus) in the center will act as a \delta function: it will affect the energy every time an e^- crosses it in the particle-in-a-box example.
Example 3: linear potential
Sketch: V(x) rising linearly from 0 at x = 0 to V_{max} at x = L:
V_{ext}(x) = \frac{V_{max}\,x}{L}
e_{tot}[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\rho^2 + \frac{x}{L}V_{max}
\qquad
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_0^L \rho^3\,dx + \int_0^L \frac{V_{max}}{L}x\,\rho\,dx
Lagrange multiplier:
\frac{\partial F}{\partial\rho} = 0 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2 + \frac{V_{max}\,x}{L} - \mu
\quad\therefore\quad
\rho_{min} = \sqrt{\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\left(\mu - \frac{V_{max}\,x}{L}\right)} \;\; (\rho_{min} \text{ is not constant})
Finding \mu from \int_0^L \rho_{min}\,dx = N:
\int_0^L \sqrt{\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\left(\mu - \frac{V_{max}\,x}{L}\right)}\,dx = N
\;\xrightarrow{\;u\text{-sub},\; u = \mu - V_{max}x/L\;}\;
(\mu - V_{max})^{3/2} - \mu^{3/2} = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{V_{max}N}{L}\sqrt{\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}}
Either solve numerically or solve for small V_{max}/\mu:
\mu \approx \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{N^2}{L^2} + O(V_{max})
\quad\hookrightarrow\quad
\boxed{\rho_{min}(x) = \frac{N}{L}\left[1 - \frac{V_{max}\,x}{L}\,\frac{2mL^2}{\pi^2\hbar^2N^2}\right]}
Sketch: \rho_{min} decreasing linearly from x = 0 to x = L — the electric field pushes on the particle, so there is less probability for it to be on that side of the box.
Write \gamma = \dfrac{N}{L} and \beta = \dfrac{V_{max}}{L}\dfrac{2mL^2}{\pi^2\hbar^2N^2}, so \rho = \gamma(1 - \beta x):
\begin{aligned}
E[\rho_{min}] &= \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_0^L \gamma^3(1-\beta x)^3\,dx + \frac{\gamma V_{max}}{L}\int_0^L x(1-\beta x)\,dx \\
&= -\frac{1}{\beta}\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\frac{\gamma^3}{4}\underbrace{\Big[(1-\beta L)^4 - 1\Big]}_{\approx\,-4\beta L \text{ (small } \beta)} + \frac{V_{max}}{L}\gamma\left(\frac{L^2}{2} - \beta\frac{L^3}{3}\right)
\end{aligned}
\boxed{E_{min} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6mL^2}N^3 + \frac{1}{2}V_{max}N} \qquad \text{for small } V_{max}
\hookrightarrow So we add \tfrac{1}{2}V_{max} to the energy of each particle (on average).
HW preview: the 1D Thomas–Fermi atom
Sketch: a wall at x = 0 with a Coulomb potential V_{ext}(x) = -\alpha/x; \rho_{min} decays away from the wall.
\mu < 0 \rightarrow need absolute values (replace \mu = -|\mu|).
Answer:
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_0^\infty \rho^3\,dx - \alpha\int_0^\infty \frac{\rho(x)}{x}\,dx
0 = \frac{\partial F}{\partial\rho} \;\rightarrow\; \rho_{min}(x) = \left(\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\right)^{1/2}\left(\mu + \frac{\alpha}{x}\right)^{1/2}
\Rightarrow\; N = \int_0^\infty \rho_{min}\,dx = \left(\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\right)^{1/2}|\mu|^{1/2}\int_0^{\infty}\left(\frac{\alpha/|\mu|}{x} - 1\right)^{1/2}dx
\rho can never be imaginary! So truncate the domain to \alpha/|\mu| to keep \rho_{min} real:
\Downarrow \qquad \mu = -\frac{m}{2\hbar^2}\frac{\alpha^2}{N^2}
E_{min}[\rho_{min}] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6mL^2}N^3 + \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\underbrace{\int_0^{\alpha/|\mu|}\left(\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}|\mu|^{3/2}\left(\frac{\alpha/|\mu|}{x} - 1\right)^{3/2}dx}_{\text{diverges}}
The integral diverges because we are modelling an atom in 1D → larger N means the particles start to pack into the lower-potential region with nowhere for them to go → unphysically packed.
Interactions between particles
1) Coulomb: classic electrostatic interactions. E \sim \dfrac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x}, repulsion between electrons.
Electrostatic functional (x' is a dummy variable; the \tfrac12 avoids double counting):
E_{Coul} = \frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{\rho(x)\,\rho(x')}{|x - x'|}\,dx\,dx'
2) Exchange: a purely QM property/interaction (attractive, and between charged particles).
\hookrightarrow Fully accounted for in the TISE, but DFT requires extra terms. Simple approximation with dimensional analysis:
E_{exch} \sim \int\frac{e^2}{\varepsilon_0}\rho^n\,dx, \qquad n = 2 \text{ gives dimensional consistency}
Putting it together (in 1D)
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int\rho^3\,dx + \frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{\rho(x)\,\rho(x')}{|x-x'|}\,dx\,dx' - C_x\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\rho^2\,dx + \int V_{ext}\,\rho\,dx
where V_{ext} could be -\dfrac{\alpha}{x}, \dfrac{1}{2}kx^2, …

Start thinking of term projects → list 2–3 thoughts
Tutorial session → next Thursday



One-dimensional atom
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int\rho^3\,dx + \frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{\rho(x)\,\rho(x')}{|x-x'|}\,dx\,dx' \underbrace{- C_x\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\rho^2\,dx}_{\text{exchange energy}} + \int V_{ext}(x)\,\rho\,dx
Simplify the Coulomb terms using delta functions:

e^-–e^- repulsion: replace the full Coulomb U(|x-x'|) with U \sim \alpha\,\delta(x - x') (sketch: decaying Coulomb curve → a spike at |x-x'| = 0).
V_{ext} = -\gamma\,\delta\!\left(x - \tfrac{L}{2}\right) (sketch: box from 0 to L with a downward spike at L/2). From an e^- perspective, the nucleus is external.

Thus our 1D atom becomes:
\begin{aligned}
E[\rho] &= \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_0^L\rho^3\,dx - C_x\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\rho^2\,dx + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^L\!\!\int_0^L\delta(x-x')\,\rho(x)\,\rho(x')\,dx'\,dx}_{e^-\text{–}e^- \text{ interactions}} \underbrace{- \gamma\int_0^L\delta\!\left(x-\tfrac{L}{2}\right)\rho\,dx}_{e^-\text{–nucleus interaction}} \\
F[\rho] &= \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_0^L\rho^3\,dx + \frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^L[\rho(x)]^2\,dx - C_x\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_0^L\rho^2\,dx - \gamma\,\rho\!\left(\tfrac{L}{2}\right) - \mu\left(\int_0^L\rho\,dx - N\right)
\end{aligned}
\frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho} = 0 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2 + \frac{2e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\Big(\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}}_{\text{Coulomb}} - \underbrace{C_x}_{\text{exchange}}\Big)\rho_{min} - \mu
\rho_{min} = constant \rightarrow \int_0^L\rho_{min}\,dx = N \Rightarrow \rho_{min} = N/L. Plugging back into the energy functional:
\boxed{E_{GS} = E[\rho] = \underbrace{\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6mL^2}N^3}_{\text{KE}} + \underbrace{\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 L}\left(\frac{1}{2} - C_x\right)N^2}_{\text{interaction term}} - \underbrace{\frac{\gamma}{L}N}_{\text{attraction to nucleus}}}


                  
                  These treatments work okay for atoms but not for molecules. 
                  
                

DFT and the TISE with periodic boundary conditions
(e.g. heterogeneous catalysis might have some periodicity)
1) Basic idea: V_{ext}(x) = V_{ext}(x + a) (sketch: periodic potential with period a along x). If V_{ext}(x) is periodic, observable properties are also periodic: \rho(x) = \rho(x+a).
Approach (n = some integer):
E[\rho] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\int_{-na}^{+na}\rho^3\,dx + \int_{-na}^{na}V_{ext}(x)\,\rho\,dx
(transcriber’s note: the notes show \rho^2 in the first integral; \rho^3 is consistent with the derivative below)
\hookrightarrow\; \frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho} = 0 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2 + V_{ext}(x) - \mu
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\rho_{min}(x) = \left(\frac{2m}{\pi^2\hbar^2}\big(\mu - V_{ext}(x)\big)\right)^{1/2} \;\rightarrow\; \text{periodic in } x \;\checkmark 
Example: Dirac comb
V_{ext}(x) = \alpha\sum_n \delta(x - na), n a positive or negative integer (sketch: spikes at \dots,-2a,-a,a,2a,\dots). P periods are analyzed.
E[\rho] = \int_{-Pa/2}^{Pa/2}\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\rho^3\,dx + \int_{-Pa/2}^{Pa/2}\alpha\sum_n\delta(x-na)\,\rho\,dx
\frac{\delta F}{\delta\rho} = 0 = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\rho_{min}^2 - \mu \;;\qquad \rho_{min} = \text{constant} = \frac{N}{L} \quad (N = \text{total number of particles in all } P \text{ periods})
E[\rho_{min}] = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6m}\frac{N^3}{(Pa)^2} + \alpha\,\underbrace{\rho(na)}_{N/L}\,P\;;\qquad \text{let } N_{cell} = \frac{N}{P}
\boxed{\frac{E_{GS}}{P} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{6ma^2}N_{cell}^3 + \frac{\alpha}{a}N_{cell}} \qquad \text{energy per unit cell in a Dirac potential}
Kohn–Sham DFT (preview): periodic TISE

Shares many features with the TISE treatment of non-interacting particles ⇒ need to study the periodic treatment of the TISE.
As with DFT, assume V(x) = V(x + na), n = integer.
All measurable quantities are also periodic: \rho(x) = \rho(x+a), i.e. |\psi(x)|^2 = \psi^*\psi = |\psi(x+a)|^2; but wavefunctions are complex, so \psi(x) \neq \psi(x+a).
Most general periodicity: \psi(x+a) = \lambda\,\psi(x) with \lambda^*\lambda = 1.
If we have P total periods and assume periodic BCs (the system “wraps around” itself):

\psi(x + Pa) = \lambda^P\psi(x) = \psi(x)\;;\qquad \lambda^P = 1 = e^{2n\pi i} = \cos(2n\pi) + i\sin(2n\pi)\;;\quad n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \dots
\lambda = e^{\frac{2\pi n}{P}i} \equiv e^{iKa}\;;\qquad K = \frac{2\pi n}{Pa} \quad (K = \text{wave number},\; Pa = \text{total length of system})


                  
                  Bloch's theorem 
                  
                

\psi_K(x+a) = \psi_K(x)\,e^{iKa}\;;\qquad K = \frac{2\pi n}{Pa}\;;\quad n = 0, \pm1, \pm2, \dots
The wavefunction displaced by a period picks up a phase; K is a quantum number depending on the periodicity.


Example: Dirac comb with the TISE
For 0 < x < a, V(x) = 0, so the TISE is
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} = E\psi \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} = -k^2\psi\;;\quad k = \sqrt{\frac{2mE}{\hbar^2}}
\qquad
\psi(x) = A\sin(kx) + B\cos(kx)\;;\;\; 0<x<a
From Bloch’s theorem, for -a < x < 0:
\psi(x + a) = e^{iKa}\Big[A\sin\big(k(x+a)\big) + B\cos\big(k(x+a)\big)\Big]
Initial conditions: at x = 0, \psi_{0^-} = \psi_{0^+} (\psi is continuous)
\hookrightarrow\; B = e^{-iKa}\Big[A\sin(ka) + B\cos(ka)\Big]
Also, the derivative has a jump (“cusp” at x = 0, sketch):
\left.\frac{d\psi}{dx}\right|_{0^+} - \left.\frac{d\psi}{dx}\right|_{0^-} = \frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}\psi(0)
\;\Rightarrow\;
kA - e^{-iKa}k\Big[A\cos(ka) - B\sin(ka)\Big] = \frac{2m\alpha}{\hbar^2}B
Eliminate A and B:
\boxed{\cos(Ka) = \cos(ka) + \frac{m\alpha a}{\hbar^2}\frac{\sin(ka)}{ka}}
Solve for k given K (graphically). For \dfrac{m\alpha a}{\hbar^2} = 1, K = \dfrac{2\pi n}{Pa}: sketch of the right-hand side vs ka — the cosine has to exist between -1 and 1, so the regions where the curve goes above 1 or below -1 are forbidden energy regions.
Certain values of k (\sim E^{1/2}) are forbidden by periodicity. This causes band structure in periodic systems.
K is quantized; as P\to\infty, K becomes continuous.
\hookrightarrow Try P = 10 (sketch: states n = 0, \pm1, \dots, \pm10 marked along the allowed parts of the curve). There are P + 1 states for non-interacting fermions in the first band (ignoring spin) and P states for all other bands.
To get the total E, sum the energies of the (non-interacting) particles:
\begin{aligned}
E_{tot} &= \sum_{\text{particles}}\varepsilon_n = \sum_{\text{particles}}\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}k_n^2 \qquad\text{(if } N \text{ is large we can approximate the sum with an integral)} \\
&= \sum\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}k_n^2\,\Delta n\;;\qquad \Delta n = \frac{Pa}{2\pi}\Delta K \\
&= \frac{Pa}{2\pi}\sum\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}k_n^2\,\Delta K \approx \frac{Pa}{2\pi}\int\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}[k(K)]^2\,dK
\end{aligned}
\boxed{\frac{E_{tot}}{P} \approx \frac{a}{2\pi}\int_{\text{occupied bands}}\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}[k(K)]^2\,dK}
Energy per cell in a periodic system of non-interacting particles (P\to\infty, K is continuous).

Email Purdue username; send 2–3 preliminary ideas for term projects.


Periodic TISE solution
V(x + a) = V(x)
\frac{E}{P} = \frac{a}{2\pi}\int_{\text{occupied levels}}\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}[k(K)]^2\,dK\;;\qquad K = \frac{2\pi n}{Pa}\;;\quad n = 0,\pm1,\pm2,\dots
Algorithm to solve:

Pick values of K for numerical integration — “K points”.
At each K point, find k(K) from the TISE solution or Kohn–Sham (K-S).
Advantage: only need TISE / K-S solutions for a single unit cell.
Small lattice constant a → larger range of K for integration → need more K points to converge the integral. Large a → fewer K points.



                  
                  K-point analysis — rule of thumb 
                  
                

Number of K points \approx \dfrac{2\pi}{0.3\,a} (in each dimension).


Kohn–Sham DFT
Normal DFT: extremely efficient, but kinetic-energy functionals aren’t good enough (except for low atomic numbers).
\therefore Idea: use a more accurate treatment of KE, at the cost of (much) greater computational expense.
\downarrow Introduce a fictitious, non-interacting gas of e^-‘s that has the true, total e^- density \rho(\underline{r}):
\rho(\underline{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N}|\psi_i(\underline{r})|^2
where \psi_i(\underline{r}) are fictitious single-e^- orbitals that don’t interact (note: \rho(\underline{r}) = N\iiint\Psi^*\Psi\,dx_1\,dx_2\,dx_3\cdots dx_N). The total \Psi is a Slater determinant of the \psi_i‘s (→ antisymmetric).
KE for non-interacting particles:
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\int\psi_i^*(\underline{r})\,\nabla^2\psi_i(\underline{r})\,d\underline{r}


                  
                  In the PIB 
                  
                

Multiply -\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\dfrac{d^2\psi}{dx^2} = E_{KE}\psi by \psi^* and integrate: -\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\displaystyle\int\psi^*\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2}\,dx = E_{KE}


Total K-S functional:
E[\rho] = \underbrace{-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\int\psi_i^*(\underline{r})\,\nabla^2\psi_i(\underline{r})\,d\underline{r}}_{T_s[\rho]} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\iint\frac{\rho(\underline{r})\,\rho(\underline{r}')}{|\underline{r}-\underline{r}'|}\,d\underline{r}\,d\underline{r}' + E_{xc}[\rho] + \int V_{ext}(\underline{r})\,\rho\,d\underline{r} \qquad \text{(Eq. 1)}
where E_{xc}[\rho] = residual KE excess + exchange + correlation.
Now the Lagrangian (with the constraint \int\rho(\underline{r})\,d\underline{r} = N):
\frac{\partial F[\rho]}{\partial\rho} = \frac{\partial T_s[\rho]}{\partial\rho} + V_{ext}(\underline{r}) + \frac{\partial E_{xc}[\rho]}{\partial\rho} + \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{\rho(\underline{r}')}{|\underline{r}-\underline{r}'|}\,d\underline{r}' - \mu
Define
V_{eff}(\underline{r}) = V_{ext}(\underline{r}) + \frac{\partial E_{xc}}{\partial\rho} + \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int\frac{\rho}{|\underline{r}-\underline{r}'|}\,d\underline{r}'
\frac{\partial T_s[\rho]}{\partial\rho} + V_{eff}(\underline{r}) = \mu
\qquad\text{compare non-interacting systems:}\qquad
\frac{\partial T_s[\rho]}{\partial\rho} + V_{ext}(\underline{r}) = \mu
Since the full TISE separates into single-particle equations for non-interacting particles, Kohn and Sham reasoned this must also be possible for their “fictitious” system ⇓


                  
                  Kohn–Sham equations 
                  
                

\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_i^2 + V_{ext}(\underline{r}) + \frac{\partial E_{xc}}{\partial\rho} + \int\frac{\rho(\underline{r}')}{|\underline{r}-\underline{r}'|}\,d\underline{r}'\right]\psi_i = \varepsilon_i\psi_i\;;\qquad i = 1\dots N


Algorithm:

Guess fictitious \psi_i
Find \rho = \sum|\psi_i|^2
Evaluate V_{eff}(\underline{r}) ← Kohn–Sham potential
Solve the K-S equations to get new \psi_i‘s
Repeat 1–4

Once converged: \Psi(\underline{r}_{all}) = Slater determinant of the \psi_i‘s. Then find the total energy:
E[\rho_{min}] = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\varepsilon_i - \frac{1}{2}\iint\frac{\rho(\underline{r})\,\rho(\underline{r}')}{|\underline{r}-\underline{r}'|}\,d\underline{r}\,d\underline{r}' - \int\frac{\partial E_{xc}}{\partial\rho}\rho\,d\underline{r} + E_{xc}[\rho]
or use the earlier Eq. (1).
Example: two fermions in a 1D box with “δ-function repulsion”
The K-S energy is (ignoring exchange & correlation — we can only do this to simplify the problem; in a real case we need guesses for these):
E[\rho] = -\frac{1}{2}\left(\int_0^1\psi_1^*\frac{d^2\psi_1}{dx_1^2}\,dx_1 + \int_0^L\psi_2^*\frac{d^2\psi_2}{dx_2^2}\,dx_2\right) + \frac{\alpha}{2}\left(\int_0^L\!\!\int_0^L\rho(x)\,\rho(x')\,\delta(x-x')\,dx_1\,dx_2\right)
\therefore the K-S equations are \left[-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d^2}{dx_i^2} + \alpha\rho(x)\right]\psi_i = \varepsilon_i\psi_i. For 2 particles, with \rho(x) = |\psi_1|^2 + |\psi_2|^2:
-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2\psi_1}{dx_1^2} + \alpha\rho\,\psi_1 = \varepsilon_1\psi_1\;;\qquad -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2\psi_2}{dx_2^2} + \alpha\rho\,\psi_2 = \varepsilon_2\psi_2
Basis expansion: \psi_1 = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\phi_{1n}(x_1), \;\psi_2 = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n\phi_{2n}(x_2), with PIB solutions \phi_n(x) = \sqrt{2}\sin(n\pi x) (assume L = 1).
-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx_1^2}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\phi_{1n}(x_1) + \alpha\left[\Big(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\phi_{1n}\Big)^2 + \Big(\sum b_m\phi_{2m}\Big)^2\right]\sum_{j}^{\infty}a_j\phi_{1j}(x_1) = \varepsilon_1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\phi_{1n}(x_1)
(similar for x_2) \;\Rightarrow\; -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\pi^2}{2}\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}n^2a_n\phi_{1n}(x_1) + \dots — an eigenvalue problem (to determine the coefficients and basis functions).
Basis functions are orthonormal \therefore multiply by \phi_{1k}(x_1) and integrate from 0 to 1:
\frac{\pi^2}{2}k^2a_k + \underbrace{\alpha\int_0^1\sum_n\sum_m(a_na_m + b_nb_m)\,\phi_{1n}\phi_{1m}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}a_j\phi_{1j}\phi_{1k}\,dx_1}_{\text{represents particle interactions}} = \varepsilon_1a_k
Similar for \varepsilon_2, but we don’t need to solve that since the particles are indistinguishable.


                  
                  Note 
                  
                

\int_0^1\phi_{1n}\phi_{1m}\phi_{1j}\phi_{1k}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\Big[\delta_{n-m-j+k} + \delta_{n-m+j-k} - \delta_{n-m-j-k} - \delta_{n-m+j+k} - \delta_{n+m-j+k} - \delta_{n+m+j-k} + \delta_{n+m-j-k} + \delta_{n+m+j+k}\Big]


\Rightarrow\; \frac{\pi^2}{2}k^2a_k + \frac{1}{2}\alpha\sum_n\sum_m(a_na_m + b_nb_m)\Big(a_{n-m+k} + a_{k-n+m} - a_{n-m-k} - a_{m-n-k} - a_{n+m+k} - a_{k-n-m} + a_{n+m-k} + a_{-n-m-k}\Big) = \varepsilon_1a_k
This is a non-linear eigenvalue problem, solved self-consistently with an initial guess for \{a_i\} and \{b_i\}.
If n_{max} = 2: \psi_1^0 = a_1^0\phi_{11}(x_1) + a_2^0\phi_{12}(x_1), \;\psi_2^0 = b_1^0\phi_{21}(x_2) + b_2^0\phi_{22}(x_2).
Guess a_1^0 = 1, a_2^0 = 0, b_1^0 = 0, b_2^0 = 1 \Rightarrow \rho^0 = a_1^{0\,2} + b_2^{0\,2} = 2. Plugging in (the bracketed coefficients come from \rho^0):
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\pi^2}{2}a_1' + \frac{1}{2}\alpha\big[1\cdot3a_1' + 1\cdot2a_1'\big] &= \varepsilon_1a_1'\;;\quad k = 1 \\
2\pi^2a_2' + \frac{1}{2}\alpha\big[1\cdot2a_2' + 1\cdot3a_2'\big] &= \varepsilon_1a_2'\;;\quad k = 2
\end{aligned}
\frac{\pi^2}{2}a_1 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha a_1 = \varepsilon_1a_1\;;\qquad 2\pi^2a_2 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha a_2 = \varepsilon_1a_2
\therefore\quad
\begin{bmatrix}\frac{\pi^2}{2} + \frac{5}{2}\alpha - \varepsilon_1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\pi^2 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha - \varepsilon_1\end{bmatrix} = 0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\left(\frac{\pi^2}{2} + \frac{5}{2}\alpha - \varepsilon_1\right)\left(2\pi^2 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha - \varepsilon_1\right) = 0
\therefore\quad \varepsilon_1 = \frac{\pi^2}{2} + \frac{5}{2}\alpha\;;\qquad \varepsilon_2 = 2\pi^2 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha
Solve for a_1 and a_2:

\varepsilon_1 = \frac{\pi^2}{2} + \frac{5}{2}\alpha \rightarrow a_2' = 0,\; a_1' = 1
\varepsilon_1 = 2\pi^2 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha \rightarrow a_1' = 0,\; a_2' = 1

The iteration has converged.
\psi_{min}(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\Big\{\phi_{11}(x_1)\,\phi_{21}(x_2) - \phi_{21}(x_2)\,\phi_{12}(x_1)\Big\}
\qquad
\rho_{min} = 2\sin^2(\pi x) + 2\sin^2(2\pi x)
E[\rho_{min}] = \frac{5}{2}\pi^2 + \frac{5}{2}\alpha \qquad (\text{not the sum of the one-particle energies})
Normal DFT (\hbar = m = 1) \Rightarrow \rho_{min} = N/L = 2 (constant), E[\rho_{min}] = \frac{4}{3}\pi^2 + 2\alpha.
Exact TISE: E_{GS} = \frac{5}{2}\pi^2.


                  
                  K-S is more accurate for Al and beyond (heavier atoms), but normal DFT approaches K-S for smaller atomic sizes.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 7 (Thermo)
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 21-23) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Stationary states: solutions to the TISE. From i\hbar\dfrac{\partial\psi}{\partial t} = H\psi \;\rightarrow\; H\psi_n = E_n\psi_n, where \psi_n is a stationary state (physically observable properties are constant).
Basis sets
Basis functions are used to solve the K-S equations. A larger basis set → more accurate solutions but more computational time (check with convergence tests; consistent for all DFT codes).
The basis set size is given as an energy cutoff. For a PIB, the plane-wave (PW) energies are
E_{PW's} = \frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2m}\left(\left(\frac{n_x}{L_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{n_y}{L_y}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{n_z}{L_z}\right)^2\right),\qquad n_x,n_y,n_z = 1,\dots,\infty
Choose the total plane-wave “cutoff energy” → this determines the number and type of plane waves that fall within this energy bound.

In 1D, for a unit cell with d \sim 1 nm, usually 4–6 basis functions are needed for convergence → E \sim 10–15 eV.
In 3D, for a unit cell with V \sim 1\,\text{nm}^3, thousands of plane waves are needed → cutoff \approx 400 eV.

Codes can be sped up with lots of tricks.
Exchange–correlation functionals
Recall the K-S equations:
\left[-\frac{1}{2}\nabla_i^2 + V_{ext}(r) + \int\frac{\rho(r')}{|r - r'|}\,dr' + \frac{\delta E_{xc}}{\delta\rho}\right]\psi_i = \varepsilon_i\psi_i
The \dfrac{\delta E_{xc}}{\delta\rho} term is where most approximations are made. Possible choices:
1) LDA — local density approximation

Similar to the class functionals → a function of \rho(\underline{r}) only.
Fit to quantum Monte Carlo calculations of the homogeneous e^- gas (very expensive) ⇒ E_{xc}^{LDA} = E_{xc}^{LDA}[\rho] (closed form).
Works best for bulk materials / systems with slowly varying (with respect to space) \rho‘s.
Does not work well for surfaces or systems with sharp \rho gradients.

2) Generalized gradient approximation (GGA)

All are explicit in \rho and \nabla\rho: E_{xc}^{GGA} = E_{xc}^{GGA}(\rho, \nabla\rho)
Standard for surfaces and interfaces.
Examples: PBE (Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof), RPBE (revised PBE), PW91, BEEF (Bayesian error estimation).

3) Meta-GGA

Incorporates second derivatives: E_{meta} = E_{meta}[\rho, \nabla\rho, \nabla^2\rho]
Example: SCAN.
The improvement in performance is relatively small.

4) Hybrid / hyper functionals

Based on GGA functionals, but add a fraction of exact exchange from Hartree–Fock. HF exchange is calculated using the \psi_i from DFT:

E_{xc}^{hyb} = E_x^{GGA} + a\left(E_x^{HF} - E_x^{GGA}\right) + E_c^{GGA}

E_{xc} depends on the \psi_i‘s, so this leads to much longer computation times.
Examples: B3LYP, M06, PBE0 (a = 0.25), HSE06 (hybrid screened exchange, a = 0.25, with exact exchange applied over short distances).
Full hybrids don’t work well on metals because e^- clouds screen out exchange effects.
Screened hybrids are better, but not great.
Hybrids work well for oxides (especially semiconductors).

Major limitations of existing DFT techniques
1) Band gaps (HOMO–LUMO gaps) in semiconductors or molecules
\Delta \equiv \varepsilon_{valence} - \varepsilon_{conduction}\;;\qquad \varepsilon_{LUMO} - \varepsilon_{HOMO}
Typically \Delta_{GGA,\,LDA} < \Delta_{exp}, because they don’t localize e^- properly (i.e. errors in e^- localization).
2) Self-interaction error (SIE)
In DFT, e^- feel themselves:
\text{Exact Coulomb: } U = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|r_i - r_j|}
\qquad
\text{DFT: } \frac{1}{2}\iint\frac{\rho(\underline{r})\,\rho(\underline{r}')}{|\underline{r}-\underline{r}'|}\,d\underline{r}\,d\underline{r}' \;\;(\text{no } j\neq i \text{ equivalent})
Therefore the issue is that DFT under-localizes e^-; for metals the errors cancel. However, in oxides, redox processes give errors that do not cancel (as much). Most important for d and f electrons, which are highly localized.
Two practical approaches:

DFT + U (Hubbard U) → an empirical term that penalizes delocalized orbitals; U depends on the material.
Exact-exchange functionals: SIE is smaller because of Hartree–Fock (SIE exactly cancels in HF).

3) Van der Waals interactions
In standard GGA calculations, \rho(r) decays exponentially from the nucleus, while vdW decays as 1/r^6; the exponential is faster, so intermolecular interactions are underestimated.

Correlated fluctuations in e^- density result in vdW (sketch: two fluctuating electron clouds inducing each other).
In metals, this is reduced due to the presence of metallic delocalized e^-.
vdW is essential for zeolites and hydrocarbon interactions on surfaces.

Empirical corrections:

(a) DFT-Dx (x = 1, 2, 3): add C_i/r^6 terms to the energy. Not great for metals (does not account for e^- screening).
(b) Explicit non-local functionals that include vdW-like terms (→ self-consistently incorporated into energies) → OK for metals. E.g. DFT-vdW, optPBE, optB86b, BEEF-vdW.

Surface thermodynamics
Sketch: DFT + surface thermodynamics + kinetics → computational catalysis.
DFT + thermo gives:

What is the state of the catalyst surface (structure, adsorbate coverage, e^- properties) for given environmental conditions (T, P, V)?
How can we determine adsorption isotherms for use in microkinetic models?

For surfaces, a convenient free energy is the grand potential:
\Omega = \underbrace{E - TS}_{\text{Helmholtz energy } (F)} - \sum_i\mu_iN_i\;;\qquad d\Omega = -S\,dT - P\,dV - \sum_i N_i\,d\mu_i
(\Omega, S, V, N are extensive; T, V, \mu_i are the fundamental variables.)

Convenient free energy because P is hard to define for a surface.
Also, the surface is often in quasi-equilibrium with a gas or solid bulk phase → easier to find the \mu_i‘s.

Consider two phases \alpha (top) and \beta (bottom). If the interphase is planar: T^\alpha = T^\beta; P^\alpha = P^\beta; \mu_i^\alpha = \mu_i^\beta.
\boxed{\Omega^{total} = \Omega^\alpha + \Omega^\beta + \Omega}
where \Omega is the excess grand potential from the interface.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 8 (Thermo)
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 24-27) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Grand potential of an interface
d\Omega = \underbrace{-S\,dT - P\,dV}_{dF} - \sum_i N_i\,d\mu_i\;;\qquad \Omega(T, V, \mu_i)
Two phases \alpha (volume V^\alpha) and \beta (volume V^\beta) at constant V_{tot}:
\Omega^{tot} = \Omega^\alpha + \Omega^\beta + \Omega\;,\qquad \Omega^\alpha = \omega^\alpha V^\alpha \;\;(\omega^\alpha = \text{free energy per volume in bulk } \alpha)
d\Omega^t = d\Omega^\alpha + d\Omega^\beta + d\Omega
d\Omega^\alpha = -S^\alpha dT - P\,dV^\alpha - \sum_i N_i^\alpha d\mu_i\;;\qquad d\Omega^\beta = -S^\beta dT - P\,dV^\beta - \sum_i N_i^\beta d\mu_i
with T^\alpha = T^\beta = T^{interface}, P^\alpha = P^\beta = P^{int}, \mu_i^\alpha = \mu_i^\beta = \mu_i^{int}.
Including the interfacial term:
d\Omega^t = -S^t dT - P\,dV^t + \underbrace{\gamma\,dA}_{\substack{\text{work associated with}\\\text{changes in interfacial area}}} - \sum_i N_i^t d\mu_i
Also: S^t = S^\alpha + S^\beta + S (with S^\alpha = s^\alpha V^\alpha, per volume); N_i^t = N_i^\alpha + N_i^\beta + N_i; V^t = V^\alpha + V^\beta.


                  
                  Where is the boundary? 
                  
                

The interface region is a couple of atomic layers thick; the dividing boundary is often placed where there is a maximum concentration gradient. How are N_i and V_i defined? N_m = N_t - \rho_m V_{m,bulk} - N_m^{vapor} → the excess amount of interfacial metal.


\begin{aligned}
d\Omega &= \Big(-S^t dT - P\,dV^t + \gamma\,dA - \sum N_i^t d\mu_i\Big) + \Big(S^\alpha dT + P\,dV^\alpha + \sum N_i^\alpha d\mu_i\Big) + \Big(S^\beta dT + P\,dV^\beta + \sum N_i^\beta d\mu_i\Big) \\
d\Omega &= -\underbrace{(S^t - S^\alpha - S^\beta)}_{S}\,dT - P\,d\underbrace{(V^t - V^\alpha - V^\beta)}_{0 \text{ (no excess interfacial volume)}} + \gamma\,dA - \sum_i\big(N_i^t - N_i^\alpha - N_i^\beta\big)\,d\mu_i
\end{aligned}
\therefore\quad \boxed{d\Omega = -S\,dT + \gamma\,dA - \sum_i N_i\,d\mu_i}
All quantities are excess interfacial quantities: \Omega = \Omega(T, A, \mu_i).
Euler integration → \Omega = \gamma A → \boxed{\gamma = \Omega/A}: the surface tension is the excess \Omega per unit area.


                  
                  Aside: Gibbs–Duhem for interfaces 
                  
                

\Omega = \gamma A \Rightarrow d\Omega = \gamma\,dA + A\,d\gamma, so A\,d\gamma = -S\,dT - \sum_i N_i\,d\mu_i:
d\gamma = -\frac{S}{A}dT - \sum_i\frac{N_i}{A}d\mu_i
This relates to the Gibbs–Duhem isotherm, \gamma = \gamma(T, \mu_i). Calculate \gamma at a given \{T, \mu_i\} and find the structure with the lowest \gamma → surface phase diagram.


Idea: compute \gamma with DFT + statistical mechanics
Calculate \Omega/A\;(\gamma) using DFT + stat mech, assuming the surface is in equilibrium with bulk phases (because \mu_i = \mu_i^{gas}, \mu_i = \mu_i^{bulk\ metal}):
\boxed{\gamma = \big(U - TS - \textstyle\sum_i\mu_iN_i\big)\frac{1}{A}}
(U = excess interfacial internal energy, S = excess entropy, N_i = excess moles of i.) Find the lowest \gamma for the desired T, \mu_i.
Algorithm
① U can be approximated in many ways:

Ignore the kinetic energy of surface molecules, and assume U \approx E_{DFT} (the potential energy for the atoms):
U = \frac{E_{DFT} - \rho_{bulk}V^\alpha}{A}\;\;(\rho_{bulk} = \text{bulk energy density})
Often people ignore this excess aspect of the surface energy in phase diagrams.
Better: U \approx E_{DFT} + \text{ZPE} (zero-point energy: the lowest vibrational energy state for molecules). Note: we typically neglect the ZPE of the surface itself.
Best: calculate Q = \sum_j e^{-\beta E_j} (the partition function over states of the surface; we have to make approximations since there are infinitely many) and use U = -\dfrac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial\beta}.



                  
                  Term project ideas 
                  
                


Methods of approximation for Q
Phonon interactions in the ZPE



② TS — excess surface entropy approximations:

Assume TS = 0 (surfaces are not bulk phases → reduced dimensionality, a large decrease in entropy). A first approximation.
Adsorbates: count all possible arrangements of adsorbate i; then S_i = k_B\ln\Omega (\Omega = number of states) ↳ configurational entropy: mean-field treatment.
Partition function: S = k_B\ln Q - \dfrac{1}{T}\dfrac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial\beta} (calculated from stat mech).
Use empirical correlations for S_i of surface adsorbates.

③ \{\mu_i\}:


Leave these as undetermined independent parameters (sketch: \gamma plotted vs \mu_i).


Evaluate \mu_i by equilibrium with a bulk phase → \mu_i = \mu_i^{gas}.
↳ Use measured data (ideal gas):


\begin{aligned}
\mu_{gas}(T,P) &= \mu_{gas}(T,P^\circ) + k_BT\ln\left(\frac{P}{P^\circ}\right) \\
&= h_{gas}(T,P^\circ) - TS_{gas}(T,P^\circ) + k_BT\ln\left(\frac{P}{P^\circ}\right) \\
&= \underbrace{\Big[h_{gas}(T,P^\circ) - h_{gas}(0,P^\circ)\Big]}_{\int_0^T C_p\,dT \text{ at } P^\circ} + \underbrace{\Big[h_{gas}(0,P^\circ) - E_{DFT,gas}\Big]}_{\text{ZPE}} + \Big[\underbrace{E_{DFT,gas}}_{\text{DFT}} - \underbrace{TS_{gas}(T,P^\circ)}_{\text{tables}}\Big] + k_BT\ln\left(\frac{P}{P^\circ}\right)
\end{aligned}
(adding and subtracting various reference states). The C_p integral can be extrapolated, assumed constant, etc.; the only KE at 0 K is the zero-point energy, h_{gas}(0,P^\circ) - E_{DFT,gas} = \text{ZPE}; E_{DFT,gas} is the potential energy from a DFT calculation of the gas phase; the entropy is the absolute value from tables.
↳ Alternatively, \mu_{gas} = h_{gas}(T,P) - TS_{gas}(T,P) with h_{gas}(T,P) = U_{gas}(T,P) + k_BT (if ideal gas). Find U_{gas} with:
(i) Equipartition theorem (high T; the total number of degrees of freedom is always 3N):

Each translational mode (3 total) gives \tfrac{1}{2}k_BT
Each vibrational mode (3N-6 non-linear, 3N-5 linear) gives k_BT
Each rotational mode (3 non-linear, 2 linear) gives \tfrac{1}{2}k_BT

\Rightarrow\; U_{gas} = 3k_BT + (3N-6)k_BT + E_{DFT,gas}\;\;(\text{non-linear})\;;\qquad U_{gas} = \frac{5}{2}k_BT + (3N-5)k_BT + E_{DFT,gas}\;\;(\text{linear})
(ii) Real statistical mechanics for U_{gas} (and S_{gas}):
\text{Vibrational (per molecule): } Q_{vib} = \prod_i\frac{e^{-h\nu_i\beta/2}}{1 - e^{-h\nu_i\beta}}
(\nu_i = vibrational frequencies, measured or calculated; i runs over all normal modes of the molecule.)
\text{Rotational: } Q_{rot} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{\sigma}\prod_{j=1}^{3}\left(\frac{2I_j}{\hbar^2\beta}\right)^{1/2}\;\;(\text{non-linear})\;;\qquad Q_{rot} = \frac{I}{\sigma\beta\hbar^2}\;\;(\text{linear})
(\sigma = symmetry factor, \beta = 1/k_BT, I_{1,2,3} = principal moments of inertia.)
\text{Translational (for 1 molecule): } Q_{trans} = \left(\frac{m}{2\pi\beta\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}V\;\;(V = \text{total volume of system})
U = \langle E\rangle = \frac{\sum_i E_ie^{-\beta E_i}}{Q} = -\frac{1}{Q}\frac{\partial Q}{\partial\beta} = -\frac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial\beta}
where e^{-\beta E_i}/Q is the probability of the system being in state i.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 28-30) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Partition functions for ideal gases
Translation, rotation, vibration → Q for ideal gases: \langle U\rangle = -\dfrac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial\beta}, \beta = \dfrac{1}{k_BT}
U_{vib} = \sum_i\Bigg(\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}h\nu_i}_{\text{ZPE}} + \underbrace{\frac{h\nu_i}{e^{\beta h\nu_i} - 1}}_{\text{thermal excitation}}\Bigg)\qquad (i = \text{normal vibrational modes of the molecule})
U_{rot} = \begin{cases}\tfrac{3}{2}k_BT & \text{non-linear} \\ k_BT & \text{linear}\end{cases}
\qquad(\text{same as equipartition, since } Q_{rot} \text{ is already for "high" } T)
\qquad
U_{trans} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT
Add E_{DFT} to these terms.
S_{gas}(T,P) can also be found from Q_{gas} (F = Helmholtz):
S = \underbrace{k\ln Q}_{-F/T} - \frac{1}{T}\frac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial\beta} = k\ln Q + \frac{U}{T}
S_{vib} = \sum_i\left(-\frac{h\nu_i}{2T} - k_B\ln\big(1 - e^{-h\nu_i\beta}\big)\right) + \frac{1}{T}\sum_i\left(\frac{1}{2}h\nu_i + \frac{h\nu_i}{e^{\beta h\nu_i} - 1}\right)
S_{rot} = k_B\ln\left[\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{\sigma}\prod_{i=1}^{3}\left(\frac{2I_i}{\hbar^2\beta}\right)^{1/2}\right] + \frac{3}{2}k_B\;\;(\text{non-linear})\;;\qquad S_{rot} = k_B\ln\left[\frac{I}{\sigma\beta\hbar^2}\right] + k_B\;\;(\text{linear})
For translation, with N indistinguishable molecules:
Q_{trans}^{tot} = \frac{\big(Q_{trans}^{molec}\big)^N}{N!}
\begin{aligned}
S_{trans}^{tot} &= Nk\ln Q_{trans}^{mol} - k\ln N! + \frac{3}{2}k_BN \\
&\approx Nk\ln Q_{trans}^{mol} - kN\ln N + kN + \frac{3}{2}k_BN \\
&= Nk\ln\left[\left(\frac{m}{2\pi\beta\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}\frac{Nk_BT}{P}\frac{1}{N}\right] + \frac{5}{2}k_BN
\end{aligned}
\therefore\quad \boxed{\frac{S_{trans}^{tot}}{N} = k_B\ln\left[\left(\frac{m}{2\pi\beta\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}\frac{k_BT}{P}\right] + \frac{5}{2}k_B} \qquad \text{per molecule}
(transcriber’s note: the notes write the last terms as \tfrac{3}{2}k_BT / \tfrac{5}{2}k_BT; for an entropy they should be k_B, as written here)
(iii) Real gases
\mu_{gas}(T,P) = \mu_{gas}(T,P^\circ) + k_BT\ln\left(\frac{f(T,P)}{f(T,P^\circ)}\right)
with fugacities from an equation of state. If P^\circ is 1 bar, use ideal-gas approximations for \mu_{gas}(T,P^\circ).
Examples: bulk stability limits
① H* on Ni(111). Bulk stability limit: \mathrm{Ni(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NiH(s)}. Quasi-equilibrium: \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{H_2(g)} + * \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^*, so \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2(g)} = \mu_{H^*}.
\Delta G_{molar} = \mu_{NiH} - \frac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2} - \mu_{Ni}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\Delta G_{molar} = \mu_{NiH} - \mu_H - \mu_{Ni}}
For \Delta G > 0: \;\boxed{\mu_H < \mu_{NiH(bulk)} - \mu_{Ni(bulk)}}\;, and with DFT, \mu_{bulk} \approx E_{DFT,bulk}.
② CO oxidation on RuO₂(110). \mathrm{CO(g)} \not\rightleftharpoons \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} — assume gas-phase equilibrium is not achieved; CO adsorbs as CO* and O₂ as O* (sketch). Then \mu_{CO(g)} \approx \mu_{CO^*} and \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{O_2(g)} \approx \mu_{O^*}.
Bulk stability: \mathrm{Ru(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{RuO_2(s)}
\Delta G = \mu_{RuO_2} - \mu_{O_2(g)} - \mu_{Ru} < 0
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\frac{1}{2}\mu_{O_2(g)} = \mu_{O^*} > \frac{1}{2}\big(\mu_{RuO_2(s)} - \mu_{Ru(s)}\big)}
Zeolites
Bulk zeolites are not equilibrium structures (bulk SiO₂(s) is the equilibrium phase); they are metastable → decay at high temperature.
↳ True excess quantities are not useful ⇓
\boxed{\gamma = \frac{U_{cell} - TS - \sum_i\mu_iN_i - U_{clean}}{A}}
— not a true interfacial free energy. U_{cell} = DFT energy (includes adsorbates); S = entropy in zeolites; U_{clean} = DFT energy of the clean zeolite; A = area in pores.

U_{cell} and U_{clean} are taken from DFT energies + thermal corrections (as before).
\mu_i are evaluated similarly, unless significant mass-transport barriers exist.
Entropy effects are similar (see upcoming lecture).
No point in estimating bulk stability ranges.
If pores have a wetting / non-wetting transition, both energies and entropies are best evaluated using ab-initio molecular dynamics.

Dealing with nanoparticles
We need to know what the surface looks like.
1) Simple case: surface energy in a vacuum
\gamma = \left(U^{xs} - TS^{xs} - \sum_i\mu_iN_i^{xs}\right)\frac{1}{A}\;;\qquad U^{xs} = U_{surf,DFT} - \sum_{metal}\mu_{metal,bulk}N_{metal,DFT}
For an ordered surface, N_{metal}^{xs} \approx 0 and TS^{xs} \to 0:
\therefore\quad \gamma = \frac{1}{A}\Big(U_{surf,DFT} - \sum\mu_{metal}N_{metal}\Big)\qquad (N_{metal} = \text{total})
Typically \mu_{metal} = g_{metal} \approx e_{DFT,metal}^{bulk} = the DFT energy per bulk metal atom.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 10 (Wulff & Langmuir)
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 31-35) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Surface thermodynamics / free energy
\gamma = \frac{1}{A}\Big(U_{DFT} - \underbrace{TS_{excess}}_{\approx\,0 \text{ (first approx.)}} - \sum\mu_{metal}N_{metal,slab}\Big)\;;\qquad \mu_{metal} = g_{metal,bulk} \approx e_{DFT,bulk}
(\gamma = free energy change per area.)
Approach: calculate \gamma‘s for different surfaces [(111), (100), (110), …] → the goal is to figure out which surfaces are present at equilibrium for a catalyst nanoparticle.
Wulff theorem
The distance from the center of the NP to a given facet is proportional to the energy of that facet.
Sketch (2D): facets along 10, 01, \bar{1}0, 0\bar{1} with \gamma_{10} = 1 and along 11-type directions with \gamma_{11} = 3/4 (by symmetry \gamma_{10} = \gamma_{01} = \gamma_{\bar{1}0} = \gamma_{0\bar{1}}, \gamma_{11} = \gamma_{1\bar{1}} = \dots). The inner envelope of the facet planes is the equilibrium shape of the NP (edges are the surfaces). Ref: Scholl book, Ch. 2, 4.4.
→ It doesn’t say anything about how the particles are formed.
”Proof”
G = \sum_i\gamma_iA_i\;\;(\text{over facets})\;;\qquad \text{constant } V \rightarrow \text{constant bulk energy}
Constraint: V = \sum_i\tfrac{1}{3}h_iA_i (a sum of a series of cones; h_i = distance from facet i to the center of the NP).
Lagrangian functional:
F = G - \lambda\left(\sum\tfrac{1}{3}h_iA_i - V\right)
\delta F = \delta G - \lambda\,\delta\Big(\sum\tfrac{1}{3}h_iA_i\Big) = \delta\Big[\gamma_iA_i - \lambda\tfrac{1}{3}\sum h_iA_i\Big] = \sum\delta\Big[\gamma_iA_i - \tfrac{1}{3}\lambda h_iA_i\Big] = 0
If the A_i can be varied independently, each term is zero:
\therefore\quad \gamma_iA_i = \frac{1}{3}\lambda h_iA_i \;\Rightarrow\; h_i = \frac{3\gamma_i}{\lambda}\;;\qquad \text{from the constraint: } \lambda = \frac{\sum_iA_i\gamma_i}{V}
\boxed{h_i = \frac{3V}{\sum_jA_j\gamma_j}\gamma_i} \qquad \bigstar\;\; h_i \propto \gamma_i
Not a full proof, since we do not consider directions.
Generalizing Wulff to supports and adsorbates
1) Supports. Start with a suspended NP (facets a_1, a_2, b, c) above a support of area A_s.
No interaction:
\Omega = 2\gamma_aA_a + 2\gamma_bA_b + 2\gamma_cA_c + \underbrace{A_s\gamma_s}_{\text{constant}}
\qquad
\Omega - \gamma_sA_s = \underbrace{2\gamma_aA_a + 2\gamma_bA_b + 2\gamma_cA_c}_{\text{standard Wulff construction}}
(so we get the same shape as the unsupported case).
Interaction (facet a_2 sits on the support over area A_{int}):
\Omega = A_{a_1}\gamma_{a_1} + A_{a_2}\gamma_{a_2} + 2\gamma_bA_b + 2\gamma_cA_c + \gamma_{int}A_{int} + \gamma_s(A_s - A_{int})
\Omega - A_s\gamma_s = \gamma_{a_1}A_{a_1} + \gamma_{a_2}A_{a_2} + 2\gamma_bA_b + 2\gamma_cA_c + A_{int}(\gamma_{int} - \gamma_s)
Excess quantities at the interface (total quantities in the calculation):
\gamma_{int}A_{int} = E_{int} - TS - \sum\mu_iN_i \approx E_{int}^{DFT} - \mu_sN_s^{DFT}\,(\text{support}) - \mu_mN_m^{DFT}\;\;(m = a_2)
Freestanding surfaces:
A_{int}\gamma_s = E_s^{DFT} - \mu_sN_s^{DFT}\;;\qquad A_{int}\gamma_m = E_m^{DFT} - \mu_mN_{m(a_2)}^{DFT}
\Rightarrow\; A_{int}\big(\gamma_{int} - \gamma_{m,a_2} - \gamma_s\big) = E_{int}^{DFT} - E_s^{DFT} - E_m^{DFT} = \text{adhesion energy}
\Omega - A_s\gamma_s = \underbrace{\gamma_{a_1}A_{a_1} + 2\gamma_cA_c + 2\gamma_bA_b + A_{int}\left(\gamma_{m,a_2} + \frac{\Delta E_{adh}}{A_{int}}\right)}_{\text{Wulff theorem}}
Effectively, replace \gamma_{m,a_2} with \gamma_{m,a_2} + \dfrac{\Delta E_{adh}}{A_{int}}.
e.g. (sketches): \Delta E_{adh} < 0 → the particle spreads (flatter) on the support; \Delta E_{adh} > 0 → de-wetting (the particle balls up).
2) Adsorbates — “easy”: just replace \gamma_{m,vacuum} with \gamma calculated from an ab-initio phase diagram:
\gamma(\theta_i) \rightarrow \gamma(\mu_i) \rightarrow \gamma(T, P_i)
e.g. strong adsorption on one facet grows that facet (sketch) → re-optimizing the shape of the NP depending on T, P. Assumption → the NP is at equilibrium.


                  
                  Why does the equilibrium shape still have high-energy facets? 
                  
                

The volume constraint! We need other facets, or else the particle would have a higher bulk free energy → penalized.


Isotherm development

Pros: DFT calcs not necessary; better treatment of surface entropies.
Cons: must parameterize surface energies and adsorption energies.

① Langmuir isotherm (the classic isotherm)
Key assumptions:

no interaction between adsorbates
uniform surface sites (each can be occupied or unoccupied)
constant adsorption energies

Minimize \Omega (grand potential) for given values of \mu and T: \Omega(\mu, T, N_s)
\Omega = U - TS - \mu N = -k_BT\ln\Xi
\qquad
\Xi = \sum_je^{-\beta(E_j - \mu N_j)} = \sum_je^{-\beta[\varepsilon(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \dots + \sigma_{N_s}) - \mu(\sigma_1 + \sigma_2 + \dots + \sigma_{N_s})]}
(\Xi = grand canonical partition function, \varepsilon = binding energy of 1 molecule, N_s = total sites, \sigma_i = 0 unoccupied / 1 occupied, so \sum_i^{N_s}\sigma_i = N.)
\therefore\quad \Xi = \sum_{\sigma_1=0}^{1}e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)\sigma_1}\sum_{\sigma_2=0}^{1}e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)\sigma_2}\cdots\sum_{\sigma_{N_s}=0}^{1}e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)\sigma_{N_s}}
= \prod_{i=1}^{N_s}\sum_{\sigma=0}^{1}e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)\sigma}
= \prod_{i=1}^{N_s}\left(1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\right)
\boxed{\Xi = \left[1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\right]^{N_s}}
\therefore\quad \Omega = -k_BTN_s\ln\left(1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\right)
\qquad
\langle N\rangle = -\frac{\partial\Omega}{\partial\mu} = \frac{e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}\cdot N_s
\therefore\quad \boxed{\frac{\langle N\rangle}{N_s} = \theta = \frac{e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}}
If the surface is in equilibrium with an ideal gas, \mu = \mu_{gas} = \mu_{gas}^\circ + k_BT\ln(P/P^\circ):
\boxed{\theta = \frac{\frac{P}{P^\circ}e^{-\beta(\varepsilon - \mu^\circ)}}{1 + \frac{P}{P^\circ}e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu^\circ)}}}


                  
                  Note 
                  
                

This assumes that S is only configurational entropy. \varepsilon can be replaced with a surface free energy without losing generality:
\varepsilon \rightarrow \varepsilon + \text{ZPE} + \text{thermal vibrations} - TS_{loc}^\circ \approx \mu_{surf}^\circ
where S_{loc}^\circ is the local (not configurational) entropy.


\therefore\quad \boxed{\theta = \frac{\frac{P}{P^\circ}e^{-\beta\Delta\mu^\circ}}{1 + \frac{P}{P^\circ}e^{-\beta\Delta\mu^\circ}}}

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 36-37) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



① Langmuir (recap)
\frac{\langle N\rangle}{N_s} = \theta = \frac{e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}
Ignores interactions. Sketch: \theta vs \log(P/P^\circ) \sim \mu, rising from 0 to 1. With \Delta\mu^\circ = 0 and \beta \gg 1 the step is sharp; with \Delta\mu^\circ > 0 or \beta < 1 (high T) the curve is broader / shifted.
② Interactions between adsorbates

Use the Ising isotherm: assume interactions have a constant value and only exist between nearest neighbors.
We can analyze it analytically in 1D:

E = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}J}_{\text{interaction}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\sigma_i}_{\text{Langmuir part}}\;;\qquad \sigma_i = 0, 1 \text{ (unoccupied or occupied)}
J = interaction (a constant; J < 0 → attraction).
As before:
\begin{aligned}
\Xi(\mu, T, N_s) &= \sum_{j,\,\text{states}}e^{-\beta(E_j - \mu N_j)} = \sum_{N=0}^{N_s}\;\sum_{\substack{\text{states}\\\text{with } N}}e^{-\beta E + \beta\mu N} \qquad (N = \text{total adsorbates on surface}) \\
&= \sum_{N=0}^{N_s}\sum e^{-\beta\left[\sum_i^{N_s}(\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}J + \varepsilon\sigma_i - \mu\sigma_i)\right]}\;;\qquad \sum\sigma_i = N
\end{aligned}
Writing it as a nested sum:
\Xi = \sum_{\sigma_1=0}^{1}\sum_{\sigma_2=0}^{1}\cdots\sum_{\sigma_{N_s}=0}^{1}e^{-\beta\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N_s}\left(\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}J + \frac{\sigma_i + \sigma_{i+1}}{2}(\varepsilon-\mu)\right)\right]}
Introduce the transfer matrix (for a lattice statistical mechanics problem; symmetric matrices are diagonalizable):
P = \begin{bmatrix}P_{00} & P_{01} \\ P_{10} & P_{11}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1 & e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(\varepsilon-\mu)} \\ e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(\varepsilon-\mu)} & e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)}\end{bmatrix}
\Xi = \sum_{\sigma_1=0}^{1}\sum_{\sigma_2=0}^{1}\cdots\sum_{\sigma_{N_s}=0}^{1}\langle\sigma_1|P|\sigma_2\rangle\langle\sigma_2|P|\sigma_3\rangle\cdots\langle\sigma_{N_s}|P|\sigma_1\rangle
(periodic BCs), where \sigma_i = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix} if site i is unoccupied and \sigma_i = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix} if it is occupied.
E.g. N_s = 2: \Xi = P_{00}P_{00} + P_{01}P_{10} + P_{10}P_{01} + P_{11}P_{11} (with P_{01} = P_{10}; P_{00} = element (0,0) of P) — the sum of the eigenvalues of the matrix P\cdot P = P^2.
In general, \Xi = largest eigenvalue of P^{N_s} (P^{N_s} = P\cdot P\cdot P\cdots, N_s times) = (\text{eigenvalue of } P)^{N_s}:
\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda & e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(\varepsilon-\mu)} \\ e^{-\frac{\beta}{2}(\varepsilon-\mu)} & e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)} - \lambda\end{vmatrix} = 0
\;;\qquad
\Xi \approx \lambda_+^{N_s} = \left[\frac{1 + e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)} + \sqrt{\big(1 + e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)}\big)^2 - 4\big(e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)} - e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\big)}}{2}\right]^{N_s}
(\lambda_+ = largest eigenvalue.)
\langle N\rangle = -\frac{\partial\Omega}{\partial\mu} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\mu}\big(k_BT\ln\Xi\big)
\therefore\quad \frac{\langle N\rangle}{N_s} = \theta = \frac{e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)} + \dfrac{-e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)} + e^{-2\beta(\varepsilon+J-\mu)} + 2e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{\Big[\big(1 - e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)}\big)^2 + 4e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\Big]^{1/2}}}{1 + e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)} + \Big[\big(1 - e^{-\beta(J+\varepsilon-\mu)}\big)^2 + 4e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\Big]^{1/2}}
If J = 0: \;\theta = \dfrac{e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}} (Langmuir).
If |\beta J| \ll 1:
\boxed{\theta \approx \frac{e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}\left[1 - \frac{2e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}}{\big(1 + e^{-\beta(\varepsilon-\mu)}\big)^2}\beta J\right]}

In 2D, a partial analytical solution exists for \theta = \tfrac{1}{2} (Onsager, 1942).
For more complex interactions, use cluster-expansion methods (power series) or machine-learning potentials. (Term project idea: different interactions.)

How interactions reshape isotherms
Sketch: \theta vs \log(P/P^\circ) for \beta J = -5 and \beta J = 8 (\beta J is of order kT).

Strong attraction (\beta J = -5): islanding behaviour — an S-shape (phase separation), jumping from \theta = 0 to 1 with a very small change in P.
Strong repulsion (\beta J = 8): two Langmuir isotherms → bimodal Langmuir behaviour:

at low pressure → empty / vacant sites;
as P\uparrow → sites fill randomly, with no nearest neighbors;
at \theta = 0.5 → the maximum number of adsorbates with no nearest neighbors (alternate filling, ○●○●○●), giving a plateau;
we then have to increase P by a tremendous amount to get more populated sites → a second Langmuir isotherm (i.e. you basically have two different sites).


For the 2D case, binding starts to minimize repulsion (i.e. \beta J will increase by a factor of 4 for a site surrounded by 4 neighbors).
Given any surface, you can intuitively get the shape / plateaus for adsorption.
The definition of a monolayer can differ depending on how you define what the surface sites are (and how many bonds they make).
H₂O adsorption on electrodes? ↳ quite attractive (H-bonding) ↳ complex structure.

Kinetics with DFT — roadmap

Discuss TST and calculating k‘s from DFT data
Review the basic principles of microkinetic modelling
Scaling relationships, BEP relations, volcano plots, trends in catalytic properties

Transition state theory (TST)
A strategy for estimating rate constants from DFT (or experimental) results.
Elementary surface reaction: \mathrm{A^* + B^* \rightleftharpoons C^* + *} (sketch: energy vs reaction coordinate from \mathrm{A^*+B^*} over the barrier [\mathrm{A^*\cdots B^*}]^\ddagger to \mathrm{C^* + *}; can be endo- or exothermic).
Two key assumptions:

To a first-order perturbation, reactants are in (quasi-)equilibrium with the TS (or else there would be no rate if exactly at equilibrium; sketch of forward/back rates across \delta r).
The rate of conversion of the TS to products is governed by an attempt frequency \nu (the vibrational frequency that dictates how it “vibrates” away from the TS).

(i)
K^\ddagger = e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT} = \frac{a_{TS}}{a_{A^*}a_{B^*}}\;;\qquad \Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger} = \mu_{TS}^\circ - \mu_{A^*}^\circ - \mu_{B^*}^\circ
(\mu^{\circ\ddagger} = standard-state chemical potential for the transition state.)
Recall: \mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + k_BT\ln a_i; a_i = f_i/f_i^\circ; \mu_i^\circ depends on T.

(a) Ideal gases: a_i = P_i/P^\circ
(b) Liquid species: a_i \approx 1 if concentrated (usually the solvent); a_i \approx C_A/C_A^* if i is dilute (C_A^* = infinitely dilute solute extrapolated to 1 M, cf. Henry’s law)
(c) Surface species: use partition functions and divide into a purely local part and a configurational part. Note: a_{A^*} \approx \theta_A (this usually gives the right answer but is not that rigorous).

Assume non-interacting adsorbates on a lattice of N_s sites, with adsorption energy \varepsilon for each adsorbate. Each adsorbate has a local energy characterized by q_{loc} (vibration, rotation). Canonical:
Q_{tot}(T, N_s, N) = \frac{N_s!}{(N_s - N)!\,N!}\left(e^{-\beta\varepsilon}q_{loc}\right)^N\;;\qquad F = -k_BT\ln Q_{tot}\;\;(\text{extensive})
\begin{aligned}
\ln Q_{tot} &= -\beta\varepsilon N + N\ln q_{loc} + \ln N_s! - \ln(N_s - N)! - \ln N!\;;\qquad \ln x! \approx x\ln x - x \\
&= N_s\ln\left(\frac{N_s}{N_s - N}\right) + N\ln\left(\frac{N_s - N}{N}\right) - \beta\varepsilon N + N\ln q_{loc}
\end{aligned}
F = -k_BT\ln Q\;,\qquad \mu = \left.\frac{\partial F}{\partial N}\right|_{T,N_s} = \underbrace{\varepsilon - k_BT\ln q_{loc}}_{\substack{\text{adsorption free energy}\\\text{for an isolated molecule}}} + \underbrace{k_BT\ln\frac{\theta}{1-\theta}}_{\substack{\text{differential}\\\text{configurational entropy}}}\;;\qquad \theta = \frac{N}{N_s}
(the only approximation is that they are non-interacting).
If more than one adsorbate is present:
\mu_i = \varepsilon_i - k_BT\ln q_{loc,i} + k_BT\ln\frac{\theta_i}{\theta_*}\;;\qquad \theta_* = 1 - \theta_A - \theta_B - \theta_C - \dots
We say that \mu_i^\circ = \varepsilon_i - k_BT\ln q_{loc,i} and a_i = \theta_i/\theta_*. Standard state: an isolated molecule with no configurational entropy.
↳ For the reaction \mathrm{A^* + B^* \xrightarrow{TS} C^* + *}:
K^\ddagger = \frac{a_{TS^*}}{a_{A^*}a_{B^*}} = \frac{\theta_{TS}\,\theta_*}{\theta_A\,\theta_B}\;;\qquad \ln K^\ddagger = -\frac{\mu_{TS}^\circ - \mu_{A^*}^\circ - \mu_{B^*}^\circ}{k_BT}
Second assumption: r \approx \nu\,\theta_{TS}\,\theta_* (assumes a monodentate TS, Langmuir–Hinshelwood)
\therefore\quad r = \nu K^\ddagger\theta_A\theta_B = \underbrace{\nu e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}}_{\text{what about these?}}\theta_A\theta_B \qquad (\text{law of mass action})
For particles on the surface:
\mu_i^\circ = \varepsilon_i - k_BT\ln q_{loc} = -k_BT\ln e^{-\beta\varepsilon_i} - k_BT\ln q_{loc} = -k_BT\ln\Big[\underbrace{q_{loc,i}\,e^{-\varepsilon_i/k_BT}}_{q_i \text{ (local kinetic and potential energies)}}\Big]
\therefore\quad \mu_i^\circ = -k_BT\ln q_i
\;\hookrightarrow\;
\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger} = \mu_{TS}^\circ - \mu_{A^*}^\circ - \mu_{B^*}^\circ = -k_BT\ln\left(\frac{q_{TS}}{q_{A^*}q_{B^*}}\right)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\boxed{r \approx \nu\frac{q^\ddagger}{q_{A^*}q_{B^*}}\theta_A\theta_B}\;,\quad q^\ddagger = q_{TS}
To find \nu, write the q_i‘s as (assuming only harmonic — parabolic energy potential — vibrational modes; E_{DFT} is like \varepsilon):
q_i = \sum e^{-\beta E_{vib,i}} = e^{-\beta E_{DFT,i}}\,q_{vib,i} = e^{-\beta E_{DFT,i}}\,e^{-\beta(\text{ZPE})_i}\prod_{j=1}^{3N}\left(\frac{1}{1 - e^{-h\nu_j/k_BT}}\right)
For mode j along the reaction coordinate (\mathrm{A^*\cdots B^*}): sketch — at the TS the energy is a maximum along the reaction coordinate, and the back-and-forth motion there is the attempt to cross. It is generally assumed we can treat this as a curvature of zero, but the attempt frequency is accurate:
\frac{1}{1 - e^{-h\nu_j/k_BT}} \approx \frac{k_BT}{h\nu_j}
\qquad\therefore\quad
q^\ddagger = e^{-\beta E_{TS}^{DFT}}\,\underbrace{q_{vib}^\times}_{\substack{\text{all modes except}\\\text{rxn coord.}}}\,\frac{k_BT}{h\nu_j}
r \approx \frac{\nu\frac{k_BT}{h\nu_j}e^{-\beta E_{TS,DFT}}\,q_{vib,TS}^\times}{e^{-\beta E_{A^*,DFT}}\,e^{-\beta E_{B^*,DFT}}\,q_{vib,A^*}\,q_{vib,B^*}}\;;\qquad \text{if } \nu = \nu_j:\quad
\boxed{r = \frac{k_BT}{h}\frac{q_{vib,TS}^\times}{q_{A^*,vib}\,q_{B^*,vib}}e^{-\beta\Delta E_a^{tot}}\theta_A\theta_B}
(the q_{vib} here do not include the ZPE; \Delta E_a^{tot} includes the potential energy and the \DeltaZPE.)
This can be written as
r = \nu e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}\theta_A\theta_B = \nu\frac{k_BT}{h\nu}e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}\theta_A\theta_B
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{r = \underbrace{\frac{k_BT}{h}e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}}_{k \text{ (rate constant)}}\theta_A\theta_B}
(Typed note in the original: Rate is proportional to the coverage of TS on substrate.)
TST with gaseous species
\mathrm{A(g) + B^* \xrightarrow{TS^*} C^*} (treat the TS as a surface species, which is often a good assumption):
K^\ddagger = \frac{a_{TS^*}}{a_Aa_{B^*}} = \frac{\theta_{TS}/\theta_*}{\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\frac{\theta_B}{\theta_*}} \;\Rightarrow\; \theta_{TS} = K^\ddagger\theta_B\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}
Thus,
r \approx \nu\theta_{TS} = \nu K^\ddagger\theta_B\frac{P_A}{P^\circ} = \frac{k_BT}{h}K^\ddagger\theta_B\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}
where K^\ddagger now does not include the reaction coordinate.
