                  Announcement 
                  
                

Thursday midterm — 2 questions, open book?


TST for gas–solid reactions
Eley–Rideal: \mathrm{A(g) + B^* \xrightarrow{TS} C^*}. Assuming the TS is close to the surface (adsorbed):
\Rightarrow\; K^\ddagger = \frac{a_{TS^*}}{a_Aa_{B^*}} = \frac{\theta_{TS}/\theta_*}{\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\frac{\theta_B}{\theta_*}} = \frac{\theta_{TS}}{\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_B}
\qquad
\theta_{TS} = K^\ddagger\theta_B\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\;\;(\text{only 1 adsorbed species})
TST assumption (rate proportional to the coverage of the TS):
r = \nu\theta_{TS} = \nu K^\ddagger\theta_B\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{r = \frac{k_BT}{h}K^\ddagger\theta_B\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}}\;\;(K^\ddagger \text{ has no reaction coordinate})
K^\ddagger = e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}\;,\quad \text{where } \Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger} = \mu^{\circ\ddagger} - \mu_{A(g)}^\circ - \mu_{B^*}^\circ
\begin{aligned}
\mu^{\circ\ddagger} &= -k_BT\ln q_{vib,TS}^\circ\cdot e^{-\beta(E_{DFT,TS} + ZPE_{TS})} \qquad (\text{adsorbed TS}) \\
\mu_{B^*}^\circ &= -k_BT\ln q_{vib,B^*}^\circ\cdot e^{-\beta(E_{DFT,B^*} + ZPE_{B^*})} \\
\mu_A^\circ &= -k_BT\frac{\partial}{\partial N_{A(g)}}\Big[\ln\Big\{Q_{trans,A}\,q_{vib,A}^{N_A}\,q_{rot,A}^{N_A}\,e^{-\beta N_A(E_{DFT,A} + ZPE_A)}\Big\}\Big] \\
&= -k_BT\ln q_{vib,A}^\circ - k_BT\ln q_{rot,A}^\circ - k_BT\frac{\partial}{\partial N_A}\big(\ln Q_{trans,A}^\circ\big) + E_{DFT,A} + ZPE_A
\end{aligned}
\therefore\quad K^\ddagger = \frac{q_{vib,TS^*}}{q_{vib,B^*}^\circ\,q_{vib,A}^\circ\,q_{rot,A}^\circ\,e^{\frac{\partial}{\partial N_A}\ln Q_{trans,A}^\circ}}\cdot e^{-\beta(\Delta E_{DFT} + \Delta E_{ZPE})}
where \Delta E_{DFT} + \Delta E_{ZPE} is the activation energy. With Q_{trans}^\circ = \dfrac{(q_{trans}^\circ)^N}{N!}, \;e^{\frac{\partial\ln Q_{trans,A}^\circ}{\partial N_A}} = \left(\dfrac{q_{trans,A}^\circ}{N}\right):
\boxed{r = \frac{k_BT}{h}\frac{q_{vib,TS^*}^\circ}{q_{vib,B^*}^\circ\,q_{vib,A}^\circ\,q_{rot,A}^\circ\left(\frac{q_{trans,A}^\circ}{N}\right)}e^{-\beta(\Delta E + \Delta E_{ZPE})}\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_B}


                  
                  Notes 
                  
                


All q_{vib}‘s have the ZPE part removed.
q^\circ for the vib/rot partition functions is that of the isolated species (gas or surface).
P^\circ is often lumped into the rate constant (careful of units).
q_{electronic} is part of the E_{DFT} expression.



Alternate TST without statistical mechanics
In general (K^\ddagger with no reaction coordinate):
k = \frac{k_BT}{h}e^{-\Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}\;;\qquad \Delta\mu^{\circ\ddagger} = \Delta\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial N_i}\right)^{\circ\ddagger} = \Delta\frac{\partial}{\partial N_i}\big(U_i - TS_i\big) = \Delta\bar{U}^{\circ\ddagger} - T\Delta\bar{S}^{\circ\ddagger}
(partial molar quantities)
\boxed{k = \frac{k_BT}{h}e^{\Delta\bar{S}^{\circ\ddagger}/k_B}\cdot e^{-\Delta\bar{U}^{\ddagger}/k_BT}}
For pure species (e.g. at partial pressure P_i) or non-interacting surface species, the partial molar quantity is the same as the “normal” molar quantity.
Many ways to calculate \bar{S}^\circ:

experimental values
stat. mech.
correlations (for surface species)
\Delta S^{\circ\ddagger} \approx 0 (if the reaction is entirely on the surface)

Example: dissociative adsorption (\mathrm{AB \rightarrow A^* + B^*}, sketch)

Simple assumption: S_{TS}^\circ \approx 0, thus \Delta S^{\circ\ddagger} = S_{TS}^\circ - S_{AB(g)}^\circ \approx -S_{AB(g)}^\circ (from thermo tables), and

k = \frac{k_BT}{hP^\circ}e^{-S_{AB}^\circ/k_B}\,e^{-\Delta U^{\circ\ddagger}/k_BT}
Collision theory
(Rates of adsorption/desorption of ideal gases without dissociation.)
Kinetic theory of gases — the flux of molecules hitting a surface:
\text{flux} = \frac{P_i}{\sqrt{2\pi mk_BT}}\quad\left[\frac{1}{\text{m}^2\cdot\text{s}}\right]
On a per-site basis (\rho = sites/area, or n_s):
\boxed{k_{ads}^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi mk_BT}\cdot\rho}}
↳ If adsorption is activated, add a Boltzmann factor and scale by the number of vacant sites:
\boxed{k = k_{ads}^\circ\,e^{-\Delta E^{ads\ddagger}/k_BT}\;;\qquad r_{ads} = kP_i\theta_*^n\;;\;\; n = 1 \text{ (simple adsorption) or } 2 \text{ (dissociative adsorption)}}
↳ Same expression from TST: assume the TS is a 2D ideal gas; calculate the rate from a 3D to a 2D gas. Partition functions:
Q_{2D} = \frac{q_{2D}^N}{N!} = \left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}A\right)^N\frac{1}{N!}\;;\qquad \ln Q_{2D} = N\ln\left[\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}A\right] - N\ln N + N
Q_{3D} = \frac{q_{3D}^N}{N!} = \left[\left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}V\right]^N\frac{1}{N!}\;;\qquad \ln Q_{3D} = N\ln\left[\left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}V\right] - N\ln N + N
F_{2D} = -k_BT\ln Q_{2D}\;;\quad \mu_{2D}^{(TS)} = \frac{\partial F_{2D}}{\partial N} = -k_BT\left[\ln\left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}A\right) - \ln N\right]
F_{3D} = -k_BT\ln Q_{3D}\;;\quad \mu_{3D} = \frac{\partial F_{3D}}{\partial N} = -k_BT\left[\ln\left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}V - \ln N\right]
At quasi-equilibrium, \mu_{2D}^{TS} = \mu_{3D}:
\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\frac{A}{N_{2D}} = \left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}\frac{V}{N_{3D}}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\left(\frac{N}{A}\right)_{2D} = \frac{P}{k_BT}\sqrt{\frac{h^2}{2\pi mk_BT}}
From TST:
r = \nu\left(\frac{N}{A}\right)_{2D} = \frac{k_BT}{h}\left(\frac{N}{A}\right)_{2D} = \frac{P}{\sqrt{2\pi mk_BT}}
\qquad\text{So,}\qquad
\boxed{k_{ads}^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi mk_BT}\,\rho}} \;\;\text{— same as collision theory}
Thermodynamic consistency of rate constants
We seek to relate kinetic and thermodynamic parameters for elementary reactions.
E.g. \mathrm{A(g) + B^* \rightleftharpoons C^*}. At equilibrium,
K = \frac{a_{C^*}}{a_Aa_{B^*}} = \frac{\theta_C}{\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_B}\qquad\text{and}\qquad r_f = r_r\;(r_{net} = 0)
k_fP_A\theta_B = k_r\theta_C \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{k_f}{k_r} = \frac{\theta_C}{P_A\theta_B}
\;\;\therefore\;\; \frac{\theta_C}{\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_B} = \frac{k_fP^\circ}{k_r} = K
\;\;\therefore\;\; \boxed{k_r = \frac{k_fP^\circ}{K}}
Microkinetics
↳ Overview (Langmuir–Hinshelwood). Consider the reaction mechanism:

\mathrm{A_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2A^*} (might be QE)
\mathrm{B_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2B^*} (might be QE)
\mathrm{A^* + B^* \rightleftharpoons AB^* + *}
\mathrm{AB^* + B^* \rightleftharpoons AB_2^* + *}
\mathrm{AB(g) + * \rightleftharpoons AB^*} (simple adsorption)
\mathrm{AB_2(g) + * \rightleftharpoons AB_2^*} (simple adsorption)

Mole balances for each adsorbed species (rates must be in s⁻¹ — turnover frequencies; the r‘s are net rates and can be < 0):
\mathrm{A^*}: \frac{d\theta_A}{dt} = 2r_1 - r_3\;;\quad
\mathrm{B^*}: \frac{d\theta_B}{dt} = 2r_2 - r_3 - r_4\;;\quad
\mathrm{AB^*}: \frac{d\theta_{AB}}{dt} = r_3 - r_4 + r_5\;;\quad
\mathrm{AB_2^*}: \frac{d\theta_{AB_2}}{dt} = r_4 + r_6
At steady state, d\theta_i/dt = 0 \Rightarrow
2r_1 - r_3 = 0\;;\quad 2r_2 - r_3 - r_4 = 0\;;\quad r_3 - r_4 + r_5 = 0\;;\quad r_4 + r_6 = 0
Express in terms of the product rates r_5 and r_6 ⇓
r_4 = -r_6\;;\quad r_3 = -r_5 - r_6\;;\quad r_2 = -\tfrac{1}{2}r_5 - r_6\;;\quad r_1 = -\tfrac{1}{2}r_5 - \tfrac{1}{2}r_6
Two linearly independent rates [6 unknowns, 4 equations] ⇒ we need additional information (use TST-like rate expressions):
\begin{aligned}
r_1 &= k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2 - k_{-1}\theta_A^2 \\
r_2 &= k_2P_{B_2}\theta_*^2 - k_{-2}\theta_B^2 \\
r_3 &= k_3\theta_A\theta_B - k_{-3}\theta_{AB}\theta_* \\
r_4 &= k_4\theta_{AB}\theta_B - k_{-4}\theta_{AB_2}\theta_* \\
r_5 &= k_5P_{AB}\theta_* - k_{-5}\theta_{AB}
\end{aligned}
(A “Lecture 14” marker is written next to these rate expressions in the original.)
If the k‘s and P_i‘s are known, we have 5 variables: \theta_A, \theta_B, \theta_{AB}, \theta_{AB_2}, \theta_* — 4 equations + \theta_* = 1 - \theta_A - \theta_B - \theta_{AB} - \theta_{AB_2} → 5 equations, 5 unknowns.
Comments:

Solving the equations for the \theta_i‘s gives rigorous rates. We can always do this.
Assumption: L-H kinetics is valid.

More practical: assume some steps are rate-limiting and some are quasi-equilibrated.
↳ E.g. assume 1, 2, 5, 6 are QE (why choose these 4? Simple adsorptions are often QE):
K_1 = \frac{\theta_A^2}{\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\theta_*^2} \;\Rightarrow\; \theta_A = \sqrt{K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}}\,\theta_*
\;;\quad
\theta_B = \sqrt{K_2\frac{P_{B_2}}{P^\circ}}\,\theta_*\;,\quad \theta_{AB} = K_5\frac{P_{AB}}{P^\circ}\theta_*\;;\quad \theta_{AB_2} = K_6\frac{P_{AB_2}}{P^\circ}\theta_*
(expressing everything in terms of \theta_*). Then, using the site balance:
\theta_* = \frac{1}{1 + \underbrace{\sqrt{K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}}}_{A^*} + \underbrace{\sqrt{K_2\frac{P_{B_2}}{P^\circ}}}_{B^*} + \underbrace{K_5\frac{P_{AB}}{P^\circ}}_{AB^*} + \underbrace{K_6\frac{P_{AB_2}}{P^\circ}}_{AB_2^*}}
Finally, substitute into the r‘s that are not QE:
r_3 = k_3\sqrt{K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}}\sqrt{K_2\frac{P_{B_2}}{P^\circ}}\,\theta_*^2 - k_{-3}K_5\frac{P_{AB}}{P^\circ}\theta_*^2
\qquad
r_4 = k_4\sqrt{K_2\frac{P_{B_2}}{P^\circ}}K_5\frac{P_{AB}}{P^\circ}\theta_*^2 - k_{-4}K_6\frac{P_{AB_2}}{P^\circ}\theta_*^2
Product production rates: r_{AB(g)} = -r_5 = r_3 - r_4; \;r_{AB_2(g)} = -r_6 = r_4.
Explore a simpler case in more detail

\mathrm{A(g) + * \rightleftharpoons A^*}
\mathrm{A^* \rightleftharpoons B^*}
\mathrm{B(g) + * \rightleftharpoons B^*}

\frac{d\theta_A}{dt} = 0 = r_1 - r_2\;;\qquad \frac{d\theta_B}{dt} = 0 = r_2 + r_3
r_1 = k_1P_A\theta_* - k_{-1}\theta_A\;;\quad r_2 = k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B\;;\quad r_3 = k_3P_B\theta_* - k_{-3}\theta_B\;;\quad \theta_* = 1 - \theta_A - \theta_B
Case 1: (1) and (3) are QE
\theta_A = K_1\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_*\;;\quad \theta_B = K_3\frac{P_B}{P^\circ}\theta_*\;;\quad \theta_* = \frac{1}{1 + K_1\frac{P_A}{P^\circ} + K_3\frac{P_B}{P^\circ}}
r_{B(g)} = -r_3 = r_2 = k_2K_1\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_* - k_{-2}K_3\frac{P_B}{P^\circ}\theta_*
Case 2: (1) is QE
\theta_A = K_1\frac{P_A}{P^\circ}\theta_*; find \theta_B from the stoichiometric SS equation 0 = r_2 + r_3:
k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B = k_{-3}\theta_B - k_3P_B\theta_*
\;\Downarrow\;
\theta_B = \frac{k_2K_1\frac{P_A}{P^\circ} + k_3P_B}{k_{-2} + k_{-3}}\theta_*\;;\qquad \theta_* = 1 - \theta_A - \theta_B
r_{B(g)} = -r_3 = r_2 (either works here — we can use either rate equation since neither is QE).
Case 3: only (3) is QE (exercise)
Case 4: no steps are QE (no assumption about kinetics apart from Langmuir–Hinshelwood)
\begin{aligned}
r_1 = r_2 &\Rightarrow k_1P_A\theta_* - k_{-1}\theta_A = k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B \\
r_2 = -r_3 &\Rightarrow k_2\theta_A - k_{-2}\theta_B = k_{-3}\theta_B - k_3P_B\theta_* \\
\theta_A + \theta_B + \theta_* &= 1
\end{aligned}
(SS balances to get \theta_A, \theta_B.)
\theta_A = \frac{k_1P_A\theta_* + k_{-2}\theta_B}{\underbrace{k_{-1} + k_2}_{\Delta k_a}}\;;\qquad \theta_B = \frac{k_2\theta_A + k_3P_B\theta_*}{\underbrace{k_{-2} + k_{-3}}_{\Delta k_b}}
\theta_B = \frac{k_2}{\Delta k_b}\left[\frac{k_1}{\Delta k_a}P_A\theta_* + \frac{k_{-2}}{\Delta k_a}\theta_B\right] + \frac{k_3}{\Delta k_b}P_B\theta_*
\;;\qquad
\theta_B = \frac{\frac{k_1k_2}{\Delta k_a\Delta k_b}P_A + \frac{k_3}{\Delta k_b}P_B}{1 - \frac{k_2k_{-2}}{\Delta k_a\Delta k_b}}\theta_*
\theta_A = \left[\frac{\frac{k_1k_2k_{-2}}{\Delta k_a^2\Delta k_b}P_A + \frac{k_3k_{-2}}{\Delta k_a\Delta k_b}}{1 - \frac{k_2k_{-2}}{\Delta k_a\Delta k_b}} + \frac{k_1}{\Delta k_a}P_A\right]\theta_*
By taking various asymptotic limits of the k_i‘s, we can explore the meaning of QE.


                  
                  Non-QE = RLS (rate-limiting step) 
                  
                


We can have multiple RLS.
Each step can have a different degree of rate limitation (Campbell score): \sim 0.0001 \rightarrow QE, \;1 \rightarrow RLS.
Q2 on HW.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 14
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 46-48) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Mechanism from the previous lecture (continued on the previous lecture’s notes):

\mathrm{A_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2A^*}
\mathrm{B_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2B^*}
\mathrm{A^* + B^* \rightleftharpoons AB^* + *}
\mathrm{AB^* + B^* \rightleftharpoons AB_2^* + *}
\mathrm{AB(g) + * \rightleftharpoons AB^*}
\mathrm{AB_2(g) + * \rightleftharpoons AB_2^*}

Example: ammonia synthesis
(The heading “Scaling relations” is written here in the original; the worked example is NH₃ synthesis.)

\mathrm{N_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2N^*}
\mathrm{N^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH^* + *} — QE
\mathrm{NH^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH_2^* + *}
\mathrm{NH_2^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + 2*} — QE
\mathrm{H_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2H^*} — QE

These don’t happen in any specific sequence.
2r_1 = r_2\;;\quad r_2 = r_3\;;\quad r_3 = r_4 \qquad\hookrightarrow\qquad 2r_1 = r_3
“Full solution”:
2\left(k_1P_{N_2}\theta_*^2 - k_{-1}\theta_N^2\right) = k_3\theta_{NH}\theta_H - k_{-3}\theta_{NH_2}\theta_*
K_2 = \frac{\theta_{NH}\theta_*}{\theta_N\theta_H}\;;\qquad K_4 = \frac{\theta_*^2\,P_{NH_3}/P^\circ}{\theta_{NH_2}\theta_H}\;;\qquad K_5 = \frac{\theta_H^2}{\theta_*^2\,P_{H_2}/P^\circ}
Limiting analysis
Write P_i' = P_i/P^\circ.
Case 1: (1) is the RLS, (3) is QE
K_3 = \frac{\theta_{NH_2}\theta_*}{\theta_{NH}\theta_H}\;;\qquad r_{ov} = 2r_1 = 2\left(k_1P_{N_2}\theta_*^2 - k_{-1}\theta_N^2\right)
\theta_H = \sqrt{K_5\frac{P_{H_2}}{P^\circ}}\,\theta_*\;;\qquad
\theta_{NH_2} = \frac{P_{NH_3}/P^\circ}{K_4\sqrt{K_5\frac{P_{H_2}}{P^\circ}}}\theta_*
\theta_{NH} = \frac{\theta_{NH_2}}{K_3\sqrt{K_5\frac{P_{H_2}}{P^\circ}}} = \frac{P_{NH_3}/P^\circ}{K_3K_4K_5\frac{P_{H_2}}{P^\circ}}\theta_*\;;\qquad
\theta_N = \frac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_2K_3K_4\left(K_5P_{H_2}'\right)^{3/2}}\theta_*
r = 2k_1P_{N_2}\theta_*^2\left[1 - \frac{k_{-1}}{k_1}\frac{P_{NH_3}^2}{P_{N_2}K_2^2K_3^2K_4^2K_5^3P_{H_2}^3}\right]
\boxed{r_{1,lim} = \frac{2k_1P_{N_2}(1 - \gamma)}{\left(1 + \sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_4\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_3K_4K_5P_{H_2}'} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_2K_3K_4(K_5P_{H_2}')^{3/2}}\right)^2}}
\gamma = \frac{1}{K_1K_2^2K_3^2K_4^2K_5^3}\frac{P_{NH_3}'^{\,2}}{P_{N_2}'P_{H_2}'^{\,3}}\;;\qquad 0 < \gamma < 1
(\gamma is the approach to equilibrium.)
Case 2: (3) is the RLS, (1) is QE
r_{overall} = r_3 = k_3\theta_{NH}\theta_H - k_{-3}\theta_{NH_2}\theta_*\;;\qquad K_1 = \frac{\theta_N^2}{\theta_*^2\frac{P_{N_2}}{P^\circ}} \Rightarrow \theta_N = \sqrt{K_1P_{N_2}'}\,\theta_*
\theta_{NH_2} = \frac{P_{NH_3}'\,\theta_*}{K_4\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}}\;;\qquad \theta_H = \sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}\,\theta_*\;;\qquad \theta_{NH} = K_2\sqrt{K_1P_{N_2}'}\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}\,\theta_*
\boxed{r_{3,lim} = \frac{k_3K_2K_1^{1/2}K_5\sqrt{P_{N_2}'}\,P_{H_2}'\,(1 - \sqrt{\gamma})}{\left(1 + \sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'} + \sqrt{K_1P_{N_2}'} + K_2\sqrt{K_1P_{N_2}'}\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_4\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}}\right)^2}}


                  
                  Principle 
                  
                

Many catalysts follow either the r_{1,lim} or the r_{3,lim} expression.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 15
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 49-52) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF





                  
                  Project topic 
                  
                

HER on Pt(111) → aqueous acidic solution.


Volcano plots for heterogeneous catalysis
Example 1:

\mathrm{A_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2A^*}
\mathrm{A^* + B(g) \rightleftharpoons AB(g) + *}

This is appropriate if \theta_B is small: for \mathrm{B(g) + * \rightarrow B^*}, \theta_* = \dfrac{1}{1 + KP_B/P^\circ + \dots}; if KP_B/P^\circ \ll 1 → we can assume \theta_B is small.
r = r_1 = k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2 - k_{-1}\theta_A^2\;;\qquad K_2 = \frac{\theta_*P_{AB}'}{\theta_AP_B'}
r = k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2 - \frac{k_{-1}}{K_2^2}\left(\frac{P_{AB}'}{P_B'}\right)^2\theta_*^2 = k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2\left(1 - \underbrace{\frac{k_{-1}}{k_1}}_{=\,P^\circ/K_1}\frac{P_{AB}'^{\,2}}{K_2^2P_{A_2}P_B'^{\,2}}\right)
r = k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2\Bigg(1 - \underbrace{\frac{1}{K_1K_2^2}\frac{P_{AB}'^{\,2}}{P_B'^{\,2}P_{A_2}'}}_{\gamma}\Bigg)
\gamma = approach to equilibrium (set by the conditions in the reactor).
Site balance: \theta_* + \theta_A = 1 \Rightarrow \theta_* + \theta_*\dfrac{P_{AB}'}{K_2P_B'} = 1
\boxed{r = \frac{k_1P_{A_2}'(1-\gamma)}{\Big(1 + \underbrace{\sqrt{K_1P_{A_2}'\gamma}}_{A^*}\Big)^2}}
(the denominator reflects the vacant sites), with
K_1 = e^{\Delta S_1^\circ/k_B}\,e^{-\Delta E_1/k_BT}\;\;(\text{ignoring the difference between } H \text{ and } E)\;;\qquad k_1 = \frac{k_{10}}{P^\circ}e^{-\Delta E_{act,1}/k_BT}\;\;(\text{find } k_{10} \text{ from TST})
Energy diagram for (1) (sketch): \mathrm{A_2(g)} → a molecular well \mathrm{A_2^*} → barrier E_{act,1} → \mathrm{2A^*}, with reaction energy \Delta E_1.
If the reaction follows a BEP relation, E_{act,1} = \alpha_1\Delta E_1 + \beta_1:
\ln\left(\frac{r}{k_{10}}\right) = -\frac{\alpha_1\Delta E_1 + \beta_1}{k_BT} + \ln\left(\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\right) + \ln(1-\gamma) - 2\ln\left[1 + \sqrt{e^{\Delta S_1^\circ/k_B}e^{-\Delta E_1/k_BT}\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\gamma}\right]
With the RPBE functional: \alpha_1 = 0.9, \beta_1 = 1.34 eV; P_{A_2}/P^\circ \approx 25; \Delta S_1^\circ = -200 J/(mol·K). We assume everything else is independent of the catalyst surface, i.e. variations in the catalyst are given by \Delta E_1.
Sketch: \ln(r/k_{10}) vs \Delta E_1 (from −5 to 0 eV) — a volcano with its peak near \Delta E_1 \approx -2 for \gamma = 10^{-7}, and a lower volcano peaking near -1 for \gamma = 10^{-2}.

Left branch (reaction becoming more and more exothermic for step 1): the rate decreases → a small number of vacant sites (A is binding very strongly) ↳ \theta_A approaches 1.
Right branch: similarly, from BEP relations E_{act} \propto \Delta E_1 (the activation energy increases).

Observations:

There are two physical processes that limit the rate (even with 1 RLS).
The rate decreases as \gamma \to 1.
The volcano maximum moves to higher \Delta E_1: from r = \dfrac{k_1P_{A_2}(1-\gamma)}{\left(1 + \sqrt{K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\gamma}\right)^2}, as \gamma \to 1 there is more A* on the surface, so the catalyst compensates by weaker binding of A*.
A decrease of P_{A_2} shifts the maximum to stronger binding of A* (to compensate for the reduced \theta_A).
If T\uparrow, the maximum moves to stronger binding (same idea; Langmuir isotherm → decreased A on the surface).

For a given catalyst, there is just one E_r → the volcano plot actually tells you which catalyst would be optimal at the new T, P — also assuming that the RLS is the same across these changing conditions.
Example 2: same idea, but assume \theta_{A_2} is not small

\mathrm{A_2(g) + * \rightleftharpoons A_2^*}
\mathrm{A_2^* + * \rightleftharpoons 2A^*} — RLS
\mathrm{A^* + B(g) \rightleftharpoons AB(g) + *}

r = r_2 = k_2\theta_{A_2}\theta_* - k_{-2}\theta_A^2\;;\qquad K_1 = \frac{\theta_{A_2}}{P_{A_2}'\theta_*}\;;\qquad K_3 = \frac{P_{AB}'\theta_*}{P_B'\theta_A}
\theta_* = \frac{1}{\underbrace{1}_{(*)} + \underbrace{K_1P_{A_2}'}_{(A_2^*)} + \underbrace{\frac{P_{AB}}{P_B}\frac{1}{K_3}}_{(A^*)}}
r = \frac{k_2K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}(1-\gamma)}{\left(1 + K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ} + \sqrt{K_1K_2\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\gamma}\right)^2}\;;\qquad \gamma = \frac{1}{K_1K_2K_3^2}\left(\frac{P_{AB}^2}{P_B^2\,P_{A_2}/P^\circ}\right)
K_1 = e^{\Delta S_1^\circ/k_B}\,e^{-\Delta E_{A_2}/k_BT}\;;\qquad K_2 = e^{0}\,e^{-(-\Delta E_{A_2} + \Delta E_1)/k_BT}\;;\qquad k_2 = k_{20}\,e^{-(\alpha\Delta E_1 + \beta_1 - \Delta E_{A_2})/k_BT}
(sketch: energy diagram with the molecular well \Delta E_{A_2} and the step-2 barrier \alpha\Delta E_1 + \beta — the energy difference for step 2.)
\ln\left(\frac{r}{k_{20}}\right) = -\frac{\alpha_1\Delta E_1 + \beta_1}{k_BT} + \frac{\Delta S_1^\circ}{k_B} + \ln\left(\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\right) + \ln(1-\gamma) - 2\ln\left[1 + K_1\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ} + \sqrt{K_1K_2\frac{P_{A_2}}{P^\circ}\gamma}\right]
With some parameters (\gamma = 10^{-13}), sketch: three volcanoes in \ln(r/k_{10}) vs \Delta E_1 for \Delta E_{A_2} = -2.5, -1.5 and 0, with the maximum shifting as \Delta E_{A_2} changes.


                  
                  Questions 
                  
                


Why does the maximum shift as \Delta E_{A_2} increases?
What happens if \Delta E_1 and \Delta E_{A_2} are correlated?

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 16
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 53-55) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Recall

\mathrm{A_2(g) + * \rightleftharpoons A_2^*} (QE)
\mathrm{A_2^* + * \rightleftharpoons 2A^*} (RLS)
\mathrm{A^* + B(g) \rightleftharpoons AB(g) + *} (QE)

Sketch: \ln r vs \Delta E_1 volcanoes for \Delta E_{A_2} = -2.5, -1.5 and 0 eV, plus the energy diagram (step 2 is the RLS): \mathrm{A_2(g)} → \mathrm{A_2^*} (well depth \Delta E_{A_2^*}) → TS (intrinsic barrier) → \mathrm{2A^*} (\Delta E_1).

Moving \mathrm{A_2^*} will increase the energy of the TS → so \Delta E_1 has to move proportionally down to keep the same barrier.
\mathrm{A_2^*} corresponds to the binding energy → if \mathrm{A_2^*} goes really high up, then the RLS will change.

What if there is more than one rate-controlling step?

\mathrm{A_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2A^*}
\mathrm{A^* + B(g) \rightleftharpoons AB(g) + *}

r_1 = k_1\theta_*^2P_{A_2} - k_{-1}\theta_A^2\;;\qquad r_2 = k_2\theta_AP_B - k_{-2}\theta_*P_{AB}
r_1 = k_1\theta_*^2P_{A_2}(1 - \gamma_1)\;,\;\; \gamma_1 = \frac{\theta_A^2/(\theta_*^2P_{A_2}')}{K_1}\;;\qquad
r_2 = k_2\theta_AP_B(1 - \gamma_2)\;,\;\; \gamma_2 = \frac{\theta_*P_{AB}'/(\theta_AP_B')}{K_2}
\gamma_{overall} = \gamma_1\gamma_2^2
Steady state for A*: 2r_1 = r_2; site balance: \theta_* + \theta_A = 1:
2k_1P_{A_2}(1-\theta_A)^2 - 2k_{-1}\theta_A^2 = k_2\theta_AP_B - k_{-2}P_{AB}(1-\theta_A)
\qquad(\text{quadratic in } \theta_A)
\theta_A = \frac{\dfrac{1 + \frac{k_{-2}P_{AB}}{4k_1P_{A_2}}\left(1 + K_2\frac{P_B}{P_{AB}}\right)}{1 - \frac{1}{K_1P_{A_2}'}}}{}\left[1 - \sqrt{1 - \left(1 - \frac{1}{K_1P_{A_2}}\right)\frac{\left(1 + \frac{k_{-2}P_{AB}}{2k_1P_{A_2}}\right)}{\left(1 + \frac{k_{-2}P_{AB}\left(1 + K_2\frac{P_B}{P_{AB}}\right)}{4k_1P_{A_2}}\right)^2}}\;\right]
r = r_1 = k_1P_{A_2}(1-\theta_A)^2 - k_{-1}\theta_A^2 = k_1P_{A_2}(1-\theta_A)^2\left[1 - \frac{\theta_A^2/\big((1-\theta_A)^2P_{A_2}'\big)}{K_1}\right]


                  
                  Exercise 
                  
                

Show that \theta_A reduces to the QE expression when (a) k_{-2}/k_1 \ll 1 (step 2 is RLS) and (b) k_{-2}/k_1 \gg 1 (step 1 is RLS).


Overall energy diagram
Sketch: \mathrm{A_2(g) + 2B(g)} → \mathrm{A_2^*} (\Delta E_{A_2}) → barrier \Delta E_{a_1} → \mathrm{2A^*} (\Delta E_1) → barriers \Delta E_{a_2} (twice, \Delta E_2 each) → \mathrm{2AB(g)} (overall \Delta E). Mechanism: \mathrm{A_2 \xrightarrow{(1)} 2A^* \xrightarrow{(2)} AB}.
k_1 = k_{10}e^{-\Delta E_{a_1}/k_BT}\;;\qquad k_{10} = \frac{k_BT}{hP^\circ}e^{\Delta S_1^{\circ\ddagger}/k_B}\;;\qquad \Delta S_1^{\circ\ddagger} = -200\ \text{J/(mol K)}
K_1 = e^{\Delta S_1^\circ/k_B}e^{-\Delta E_1/k_BT}\;;\qquad \Delta E_{a_1} = \alpha_1\Delta E_1 + \beta_1\;;\qquad K_2 = e^{\Delta S_2/k_B}e^{-\Delta E_2/k_BT}
k_2 = \frac{k_BT}{hP^\circ}e^{\Delta S_2^{\circ\ddagger}/k_B}e^{-\Delta E_{a_2}/k_BT}\;;\qquad k_{-2} = \frac{k_2}{K_2}\;;\qquad \Delta S_2^{\circ\ddagger} \approx -200\ \text{J/(mol K)}
\Delta E_{a_2} \approx \alpha_2\Delta E_1 + \beta_2\;,\quad \alpha_2 < 0\;;\qquad \alpha_2 \approx -\tfrac{1}{2}\;;\;\; \beta_2 \approx 0.8\ \text{eV} \qquad (\text{values can vary in the literature})
\Delta E_2 = \frac{\Delta E_{ov} - \Delta E_1}{2}\;;\quad \text{choose } \Delta E_{ov} \approx -1\ \text{eV}\;;\qquad \Delta S_2^\circ \approx S_{AB(g)}^\circ - S_{B(g)}^\circ \approx 0 \;\;(\text{standard entropy change for step 2})
\gamma = \frac{(P_{AB}/P_B)^2}{K_1K_2^2P_{A_2}'}\;\;\Downarrow\;\; \frac{P_{AB}}{P_B} = \sqrt{K_1K_2P_{A_2}'\gamma}\;;\qquad \text{assume } P_{A_2}' = 25,\; P_B' \approx 50
(Where does this come from? Physical meaning?) Treat \gamma as a parameter, or add a reactor model — design equations for a PFR or PBR — and solve the microkinetic and reactor equations together for the partial pressures across the reactor.


                  
                  Notes 
                  
                


Values of S^{\circ\prime}s, P's and \gamma have a big effect on the rate, but a smaller effect on the volcano maximum.
BEP relationships affect everything!



Volcano
Assuming the first step is a lumped step → we don’t need the binding/activation energy of step 2!
Sketch: \ln r vs \Delta E_1 — the true volcano for \gamma = 10^{-2} (and a lower one for \gamma = 0.99), with leg ② on the left (step 2 is RLS) and leg ① on the right (in this region step 1 is RLS); the Sabatier bound is the dashed curve above.
The different “legs” of the volcano (① and ②) correspond (approximately) to different assumptions about the RLS.
Leg ①: assume step 1 is the RLS (as before; \gamma = overall approach to equilibrium):
r = r_1 = k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2 - k_{-1}\theta_A^2\;;\quad \theta_A = K_2^{-1}\frac{P_{AB}}{P_B}\theta_*\;;\quad r = k_1P_{A_2}\theta_*^2(1-\gamma)
r_{(1)} = \frac{k_1P_{A_2}}{\left(1 + K_2^{-1}\frac{P_{AB}}{P_B}\right)^2}(1-\gamma) \quad(\text{sketched on the graph above})
Sabatier: assume maximum rates ↳ \theta_* = 1: \;r_{Sab} = k_1P_{A_2}(1-\gamma) (upper bound).
Leg ②: assume step 2 is the RLS:
r = \tfrac{1}{2}r_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(k_2P_B\theta_A - k_{-2}P_{AB}\theta_*\big)\;;\qquad \text{step 1 is QE: } \theta_A = \sqrt{K_1P_{A_2}'}\,\theta_*\;,\;\; \theta_A + \theta_* = 1
r_{(2)} = \tfrac{1}{2}k_2P_B\theta_A(1-\sqrt{\gamma}) = \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}k_2\sqrt{K_1P_{A_2}'}}{1 + \sqrt{K_1P_{A_2}'}}(1-\sqrt{\gamma}) \;<\; \text{upper bound } \tfrac{1}{2}k_2P_B\dots


                  
                  Notes 
                  
                


The legs (sides) are determined by assuming different RLS’s. The maximum of the volcano is a transition between different RLS’s. [Each RLS has its own volcano — a competition between rate constants and coverage effects.]
The limiting expressions approximate the true volcano except where the volcanoes cross.
Sabatier rates are useful if \gamma \ll 1.
Volcanoes assuming only 1 RLS can wildly overestimate rates. ↳ Volcanoes with > 2 steps may have many legs!

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 17
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 56-58) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Term projects
General:

Literature survey: key papers
Calculations: mostly structural and thermodynamics, but basic transition states for experimental students

Example topics: epoxidation (C=C → epoxide), ethers (R–O–R).
HER on a Pt(111) surface (no water):

\mathrm{H^+ + e^- + * \rightleftharpoons H^*} (don’t need the kinetics, just the thermodynamics)
\mathrm{2H^* \rightleftharpoons H_2(g) + 2*} (Langmuir–Hinshelwood step)

\mathrm{BE_H} (binding energy of H) vs \theta_H (coverage) ⇒ calculate the H₂ formation barrier vs \theta_H (a surface-graph algorithm helps with symmetry). Then make a microkinetic model!
Scaling relationships and volcano plots

\mathrm{A_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2A^*}
\mathrm{A^* + B(g) \rightleftharpoons AB(g) + *}

(sketch: the volcano \ln r vs \Delta E_1). Interactions between adsorbates matter for surface phase diagrams and isotherms.

It is difficult to find relationships that are general enough to describe all of a volcano plot.
Coverage-dependent binding energies (if deviations from mean field are small). Sketch: \mathrm{BE}(\theta) rising linearly from −1 at \theta = 0 toward \theta = 1 — more weakly adsorbed at higher coverages (more endothermic due to repulsion).

\Delta E_1 = \frac{E(N) - E(N-1)}{1} - E_{A(g)}
is the differential energy (given that there are already some adsorbates on the surface). E.g. \Delta E_1(\theta) = \Delta E_1(\theta = 0) + 0.75\theta (an arbitrary slope).
If we assume that the BEP relation does not change with coverage (slope and intercept are the same):
E_{a_1}(\theta) = \alpha_1\Delta E_1(\theta) + \beta_1 \qquad (\alpha_1, \beta_1 \text{ do not depend on coverage — although not always true})
Sketch: \log(r/\text{s}^{-1}) vs \Delta E_1 (evaluated at \theta = 1 — this is the descriptor you choose), with and without coverage effects:

Strong-binding side: interactions give a larger rate → strong binding can only lead to higher coverage; site blocking; repulsion will increase the energy of A on the surface ↳ but actually reduce the activation barrier of A reacting ↳ although there is a volcano, so this will fall off. For a given \Delta E_1, the repulsive case will have a higher rate.
Weak-binding side: no effect of the repulsive interaction on the rate (since binding is weak, so there is automatically less coverage) — no coverage effects.
Sketch (energy diagram): repulsion weakens the binding of A*, raising A* + B(g) relative to the TS to AB(g) + *.

We usually consider interactions between the MASI (most abundant surface intermediate) and other intermediates on the surface.
Ammonia synthesis

\mathrm{N_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2N^*}
\mathrm{N^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH^* + *}
\mathrm{NH^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH_2^* + *}
\mathrm{NH_2^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH_3(g) + 2*}
\mathrm{H_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2H^*}

Steps 1 and 3 are the 2 competing RLS.
Limiting analysis
1) Step 1 is the RLS (from the earlier analysis; \gamma for the overall reaction):
r_1 = \frac{2k_1P_{N_2}(1-\gamma)}{\left[1 + \sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_4\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_3K_4K_5P_{H_2}'} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_2K_3K_4(K_5P_{H_2}')^{3/2}}\right]^2}
2) Step 3 is the RLS:
r_3 = \frac{k_3K_2K_1^{1/2}K_5P_{N_2}'^{\,1/2}P_{H_2}'(1-\sqrt{\gamma})}{\left[1 + \sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'} + \sqrt{K_1P_{N_2}'} + K_2\sqrt{K_1P_{N_2}'}\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'} + \dfrac{P_{NH_3}'}{K_4\sqrt{K_5P_{H_2}'}}\right]^2}
Parameters: P_{H_2}' = 75, P_{N_2}' = 25; S_{H_2}^\circ \approx 192 J/(mol K), S_{NH_3(g)}^\circ \approx 193 J/(mol K) (from tables or partition-function approaches).
↳ Ignoring the entropy of surface species: \Delta S_1^\circ = -192, \Delta S_2^\circ \approx \Delta S_3^\circ \approx 0, \Delta S_4^\circ = 193, \Delta S_5^\circ \approx -131.
E_{a_1} \approx 0.9\Delta E_1 + 1.34 eV (RPBE) ↳ the defects/steps are taken as active sites.
→ 4 adsorbed intermediates ↳ can we express all energies in terms of \Delta E_1? Many parameters are correlated (DFT, RPBE):
\Delta E_{NH_2} = 0.37\,\Delta E_N - 1.26\;;\qquad \Delta E_{NH} \approx 0.67\,\Delta E_N - 1.04
Note (definition): \Delta E_{NH^*} \equiv E_{NH^*} - E_* - E_{NH(g)}.
These relations result from bond-order conservation. Thus
K_2 = e^{-(\Delta E_2 - T\Delta S_2^\circ)/k_BT}
(we need to find the \Delta E_2 expression, the \Delta E for reaction 2):
\Delta E_2 \equiv E_{NH^*} + E_* - E_{N^*} - E_{H^*} \quad\to\quad \text{express in terms of } \Delta E_1

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 18
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 59-61) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF





                  
                  Announcement 
                  
                

Tutorial on Thursday; final project/presentation due the last week.


Ammonia synthesis as a model reaction (Nørskov group)

\mathrm{N_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2N^*} → \Delta E_1
\mathrm{N^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH^* + *} → \Delta E_{NH} = E_{NH^*} - E_* - E_{NH(g)}
\mathrm{NH^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH_2^* + *} → \Delta E_{NH_2}
\mathrm{NH_2^* + H^* \rightleftharpoons NH_3^* + 2*}
\mathrm{H_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2H^*} → \Delta E_H

How many independent descriptors do we need to describe trends in activities?
Scaling relationships
(Real relationships that must be accounted for; most accurate for species that bind using the same atom → H and N are linked via a scaling relationship.)
\Delta E_{NH} = 0.67\,\Delta E_N - 1.04\;;\qquad \Delta E_{NH_2} = 0.37\,\Delta E_N - 1.26 \qquad (\text{RPBE, eV})
Intercepts will change with the functional (but slopes usually don’t).
\Delta E_2 = E_{NH^*} + E_* - E_{H^*} - E_{N^*} = -\Delta E_N - \Delta E_H + \Delta E_{NH} + \underbrace{(E_{NH} - E_N - E_H)_{gas}}_{\Delta E_{gas}}
(we can also use DFT to calculate the energy of isolated species in the gas phase). Plugging in the \Delta E_{NH} scaling relationship:
\Delta E_2 = (0.67 - 1)\Delta E_N - 1.04 + \Delta E_{gas} - \Delta E_H\;;\qquad \Delta E_H \approx -2.6\ \text{eV}
(approximate this because H adsorption does not vary too much across different surfaces ↳ alternatives: ① find a scaling relation between \Delta E_H and \Delta E_N; ② keep \Delta E_H as an independent descriptor.)
Recall:
\Delta E_1 = (2E_N - E_{N_2})_{gas} + 2\Delta E_N \;\hookrightarrow\; \Delta E_N = \frac{\Delta E_1}{2} + \frac{(E_{N_2} - 2E_N)_{gas}}{2}
\therefore\quad \Delta E_2 = -0.16\,\Delta E_1 - 0.16\underbrace{(E_{N_2} - 2E_N)_g}_{-9.47\ \text{eV}} - 1.04 - (-2.6) + \underbrace{(E_{NH} - E_N - E_H)_g}_{-3.76}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\Delta E_2 = -0.16\,\Delta E_1 - 0.69}
\Delta E_5 = \underbrace{(E_{H_2} - 2E_H)_{gas}}_{4.58\ \text{eV} \text{ (constant for all catalysts)}} + 2\Delta E_H = -0.62\ \text{eV}
\Delta E_3 = -0.15\,\Delta E_1 - 0.32\;;\qquad \Delta E_4 = -0.19\,\Delta E_1 + 0.97
→ Slopes are similar due to the similarity of the elementary steps.
Combining BEP and TST
(Literature: J. Catal. 192, 31 (2000).)
k_1 = \frac{1.2\times10^6}{\sqrt{T}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{K}}{\text{bar}}\right)\exp\Bigg[\underbrace{-\frac{0.9\,\Delta E_1 + 1.34}{k_BT}}_{\text{BEP relation}}\Bigg]
(Lit.: J. Catal. 220, 273 (2003).) E_{a_3}(Ru step) = 1.35 eV; \Delta E_1(Ru step) = −0.83 eV. Assume
\Delta E_{a_3} = \alpha_3\Delta E_3 + \beta_3\;;\qquad \alpha_3 = 0.9\;,\;\; \Delta E_3 = -0.15\,\Delta E_1 - 0.32\;,\;\; \beta_3 = 1.51\ \text{eV} \qquad (\text{very approximate results})
Sketch: \ln(r/\text{s}^{-1}) vs \Delta E_1 — two curves crossing near \Delta E_1 \approx -1, and the overall volcano is the lower envelope:

strong binding (left): r_3 is limiting — slow reaction of NH* + H* (low \theta_{NH}) and N* site blocking;
weak binding (right): r_1 is limiting — slow dissociation of N₂.



                  
                  Caution 
                  
                

Nørskov papers often assume that step 1 is always rate-limiting → not always true.
Q: How can you have r_3 limiting and still be varying with the \Delta E_1 descriptor???


Physical basis of scaling relationships
Scaling usually results from the bond-order conservation (BOC) principle: when N-containing species adsorb, they maintain valency by making an appropriate number of bonds to the surface.
E.g. \Delta E_{NH} vs \Delta E_N; N can form 3 bonds. Thus
\Delta E_N \approx 3\,\underbrace{e_{N\text{-}M}}_{\text{average strength of the N–metal bond}} + \text{const.} = \big(E_{N^*} - E_* - E_{N(g)}\big)
(N forms 3 bonds to the surface), while NH has only 2 bonds to the surface (since 1 is bonded to H):
\Delta E_{N\text{-}H} \approx 2e_{N\text{-}M} + \text{const.}\;;\quad e_{N\text{-}M} = \tfrac{1}{3}\Delta E_N \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\Delta E_{NH} = \frac{2}{3}\Delta E_N + \text{const.}} \;\bigstar
This is very robust on metal surfaces, simple (reducible) oxides, zeolites, and 3-phase boundaries (if charge-balanced).
In general (A binds to the surface; B is often H):
\boxed{\Delta E_{AB_x} = \frac{n_{max,A} - x}{n_{max,A}}\Delta E_A + \text{const.}}
→ a first-order approximation (using just the simple bond-order analysis as done previously). One data point (e.g. on Pt) will give the constant:
\text{const.} = \Delta E_{AB_x/Pt} - \frac{n_{max} - x}{n_{max,A}}\Delta E_{A/Pt}
\qquad\therefore\qquad
\Delta E_{AB_x} - \Delta E_{AB_x/Pt} = \frac{n_{max} - x}{n_{max,A}}\big(\Delta E_A - \Delta E_{A/Pt}\big)
The slope is relatively insensitive to the facet, but the intercept is sensitive.
Multidentate species
Consider e.g. a species bound through C, A and D, each carrying B groups (sketch). The contribution from binding through C:
\Delta E_{CAB_2} - \Delta E_{CAB_2/Pt} = \frac{n_{max,C} - n_{CAB_2}}{n_{max,C}}\big(\Delta E_C - \Delta E_{C/Pt}\big)
Assume the contributions from C, A, D are independent → use a linear sum (all bonds contribute a single bond order):
\Delta E - \Delta E_{Pt} = \sum_i\frac{n_{max,i} - n_i}{n_{max,i}}\big(\Delta E_i - \Delta E_{i/Pt}\big)
This fails if we have multiple bonds between adsorbed species (e.g. H₂C=CH₂ on a surface; or aromatics).

In practice, higher-order bonds are broken on the surface, so scaling still holds (exceptions: Au, Ag, Cu). Observation: once in a while, species can form more than “one effective” bond to the surface.
Scaling is more accurate when correlating binding energies of species bound to the same site geometries ↳ create separate scaling relations for different site types.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 62-64) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF





                  
                  Announcements 
                  
                

Start the project! Send an email about the bonus lecture.


Alternate scaling relationships
Traditionally: correlate the binding of 2 adsorbates across many surfaces.
↳ Instead, correlate the binding energies of many adsorbates on a single surface (cf. group-contribution methods).
Bond-order parameter: \dfrac{x_{max} - x}{x_{max}} → use this to correlate many adsorbates:
\text{BE}_{(\text{"any" adsorbate})} = \sum_i P_i\left(\frac{x_{max} - x}{x_{max}}\right) + \text{const.}
where i runs over the atoms that bind covalently to the surface, and the P_i are parameters fit to DFT data (different for each surface) — a simple regression analysis. With a small number of DFT calculations, we can estimate the BEs of many species.
↳ We can add higher-order corrections (interactions between nearest-neighbor atoms i,j):
\text{BE} = \sum_iP_i\left(\frac{x_{max} - x}{x_{max}}\right) + \sum_{ij}P_{ij}\left(\frac{x_{max,i} - x_i}{x_{max,i}}\right)\left(\frac{x_{max,j} - x_j}{x_{max,j}}\right)
Classic example: scaling/BEP analysis (Mavrikakis et al., JACS 2009)
Consider ethanol partial oxidation on transition-metal surfaces:
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{C_2H_5OH(g) + * \rightleftharpoons C_2H_5OH^*} \\
&\mathrm{C_2H_5OH^* + * \xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}H} C_2H_4OH^* + H^*} \qquad \mathrm{C_2H_5OH^* \xrightleftharpoons{O\text{–}H} C_2H_5O^* + H^* \xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}H} C_2H_4O^* + H^*} \\
&\mathrm{C_2H_4OH^* + * \xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}H} C_2H_3OH^* + H^*} \qquad \mathrm{C_2H_4OH^* \xrightleftharpoons{O\text{–}H} C_2H_4O^* + H^*} \\
&\qquad\vdots
\end{aligned}
More dehydrogenation can occur, down to CCO* (never achieved in practice).
Intermediates (C–C and C–O scission; similar steps for other intermediates):
\mathrm{C_2H_3OH^* + * \xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}C} CH^* + CH_2OH^*}\;;\quad \mathrm{\xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}C} CH_2^* + CHOH^*}\;;\quad \mathrm{\xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}C} CH_3^* + COH^*}\;;\quad \mathrm{\xrightleftharpoons{C\text{–}O} C_2H_3^* + OH^*}
To get the maximum H₂ yield, suppress C–O bond scission (it usually gives alkanes + H₂O).
How can one analyze such a complex mechanism?
(a) Surface adsorption energies and surface coverages
↳ Starting with a complete database of binding energies on Ru(0001), use the scaling relationship (i = C, O atoms):
\Delta E - \Delta E_{Ru} = \sum_i\left(\frac{x_{max,i} - x_i}{x_{max,i}}\right)\big(\Delta E_i - \Delta E_{i/Ru}\big)
↳ From these values, estimate the \theta‘s of all intermediates on all surfaces by assuming QE with the appropriate gas species (assume net rate limiting):
\mathrm{C_2H_x^* \rightleftharpoons C_2H_6(g) + yH_2(g) + *}\;;\qquad
\mathrm{C_2H_xO_y^* \rightleftharpoons C_2H_5OH(g) + zH_2(g) + *}\;;\qquad
\mathrm{CH_x^* \rightleftharpoons CH_4(g) + mH_2(g) + *}
⇓ For all metals except Cu, Ag, Au, CO* is the MASI (Cu, Ag, Au had * — empty sites — as the MASI). This is an approximation as well, assuming that C–H bond breaking is QE?
→ Since CO* is at high coverage, account for interactions of species with CO*. On Pt(111) [PW91, differential BE = d\varepsilon/d\theta]:
\text{BE}_{CO}(\theta_{CO}) = -1.78 + 0.0065\,e^{4.79\theta_{CO}} + 0.314\,\theta_{CO}\,e^{4.79\theta_{CO}}
↳ Crude first approximation: assume these \theta_{CO}-dependent terms for all adsorbates on all metals.
(b) Kinetics

Use a BEP relationship to estimate barriers (energies of the TS) for all possible reactions with C–C or C–O cleavage. Two approaches for the barriers: (i) correct the reactant/product BEs for \theta_{CO}, then apply BEP; (ii) apply BEP without \theta_{CO}, then correct the TS and reactant/product separately for \theta_{CO}.
Use coverages from the thermodynamic analysis.
Calculate rates on each metal according to the most stable TS for C–C and C–O bond breaking:

R = 10^{13}\,\text{s}^{-1}\,\theta_{TS}\,\theta_*\qquad\left(\approx\frac{k_BT}{h}K_{TS}\,\theta_{TS}\,\theta_*\right)
(c) Steps / structure sensitivity

The general approach is to calculate \Delta E to dissociate CO* on steps:

if \Delta E < 0, steps will be poisoned with C* ↔ they do not contribute;
if \Delta E > 0, steps must be considered → redo the calculations on steps.


Con: it is not stated which approach is better.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 20 (CHE)
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 65-68) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Electrochemistry
Applications: electrocatalysts, batteries, capacitors, devices, corrosion.
Key features:

Solvent/solid interfaces (water – electrocatalysis; organic – batteries).
The existence of a charged double layer near the surface of an electrode that establishes potential drops across surfaces.

Sketch: anode and cathode with the electrolyte between, connected through an external circuit; different charge densities on the anode and cathode (so the overall sign will be determined by that). The potential profile V drops across each double layer (and also in the solid itself), giving \Delta V_{cell}.
Reactions at electrified interfaces
Chemical (e.g. N₂ → 2N* near the charged surface):

No e^- transfer
Small voltage dependence (rearrangement of anions)
↓ Can use normal DFT (possibly including solvent molecules)

Electrochemical (e.g. \mathrm{* + H_2O \rightarrow OH^* + H^+ + e^-}; e^- goes into the electrode, H⁺ into solution across the potential V):

Generates positive/negative charges, and so these steps are hugely affected by voltage.

Analyzing thermodynamics
Calculating \Delta G:
\Delta G = \mu_{OH^*} + \underbrace{\mu_{H^+} + \mu_{e^-}}_{} - \mu_* - \mu_{H_2O}
\mu_{OH^*} \approx E_{OH^*} - TS_{OH^*} + ZPE_{OH^*} + \dots\;;\qquad \mu_* \approx E_*\;;\qquad \mu_{H_2O} \approx E_{H_2O} - TS_{H_2O} + ZPE_{H_2O}
\mu_{H^+} + \mu_{e^-}:

Assume the proton entropy (activity) is \sim k_BT\ln[\mathrm{H^+}], assuming that H⁺ don’t interact with each other (even at pH 0 there is 1 H⁺ per 55 H₂O molecules, so a pretty good assumption unless at negative pHs).
Assume the electrostatic energy to separate charges across the double layer is \sim qV = -eV.

\text{Thus,}\quad \mu_{H^+} + \mu_{e^-} = \underbrace{\text{const.}}_{\text{undetermined}} + k_BT\ln[\mathrm{H^+}] - eV
Standard conditions: \mu_{H^+}^\circ + \mu_{e^-}^\circ = \text{const.} + k_BT\ln[\mathrm{H^+}]_0 - eV_0
\therefore\quad \boxed{\mu_{H^+} + \mu_{e^-} = \mu_{H^+}^\circ + \mu_{e^-}^\circ + k_BT\ln\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]_0} - e(V - V_0)}
V_0 is an arbitrary reference (standard state) for voltage; it is often chosen to be the standard hydrogen electrode reference:
-eV_0 \equiv \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2(g)}^\circ - \big(\mu_{H^+}^\circ + \mu_{e^-}^\circ\big)
↳ Experimentally, use a counter electrode where [\mathrm{H_2}]^\circ and [\mathrm{H^+}]_0 are in equilibrium with the electrode surface (\mathrm{H_2(g)}^\circ: typically 1 bar; \mathrm{H^+}^\circ: typically 1 M). We get:
\boxed{\mu_{H^+} + \mu_{e^-} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ + k_BT\ln\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]_0} - eV_{SHE}}\;;\qquad \mu_{H_2}^\circ = E_{H_2(g)} - TS_{H_2(g)}^\circ + ZPE_{H_2(g)}
The log term is related to pH; V_{SHE} carries the \mu_{H^+} dependence. So \Delta G = \Delta G(V, \text{pH}, \text{BE}).
Example: ORR

\mathrm{O_2(g) + 2* \rightleftharpoons 2O^*}
\mathrm{O^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons OH^*}
\mathrm{OH^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons * + H_2O(l)}

\Delta G_1 = 2\mu_{O^*} - 2\mu_* - \mu_{O_2(g)}\qquad[\text{independent of } V]
\Delta G_2(V,\text{pH}) = \mu_{OH^*} - \mu_{O^*} - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ + k_BT\ln\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]_0} - eV_{SHE}\right) = \Delta G_2(0,0) - k_BT\ln\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]_0} + eV_{SHE}
\Delta G_3(V,\text{pH}) = \mu_{H_2O(l)} + \mu_* - \mu_{OH^*} - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ + k_BT\ln\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]_0} - eV_{SHE}\right)
All quantities can be estimated with DFT → make a free-energy diagram.
Sketch (G vs reaction steps on Pt(111), pH = 0): at V_{SHE} = 0 the path goes \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2(\mathrm{H^+ + e^-}) → up to \mathrm{O^*} + 2(\mathrm{H^+ + e^-}) → down to \mathrm{OH^* + H^+ + e^-} → down to \mathrm{H_2O(l) + *}; at V_{SHE} = 1.23 V the electrochemical steps are shifted up and the profile flattens.

At V_{SHE} = 0 V: O₂ dissociation is the RLS.
At V_{SHE} = 1.23 V: conversion of OH* to water may be the RLS.

→ The RLS can change with voltage in electrochemical systems [the RLS may be voltage-dependent].


                  
                  Onset potential 
                  
                

The potential at which all electrochemical steps are thermodynamically exergonic is called the onset potential — an approximation of the V where the rate becomes non-negligible.
↳ We know this because when you lower the voltage from 1.23 V there will be a point where the plateaus are level (that doesn’t mean they are at equilibrium).


Alternate ORR mechanism (associative, via OOH*)

\mathrm{O_2(g) + H^+ + e^- + * \rightleftharpoons OOH^*}
\mathrm{OOH^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons O^* + H_2O(l)}
\mathrm{O^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons OH^*}
\mathrm{OH^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons H_2O(l) + *}

Overall: \mathrm{O_2(g) + 4(H^+ + e^-) \rightleftharpoons 2H_2O}
\Delta G_1(V_{SHE},\text{pH}) = \mu_{OOH^*} - \mu_* - \mu_{O_2(g)} - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ + k_BT\ln\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]_0} - eV_{SHE}\right) = \Delta G_1(0,0) + eV_{SHE}\;\;@\;\text{pH} = 0
\Delta G_2 = \mu_{O^*} + \mu_{H_2O(l)} - \mu_{OOH^*} - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ - eV_{SHE}\right)\;;\qquad
\Delta G_3 = \mu_{OH^*} - \mu_{O^*} - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ - eV_{SHE}\right)
\Delta G_4 = \mu_{H_2O(l)} + \mu_* - \mu_{OH^*} - \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ - eV_{SHE}\right)
Example: \Delta G_2^\circ(0,0) = \mu_{O^*}^\circ + \mu_{H_2O(l)}^\circ - \mu_{OOH^*}^\circ - \tfrac{1}{2}\mu_{H_2}^\circ, with
\mu_{H_2O(l)} = \mu_{H_2O(g)}^\circ - \underbrace{\Delta G_{vap}^\circ}_{\text{from exp.}} = E_{H_2O(g)} - TS_{H_2O(g)}^\circ + ZPE_{H_2O(g)} - \Delta G_{vap}^\circ
\mu_{O^*}^\circ = E_{O^*} + ZPE_{O^*} - TS_{O^*}^\circ\;;\quad \mu_{OOH}^\circ = E_{OOH^*} + ZPE_{OOH^*} - TS_{OOH^*}^\circ\;;\quad \mu_{H_2}^\circ = E_{H_2(g)} + ZPE_{H_2(g)} - TS_{H_2(g)}^\circ
\begin{aligned}
\Delta G_2^\circ &= \Big(E_{O^*} + E_{H_2O(g)} - E_{OOH^*} - \tfrac{1}{2}E_{H_2(g)}\Big) + \Big(ZPE_{O^*} + ZPE_{H_2O(g)} - ZPE_{OOH^*} - \tfrac{1}{2}ZPE_{H_2(g)}\Big) \\
&\quad - T\Big(S_{O^*}^\circ + S_{H_2O(g)}^\circ - S_{OOH^*}^\circ - \tfrac{1}{2}S_{H_2(g)}^\circ\Big) - \Delta G_{vap}^\circ \\
&= \Delta E_{DFT}^\circ + \Delta ZPE - T\Delta S^\circ - \Delta G_{vap}^\circ
\end{aligned}
Often, define O* and OOH* with respect to a common reference:
\Delta E_O \equiv E_{O^*} + E_{H_2(g)} - E_{H_2O(g)} - E_*\quad[\mathrm{H_2O(g) + * \rightleftharpoons O^* + H_2(g)}]
\Delta E_{OOH} = E_{OOH^*} + \tfrac{3}{2}E_{H_2(g)} - 2E_{H_2O(g)} - E_*\quad[\mathrm{2H_2O(g) + * \rightleftharpoons OOH^* + \tfrac{3}{2}H_2(g)}]
\boxed{\Delta G_2^\circ = \Delta E_O - \Delta E_{OOH} + \Delta ZPE_2 - T\Delta S_2^\circ - \Delta G_{vap}^\circ}
Scaling relations (PCCP 2007, RPBE):
\Delta E_{OOH} = 0.53\,\Delta E_O + 3.18\ \text{eV}\;;\qquad \Delta E_{OH} = 0.5\,\Delta E_O + 0.05\ \text{eV}
\Delta G_2^\circ = \underbrace{0.47\,\Delta E_O}_{\text{depends on catalyst}} \underbrace{- 3.18\ \text{eV} + \Delta ZPE_2 - T\Delta S_2^\circ - \Delta G_{vap}^\circ}_{\text{independent of catalyst}}
\begin{aligned}
\Delta G_1^\circ &= 0.53\,\Delta E_O + 3.18\ \text{eV} + \big(2E_{H_2O(g)} - E_{O_2(g)} - 2E_{H_2(g)}\big) + \Delta ZPE_1 - T\Delta S_1^\circ \\
\Delta G_3^\circ &= -0.5\,\Delta E_O + 0.05\ \text{eV} + \Delta ZPE_3 - T\Delta S_3^\circ \\
\Delta G_4^\circ &= -0.5\,\Delta E_O - 0.05\ \text{eV} + \Delta ZPE_4 - T\Delta S_4^\circ - \Delta G_{vap}^\circ
\end{aligned}

                  Announcements 
                  
                


Final report: 20-page report; decent literature review (key papers, intro, why the interest, methods + results, discussion, conclusion).
Geometrical algorithm to match the surfaces of two solids (with different lattice constants and periodicities).



Electrocatalysis (continued)
ORR:

\mathrm{O_2(g) + H^+ + e^- + * \rightleftharpoons OOH^*}
\mathrm{OOH^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons O^* + H_2O(l)}
\mathrm{O^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons OH^*}
\mathrm{OH^* + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons H_2O(l) + *}

Find \Delta G_1, \Delta G_2, \Delta G_3, \Delta G_4 in terms of \Delta E_O. Use a “limiting legs” analysis, combined with a Sabatier analysis (assume idealized surface energies).
Step 1 is the RLS:
r = r_1 = k_1(U)\,P_{O_2}C_{H^+}\theta_* - k_{-1}(U)\,\theta_{OOH} = k_1P_{O_2}C_{H^+}\theta_*\Bigg[1 - \underbrace{\frac{k_{-1}}{k_1}\frac{\theta_{OOH}}{P_{O_2}C_{H^+}\theta_*}}_{\gamma_1}\Bigg]
(U = potential.) Assume maximum rates: irreversibilities and idealized \theta‘s = 1. Similarly:
r_1^{max} = k_1P_{O_2}C_{H^+}\;;\quad r_2^{max} = k_2C_{H^+}\;;\quad r_3^{max} = k_3C_{H^+}\;;\quad r_4^{max} = k_4C_{H^+}
Example for k_1 — voltage-dependent (use a BEP relation):
k_1 = \frac{k_{10}}{C_{H^+}^\circ P^\circ}\exp\left(-\alpha\left(\frac{\Delta G_1^\circ + eU}{k_BT}\right)\right)
(\Delta G_1^\circ + eU is the voltage-dependent \Delta G_1; usually \tfrac{1}{2} < \alpha < 1.) ⇓ Assume \alpha = 1 for now:
-k_BT\ln\left(\frac{r_1}{k_{10}}\right) = \underbrace{\Delta G_1^\circ}_{\text{expressed in terms of } \Delta E_O} + eV_{SHE} - k_BT\ln\left(\frac{P_{O_2}C_{H^+}}{P^\circ C_{H^+}^\circ}\right)
k_{10} is a pre-exponential factor for H⁺ transfer through the double layer. Use TST or fit to experiment.
Plot activity vs \Delta E_O for a given U_{SHE} (sketch: activity = -k_BT\ln(r/k_0) vs \Delta E_O (eV), volcanoes for U = 0.8\,V_{SHE} and U = 1.23\,V_{SHE}; left leg: step 4 is RLS; right leg: step 1 is RLS):

U affects the location of the maximum a little.
The rate increases as U decreases (but the cell efficiency decreases) — you want the potential difference between the anode and cathode to be the highest (but the rate is slow when operating at 1.23 V).

d-band analysis
K-S equations → K-S wave functions → eigenvalues (\varepsilon_i) ≈ the energies of 1-e^- orbitals.
Density of states → electronic properties (sketch: \rho(E) for a molecule — discrete lines — vs a broadened band).
Nørskov d-band theory: tight binding (molecular-orbital theory). Sketch: two atomic levels A and B combining:
\psi_{AB} = c_A\psi_A + c_B\psi_B
(we can have more orbitals than particles also involved).
H_{AB} = -\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2 + v_A + v_B
The (approximate) 1-e^- Hamiltonian → write it in matrix form and set the determinant equal to zero → a formal way of understanding molecular-orbital theory.
Newns–Anderson theory

↳ Especially for metals (using the density of states instead of metal orbitals).
So we are not completely ignoring the s and p bands ↳ just prioritizing the d-band? The d-band acts like a “molecule” → the expression is the same as the molecular-orbital theory expression (\Delta E).
Binding parameters: f and V_{ad}^2.
E_0 → estimate (interaction with the s-p band).
\varepsilon_d → the d-band center (independent of adsorbate).
\varepsilon_a → (adsorbate level).
f = 1 (full d-band) → post-transition metals.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Lecture 23
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 75-78) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF





                  
                  Announcements 
                  
                


HWs: can ask for solutions
Course evaluation → Friday deadline

(Useful conversion: 0.1\ \text{eV} \sim 10\ \text{kJ/mol}.)


Zeolites (continued): DEE (diethyl ether) formation

Microkinetic model → degree of rate control (sensitivity analysis), using a higher-accuracy functional to get better elementary-step endothermic values.
The rate constants changed a lot? ↓ Maybe other steps were the RDS / important? ↓ Need to compare to the experimental values/data.
The MASI would depend on changing T, P and reactor conditions.

Review of surface and gas-phase chemical potential analysis
① (Ideal) gas treatments
Divide them into translational, rotational, vibrational and electronic (DFT) parts:
q_{vib} = \prod_i^{modes}\frac{e^{-h\nu_i\beta/2}}{1 - e^{-h\nu_i\beta}}\;\;(\text{per molecule; includes ZPE})\;;\qquad
q_{rot} = \frac{I}{\sigma\beta\hbar^2}\;\;(\text{linear, per molecule})
q_{trans} = \left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}V\;\;(\text{per molecule})\;;\qquad q_{el} = e^{-E_{DFT}/k_BT}\;\;(\text{total energy})
Q_{tot} = \frac{q_{trans}^N}{N!}q_{vib}^Nq_{rot}^Ne^{-E_{DFT}/k_BT}\;;\qquad F_{tot} = -k_BT\ln Q_{tot}\;,\quad \mu = \frac{\partial F_{tot}}{\partial N} = -k_BT\frac{\partial}{\partial N}\big(\ln Q_{tot}\big)
With \ln N! \approx N\ln N - N:
\boxed{\mu = -k_BT\ln\left[\left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right)^{3/2}\underbrace{\left(\frac{V}{N}\right)}_{k_BT/P}\right] - k_BT\ln q_{vib} - k_BT\ln q_{rot} + \frac{\partial E_{DFT}}{\partial N}}
Standard state: \mu^\circ = \mu(P = P^\circ):
\mu^\circ = -\frac{3}{2}k_BT\ln\left(\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\right) - k_BT\ln\left(\frac{k_BT}{P^\circ}\right) - k_BT\ln q_{vib} - k_BT\ln q_{rot} + \frac{\partial E_{DFT}}{\partial N}
\qquad\therefore\quad \mu = \mu^\circ + k_BT\ln\left(\frac{P}{P^\circ}\right)
(use this to calculate K‘s in the microkinetic model). Equivalently, \mu^\circ = \varepsilon_{DFT} + \text{ZPE} - T\bar{S}, with \bar{S} = \partial S/\partial N, and \dfrac{\partial E_{DFT}}{\partial N} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial N}\big(N\varepsilon_{DFT}\big) = \varepsilon_{DFT} (per molecule).
② Liquid-phase treatments — complicated
③ Surface processes
(a) First-order treatment: calculate harmonic modes on the surface (3N_{atoms} modes) and use the harmonic partition function:
Q_{tot} = q_{vib}^Ne^{-E_{DFT}/k_BT}\frac{N_s!}{N!(N_s - N)!}
\mu = \frac{\partial E_{tot}}{\partial N} = \underbrace{-k_BT\ln\left[\prod_i^{modes}\frac{e^{-h\nu_i\beta/2}}{1 - e^{-h\nu_i\beta}}\right] + \frac{\partial E_{DFT}}{\partial N}}_{\mu^\circ \text{ (includes ZPE)}} + \underbrace{k_BT\ln\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta_*}\right)}_{\text{activity}}\;;\qquad \theta_* = 1 - \theta_A - \theta_B - \theta_C
\therefore\quad \boxed{\mu = \mu^\circ + k_BT\ln\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta_*}\right)} \qquad (\text{for a TS, do not include the reaction coordinate})


                  
                  Caution 
                  
                

This approach fails for low-frequency modes (\nu_i \lesssim 150\ \text{cm}^{-1}): low frequencies imply low diffusion barriers — anharmonic. (Sketch: a corrugated potential V(x) along the surface; the frequency is \sqrt{\text{curvature}}; at higher T, adsorbates access anharmonic states or are not even bound.) These modes make the largest contribution to the entropy.
Crude correction: take all modes with \nu_i \lesssim 150\ \text{cm}^{-1} and assume their entropies are all equal to that of a mode with \nu = 150\ \text{cm}^{-1} (!?).


(b) Better treatments of low-frequency modes
(i) Particle-in-a-box (for adsorbates). Sketch: a box from 0 to L; in 2D, free diffusion in a box, but the molecules are still localized.
\text{In 2D:}\quad E_{n,l} = \frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2m}\left[\frac{n^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{l^2}{L_y^2}\right]\;,\quad n, l = 1, 2, \dots
q_{trans}^{(per\ molecule)} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\exp\left[-\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mk_BT}\left(\frac{n^2}{L_x^2} + \frac{l^2}{L_y^2}\right)\right]
\approx \int_0^\infty\!\!\int_0^\infty e^{-\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2n^2}{2mk_BTL^2}}e^{-\frac{\pi^2\hbar^2l^2}{2mk_BTL^2}}\,dn\,dl \;\;(\text{if } L_x = L_y = L)
= \frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}A_{box}
where A_{box} = L^2 = the area of free diffusion for each adsorbate (define this for the area that you care about around the active site).
Q_{trans} = q_{trans,box}^N\;;\qquad \mu_{trans} = -k_BT\ln\left[\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}A_{box}\right]


                  
                  Important
                  
                

\mu^\circ = -k_BT\ln\left[\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}A_{box}\right]
Replace the low-frequency translational modes with this; everything else is the same. Useful for zeolites and surfaces at high coverages.


(ii) Two-dimensional ideal gases (simple adsorption/desorption, weakly bound adsorbates):
q_{trans} = A\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}\;\;(\text{per molecule})\;;\qquad Q_{tot} = \frac{q_{trans}^N}{N!}q_{vib}^Nq_{rot}^Ne^{-E_{DFT}/k_BT}
(identify the low-frequency modes and the high-frequency modes). This gives \dfrac{A}{N} = \dfrac{a_s}{\theta}, with \theta = N/N_s:
\mu = -k_BT\ln\left[\frac{2\pi mk_BT}{h^2}a_s\right] - k_BT\ln\big(q_{vib}q_{rot}\big) + \frac{\partial E_{DFT}}{\partial N} + k_BT\ln\theta\qquad(q_{vib} \text{ includes ZPE})
\boxed{\mu = \mu^\circ + k_BT\ln\theta}
There is no \theta_* because ideal gases have no volume (so no site-blocking term).

→ Not correct for real molecules at high coverages.
→ Still approximately true if \theta_* \approx 1: \mu = \mu^\circ + k_BT\ln(\theta/\theta_*).

Rough correction: change A \to A - Na_{ads} (the area excluded by adsorbates). Then
\frac{A}{N} \to \frac{A - Na_{ads}}{N} = \frac{N_sa_s - Na_{ads}}{N} = a_s\frac{\left(1 - \frac{a_{ads}}{a_s}\theta\right)}{\theta}
\Rightarrow \mu^\circ is the same: \;\mu = \mu^\circ + k_BT\ln\dfrac{\theta}{\theta_*}, with \theta_* = 1 - \dfrac{a_{ads}}{a_s}\theta.
If the coverage is getting too high (\theta_* \ll 1), consider the particle-in-a-box (or a different model).

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Notes on density functional theory (DFT 697)
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Handwritten class notes from DFT 697 (Spring 2023), transcribed into Markdown and LaTeX. Each lecture page has the typed version first, with the original handwritten pages in a collapsible box underneath.

Original handwritten notes (PDF, 43 MB)

Lectures

Lecture 03 · 2023-01-17 — Many particles in a box, fermion antisymmetry and Slater determinants, the Hohenberg–Kohn theorems, functionals, and the 1D kinetic-energy functional.
Lecture 04 · 2023-01-19 — Using the simple kinetic-energy functional with Lagrange multipliers — particle in a box, a delta-function spike, a linear potential, the 1D Thomas–Fermi atom — and adding Coulomb and exchange terms.
Lecture 05 · 2023-01-24 — A one-dimensional atom with delta-function interactions, DFT and the TISE with periodic boundary conditions, the Dirac comb, Bloch’s theorem and the origin of band structure.
Lecture 06 · 2023-01-26 — Solving the periodic TISE with k-points, then Kohn–Sham DFT — the fictitious non-interacting system, the Kohn–Sham equations, the self-consistent algorithm, and a worked two-fermion example.
Lecture 07 (Thermo) · 2023-01-31 — Basis sets and energy cutoffs, the hierarchy of exchange–correlation functionals (LDA, GGA, meta-GGA, hybrids), major limitations of DFT (band gaps, self-interaction, van der Waals), and an introduction to surface thermodynamics and the grand potential.
Lecture 08 (Thermo) · 2023-02-07 — Interfacial thermodynamics with the grand potential — excess quantities, surface tension and the Gibbs–Duhem relation for interfaces — and how to approximate the internal energy, entropy and chemical potentials (equipartition and statistical mechanics) to build surface phase diagrams.
Lecture 09 (Thermo) · 2023-02-09 — Ideal-gas partition functions for internal energy and entropy, real gases via fugacity, bulk stability limits for H on Ni(111) and CO oxidation on RuO₂(110), zeolite “surface” energies, and surface energies of metals in vacuum.
Lecture 10 (Wulff & Langmuir) · 2023-02-14 — Nanoparticle shapes from surface free energies — the Wulff theorem and its “proof”, generalizing Wulff to supports (adhesion energy) and adsorbates — and deriving the Langmuir isotherm from the grand canonical partition function.
Lecture 11 (Langmuir) · 2023-02-16 — Langmuir isotherm behaviour, then adsorbate–adsorbate interactions with the 1D Ising model solved by a transfer matrix, the weak-interaction limit, and how attractive or repulsive interactions reshape isotherms.
Lecture 12 (Kinetics) · 2023-02-23 — Kinetics with DFT — transition state theory for surface reactions, activities of gas, liquid and surface species, chemical potentials of adsorbates from partition functions, and the harmonic TST rate expression, including reactions with gas-phase species.
Lecture 13 · 2023-02-28 — TST for gas–solid (Eley–Rideal) reactions, TST without statistical mechanics, collision theory for adsorption (and its equivalence to TST), thermodynamic consistency of rate constants, and an introduction to microkinetic modelling with quasi-equilibrium and rate-limiting steps.
Lecture 14 · 2023-03-02 — Microkinetic analysis of ammonia synthesis — the full steady-state solution and limiting cases where N₂ dissociation or NH hydrogenation is rate-limiting, with the approach-to-equilibrium factor.
Lecture 15 · 2023-03-07 — Volcano plots for heterogeneous catalysis — deriving the rate vs. dissociative adsorption energy with a BEP relation, how the volcano maximum shifts with approach to equilibrium, pressure and temperature, and a second example with a molecular precursor state.
Lecture 16 · 2023-03-21 — Volcanoes with more than one rate-controlling step — the full steady-state solution, the overall energy diagram and parameter choices, and how the legs of a volcano correspond to different rate-limiting steps, with Sabatier upper bounds.
Lecture 17 · 2023-03-30 — Term-project guidance (e.g. HER on Pt(111)), coverage-dependent binding energies and their effect on volcano plots, and setting up an ammonia-synthesis volcano with entropies, BEP relations and scaling relations between intermediates.
Lecture 18 · 2023-04-04 — Ammonia synthesis as a model reaction — expressing all step energies through scaling relations in one descriptor, combining BEP and TST, the resulting two-legged volcano, and the bond-order-conservation basis of scaling relationships (including multidentate species).
Lecture 19 · 2023-04-11 — Group-additivity style scaling relations across many adsorbates on one surface, and the classic scaling/BEP analysis of ethanol decomposition on transition metals — coverages from thermodynamics, CO* interactions, BEP barriers for C–C and C–O scission, and step sites.
Lecture 20 (CHE) · 2023-04-18 — Electrochemistry with DFT — electrified interfaces, chemical vs electrochemical steps, the computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) for μ(H⁺)+μ(e⁻), and free-energy diagrams, onset potentials and scaling relations for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR).
Lecture 21 (D-band) · 2023-04-20 — Electrocatalysis continued — limiting-legs and Sabatier analysis of the ORR with voltage-dependent rate constants and activity volcanoes vs ΔE_O — followed by an introduction to d-band analysis (density of states, tight binding, Newns–Anderson model).
Lecture 22 (Zeolites) · 2023-04-25 — Guest lecture on zeolites — k-point density, levels of solvent modelling in microporous materials, water in Sn-Beta zeolites, AIMD-based entropies (solid-like + gas-like), and TST/DFT kinetic modelling with low-frequency modes.
Lecture 23 · 2023-04-27 — Final lecture — degree of rate control in a zeolite microkinetic model, then a review of chemical potentials for ideal gases and surface species, the failure of the harmonic approximation for low-frequency modes, and particle-in-a-box and 2D ideal-gas treatments of adsorbates.

Homework

HWs · 2023-01-30 — Section divider page for the DFT 697 homework sets (no content on this page).
HW 01 · 2023-01-27 — Homework 1 solutions — two fermions in a box via a Slater determinant and their expectation energy, the 1D δ-function well with simple DFT (diverges), the DFT harmonic oscillator vs the exact result, and a spherical Thomas–Fermi-like atom.
HW 02 · 2023-02-15 — Homework 2 solutions — band energies of a periodic Dirac comb from the Bloch condition (discrete sums vs integrals for P = 10 and 20, one to three bands) compared with DFT, and simple DFT for a sinusoidal potential.
HW 03 · 2023-03-01 — Homework 3 solutions — an ab-initio phase diagram for H adsorption on Pt(111) (surface and subsurface sites), T/P relations for μ_H and a coverage heat map, and the Wulff shape of a Pt nanoparticle with support and adsorbate effects.
HW 04 · 2023-04-04 — Homework 4 solutions — showing that the fully steady-state A ⇌ A* ⇌ B* ⇌ B mechanism reduces to quasi-equilibrium of steps 1 and 3, both by direct limits and by a perturbation expansion in the slow rate constants.

Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.title: Data 100 Bias-Variance
Coursework/Computational_and_Data_Method.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 1-5) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF







Five handwritten pages from Data 100 (UC Berkeley, principles and techniques of data science).
Bias–variance
\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[D^2]\;(\text{expectation of deviation squared, }D = X - E[X]) = E[(X - E[X])^2] = E[X^2 - 2XE[X] + (E[X])^2] = E[X^2] - 2E[X]E[X] + (E[X])^2 = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2
Similarly:
\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = E[(X + Y - E(X + Y))^2] = E[(\underbrace{X - \mu_x}_{a} + \underbrace{Y - \mu_y}_{b})^2] = E[a^2 + b^2 + 2ab] = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) + \underbrace{2E(D_xD_y)}_{\text{covariance}}
\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = E[(X - E(X))(Y - E(Y))] = E[XY - XE(Y) - YE(X) + E(Y)E(X)] = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y)
Since we express r = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}: for covariance = 0, X & Y are uncorrelated (since r(X, Y) = 0) (but that doesn’t make them independent) or X & Y are independent.

↳ Model bias: average difference between our predicted value and the true value: E[\hat{Y}(x)] - g(x)
↳ Model risk: mean squared error of prediction: E[(Y - \hat{Y}(x))^2]
↳ Model variance: average of predictions across all possible samples: E[(\hat{Y}(x) - E(\hat{Y}(x)))^2] → has got nothing to do with the true model value (just variations in our own predictions)

Bias–variance decomposition:
\text{Model risk} = \underbrace{\text{observation variance}}_{\sigma^2} + (\text{model bias})^2 + \text{model variance}
(sketch: error vs. model complexity — bias² falling, model variance rising, test error U-shaped with its minimum where they cross.)
PCA
The goal of PCA is to identify the most meaningful basis to re-express a data set ↳ our hope is that these new bases will filter out the noise and reveal hidden structure, i.e. re-expressing the data as a linear combination of its basis vectors.
Assumptions: (1) linearity; (2) large variances have important structure (PCs corresponding to large variances represent interesting structure); (3) principal components are orthogonal.
A 2D overview of PCA: transforms an N×d matrix (X) into an N×m matrix (Y) (if d = m, then there is no loss of information). Steps:

Centralize data (subtract mean)
Calculate the d×d covariance matrix (diagonals are variances while off-diagonals are covariances b/w i & j)
Calculate the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (orthonormal)
Select m eigenvectors w/ largest eigenvalues

(sketches: a correlated point cloud in x–y; after finding the covariance matrix & using that to get eigenvalues/eigenvectors, v_1 and v_2 are orthonormal vectors that capture the data variance; plotting on the new axes, the data spread mainly along v_2.)
These eigenvectors obtained are called principal components ↓ we see that v_2 captures the majority of the data while v_1 captures some of it. Therefore, using only v_2 we can get back projected data, Y = XV (sketch: points collapsed onto a line). Using only PC1 we lose variance in the other direction but retain the majority of the structure of the data.
Linear regression
SLR: slope = r\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}; intercept = \mu_x - \text{slope}\cdot\mu_y.
Transcriber’s note: the SLR intercept is \mu_y - \text{slope}\cdot\mu_x; the subscripts are swapped on the sheet.
Linear regression [w/ changing X, Y parameters], \hat{Y} = X\hat{\theta}:

→ Shifting x and y: SD of x and y stay the same (mean changes); parameters don’t change (apart from the intercept); MSE same; r same.
→ Shifting only x or only y: no change in SD (means change); MSE same; intercept changes.
→ Scaled both x and y: everything changes (points move closer or further away to the regression line).
→ Scaling only x: intercept stays the same; MSE same.
→ Scaling only y: everything changes; if scaled by ½ → MSE will drop (since predicted values are closer to [the sentence is unfinished on the page]).

Midterm 1 cheat sheet for CBE 176, electrochemical engineering (UC Berkeley). Three handwritten pages; the third repeats the title and continues with transport.
Page 1 — “CBE 176: MT#1 Cheat Sheet”

Red Cat → reduction @ cathode (e⁻ →); An Ox → oxidation @ anode (→ e⁻)
F = 96485 C/mol
e⁻ flow from low potential → high potential (high free energy → low free energy)

Electroneutrality

iA_{Anode} + iA_{Cathode} = 0 (i = current density [mA/cm²]; A = surface area)
\sum_iz_ic_i = 0 (z_i = charge on species; c_i = conc. of species)
i = F\sum z_iN_i = F(z_+N_+ + z_-N_-) — flux: diffusion, migration, convection
M_i = \frac{s_i(MW_i)Q}{nF} (total mass consumed/formed); Q = \int I(t)\,dt = I\cdot t [=] mAh [sign convention written as reduction rxn]
Total e⁻ = \frac{Q}{F}\cdot(6.023\times10^{23}); W = \int I(t)V(t)\,dt
Faradaic efficiency = \frac{Q_{desired}}{Q_{total}}\times100

Thermodynamics
Equilibrium / open-circuit potential: \Delta G_{rxn}^\circ = -nFU_{rxn}^\circ [U^\circ > 0, \Delta G < 0 → spontaneous]
\bar{\mu}_i = \mu_i + z_iF\Phi\;;\qquad \mu_i = f(N, T, P)\;;\qquad \bar{\mu}_{e^-} = -F\Phi = -FU^\circ\;;\quad \mu_{e^-} = 0\;;\quad \bar{\mu}_i = \mu_i\;(\text{for an uncharged species})
\eta = \Phi - U; \Phi > U → decreases energy of e⁻ (when a positive potential is applied) → e⁻ transfer from reactants to electrode → anodic process/oxidation.
V_{cell} = U_{right} - U_{left} @ equilibrium [V_{cell} > 0 for a galvanic cell].
Phase equilibrium (sketch: a cell β | S | ε with phases α and α′):

\bar{\mu}_i^\alpha = \bar{\mu}_i^\beta [adjacent phases have equal (electro)chemical potentials of the same species ‘i’] } same species, diff. phase rule
U = \Phi^{\alpha'} - \Phi^\alpha; FU = \mu_{e^-}^\alpha - \mu_{e^-}^{\alpha'} [left − right]
μ are G_f values from the NBS table @ 1 bar, 25 °C, 1 mol/kg
For a strong electrolyte → we assume complete dissociation & therefore can use the starting species.

Pourbaix diagram (sketch: V vs. SHE against pH — water stable between the O₂ line (1.23 V at pH 0) and the H₂ line (0 V), both sloping down; 0.816 and −0.828 V marked at pH 7 and 14; a vertical line has no V dependence (no e⁻), a horizontal line no pH dependence (no H⁺ or OH⁻); 0.401 V marked.)

M \leftrightarrow M^{n+} + ne^- [horizontal line]
M + nH_2O \leftrightarrow M(OH)_n + nH^+ + ne^-; M + nH_2O \leftrightarrow MO_n + 2nH^+ + ne^- } slanted
M + nH_2O \leftrightarrow MO_n^{n-} + nH^+ + ne^- [vertical]

Transcriber’s note: the “vertical” example as written still transfers electrons; a vertical Pourbaix line is a reaction with H⁺ but no e⁻.
Page 2 — kinetics and activity corrections
Kinetics: i = i_0\left[\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_AF\eta_s}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)\right]; \alpha_A = 1 - \alpha_c. \vec{i} = -\kappa\nabla\Phi; we want high κ, high current, low η.
Deviations from 1 mol/kg molalities:

Non-ionizing solutes/weak electrolytes: \mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + RT\ln\left(\frac{m_i}{m_0}\right) + RT\ln(\gamma_i) (m_i = molality of i)
Ionizing solutes/strong electrolytes: \mu_i = \mu_i^\circ + \nu RT\ln(m_A\gamma_{\pm}) + RT\ln(\nu_+^{\nu_+}\nu_-^{\nu_-}); \nu = \nu_+ + \nu_-
Solvents: \mu_0 = \mu_0^\circ - \nu(MW)RTm_A\phi (φ = osmotic coefficient)
Gases: \mu_A = \mu_A^\circ + RT\ln(p_A); p_A = x_APf_A
Solids: (pure) \mu_A = \mu_A^\circ; (alloys) \mu_A = \mu_A^\circ + RT\ln a_A (a_A = activity of A in alloy)

Deviations from T & P:

Pressure: U - U^\circ = -\frac{2.303RT}{nF}\log\left(\frac{P}{P^\circ}\right); \ln(x) = 2.303\log(x); @ n = 1, 25 °C ⇒ U - U^\circ = 60\text{ mV}\log\left(\frac{P}{P^\circ}\right)
Temp.: \Delta H = \Delta G - T\Delta S = -T^2\frac{\partial(\Delta G/T)}{\partial T} [Gibbs–Helmholtz]; closed system: \Delta U = \frac{S^\circ}{nF}(T - T^\circ) → small temp. changes

Transcriber’s note: \Delta H = \Delta G - T\Delta S is as written; the identity is \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S, i.e. \Delta H = \Delta G + T\Delta S.
pH vs. V — Nernst:
U = U^\circ - \frac{RT}{nF}\ln\left(\prod m_i^{s_i}\right)\;;\qquad U = U^\circ - \frac{0.05916}{n}\log\left[\prod\frac{m_{reduced}^{s_i}}{m_{oxidized}^{s_i}}\right]\;@\;T = 25\,°\mathrm{C}
Page 3 — transport
\frac{\partial c_i}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\underbrace{\left[-z_iu_iFc_i\nabla\Phi + c_i\vec{v} - D_i\nabla c_i\right]}_{N_i} + R_i\;\rightarrow\;\text{for strong electrolytes: }\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\nabla^2c - \vec{v}\cdot\nabla c
\vec{i} = F\sum z_i\vec{N}_i; \sum z_ic_i = 0.
Conductive diffusion: i = -\nabla\Phi\cdot\underbrace{\left[F^2\sum z_i^2u_ic_i\right]}_{\kappa} - F\sum z_iD_i\nabla c_i; \kappa = z_+c_+(\lambda_+ + \lambda_-).

↳ \nabla c = 0: i = -\kappa\nabla\Phi; R = \frac{\rho l}{A}; \kappa = \frac{1}{\rho}
↳ \nabla c \neq 0: \nabla\Phi = \frac{-i}{\kappa} - \underbrace{\frac{F}{\kappa}\sum z_iD_ic_i}_{\text{diffusion potential}} (z = charge of species i)

Nernst–Einstein relationship: D_i = RTu_i; D = \frac{z_+u_+D_- - z_-u_-D_+}{z_+u_+ - z_-u_-} = \frac{D_+D_-(z_+ - z_-)}{z_+D_+ - z_-D_-}
Transference number: t_+ = \frac{z_iF\vec{N}_i}{\vec{i}} = \frac{z_i^2u_ic_i}{\sum_jz_j^2u_jc_j} = \frac{z_+D_+}{z_+D_+ - z_-D_-} = 1 - t_-
Ion diffusion: D_+ = \frac{RT}{6\pi\eta r}; D_+ \propto \frac{1}{\eta}; D_+ \propto \frac{1}{r}.
(sketch: an electric field between − and + charges; two parallel plates with the potential V falling linearly with distance d; V = Ed.)

Q1. Cost of gold in the connector?

V_{Au} &= \pi\big(r_{pin} + Au_{thickness}\big)^2(l + 1\,\mu\text{m}) - \pi r_{pin}^2\,l \\
&= \pi\big[(0.5\,\text{mm} + 1\,\mu\text{m})^2\big](3\,\text{mm} + 1\,\mu\text{m})\,[?] - \pi\big[0.5\,\text{mm}\big]^2\cdot 4\,\text{mm} \\
&= \pi\big[(0.5\times10^{-3} + 1\times10^{-6})^2(3.001\times10^{-3})\big] - \pi(0.5\times10^{-3})^2\cdot4\times10^{-3} \\
&= 1.258\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}^3
\end{aligned}
Transcriber’s note: the length is written as 3 mm in the first term but 4 mm in the second, as in the original.
Total volume: 1.258\times10^{-11} m³ (1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2} m).
Mass of Au = density of Au · volume of Au:

@ LBMA UK [lbma.org.uk]: \rho_{Au} = 19.32 g/cm³ = 19.32\times10^{6} g/m³
↳ mass of Au = (19.32)(1.258\times10^{-5}) g
@ Monex Metals [monex.com/gold-prices/]: $61.38 g⁻¹

\text{Total cost of gold for 1 pin} = (61.38)(19.32)(1.258\times10^{-5}) = \$0.015 \;\xrightarrow{\times25}\; \boxed{\text{Cost of connector} \Rightarrow \$0.38}
Q2. Cost/L of Au electrolyte (conc. = 40 mM)?

Conc. = mol/L; 1 L of electrolyte has 40\times10^{-3} mol of Au.
MW_{Au} = 196.967 g/mol
Mass of Au (per L electrolyte): 40\times10^{-3}\cdot(196.967) = 7.878 g/L

\boxed{\text{Cost of electrolyte} = \frac{\$61.38}{\text{g}}\cdot\frac{7.878\ \text{g}}{\text{L}} = \$483.6}
Q3. Supporting electrolyte?
Adding another electrolyte will result in a reduction in efficiency of the E-cell, since another side reaction at the counter electrode is likely to take place. This may allow for greater control of the gold electroplating process?
Problem 1.4
Batteries vs fuel cells
Similarities:

Both batteries and fuel cells are devices that generate electricity via electrochemical reactions (i.e. transfer of electrons) at an electrode interface. Both technologies depend on a species being oxidised at the anode, resulting in a flow of electrons around an external circuit that can then be used as a voltage difference across a load.

Differences:

A battery needs to be replenished by charging, or adding in “electricity” to be stored for later use. A fuel cell needs chemical compounds (such as hydrogen in the case of a hydrogen fuel cell) in order to provide electricity.
A fuel cell operates as an open (continuous) system, where it can produce electricity via the flowing fuel (hydrogen) and the outflow of by-product (such as water); a battery, on the other hand, can provide DC current continuously until it runs out (i.e. all lithium ions have been intercalated back into the cathode and need to be transported back to the graphitic anode to convert the battery into a charged state). Therefore a battery can be considered a batch process, where it would ideally need to be stopped to charge again.

Links: energy.gov, usdoe, Visual Capitalist.

Half-cell reactions in electrochemical cells.
(a) \mathrm{Cu_{(s)}\,|\,CuSO_{4(aq)}\,\|\,CuSO_{4(aq)}\,|\,Cu_{(s)}}
