Problem 5
(a)

Electron-conducting: electrode 1, electrode 2, metal wire
Ion-conducting: liquid electrolyte
Insulating: glass beaker

(b) Since e⁻ are flowing from V1 to V2 across a load R1, it is a galvanic cell.

Oxidation @ V1 (loss of e⁻) → anode
Reduction @ V2 (gain of e⁻) → cathode
Current flows in the opposite direction of the e⁻ flow (V2 → V1).

(c)

When V1 ≈ V2, there is no resistance to flow; therefore we have max current (short circuit/closed circuit).
When V1 ≫ V2, there is min current (negligible), and we have max cell voltage (open circuit potential) → V_{OC}.
Max cell power is achieved at an intermediate value, where \boxed{0 \le V_1 \le V_{OC}}.

Problem 6
Bockris 1.1–1.5, 1.12.
a. What did you know about electrochemistry before reading the chapter?
I knew that electrochemistry is essential to understanding how electrochemical cells (such as batteries) function. There are two types of electrochemical cells: galvanic and electrolytic.
b. What were 3 things you learned by reading the chapter? Even if ideas were new, were the physical and chemical concepts familiar to you?

Firstly, it was illuminating to learn about the history of electrochemistry and its profound impact on technology years down the line, starting from Volta, Debye, Hückel, Faraday and Tafel.
The field of electrochemistry can be subdivided into:

Ionics: ions in solution, solid solutions. This sub-field deals with ion–solvent interaction, ion–ion interaction, ion transport, and ionic liquids.
Electrodics: the region between an electronic and an ionic conductor — the interfacial region: electrically controlled surface reactions.


An electrochemical reaction, in its bare form, is just a transfer of electrons across an interface that results in a chemical transformation. However, this transformation occurs in a fundamentally different way than a conventional chemical reaction: reactants no longer collide with each other but with separated “charge-transfer catalysts” (i.e. electrodes). The net reaction may be the same, but electrochemical reactions differ fundamentally from conventional chemical reactions. Furthermore, this spatial separation (among other things) gives electrochemical cells an edge over other reactors, since separation may not be an added cost in the production of chemicals.
The reaction rate is the rate at which the power source pushes out and receives back electrons after their journey around the circuit. Therefore one can easily control the electrochemical reaction rate: increase the potential across the power source!

Yes, the concepts were familiar, but it was helpful to read them in an interesting thought-experiment form to understand the fundamentals.
c. What were 2 things you are still confused about?
It is described that electrons are “physically” pushed from the power source into the electrode and then “overflow” into the solution to strike and neutralize ions in the layer of solution in contact with the metal. This may be a little misleading, since it describes the electrons as “flowing” and then building up to overflow into the solution.
My understanding is that the potential difference (due to the power source) raises (or lowers) the highest occupied molecular orbital in the electrode, so electrons want to transfer to the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital of ions in solution that is at a lower (or higher) energy. This results in a transfer of electrons. The higher the potential difference (from the power source), the greater the difference between these molecular orbitals, and the faster the electron wants to jump across to the lower energy.
d. Which of the actual or potential (section 1.12) applications of electrochemistry are most intriguing to you?
It was interesting to learn about humans’ electrical dependence increasing as time goes on, where entire towns and cities would be self-sufficient in producing all that is required from electrochemical devices — including even an “internal fuel-cell powered heart” and electrically functioning body parts that would lead to a “person–machine combination”, i.e. cyborgs. This seems pretty cool!

Problem 2.1
Debye length, with ionic strength I_s:
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon RT}{F^2\sum_j z_j^2c_{j\infty}}}\;;\qquad I_s = \frac{1}{2}\sum_j z_j^2c_{j\infty}\;\;\therefore\;\; \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon RT}{F^2\cdot2I_s}} = \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon RT}{2F^2}}\cdot I_s^{-1/2}\;\Rightarrow\;\lambda \propto I_s^{-1/2}
Net charge falls exponentially over distances on the order of the Debye length → i.e. the distances over which electroneutrality breaks down. (sketch: \lambda vs I_s, decaying as I_s^{-1/2}.)
@ pH 7, pure water, I_s = 1\times10^{-3} M [?]; assuming room temperature of 20 °C:
\kappa = \frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}\;;\qquad \varepsilon_{H_2O} = 78\cdot\left(8.854\times10^{-14}\,\frac{\text{F}}{\text{cm}}\right) = 78\times\left(8.85\times10^{-16}\,\frac{\text{F}}{\text{m}}\right)\,[?]
\therefore\;\lambda = \left(\frac{78\times8.854\times10^{-14}\times8.314\times293.15}{2\times(96485)^2}\right)^{1/2}\cdot\left(1\times10^{-3}\times10^{3}\right)^{-1/2}
\;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\lambda = 9.5\times10^{-9}\ \text{m}} \approx 9.5\ \text{nm}
@ same conditions but I_s = 1 M: \boxed{\lambda = 3.01\times10^{-11}\ \text{m}} \approx 0.03 nm.
As I_s\uparrow, \lambda\downarrow ✓

Really small value ✓
Significance → the Debye length just provides a general idea of the diffuse layer ↓ a really small value would mean that charge neutrality can only be broken over an nm scale, as the concentration of electrolyte (or I_s) increases. (This might have significance when dealing with double-layer analysis.)

Problem 2.2
↳ Conductivity of an electrolyte:
\kappa = F^2\sum_j z_j^2u_jc_j\quad[\Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}]\;;\qquad u_j = \frac{D_j}{RT}\;(\text{ionic mobility; } D_j = \text{diffusion coefficient},\; c_j = \text{ionic conc.})
Water dissociates into H⁺ (H₃O⁺) and OH⁻ → @ pH 7, 10^{-7} mol of H₃O⁺ & OH⁻ ions:
\kappa = F^2\left[\frac{(+1)^2\cdot10^{-7}\cdot9.310\times10^{-9}\cdot10^3}{(8.314)(293.15)} + \frac{(-1)^2\cdot10^{-7}\cdot5.270\times10^{-9}\cdot10^3}{(8.314)(293.15)}\right]
\kappa = 5.57\times10^{-4}\,[?]\ \Omega^{-1}\text{m}^{-1} \approx \boxed{0.056\ \text{mS/cm}}
↳ Sea water: Na⁺, Cl⁻; I_s = \frac{1}{2}\sum z_j^2c_\infty = 0.5 M; @ room temp. Assuming only Na⁺, Cl⁻ in seawater:
\kappa = F^2\cdot\left((+1)^2\frac{D_{Na^+}}{RT}c_{Na^+} + (-1)^2\frac{D_{Cl^-}}{RT}c_{Cl^-}\right)
If we assume D_{Na^+} \approx D_{Cl^-} \approx 10^{-9} m²/s (D_{Na^+} = 1.33\times10^{-9} m²/s; D_{Cl^-} = 2.03\times10^{-9} m²/s — a somewhat valid assumption):

= 38.2\times10^{-3}\,[?]\ \Omega^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}\;\text{or}\;\boxed{38\ \text{mS/cm}}\quad(1\ \text{S} = 1\ \text{ohm}^{-1})
0.5 M NaCl → 0.0479 S/cm ≈ 47.9 mS/cm (@ Engineering Toolbox).

Problem 2.9
(sketch: a 150 mm-long, 1 cm-wide strip; 10 nm resistive Ru substrate with a Cu layer plated over 100 mm of it at 10 mA/cm², current collector at the left end.)
Substrate → Ru (resistive).
(a) Substrate: R = \dfrac{\rho L}{A} (\rho = resistivity) [resistance is proportional to the no. of e⁻ that can pass through a cross-section of wire]
R = \frac{(71\times10^{-9})(150\times10^{-3})}{(10\times10^{-9})(1\times10^{-2})}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{R = 106.5\ \Omega}
(b) (sketch: 200 nm Cu on top of the 10 nm Ru, 1 cm wide, 150 mm long.)
R = \frac{\rho L}{A} = \frac{(17\times10^{-9})(150\times10^{-3})}{(200\times10^{-9})(1\times10^{-2})}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{R = 1.3\ \Omega}\qquad \rho_{Cu} = 17\ \text{n}\Omega\,\text{m}
Ideally we would have to consider the resistivity of both Cu & Ru, but because Cu is much more conductive (and thicker), we only need to consider this layer.
(c) Constant deposition rate = 10 mA cm⁻² (current density i); Ohm’s law: V = IR.
Shell balance (sketch: a slab element of width a and thickness a between x and x + \Delta x, with i_n entering through the top face; m = metal, s = substrate; V_m = \rho i_mL):
\big(i_m(x) - i_m(x + \Delta x)\big)a^2 = -i_n\Delta x^2 \;\Rightarrow\; a^2\frac{di_m}{dx^2}\,[?] = i_n\;;\qquad i_m = \frac{V_m}{\rho_sL_s}
\frac{a^2}{\rho_sL_s}\frac{d^2V_m}{dx^2} = i_n\;;\quad a^2 = L_s\cdot\lambda_s\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\frac{\lambda_s}{\rho_s}\left(\frac{d^2V_m}{dx^2}\right) = i_n}

\frac{d^2V_m}{dx^2} = \frac{\rho_s\,i_n}{\lambda_s} \neq f(x)\;;\qquad \frac{dV_m}{dx} = \frac{\rho_s\,i_n}{\lambda_s}x + c\;;\qquad V_m = \frac{\rho_s\,i_n}{2\lambda_s}x^2 + cx + d
BCs:

@ x = 0, V_m = 0 (potential at the current collector is zero)

\therefore\; V_m = \frac{\rho_s\,i_nL^2}{\lambda_s\,2}

Although current flow majorly happens via Cu ↓ so the Cu potential is imp/useful.


Problem 2.13
(circuit sketch: a cell V_{oc} in series with internal resistors R_1, R_2 and an external load R_{load}.)

Simple, linear circuit.
R_{load} \to \infty, V_{oc} = 1 V ← open circuit (we assume that this is the voltage output of the cell and is constant).

(a) R_1 = R_2 = 1\ \Omega; P_{load} = V_{load}\cdot I = I^2R_{load}; V_{load} = I\cdot R_{load}.
Linear/series circuit: R_{total} = \underbrace{R_1 + R_2}_{2\,\Omega} + R_{load}, I = \dfrac{V_{oc}}{R_{total}}; V_{total} = V_1 + V_2 + V_{load}.
Bounds of I:

@ R_{load} = 1000\ \Omega, V_{load} = 1 V (very high R) → open circuit
@ R_{load} = 0.001\ \Omega, V_{load} = 0.01 V (very low R) → short circuit

Plotting using discretized values (plots: I and V_{load} vs R_{load} — I falls from 0.5 A while V_{load} rises to 1 V; and the same vs R_{load}/R_{cell}, where I falls linearly and V_{load} rises linearly).

★ The graphs show the necessary trend: max power occurs at a specific R_{load}, well below that at V_{oc}.
(c) Current at which P_{max}? P_{load} = V_{load}\cdot I; V_{load} = I\,R_{load}:
P_{load} = I^2R_{load} = \frac{V_{oc}^2}{(2 + R_{load})^2}R_{load}\;;\qquad P_{load} = \frac{V_{load}^2}{R_{load}}
\frac{\partial P_{load}}{\partial R_{load}} = V_{oc}\left[\frac{(2 + R_{load})^2 - R_{load}\cdot2(2 + R_{load})}{(2 + R_{load})^4}\right] = \cdots = \frac{(2 - R_{load})V_{oc}}{(2 + R_{load})^3}
P_{max} \Rightarrow \frac{\partial P_{load}}{\partial R_{load}} = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{(2 - R_{load})V_{oc}}{(2 + R_{load})^3} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; R_{load} = 2\ \Omega \text{ @ } P_{max}
\therefore\; I_{max} = \frac{V_{oc}}{(2 + R_{load}^{max})} = \boxed{\frac{V_{oc}}{4} = I_{max}}
Problem 3.1
Given k [s⁻¹] & T [°C]. Arrhenius relationship (A_0 = pre-exponential factor):
k = A_0\exp\left(\frac{-E_A}{RT}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\text{linearized}}\; \ln k = \underbrace{\ln(A_0)}_{y\text{-intercept}} - \underbrace{\frac{E_A}{R}}_{\text{gradient}}\left(\frac{1}{T}\right)
Plotting \ln k vs 1/T (plot: linear fit y = -6018.7x + 20.727, R^2 = 1; assuming the last point is a typo and should be 10,000) gives m = -6018.7, c = 20.727:
\Rightarrow -E_a = -6018.7(R)\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{E_a = 50039.5\ \text{J}}
To achieve a 10× reaction-rate increase (i.e. increasing the rate constant) [r \propto k] (room T = 20 °C):
\frac{k_{new}}{k_0} = 10 \Rightarrow \frac{A_0\exp\left[\frac{-E_a}{RT_{new}}\right]}{A_0\exp\left[\frac{-E_a}{RT_{room}}\right]} = 10\;\Rightarrow\;\exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{RT_{new}} + \frac{E_a}{RT_{room}}\right) = 10
\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_{room}} - \frac{1}{T_{new}}\right) = \ln10\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{1}{T_{new}} = \frac{1}{T_{room}} - \frac{R\ln10}{E_a} = \frac{1}{293.15} - \frac{8.314\ln(10)}{50039.5}
T_{new} = 330.18\ \text{K} \approx 57\ °\text{C}

Problem 3.2
Tafel plot — large overpotential (\eta \gg 0):
i = i_0\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right) \;\xrightarrow{\text{linearize}}\; \log_{10}i = \underbrace{\log_{10}i_0}_{c} + \underbrace{\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\log_{10}(e)}{RT}\right)}_{m}\eta
Plotting \log_{10}i (y) vs \eta (x) (inverse Tafel plot; plot: overpotential vs log(i), fit y = 8.7388x + 1.0014, R^2 = 0.9997): m = 8.7388 @ room temp 293.15 K.
\frac{\alpha_aF}{RT}\log_{10}(e) = 8.7388\;\Rightarrow\;\alpha_a = \frac{(8.7388)(8.314)(293.15)}{(96485)(0.4343)} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\alpha_a = 0.508}

Problem 8
\begin{aligned}
&(1) \quad \mathrm{Cu \rightleftharpoons Cu^+ + e^-}\quad(\text{RDS}) \\
&(2) \quad \mathrm{Cu^+ + 2Cl^- \rightleftharpoons CuCl_2^-}
\end{aligned}
\qquad i = f(V, c_n)
① Electrochemical: r_1 = k_{1,a}\exp\left(\dfrac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right)[\mathrm{Cu}] - k_{1,c}[\mathrm{Cu^+}]\exp\left(\dfrac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right)
② Chemical: r_2 = k_f[\mathrm{Cu^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2 - k_r[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]
r_1 is the RDS, r_2 is QE:
r_2 \approx 0 \Rightarrow k_f[\mathrm{Cu^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2 = k_r[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]\;\Rightarrow\;[\mathrm{Cu^+}] = \frac{k_r}{k_f}\frac{[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2}
r_{net} = r_1 = k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right) - k_{1,c}[\mathrm{Cu^+}]\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right]
\frac{i}{F} = k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right) - \frac{k_{1,c}k_r}{k_f}\frac{[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2}\exp\left(\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right)\quad\to\text{matches B-V kinetics (w/ 1 }e^-\text{ transfer)}
Solving for the exchange current: i = 0 when V = U. Let Z = \dfrac{k_{1,c}k_r}{k_f}\dfrac{[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2}:
k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)FU}{RT}\right) = Z\exp\left(\frac{-\beta FU}{RT}\right)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}{Z} = \exp\left(\frac{-\beta FU}{RT} - \frac{(1-\beta)FU}{RT}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{FU}{RT}\right)
\frac{FU}{RT} = -\ln\left(\frac{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}{Z}\right)\;\Rightarrow\;U = \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{Z}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}\right)\qquad\left[\exp\left(\frac{FU}{RT}\right) = \frac{Z}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}\right]
\eta = V - U; V = \eta + U → plugging into the original expression:
\begin{aligned}
\frac{i}{F} &= k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)F(\eta + U)}{RT}\right) - Z\exp\left(\frac{-\beta F(\eta + U)}{RT}\right) \\
&= k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)F\eta}{RT}\right)\exp\left(\frac{FU}{RT}\right)\exp\left(\frac{-\beta FU}{RT}\right) - Z\exp\left(\frac{-\beta FU}{RT}\right)\exp\left(\frac{-\beta F\eta}{RT}\right) \\
&= \frac{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]\,Z}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}\exp\left(\frac{-\beta FU}{RT}\right)\left[\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)F\eta}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-\beta F\eta}{RT}\right)\right] \\
&= Z\exp\left(\frac{-\beta F}{RT}\cdot\frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{Z}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}\right)\right)[\;\cdots\;] = Z\exp(-\beta)\frac{Z}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}[\;\cdots\;]
\end{aligned}
\boxed{i = \frac{Z^2\exp(-\beta)}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}\left[\exp\left(\frac{(1-\beta)F\eta}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-\beta F\eta}{RT}\right)\right]}
i_0 = \left[\frac{k_{1,c}k_r}{k_f}\frac{[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]}{[\mathrm{Cl^-}]^2}\right]^2\cdot\frac{1}{k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}]}\exp(-\beta)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\boxed{i_0 \propto \frac{[\mathrm{CuCl_2^-}]^2}{[\mathrm{Cl^-}]^4[\mathrm{Cu}]}}
Transcriber’s note: in the last steps the original drops the \ln when simplifying the exponential (writing \exp(-\beta)\cdot Z/k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}] rather than (Z/k_{1,a}[\mathrm{Cu}])^{-\beta}); transcribed as written.

Question 1
Hemicylinder electrode [W 5.6] (sketch: a hemicylinder WE of radius r_0 with the CE at r_{CE}, a finite distance away from the WE).
(a) Assuming uniform composition, \nabla^2\phi = 0. In cylindrical geometry:
\nabla^2\phi = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial\theta^2} + \frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial z^2} = 0
↳ Considering only the radial direction we get \dfrac{1}{r}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right) = 0, with BCs: \phi = V @ r = r_0; \phi = 0 @ r = r_c.
(b) Solve for the ohmic resistance (R_\Omega). Obtaining the \phi profile:
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; r\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r} = c_1 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r} = \frac{c_1}{r} \;\Rightarrow\; \phi = c_1\ln r + c_2
@ r = r_0, \phi = V ⇒ V = c_1\ln r_0 + c_2; @ r = r_{CE}, \phi = 0 ⇒ 0 = c_1\ln r_{CE} + c_2. Subtracting:
V = c_1\ln\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}} \;\Rightarrow\; c_1 = \frac{V}{\ln\left(\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}}\right)}\;;\qquad c_2 = \frac{-V\ln r_{CE}}{\ln\left(\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}}\right)}
\therefore\;\phi = \frac{V}{\ln\left(\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}}\right)}\ln r - \frac{V}{\ln\left(\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}}\right)}\ln r_{CE} = \frac{V}{\ln\left(\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}}\right)}\ln\left(\frac{r}{r_{CE}}\right)
R_\Omega = V/i_\Omega (assuming no charge-transfer resistance), with
i_\Omega = -\kappa\left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right|_{r=r_0}\;;\qquad \left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right|_{r=r_0} = \frac{c_1}{r_0} = \frac{V}{\ln\left(\frac{r_0}{r_{CE}}\right)}\cdot\frac{1}{r_0}
\therefore\;R_\Omega = \frac{V}{-\kappa V\frac{1}{r_0\ln(r_0/r_{CE})}} = \boxed{\frac{r_0}{\kappa}\ln\left(\frac{r_{CE}}{r_0}\right) = R_\Omega}\quad(\text{in }\Omega\,\text{cm}^2\,[?])
WE surface area: \pi r_0l (l = length of cylinder):
R'_\Omega = \frac{R_\Omega}{\pi r_0l} = \boxed{\frac{1}{\kappa\pi l}\ln\left(\frac{r_{CE}}{r_0}\right) = R'_\Omega}\quad(\text{in }\Omega\,[?])
Transcriber’s note: the margin units read “in Ω” for R_\Omega and “in Ω cm²” for R'_\Omega; they look swapped, so they are shown here the other way round with [?].
As r_{CE} \to \infty: R_\Omega = \dfrac{r_0}{\kappa}\ln\left(\dfrac{r_{CE}}{r_0}\right) \Rightarrow \lim_{r_{CE}\to\infty}R_\Omega = \infty ← if the CE is at an infinite distance away, there is infinite ohmic resistance.
(c)

For 1D: R_\Omega = \dfrac{L}{\kappa} → this assumes that the CE is at distance L.
For hemispherical: R_\Omega = \dfrac{r_0}{\kappa} → this assumes the CE is at ∞.
R_\Omega for hemicylindrical assumes r_{CE} at a finite distance away ↓ comparing hemisphere to hemicylinder: \ln\left(\frac{r_{CE}}{r_0}\right) \to 0 as r_0 \to \infty.



                  
                  So cylindrical approaches spherical behaviour for large r_0.
                  
                

Question 2 [W 6.2]
Linear & anodic Tafel kinetics.
(a) R_{ct} = \left.\dfrac{\partial\eta_s}{\partial i}\right|_{i=i_{avg}}. Cathodic Tafel: i = -i_0\exp\left(\dfrac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right):
\frac{\partial i}{\partial\eta_s} = -i_0\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF}{RT}\right)\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right) = \frac{\alpha_cF\,i_0}{RT}\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)
@ i = i_{avg}: i_{avg} = -i_0\exp\left(\dfrac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right) \Rightarrow \exp\left(\dfrac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right) = -\dfrac{i_{avg}}{i_0}
\therefore\;\left.\frac{\partial i}{\partial\eta_s}\right|_{i_{avg}} = \frac{\alpha_cF\,i_0}{RT}\cdot\left(-\frac{i_{avg}}{i_0}\right) = -\frac{\alpha_cF}{RT}i_{avg}
\;\Rightarrow\;
R_{ct} = \left(\left.\frac{\partial i}{\partial\eta_s}\right|_{i=i_{avg}}\right)^{-1} = \boxed{\frac{RT\,i_{avg}}{-\alpha_cF} = R_{ct}}\quad\leftarrow R_{ct}\text{ for cathodic Tafel}
Transcriber’s note: as written; inverting the derivative gives RT/(-\alpha_cF\,i_{avg}).
For B-V kinetics:
i = i_0\left[\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta_s}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)\right]\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{i_{avg}}{i_0} = \exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta}{RT}\right)
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial i}{\partial\eta_s} &= i_0\left(\frac{\alpha_aF}{RT}\right)\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta_s}{RT}\right) - i_0\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF}{RT}\right)\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right) = i_0\left(\frac{F}{RT}\right)\left[\alpha_a\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta_s}{RT}\right) + \alpha_c\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)\right] \\
&= \frac{Fi_0}{RT}\left[\alpha_a\left(\frac{i_{avg}}{i_0} + \exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)\right) + \alpha_c\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)\right] = \frac{Fi_0}{RT}\left[\alpha_a\frac{i_{avg}}{i_0} + (\alpha_a + \alpha_c)\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta_s}{RT}\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
\boxed{R_{ct} = \left(\left.\frac{\partial i}{\partial\eta}\right|_{i=i_{avg}}\right)^{-1} = \frac{RT}{Fi_0\left[\alpha_a\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right) + \alpha_c\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta}{RT}\right)\right]}}\quad\leftarrow\text{B-V kinetics } R_{ct}
(b) Graphs shown (plot: B-V kinetics — current density (mA/cm²) vs overpotential from −0.1 to 0.1 V, rising exponentially to ≈350 mA/cm²).
(c) Resistance vs \log(i) (three plots of resistance vs \log_{10}(i) for i_0 = 1, 0.1 and 10, each comparing the linear, anodic Tafel, cathodic Tafel and B-V forms of R_{ct}).

From the above graphs, it seems that the anodic Tafel approximation matches B-V the closest; linear may be accurate only at small current densities but is independent of i.
Cathodic diverges at first but then approaches B-V/anodic at higher i_0 values.
At higher i_0, the differences reduce (apart from cathodic).

Question 3 (W 6.3)
Hull cell (sketch: a trapezoidal cell — the CE across the top, the WE along the sloped bottom at angle \theta, height h_H above the WE and length L_H; with h' = h + (K - h') and an offset L/\tan\theta).
Primary current distribution (Wa = 0) (current density in the x-direction is zero).
Current density only in the y-direction: \nabla^2\phi = 0, with i = -\kappa\nabla\phi (only y-dependence):
\cancelto{0}{\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x^2}} + \frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y} = c_1 \;\Rightarrow\; \phi = c_1y + c_2
BCs (only the y-direction is needed): (i) @ y = h', \phi = 0; (ii) @ y = K - h', \phi = V.
V = c_1(K - h') + c_2\;;\quad 0 = c_1h' + c_2\;\Rightarrow\; V = c_1[K - h' - h']\;\Rightarrow\; c_1 = \frac{V}{[K - h' - h']} = \frac{V}{[K - h - K + h']}\,[?] = \frac{V}{-h}
i = -\kappa\nabla\phi = -\kappa\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y} = +\kappa\frac{V}{h}\;;\qquad i_{avg} = \int_0^L i\,dx = \frac{\kappa V\cdot L}{h}
\therefore\;\boxed{\frac{i}{i_{avg}} = \frac{\kappa V}{h}\cdot\frac{h}{\kappa VL} = \frac{1}{L}}
(crossed out: i_{avg} = \kappa V/(h + L/\tan\theta) using the total "y" length, giving \dfrac{i}{i_{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{h}\left(h + \dfrac{L}{\tan\theta}\right) = 1 + \dfrac{L}{h\tan\theta}.)
Plotting i/i_{avg} for h/L = 0.7385 & \theta = 0.22\pi we get the following graphical representation (plot: Hull cell vs straight-current approximation, i/i_{avg} vs x/L — the Hull-cell curve rises from ≈0 and diverges near x/L = 1, while the straight-current line is flat at ≈0.5).
Question 4
Microfluidic echem cell; 2 line electrodes (sketch: a channel of height 2h between y = 0 and y = 2h, fluid flowing in x; WE on the bottom wall and CE on the top wall, both from x = 0 to x = L).
Equation 4.5 [?]:
\frac{3U}{h}y\frac{\partial c_{lim}}{\partial x} = D_{lim}\frac{\partial^2c_{lim}}{\partial y^2}
Similarity transformation:
\xi = y\left(\frac{U}{3hD_{lim}x}\right)^{1/3}\;;\qquad \xi^3 = y^3\left(\frac{U}{3hD_{lim}x}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{Uy^3}{h}\,[?] = \xi^3\,3D_{lim}x
As shown in class:
\frac{\partial c}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\cdot\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial x}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial\xi}{\partial x} = y\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{1/3}\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)x^{-4/3} = \frac{-\xi}{3x}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\partial c}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\cdot\left(\frac{-\xi}{3x}\right)
Similarly,
\frac{\partial c}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\cdot\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial y}\;;\qquad \frac{\partial\xi}{\partial y} = \left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3} = \frac{\xi}{y}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{\partial c}{\partial y} = \left(\frac{\xi}{y}\right)\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}
We need:
\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial c}{\partial y}\right) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\xi}{y}\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\right) = \frac{\xi}{y}\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\right) + \frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\cancelto{0}{\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\left[\frac{U}{3hDx}\right]^{1/3}\right)}
= \frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\xi^2}\left(\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial y}\right)^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\xi^2}\left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{2/3}
Plugging into the original PDE and dividing by \left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{2/3}:
\frac{3U}{h}y\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\left(\frac{-\xi}{3x}\right) = D\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\xi^2}\left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{2/3}
\;\Rightarrow\;
3y\underbrace{\left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3}}_{\xi/y}\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}(-\xi) = \frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\xi^2}
\therefore\;\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\xi^2} + 3\xi^2\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi} = 0 \;\xrightarrow{\text{since only change w/ 1 var}}\; \boxed{\frac{d^2c}{d\xi^2} + 3\xi^2\frac{dc}{d\xi} = 0}
Transcriber’s note: the original writes 3\xi^3 in this ODE; 3\xi^2 follows from the step above and matches the e^{-x^3} solution below.
BCs:

@ x = 0, c_{lim} = c_\infty ⇒ \xi \to \infty: c_{lim} = c_\infty
@ y = \infty, c_{lim} = c_\infty ⇒ \xi \to \infty: c_{lim} = c_\infty
@ y = 0, c_{lim} = 0 ⇒ @ \xi = 0: c_{lim} = 0

Using the Frobenius solution:
\frac{c_{lim}}{c_\infty} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(4/3)}\int_0^{\xi}e^{-x^3}\,dx
N_y = -D\left.\frac{\partial c}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0} = -D\left.\frac{\partial c}{\partial\xi}\right|_{\xi=0}\left.\frac{\partial\xi}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0} = \frac{-Dc_\infty}{\Gamma(4/3)}\underbrace{\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\left(\int_0^{\xi}e^{-x^3}dx\right)\bigg|_{\xi=0}}_{\text{F.T.C.}}\left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3}
N_y = \frac{-Dc_\infty}{\Gamma(4/3)}e^{-\xi^3}\Big|_{\xi=0}\left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3} = \frac{-c_\infty D}{\Gamma(4/3)}\left(\frac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3}
Find the current: \dfrac{si}{nF} = -N_y \Rightarrow \dfrac{si}{nF} = \dfrac{Dc_\infty}{\Gamma(4/3)}\left(\dfrac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3}
i_{avg} = \left(\frac{nF}{s}\frac{Dc_\infty}{\Gamma(4/3)}\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{1/3}\int_0^Lx^{-1/3}dx\right)\frac{1}{L} = \frac{nF}{s}\left(\frac{3}{2}\frac{D^{2/3}}{\Gamma(4/3)}\right)c_\infty\left(\frac{U}{3h}\right)^{1/3}L^{-1/3}
\frac{i}{i_{avg}} = \frac{\frac{nF}{s}\frac{D^{2/3}c_\infty}{\Gamma(4/3)}\left(\frac{U}{3h}\right)^{1/3}x^{-1/3}}{\frac{nF}{s}\frac{D^{2/3}c_\infty}{\Gamma(4/3)}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\frac{U}{3h}\right)^{1/3}L^{-1/3}}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\boxed{\frac{i}{i_{avg}} = \frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{L}{x}\right)^{1/3}}
Question 5
\delta = \frac{-Dc_\infty}{N}\;;\qquad \frac{\delta}{\delta_{avg}} = \frac{-Dc_\infty/N}{-Dc_\infty/N_{avg}} = \frac{N_{avg}}{N}
From the previous part, N_y = \dfrac{-c_\infty D}{\Gamma(4/3)}\left(\dfrac{U}{3hDx}\right)^{1/3}:
\therefore\;\delta = \frac{-Dc_\infty}{-c_\infty D}\Gamma(4/3)\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{-1/3}x^{1/3}
\delta_{avg}(x) = \left(\int_0^L\Gamma(4/3)\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{-1/3}x^{1/3}dx\right)\frac{1}{L} = \Gamma(4/3)\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{-1/3}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)x^{4/3}\Big|_0^L\cdot\frac{1}{L} = \Gamma(4/3)\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{-1/3}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)L^{1/3}
\therefore\;\frac{\delta}{\delta_{avg}} = \frac{\Gamma(4/3)\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{-1/3}x^{1/3}}{\Gamma(4/3)\left(\frac{U}{3hD}\right)^{-1/3}\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)L^{1/3}} = \boxed{\frac{4}{3}\left(\frac{x}{L}\right)^{1/3} = \frac{\delta}{\delta_{avg}}}
(A crossed-out alternative via N_{y,avg}/N_y gave \frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{x}{L}\right)^{1/3}.)
Plotting i/i_{avg} & \delta/\delta_{avg} (plot: line electrode analysis vs x/L — the current density falls from ≈1.8 to ≈0.67 while the boundary layer rises from ≈0.5 to ≈1.33, crossing near x/L \approx 0.35).
Question 6
Levich plot @ a specific overpotential → find the diffusion coefficient:
m = 0.62\left(\frac{nFc_\infty}{s_{lim}}\right)\nu^{-1/6}D^{2/3}\;\Rightarrow\;\left[\frac{m}{0.62}\nu^{1/6}\left(\frac{s_{lim}}{nFc_\infty}\right)\right]^{3/2} = D

c_\infty → conc. of H₂ [?] in the bulk solution: \dfrac{0.00016\ \text{g H}_2}{100\ \text{g H}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{0.00016\ \text{g H}_2}{100\ \text{mL H}_2\text{O}} = \dfrac{0.00016\times\frac{1}{2.02}}{100\times10^{-6}} = 0.792 mol/m³
\nu → kinematic viscosity (can be approximated close to water, since 0.1 M K₂SO₄ is used). From Engineering Toolbox: \nu = 8.92\times10^{-7} m²/s.
n = 2, F = 96485, s_{lim} = 2; units: \text{mA/cm}^2 = \dfrac{10^{-3}}{(10^{-2})^2}\,\text{A/m}^2.

From the Levich plot (plot: Levich plot analysis, -i_{lim} (A/m²) vs \Omega^{1/2}, fit y = 1.1499x - 0.8706, R^2 = 0.9949): slope = 1.1499.
\therefore\;\boxed{D = 3.67\times10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}}\;;\qquad D_{lit} = 4.58\times10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}
— within a factor of 0.8!
Question 7
Koutecký–Levich analysis; magnitude of charge-transfer resistance vs MT resistance in the system.
From the plot of -\dfrac{1}{i_{lim}} vs \dfrac{1}{\Omega^{1/2}} (plot: Koutecký–Levich, fit y = 0.7306x + 0.0325, R^2 = 0.9691) we get m = 0.7306, c = 0.0325:
\therefore\;\frac{1}{i_{lim}} = \frac{1}{i_K} + \frac{1}{i_D}\;;\qquad \frac{1}{i_K} = 0.0325 \Rightarrow i_K = 30.77\ \text{A/m}^2

For 100 rpm: \dfrac{1}{i_K} = 0.0325, \dfrac{1}{i_D} = 0.2175
For 2500 rpm: \dfrac{1}{i_K} = 0.0325, \dfrac{1}{i_D} = 0.03417

↕ Similar to summing up resistors:

→ As rpm ↑, the mass-transfer resistance decreases (while the charge-transfer resistance stays the same).
→ The charge-transfer resistance is always smaller than the mass-transfer resistance (i.e. always in diffusion limitations for the range of rpms in the demo).

m = \frac{1}{(0.62)D^{2/3}\nu^{-1/6}c_\infty\cdot F\cdot n}\;\Rightarrow\;D^{2/3} = \frac{1}{(0.62)\,m\,\nu^{-1/6}c_\infty\cdot F\cdot n}\;\Rightarrow\;D = \left(\frac{1}{(0.62)\,m\,\nu^{-1/6}c_\infty\cdot F\cdot n}\right)^{3/2}
\boxed{D = 1.68\times10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\;;\qquad D_{lit} = 4.58\times10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}}
These are off by a factor of 2.73 ↳ possibly due to contributions from the ORR occurring simultaneously.
Question 8
(a)
\Delta r = O\left(\sqrt{\frac{D\nu^{1/2}}{\Omega^{3/2}r_0}}\right)\,[?]\;;\qquad D = 10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2\,\text{s}^{-1},\;\nu = 10^{-2}\,[?]\ \text{cm}^2\,\text{s}^{-1}
rpm → rad/s: 1\ \text{rpm} = \dfrac{1\ \text{rotation}}{1\ \text{min}} = \dfrac{2\pi}{60}\dfrac{\text{rad}}{\text{s}}.
The plotted graphs allow us to calculate the required r_0 value (plots: \Delta r/r_0 vs r_0 at 50 rpm and at 900 rpm, each with a horizontal line at 0.01; the crossing is at r_0 = 0.094 [?] for 50 rpm and r_0 = 0.022 [?] for 900 rpm).
rpm ↑ → r_0↓ (a smaller r_0 is needed to go below the 0.01 ratio).
(b) Solving for the \Delta r order given r_0, \Omega & \nu gives:
\Delta r^{100\,\text{rpm}} = 7.67\times10^{-4}\;;\qquad \Delta r^{3600\,\text{rpm}} = 5.21\times10^{-5}
↓ Higher rpm reduces the edge-effect region.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 1-2) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Electrochemical engineering
Electrochemical engineering → translating fundamental principles (of electrochemical transformations) to an applied/industrial context.
Why?

CO₂-free (green e^-) → decarbonization
Driven by e^- rather than heat

How?

Concepts: thermodynamics, kinetics, transport; charge, voltage, conservation of charge → fundamentals
Current distributions, rotating electrodes, electroanalytical methods → techniques and modelling to test and understand electrochemical systems
Porous electrodes/batteries, electrocatalysis, decarbonization → applied systems

Goal?

A technical working knowledge of electrochemical phenomena for e^--driven processes.

Electrochemical reactions


                  
                  Definition 
                  
                

Electrochemical reaction: a change in the molecular identity of a chemical species in which one or more electrons are a reactant or product.


e.g. \mathrm{2Cl^-_{(aq)} \rightarrow Cl_{2(g)} + 2e^-} (the reaction does not occur unless e^- transfer happens).
↳ e^- transfer to/from an electrode (conducting/semi-conducting) to a different phase; the electrons have to be free e^-.
↳ Electrochemical reactions are inherently heterogeneous.
Sketch: a Pt electrode with \mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+}} at its surface, releasing e^- into the electrode.

Driving force: thermodynamics (electrochemical potential)
Proximity: physics
Transport: the interfacial region

↳ Charge neutrality: it takes an enormous amount of energy to separate charge. Therefore we can assume charge neutrality everywhere, except over very short distances.
↓ This means that there must be another electrode.
↳ Charge transfer happens at each electrode (“half reactions”).
↳ Half-reactions are chemically independent.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 3) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Electroneutrality!
Sketch: two electrodes in an electrolyte — \mathrm{Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2} at one, \mathrm{H_2O \rightarrow OH^- + H_2} at the other — with 2e^- flowing through the external circuit and positive charge moving through the electrolyte.
Electrolyte: the phase through which ions can move. It can be:

Liquid (aqueous or organic)
Polymeric (Nafion)
Solid (ceramic with oxide vacancies, or a solid-oxide electrolyte)

Example: the chlor-alkali process
(OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.)
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{2Cl^-_{(aq)}} &\rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_{2(g)} + 2e^-} && \text{(oxidation)} \\
\mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^-} &\rightarrow \mathrm{2OH^- + H_{2(g)}} && \text{(reduction)} \\
\hline
\mathrm{2NaCl_{(aq)} + 2H_2O} &\rightarrow \mathrm{Cl_{2(g)} + 2NaOH + H_{2(g)}}
\end{aligned}
Shorthand:
\mathrm{Pt\,|\,Cl^-_{(aq)}\,||\,NaOH_{(aq)}\,|\,H_2, Cl_{2(g)}\,|\,Pt_{(s)}}
where a single bar ”|” is a phase boundary and the double bar ”||” is a transition to a different electrolyte composition.
Example: Alessandro Volta — the first battery in the 1790s
Sketches:

A cell with a Zn electrode and an Ag electrode in H₂O/NaCl, with \mathrm{H_2O \rightarrow 2OH^-} at Zn and \mathrm{Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2} at Ag — crossed out (wrong assignment of reduction/oxidation).
The corrected cell: at the Zn electrode \mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+}} (oxidation); at the Ag electrode \mathrm{Ag^{2+} \rightarrow Ag} (reduction); \mathrm{Na^+} and \mathrm{Cl^-} migrate through the separator; e^- flows from Zn to Ag through the external circuit.

\mathrm{AgO + H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow Ag + 2OH^-}\;;\qquad \mathrm{Zn + 2OH^- \rightarrow ZnO + H_2O + 2e^-}
Wind + solar → enable electrochemical processes in manufacturing to take place.


                  
                  Note 
                  
                

Valency 2^+ \rightarrow 3^+ (lost an e^-) → oxidation; i.e. the oxidation number increasing → oxidation. e^- being released (on the right-hand side) → oxidation.

                  Announcements 
                  
                


HW1 (due Thursday)
HW0, part 1 → course evaluation (due Friday)



Heterogeneous reactions
↳ Heterogeneous reaction (e^- transfer between electrodes):

→ written as half-reactions (oxidation/reduction)
→ shorthand notation for an electrochemical cell

Example 1: chlor-alkali
\mathrm{2Cl^-_{(aq)} \rightarrow Cl_{2(g)} + 2e^-}\;;\qquad \mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^- + H_{2(g)}}
\mathrm{Pt\,|\,Cl_{2(g)}\,|\,Cl^-, Na^+\,||\,Na^+, OH^-, H_2O\,|\,H_{2(g)}\,|\,Pt}
The ”||” denotes a change in composition (although in the same phase) — a separator.
Example 2: a Zn and Ag electrode cell with AgCl:
\mathrm{Zn_{(s)}\,|\,Zn^+, Cl^-\,|\,AgCl_{(s)}\,|\,Ag}
Electrochemical concepts and conventions

At least 2 electrodes:

↳ Anode → oxidation reaction (“An-Ox”): \mathrm{R \rightarrow O + e^-} (the reductant gets oxidized)
↳ Cathode → reduction reaction: \mathrm{O + e^- \rightarrow R}


Electrodes must be connected via an electrolyte (any phase in which ions can be transported).
The transition between electric/ionic conduction occurs at the electrode/electrolyte interface.
Electroneutrality states that the currents at the electrodes must be equal and opposite:

\boxed{I_{anode} + I_{cathode} = 0}\qquad\text{Convention: } I_{anode} > 0
Cell potentials (galvanic and electrolytic cells)
↳ Galvanic cell: the half-reactions sum to an overall spontaneous reaction (\Delta G < 0).

We can extract work from these types of cells (batteries).
e.g. the H₂ fuel cell: \mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}

↳ Electrolytic cell: electrical power from an external source is required to make the reaction proceed (\Delta G > 0).

We put work into the cell.
e.g. charging a battery, water electrolysis.

Sketch (galvanic): cathode and anode in a cell with internal resistance R_{cell}, connected through an external load R_{load}; potentials V_1 (at the cathode metal), V_2, V_3 (in solution), V_4 (at the anode metal), V_5, V_6 (across the load).

The anode and cathode are at different potentials, since different reactions occur at them.
I_{anode} → positive (convention) \therefore current flows opposite to electrons.
Ohm’s law: V = IR, so (V_6 - V_5) = IR_{load}.

↳ If R_{load} \gg R_{cell} → no current in the external circuit. ↳ (V_6 - V_5) then defines the open-circuit potential (V_{OC}) — measured by connecting with a large known resistor and measuring a small current.
↳ No resistance to flow [(V_6 - V_5) \sim 0]: maximum current but no work extracted → short circuit / closed circuit.
↳ Therefore, to achieve maximum power (P = I(V_6 - V_5)), we need an intermediate load (sketches: I falls and \Delta V = V_6 - V_5 rises with R_{load}/R_{cell}; P vs R_{load}/R_{cell} has a maximum).


If the wires are conductive: (1) V_6 \approx V_1, (2) V_5 \approx V_4.
At open circuit, V_2 \approx V_3.

Sketch: potential vs position in the circuit for

a flowing galvanic cell: 0 \leq (V_6 - V_5) \leq V_{OC} — the potential difference is reduced;
an electrolytic cell: V_{OC} \leq (V_6 - V_5) \leq \infty — (V_6 - V_5) is increased.

Electrolytic cell (sketch: a power supply (PS) between the electrodes):

Requires a power supply (PS).
The current is reversed.
Now the RHS electrode is the cathode.
The PS increases (V_6 - V_5) > V_{OC}; current flows from V_6 \rightarrow V_5 (high to low) [opposite to the potential] ↓ at open circuit there is no net current flow, I = 0.

→ Cathode and anode switching is confusing. Sketch: I vs \Delta V = V_6 - V_5 — the anodic current is positive for \Delta V < V_{OC}, crosses zero at V_{OC}, and becomes cathodic beyond.
So, even though I_{anode} > 0, there can be both oxidation and reduction reactions occurring; just the net should be oxidation.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 6-8) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Open-circuit potential, V_{OC}: the potential difference between electrodes when R_{load} \gg R_{cell}, I = 0.
Faraday’s law of electrolysis
1) The mass of product formed/consumed in an electrochemical reaction is directly proportional to the charge passed: m/Q = z (sketch: m vs Q lines for different materials — linear regardless of material).
2) For a given amount of charge passed on electrodes of different materials, the amount of product formed/consumed is proportional to the electrochemical equivalent weight of that product, E = \dfrac{M}{n\cdot N_A}:
m = xE = \frac{xM\cdot e}{nN_A\cdot e}
where x is the amount of e^- passed, e is the fundamental charge, ex is the amount of charge passed Q, and eN_A is Faraday’s constant, F = 96485.3\ \text{C/mol}\,e^-.
\therefore\quad \boxed{m = \frac{QM}{nF}}
→ If we know the amount of charge passed, we know how much mass is formed.
(Side note: units of \dfrac{F}{RT}V — \dfrac{\text{C}}{\text{mol}\,e}\cdot\dfrac{\text{K mol}}{\text{J}}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\text{K}}\cdot\text{V} \Rightarrow \dfrac{\text{CV}}{\text{J}} — dimensionless.)
Rates
I = \frac{\text{charge}}{\text{time}}\;[=]\;\frac{\text{C}}{\text{s}}\;[=]\;\text{A}
Faraday’s law as a rate:
\frac{m/M}{s} = \frac{Q/s}{nF} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{r = \frac{I}{nF}}\;[=]\;\frac{\text{mol}}{\text{time}}
(n = mol of e^- per mol of product; F = 96485 C/mol e^-.)
Flux at the electrode surface
(Flux is a vector quantity.) Sketch: a cathode with \mathrm{Fe^{3+}} arriving, \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} leaving, e^- supplied from the electrode, surface normal \vec{n} pointing into solution.
\mathrm{Fe^{3+} + e^- \rightleftharpoons Fe^{2+}}

↳ Flux balance at SS: \text{Flux}_{Fe^{3+}} = \text{Flux}_{e^-}, i.e. (\vec{N}_3) \leftrightarrow (\vec{N}_e)
↳ Molar flux: N_j\;\left[\dfrac{\text{mol}}{\text{cm}^2\cdot\text{s}}\right]

\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_3 = -\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_e = -\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_2\;;\qquad i = \frac{I}{\text{Area}} \Rightarrow \text{current density}
i/F → cathodic current < 0.
For a generic reaction with stoichiometric coefficients s_j (+ for products): \sum s_jN_j \rightleftharpoons ne
\boxed{\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_j = -\frac{s_j}{nF}i}\;[=]\;\frac{\text{mol}}{\text{cm}^2\cdot\text{s}} = r' = \frac{-s_ji}{nF}
— Faraday’s law as a flux. The minus sign for i would then mean it is a cathodic current density.
Electrode potentials
\Delta G = -nFU\;;\qquad \text{potential} \sim \Delta G \quad(\text{of an entire cell; } U = \text{reversible cell potential})

→ We care about the potential of one electrode (usually the working electrode).
↳ A counter electrode must exist, but it may complicate our potential measurements (since if we don’t know the reactions happening at our counter, then we don’t know what we are referencing to).
↳ Therefore, we have to reference our WE potential to a 3rd electrode with a stable and defined potential → the reference electrode (RE), which does not participate in the cell reactions. e.g. \mathrm{Ag_{(s)} + Cl^-_{(aq)} \rightarrow AgCl_{(s)} + e^-}.

Electrochemical potential
A similar concept to the chemical potential, \mu = \left.\dfrac{\partial G}{\partial n_j}\right|_{T,P,n_{j\neq i}}. The charged species involved interact with the electric field → electrochemical potential.
Fick’s law (mass transport)
Flux = convection + diffusion + electrical migration (for charged species).
↳ In dilute solution, diffusion is very important and defined by Fick’s law:
\boxed{\vec{N}_j = -D_j\nabla c_j}\;;\qquad D \approx 10^{-5}\ \text{cm}^2/\text{s}\;\;(\text{in aqueous systems; } D = \text{diffusivity})
Ohm’s law (current transport)
In a well-mixed electrolyte, Ohm’s law can describe the current flowing through the electrolyte:
\vec{i} = -\kappa\nabla\phi\qquad(\kappa = \text{conductivity},\; \phi = \text{electric potential})
Electrolyte conductivity
\boxed{\kappa = F^2\sum_jz_j^2u_jc_j}\qquad(z_j = \text{charge on species},\; u_j = \text{ionic mobility})
\boxed{u_j = \frac{D_j}{RT}} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Nernst–Einstein equation}
Electroneutrality
\sum_jz_jc_j = 0

↳ An excellent (and necessary) approximation everywhere.
↳ Only on length scales of ~nm can charges sufficiently separate (at the electrode/electrolyte interface).

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 9-10) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Double layer
The region very near the electrode surface where some charge separation occurs, but the charge built up will be exactly balanced by the electrode.
Due to Brownian motion this is not an exact single layer in solution; instead, the net charge decreases exponentially away from the electrode (sketch: e^- on the electrode, \oplus ions in solution, charge decaying with distance — a capacitive double layer) ↓ defined by the Debye length:
\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon RT}{F^2\sum_jz_j^2c_{j,\infty}}}\;;\qquad \varepsilon = (\text{dielectric constant})(\text{permittivity of free space})
with dielectric constant \kappa = 78 (for water) and \varepsilon_0 = 8.854\times10^{-14} F/cm.
Electrochemical rates

If we increase the current density, we could reduce the total number of devices needed.
We need to understand the driving force required to achieve such an increase ↳ deriving electrochemical rate laws.

↳ Changing the potential has an impact on the current → varying the potential is called polarizing an electrode.
Sketch: i (mA/cm²) vs E (V vs RHE) — zero current at the equilibrium potential V_E, negative (cathodic) below and positive (anodic) above, rising exponentially. V_E represents the equilibrium of a single reversible electrode reaction [\mathrm{R \underset{k_c}{\overset{k_a}{\rightleftharpoons}} O + e^-}], i.e. the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal, resulting in zero current at the electrode: r = k_aC_R - k_cC_O.

Voltages below and above V_{OC} lead to the flow of charge one way vs the other.
The relationship between i and V appears exponential.
i \propto reaction rate (by Faraday’s law) ↓ Arrhenius equation (k \propto e^{-E_a/RT}) → originally an empirical relationship.

The same activation-energy approach applies to electrochemical reactions:
W_{rev} = -F\Delta V\qquad(\text{work required to move 1 mol of } e^- \text{ across an energy barrier } \Delta V)
— energy is associated with the e^-.
Example: \mathrm{R \rightleftharpoons O + e^-}. Sketch: energy vs reaction coordinate from R over a barrier to O; changing the electrode potential from V_1 to V_2 lowers the product state by F(V_2 - V_1) and the barrier by (1-\beta)F(V_2 - V_1).
\beta represents the fraction of \Delta V required to reach a new transition state (0 \leq \beta \leq 1). So,
\begin{aligned}
E_{A,forward}(V_2) &= E_{A,forward}(V_1) - (1-\beta)F(V_2 - V_1) \\
E_{A,forward}(V) &= E_{A,forward}(0) - (1-\beta)FV\qquad(\text{the forward reaction is anodic}) \\
E_{A,a}(V) &= E_{A,a}(0) - (1-\beta)FV\qquad(\text{change in potential of 1 electrode, so we can just replace with } V) \\
E_{A,c}(V) &= E_{A,c}(0) + \beta FV\qquad(\text{cathodic})
\end{aligned}
k_{forward} = A\exp\left[\frac{-E_{A,a}(0) + (1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right] = k_a\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right]\;;\qquad k_a = \exp\left(\frac{-E_{A,a}}{RT}\right)\quad(\text{Arrhenius dependence})
k_{rev} = k_c\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right]
\therefore\quad \boxed{r = \frac{i}{F} = C_Rk_a\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right] - C_Ok_c\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right]}

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 6 (Kinetics)
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 11-13) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



r = \frac{i}{F} = C_Rk_a\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right] - C_Ok_c\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right]
Exchange current density and equilibrium potential
We characterize the exchange current density as the rate of the forward (or reverse) reaction when the overall reaction is at equilibrium ↳ we define the potential at which this occurs as U.
i \Rightarrow 0 \;\Rightarrow\; FC_Rk_a\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FU}{RT}\right] = FC_Ok_c\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FU}{RT}\right] = i_0
↓ Solving for U:
\exp\left[\left(\frac{(1-\beta)F}{RT} + \frac{\beta F}{RT}\right)U\right] = \frac{C_Ok_c}{C_Rk_a}
\;\Rightarrow\;
U = \frac{\ln\left(\frac{C_Ok_c}{C_Rk_a}\right)}{\frac{(1-\beta)F}{RT} + \frac{\beta F}{RT}} = \ln\left(\frac{C_Ok_c}{C_Rk_a}\right)\frac{RT}{F}
\therefore\quad \boxed{U = \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{k_c}{k_a}\right) + \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{C_O}{C_R}\right)}
Butler–Volmer equation
Introduce V = U + \eta (\eta = overpotential) → plugging into the i expression:
\therefore\quad i = \underbrace{FC_Rk_a\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)UF}{RT}\right]}_{i_0}\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)\eta F}{RT}\right] - \underbrace{FC_Ok_c\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FU}{RT}\right]}_{i_0}\exp\left[\frac{-\beta F\eta}{RT}\right]
\boxed{i = i_0\left(\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)F\eta}{RT}\right] - \exp\left[\frac{-\beta F\eta}{RT}\right]\right)} \;\rightarrow\; \textbf{Butler–Volmer equation}
For reactions where multiple e^- transfers occur, we use \alpha instead of \beta:
\boxed{i = i_0\left(\exp\left[\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right] - \exp\left[\frac{-\alpha_cF\eta}{RT}\right]\right)}\;;\qquad 0 \leq \alpha \leq n\;\;(\alpha = \text{transfer coefficient})
Simplifications
At small overpotential (\eta \to 0): linearize B-V with a 1st-order Taylor expansion:
\boxed{i = \frac{i_0(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)F\eta}{RT}} \qquad \text{linear kinetics (sketch: } i \text{ linear in } \eta\text{)}
At large overpotential, e.g. \eta \gg 0: the total current contribution from the cathodic reaction becomes small relative to the anodic reaction (the first exponent is positive and large, the second negative and small):
\therefore\quad \boxed{i = i_0\exp\left[\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right]} \qquad \text{anodic Tafel equation}
↳ Taking \log_{10} to linearize:
\log_{10}(i) - \log_{10}(i_0) = \frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\log_{10}(e) = \frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{2.303RT}
\eta = m\cdot\log_{10}(i) + b\;;\qquad m = \frac{2.303RT}{F\alpha_a}\;;\qquad b = -m\log_{10}(|i_0|)
Sketch: \eta vs \log_{10}|i|, a line with slope m = Tafel slope [mV/decade] — analogous to an Arrhenius plot.
Slope → higher would mean that a small increase in \eta leads to \uparrow i_0 (higher rate?)


                  
                  Typed correction in the original 
                  
                

“Actually, a lower slope means that a small overpotential causes a larger increase in current, therefore smaller slope is higher rate!!! (since overpotential is on the y axis)“


β (symmetry factor)
The fraction of F(V_2 - V_1) required to overcome the energy barrier → what does it physically represent?

\beta characterizes the quantum-mechanical transfer of e^- from the electrode to the chemical species.
↳ Classical mechanics of e^- predicts orders of magnitude lower i than observed for the potentials we apply.

Sketch: electron energy in the metal, M(e), filled up to the Fermi level (the highest energy level); the work function \phi is the energy required to surmount the barrier above the Fermi level. The e^- needs to escape the metal and then get transferred to another Fermi level → however, recorded energies were far lower than predicted.
↳ QM allows e^- to tunnel rather than overcome the energy barrier → this occurs without radiation energy (no light is seen) ↳ this requires the initial and final states to have the same energy.
Example: adsorption of a proton at an electrode
\mathrm{M(e^-) + H^+\text{–}OH_2 \rightleftharpoons M\text{–}H + H_2O}
Sketch: energy vs distance for the initial state (e⁻ in the metal, H⁺ attached to water) and the final state (H adsorbed on the metal) — two crossing curves.

\Delta E → the large energy barrier required to transfer the e^- from the ground state (no tunnelling possible).
\Delta\varepsilon → represents the activation barrier for tunnelling (up to the crossing point).

When we apply a potential, we vertically shift the initial state and thus change \Delta\varepsilon:
\Delta(\Delta\varepsilon) = \Delta\varepsilon_1 - \Delta\varepsilon_0\;;\qquad \frac{\Delta\varepsilon_0}{\Delta E_0} = \frac{\Delta\varepsilon_1}{\Delta E_1}\;(\text{straight line}) = \frac{\Delta\varepsilon_0 + \Delta(\Delta\varepsilon)}{\Delta E_0 + \Delta VF}
(F(V_1 - V_0) gives the energy associated with the voltage change.)
\frac{\Delta\varepsilon_0}{\Delta E_0} = \frac{\Delta(\Delta\varepsilon)}{\Delta VF} = \beta
— the change in \Delta\varepsilon represents the fraction of work applied that is required to change E_A.
Get the value of \beta from trigonometry (sketch: crossing lines with angles \gamma and \theta at the crossing point a):
\beta = \frac{\Delta\varepsilon_0}{\Delta E_0} = \frac{x\tan\gamma}{x(\tan\gamma + \tan\theta)}\;\;(\text{cathodic})\;;\qquad (1-\beta) = \frac{\tan\theta}{\tan\gamma + \tan\theta}\;\;(\text{anodic})
Straight-line assumption → validity? ↳ It has to hold near the crossing point a → the excited state (H between the electrode and water).
\beta → the fraction of energy for a \Delta V change going into the activation-energy change. If the slopes are equal, \tan\gamma \approx \tan\theta and \beta = \tfrac{1}{2}.
Sketches for \mathrm{R \rightleftharpoons O + e^-}:

\beta \approx 0 → the anodic process is greatly impacted by \Delta V → the cathodic process is not!
\beta \approx 1 → the anodic process is not impacted by \Delta V!

Electrochemical mechanisms
A similar process to heterogeneous catalysis → we have to modify the approach using electrochemical kinetics:

A series of elementary steps (1 e^- at a time)
Write the rate law for each step
Assume an RLS (rate-limiting step); set all other rates to quasi-equilibrium

(i) Eliminate intermediates/sites


Compose the overall rate law
Determine the reversible potential (U), introduce \eta, and determine i_0
Compare i_0, \alpha_a, \alpha_c and the reaction-order dependence to experiment

Example: water electrolysis → the hydrogen evolution half-reaction

















Mechanism 1Mechanism 2Volmer: \mathrm{S + H^+ + e^- \underset{k_{1,a}}{\overset{k_{1,c}}{\rightleftharpoons}} H_{ads}}Volmer: \mathrm{S + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons H_{ads}}Tafel: \mathrm{2H_{ads} \underset{k_{2,r}}{\overset{k_{2,f}}{\rightleftharpoons}} H_{2(g)} + 2S}Heyrovsky: \mathrm{H_{ads} + H^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons H_{2(g)} + S}

Tafel → non-faradaic.
Both steps involve adsorbed species (i.e. surface sites) → [S].

Volmer–Tafel mechanism
r_1 = k_{1,c}[\mathrm{H^+}][S]\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right] - k_{1,a}[\mathrm{H_{ads}}]\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right]
with C_S = number of unoccupied sites = C_t(1-\theta) and C_{H_{ads}} = C_t\cdot\theta, where \theta = fractional coverage [C_{H_{ads}}/C_t] and C_t is something we can measure (i.e. a BET isotherm):
\rightarrow\; r_1 = k_{1,c}C_{H^+}C_t(1-\theta)\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right] - k_{1,a}C_t\theta\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right]
r_2 = k_{2,f}[\mathrm{H_{ads}}]^2 - k_{2,r}[\mathrm{H_2}][S]^2 = k_{2,f}C_t^2\theta^2 - k_{2,r}C_{H_2}[C_t(1-\theta)]^2
\;\rightarrow\;
r_2 = k_{2,f}(C_t\theta)^2 - k_{2,r}P_{H_2}[C_t(1-\theta)]^2
Solving for \theta: if r_2 is rate-limiting, then r_1 is in quasi-equilibrium: r_1 = 0 \Rightarrow
k_{1,c}C_{H^+}C_t(1-\theta)\exp\left[\frac{-\beta FV}{RT}\right] = k_{1,a}C_t\theta\exp\left[\frac{(1-\beta)FV}{RT}\right]
\;\Rightarrow\;
\theta = \frac{k_{1,c}C_{H^+}}{k_{1,a}\exp\left[\frac{FV}{RT}\right] + k_{1,c}C_{H^+}}
\boxed{\theta = \frac{\frac{k_{1,c}C_{H^+}}{k_a}\exp\left[\frac{-FV}{RT}\right]}{1 + \frac{k_{1,c}C_{H^+}}{k_a}\exp\left[\frac{-FV}{RT}\right]}}
\qquad\rightarrow\;\text{similar to the Langmuir isotherm, } \theta = \frac{K}{1+K}
Net rate:
r_{net} = r_2 = \frac{i}{2F} = k_{2,f}(C_t\theta)^2 - k_{2,r}P_{H_2}[C_t(1-\theta)]^2


Even though step 2 has no e^-, it is still used to define r_{net}, and we always use this Faraday’s-law equation.


\theta = f(V) [depends on the applied potential]! ★ ↳ Non-faradaic processes can also be indirectly affected by the potential.


↓ This expression is not consistent with B-V kinetics ↳ there might be deviations from B-V (and rare exceptions).


↓ It could be other mechanisms:

Volmer (rds) – Tafel
Volmer (rds) – Heyrovsky
Volmer – Heyrovsky (rds)

These all have e^- transfer in the rds ↓ they will take the look of B-V!


Example: \mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}

\mathrm{Cu \underset{k_c}{\overset{k_{1a}}{\rightleftharpoons}} Cu^+ + e^-}
\mathrm{Cu^+ \underset{k_{2c}}{\overset{k_{2a}}{\rightleftharpoons}} Cu^{2+} + e^-} [RDS]; \beta = 0.5 \rightarrow \alpha_a = 1.5, \alpha_c = 0.5 \rightarrow i_0 \sim C_{Cu^{2+}}^{3/4} (show this)

(the notes write step 2 as \mathrm{Cu^{2+} \rightleftharpoons Cu^{2+} + e^-}; \mathrm{Cu^+} is clearly intended)

What is α, the transfer coefficient?
For a multi-step / multi-e^- electrode reaction \mathrm{A + ne^- \rightarrow Z}, composed of n e^--transfer steps, where \mathrm{O + re^- \rightleftharpoons R} is the RLS (r = number of e^- in the rate-limiting step: r = 0 → chemical step, r = 1 → electrochemical step), with stoichiometry Z = \gamma P (\gamma = stoichiometric coefficient), and assuming s e^- are transferred before the RLS and s' e^- are transferred after the RLS (n = s + s' + r):
|i_c| = k_c\cdot C_O\cdot\exp\left[\frac{-r\beta\eta F}{RT}\right]
and after applying quasi-equilibrium for all other steps:
\boxed{i = i_0\left(\exp\left(\left(\frac{n-s}{\gamma} - r\beta\right)\frac{F\eta}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(-\left(\frac{s}{\gamma} + r\beta\right)\frac{F\eta}{RT}\right)\right)}\;;\qquad \alpha_a = \frac{n-s}{\gamma} - r\beta\;,\quad \alpha_c = \frac{s}{\gamma} + r\beta
If the RLS is non-faradaic, r = 0 → \beta does not appear in \alpha_a, \alpha_c, but the rate will still depend on potential: \alpha_a + \alpha_c = n/\gamma.
Kinetics of multiple reactions
↳ More than one reaction can occur at an electrode simultaneously. E.g. CO₂ electrochemical reduction to CO:
\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow CO + 2OH^-}
— this reaction occurs in the same potential regime as water electrolysis [\mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 + 2OH^-}].

The total current observed would be the sum of the partial currents: i_T = i_{CO} + i_{H_2} → we can model each partial current with a B-V expression, assuming they are non-interacting.
↳ We might also assign a “current efficiency” or faradaic efficiency to understand selectivity.



                  
                  Side questions 
                  
                

Is every process faradaic? ↓ How can non-faradaic processes occur? ↓ vdW? But then that is not a bond? e^- coming from the same element?


Corrosion
A special type of multiple reaction (sketch: a metal surface with local anodic (A) and cathodic (C) sites; O₂ reduced to OH⁻ at C while metal dissolves at A).
↳ What must the net current of a corroding metal be?
I_{total} = 0\;,\quad i_{ox} = i_{red}\;;\qquad \text{other reactions: } \mathrm{H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 + 2OH^-}\;,\;\; \mathrm{H_2O + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2 + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^-}
We care about the potential at which this process happens → we polarize our electrode to find this point. E.g.
\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}\;;\qquad \mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow 2OH^- + H_2}
Sketch: |i| (log scale, 10^{-8}–10) vs potential (V vs RHE, 0 to −0.5) — the oxidation and reduction branches cross; the intersection gives the predicted corrosion rate (and the mixed potential).

→ Reducing potential → helping the reduction reaction.
→ For non-zero currents → you need a counter electrode??

Alloy electroplating ↳ here we desire multiple reactions.
Non-idealities that deviate from B-V

Mass transport (Ch. 5): we can have large changes in i with small changes in V, so we frequently move between reaction-limited and MT-limited regions (sketch: i vs E plateauing at i_{lim}).
Passivation: certain oxidized metals are not soluble, and therefore they do not react further. E.g. \mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} vs \mathrm{Cu \rightarrow CuOH_{(s)} + e^-} (sketch: |i| rises then falls). We can understand the regimes with potential–pH or Pourbaix diagrams — the stability of electrodes is determined from this.
Organic additives: often used in electroplating to achieve desirable feature filling. They do not take part in the electrochemical reaction but in fact affect the rate (we need to incorporate these non-reacting species into the equation).
Electrode poisoning: chemical species bind so strongly that they eat up active sites and don’t leave, e.g. \mathrm{CO + Pt \rightarrow Pt\text{–}CO}.

Contributions of the double layer to current

B-V describes the current due to charge-transfer reactions (faradaic).
Charge separation occurs in the double layer (charge accumulation) → polarizing an electrode ↓ manifesting as current (no flow of e^-, so it cannot be captured by B-V kinetics).
Qualitatively, model using a circuit: a resistor R_{Far} (the faradaic process) in parallel with a capacitor C_{dl} (the double layer), between the electrolyte (potential \phi_0) and the electrode (V). Capacitance [=] F = C/V.

i_{total} = i_{Far} + i_{dl} = \frac{V - \phi_0}{R_{Far}} + C_{dl}\frac{\partial(V - \phi_0)}{\partial t}\;;\qquad R_{Far} \text{ is given by } \frac{\partial\eta}{\partial i}\;\;(\text{from B-V; Ohm's law})
At SS, i_{dl} = 0 → the capacitive current is 0 ↳ but the DL still exists, and it can impact the transport of ions just by its presence.
How do we calculate C_{dl}?

↳ It contains a distribution of charge.
↳ A common model for a more accurate DL is the Helmholtz model (sketch: electrode charge; the inner Helmholtz plane (IHP) of specifically adsorbed ions, considered “desolvated”; the outer Helmholtz plane (OHP) of weakly associated ions, often solvated (→ H₂O); then the diffuse layer).

Total charge must be balanced (Gouy–Chapman theory):
q_{electrode} = -\big(q_{IHP} + q_{OHP} + q_d\big)\;;\qquad \frac{1}{C_{dl}} = \frac{1}{C_{IHP}} + \frac{1}{C_{OHP}} + \frac{1}{C_d}
where the minimum C_d = \varepsilon/\lambda (\varepsilon = permittivity, \lambda = Debye length).
Thermodynamics
The voltage difference (that we measure across a load attached to an electrochemical cell) is an (electrochemical potential)/F. What is the electrochemical potential?
Chemical potential:
\mu_A = \left.\frac{\partial G}{\partial N_A}\right|_{T,P,N_{[A]}}
Relative values have meaning (i.e. relative to standard states). \mu_i = f(T, P, x_i); the work/energy associated with moving a chemical species from one place to another is W_{rev} = \mu_A(2) - \mu_A(1) = -\Delta G.
Electrical potential: the energy associated with moving idealized point charges from one place to another (regardless of chemical state):
f = \frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r^2}\;;\qquad W_{rev} = -\Delta G = F(V_2 - V_1) = \mu_e(2) - \mu_e(1)
A need for something more. Issues (case studies):

The energy associated with moving e^- from one sphere to another is \sim10^8 V [a 2 cm Cu sphere, moving 1\times10^{-9} e^-], but \delta\mu_e \approx 0 (adding a small number of e^- to a very large mass/mol of e^-).
The Volta battery (uncharged electrodes make an electric current) → \mu_e can’t describe this, since it ignores the chemical state, but \mu can be used to understand the change.

\therefore Electrochemical systems need charged species in a chemical state whose energies are affected by changes in P, T, composition and the electrical state → the electrochemical potential!
\boxed{\mu_j = \mu_j^c + z_jF\phi}
(\mu_j^c = chemical potential, z_j = charge number, \phi = quasi-electrostatic potential.) This is a formal description of the electrochemical potential. However,
\boxed{\mu_j = RT\ln(\lambda_j)\;;\qquad \lambda_j = c_jf_ja_j^\circ}
(\lambda_j = electrochemical activity, f_j = activity coefficient, a_j^\circ = constant of proportionality.) This definition utilizes differences in reference/standard states ↓ more useful. The activity coefficient must depend on the electrical state for ionic species (but specific combinations of the f_j are not dependent on the electrical state):
\mathrm{MX_2 \rightleftharpoons M^{2+} + 2X^-}\;;\qquad C_{MX_2} = C = \frac{C_{M^{2+}}}{1} = \frac{C_{X^-}}{2}\;;\qquad \mu_{MX_2} = \mu_{M^{2+}} + 2\mu_{X^-}
\lambda_{MX_2} = \lambda_{M^{2+}}\lambda_{X^-}^2 = \big(C_{M^{2+}}f_{M^{2+}}a_{M^{2+}}^\circ\big)\big(C_{X^-}f_{X^-}a_{X^-}^\circ\big)^2
\;\Rightarrow\;
\lambda_{MX_2} = C^3\big(a_{M^{2+}}^\circ\big)\big(2a_{X^-}^\circ\big)^2\big(f_{M^{2+}}f_{X^-}^2\big)
All of these species are not dependent on the electrical state → so the product f_{M^{2+}}f_{X^-}^2 is not dependent on the electrical state (although individually they are)!
In general, the mean activity coefficient for a general electrolyte \mathrm{M_{\nu_+}X_{\nu_-} \rightleftharpoons \nu_+M^{z_+} + \nu_-X^{z_-}} with z_+\nu_+ + z_-\nu_- = 0 (electroneutrality):
\boxed{f_\pm^\nu = f_+^{\nu_+}f_-^{\nu_-}}
★ A neutral combination of ions will always have a mean activity coefficient independent of the electric state.
Why?

Physical properties and rates → defined in terms of activities, not concentrations.
The framework of electrochemical systems.

Electrochemical reaction equilibrium
Phase equilibrium: chemical species in different phases are in equilibrium if their chemical potentials are equal:
\mu_j^\alpha = \mu_j^\beta
e.g. O₂ dissolved in water: \mu_{O_2}^{aq} = \mu_{O_2}^g → Henry’s law, P_{O_2} = K_H[\mathrm{O_2}] — the chemical-potential equivalence between the gas phase and the liquid solubility of a species.
Chemical reaction equilibrium: a chemical reaction is in equilibrium when the chemical potentials of the reactants and products are equal:
\mathrm{A + B \rightleftharpoons C}\;;\qquad \mu_A + \mu_B = \mu_C
↳ For ideal solutions (activity coefficient = 1):
\mu_j = \mu_j^\circ + RT\ln\frac{c_j}{c_j^\circ}
(\mu_j^\circ = chemical potential at standard conditions; c_j^\circ = concentration at standard conditions.) ↓ Plugging this in for our reaction:
\underbrace{\frac{C_C^\circ}{C_A^\circ C_B^\circ}\exp\left[\frac{\mu_A^\circ + \mu_B^\circ - \mu_C^\circ}{RT}\right]}_{K} = \frac{C_C}{C_AC_B}
For an electrochemical reaction we can write \sum s_j\mu_j \rightleftharpoons ne^-. At equilibrium,
\sum s_j\mu_j = n\mu_{e^-}
where \mu_{e^-} is what we measure via a voltmeter (the electrochemical potential of e^-).
Example: consider the full cell reaction (phases labelled \alpha, \beta, \gamma_1, \gamma_2, \delta, \alpha'):
\underset{\alpha}{\mathrm{Pt}}\,|\,\underset{\beta}{\mathrm{H_{2(g)}}}\,|\,\underset{\gamma_1}{\mathrm{H_2SO_{4(aq)}}}\,||\,\underset{\gamma_2}{\mathrm{CuSO_{4(aq)}}}\,|\,\underset{\delta}{\mathrm{Cu_{(s)}}}\,|\,\underset{\alpha'}{\mathrm{Pt_{(s)}}}
(continued in Lecture 11).
