Phase + reaction equilibrium for electrochemical systems
\underset{\alpha}{\mathrm{Pt}}\,|\,\underset{\beta}{\mathrm{H_{2(g)}}}\,|\,\underset{\gamma_1}{\mathrm{H_2SO_{4(aq)}}}\,||\,\underset{\gamma_2}{\mathrm{CuSO_{4(aq)}}}\,|\,\underset{\delta}{\mathrm{Cu_{(s)}}}\,|\,\underset{\alpha'}{\mathrm{Pt_{(s)}}}

→ When the potential difference between the RHS and LHS electrodes (V^{\alpha'} - V^\alpha) creates equilibrium, we define this as U_{cell} \equiv V^{\alpha'} - V^\alpha.
→ We also know that measured potential differences across electrodes describe the electrochemical potential of e^-:

\mu_e^\alpha - \mu_e^{\alpha'} = -F\big(V^\alpha - V^{\alpha'}\big)\;[=]\;\frac{\text{J}}{\text{mol}\,e^-}\;;\quad\text{thus}\quad \boxed{\mu_e^\alpha - \mu_e^{\alpha'} = FU} \;\text{(left - right) at equilibrium}
(W_{rev} = \Delta G = -F\Delta V.)


→ Applying phase equilibrium to our example means that species in adjacent phases must be in equilibrium. So on the RHS, at \mathrm{Cu_{(s)}\,|\,Pt_{(s)}}: \mu_e^\delta = \mu_e^{\alpha'} at equilibrium.
Reaction: \mathrm{Cu^\circ \rightleftharpoons Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} (\delta, \gamma_2, \delta):


2\mu_{e^-}^\delta = \mu_{Cu}^\delta - \mu_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}\;\;\therefore\;\; 2\mu_e^{\alpha'} = 2\mu_e^\delta = \mu_{Cu^\circ} - \mu_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}

→ Repeating this process for the LHS (now only the e^--conducting phase \alpha). Reaction: \mathrm{H_{2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2H^+_{(aq)} + 2e^-}:

2\mu_e^\alpha = \mu_{H_2}^\beta - 2\mu_{H^+}^{\gamma_1}

→ Combining with the cell equilibrium potential:

U_{cell} = \frac{1}{F}\big(\mu_e^\alpha - \mu_e^{\alpha'}\big) = \frac{1}{2F}\big(2\mu_e^\alpha - 2\mu_e^{\alpha'}\big)
\qquad
\boxed{U_{cell} = \frac{1}{2F}\Big(\mu_{H_2}^\beta - 2\mu_{H^+}^{\gamma_1} - \mu_{Cu}^\delta + \mu_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}\Big)}
(the boxed expression in the notes shows \tfrac{1}{F}; \tfrac{1}{2F} follows from the line above)
We don’t typically measure \mu → apply the definition of activities to get a usable form:
\mu_{H_2}^\beta = \mu_{H_2}^* + RT\ln P_{H_2}^\beta\;\;(\mu^* = \text{standard chemical potential for a gas})\;;\qquad \mu_{Cu}^\delta = \mu_{Cu}^\circ
\mu_{H^+}^{\gamma_1} = RT\ln\big(\lambda_{H^+}^{\gamma_1}\big) = RT\ln\big(c_{H^+}f_{H^+}a_{H^+}^\circ\big)\;;\qquad \mu_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2} = RT\ln\big(c_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}f_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}a_{Cu^{2+}}^\circ\big)
U_{cell} = \frac{1}{2F}\Big[\mu_{H_2}^* + RT\ln\big(P_{H_2}^\beta\big) - 2\big(RT\ln(a_{H^+}^\circ) + RT\ln(c_{H^+}f_{H^+})\big) - \mu_{Cu}^\circ + RT\ln\big(a_{Cu^{2+}}^\circ\big) + RT\ln\big(c_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}f_{Cu^{2+}}\big)\Big]
The terms independent of concentration define U_{cell}^\circ → the standard equilibrium potential:
U_{cell}^\circ = \frac{1}{2F}\Big(\mu_{H_2}^* - 2RT\ln(a_{H^+}^\circ) - \mu_{Cu}^\circ + RT\ln(a_{Cu^{2+}}^\circ)\Big)
= \underbrace{-\frac{1}{2F}\Big(\mu_{Cu}^\circ - RT\ln(a_{Cu^{2+}}^\circ)\Big)}_{U_{RHS}^\circ\ (\text{red})} - \underbrace{\left(-\frac{1}{2F}\Big(\mu_{H_2}^* - 2RT\ln a_{H^+}^\circ\Big)\right)}_{U_{LHS}^\circ\ (\text{ox})}
(factor out minus signs so we can write U_{cell}^\circ = U_{red}^\circ - U_{ox}^\circ such that U > 0.)
\boxed{U_{cell}^\circ = U_{RHS}^\circ - U_{LHS}^\circ}
— standard potentials, when all species are at standard state: 1 M for solutes, 1 bar for gases.
\therefore\quad U_{cell} = U_{cell}^\circ + \frac{RT}{2F}\Big(\ln\big(P_{H_2}^\beta\big) - 2\ln\big(c_{H^+}^{\gamma_1}f_{H^+}^{\gamma_1}\big) + \ln\big(c_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}f_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}\big)\Big)
★ Assume all f_j = 1:
\boxed{U_{cell} = U_{cell}^\circ + \underbrace{\frac{RT}{2F}\ln\left(\frac{P_{H_2}^\beta\,C_{Cu^{2+}}^{\gamma_2}}{(C_{H^+})^2}\right)}_{\text{Nernstian correction}}}
\eta = V - U: this U was a half-cell potential (for an electrode) → not the same as U_{cell}.
Half-cell potentials and the SHE
To discuss half-cell potentials, we reference to a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) [U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ]: an ideal solution at equilibrium exposed to 1 bar H₂ and 1 M H⁺(aq) [pH = 0].
Example: \mathrm{AgCl + e^- \rightleftharpoons Ag + Cl^-} in reference to SHE:
\underset{\alpha}{\mathrm{Pt}}\,|\,\underset{\beta}{\mathrm{H_{2(g)}}}\,|\,\underset{\gamma}{\mathrm{HCl_{(aq)}}}\,|\,\underset{\delta}{\mathrm{AgCl_{(s)}}}\,|\,\underset{\beta'}{\mathrm{Ag_{(s)}}}\,|\,\underset{\alpha'}{\mathrm{Pt_{(s)}}}
Phase equilibrium: \mu_{e^-}^{\alpha'} = \mu_e^{\beta'} = \mu_e^\delta. (Writing it as \mathrm{AgCl + e^- \rightleftharpoons Ag + Cl^-} would be an equivalent reaction to look at — the thermodynamic analysis will lead to the answer both ways.)
\text{RHS: } \mathrm{Ag \rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + e^-}\;,\;\; \mu_{Ag}^{\beta'} = \mu_{Ag^+}^\delta + \mu_{e^-}^{\alpha'}\;;\qquad
\text{LHS: } \mathrm{H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2H^+ + 2e^-}\;,\;\; \mu_{H_2}^\beta = 2\mu_{H^+}^\gamma + 2\mu_e^\alpha
\mu_e^\alpha - \mu_e^{\alpha'} = FU_{cell} \;\Rightarrow\; \big(\mu_{H_2}^\beta - 2\mu_{H^+}^\gamma\big) - \big(\mu_{Ag}^{\beta'} - \mu_{Ag^+}^\delta\big) = FU_{cell}\;;\qquad U_{cell} = \frac{1}{2F}\big(2\mu_e^\alpha - \mu_e^{\alpha'}\big)


                  
                  Note 1 
                  
                

If we tabulate all reactions vs SHE (half-reaction values), then we can determine cell potentials + the Nernst correction for any combination of half-reactions:
U_{cell}^\circ = U_{AgCl}^\circ - U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}}^\circ\;;\qquad \boxed{U_{cell}^\circ = \underbrace{\big(U_{AgCl}^\circ - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ\big)}_{\text{tabulated}} - \underbrace{\big(U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}}^\circ - U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}}\big)}_{\text{tabulated}}}
— standard potentials (or standard reduction potentials); these are half-reactions.




                  
                  Note 2 
                  
                

If we experimentally measure electrode reactions at standard conditions, then we can just use the Nernst correction for deviations from the tabulated standards. E.g. \mathrm{Cu \rightleftharpoons Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} in 0.0001 M HCl in a cell with SHE:
U_{cell} = U_{cell}^\circ + \text{Nernst}_{cell} = U_{cell}^\circ + \frac{RT}{2F}\ln C_{Cu^{2+}}\;\bigstar
with U_{cell}^\circ = (U_{Cu/Cu^+} - U_{SHE}), where U_{SHE} is set to zero. (If Pt is the electrode, then the electrolyte concentration matters → that is why we correct for that.)


The tabulated values are particularly useful when conducting experiments, because it is often inconvenient to experimentally set up a SHE.
↳ Indeed, we can set up a convenient electrode like Ag/AgCl in KCl and reference our WE to that:
\big(U_{Ag/AgCl}^\circ - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ\big) = 0.222\ \text{V}\quad\text{or}\quad U_{Ag/AgCl}^\circ = 0.222\ \text{V vs SHE}
Example: the reference will have a liquid-junction potential (across the membrane). With an Ag/AgCl reference (0.222 V) and \mathrm{Cu \rightleftharpoons Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} (we want this to be in equilibrium; U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}}^\circ = 0.337 V):
U_{cell} = 0.337 - 0.222\ \text{V} = 0.115\ \text{V}
(sketch: an energy ladder — SHE at the bottom, Ag/AgCl 0.222 V above it, and Cu/Cu²⁺ a further 0.115 V above.)
A potentiostat provides a \Delta V between the WE and the reference electrode → measures the I, and then provides a \Delta V at the CE to match that i.
Tafel kinetics (worked example):
i_a = i_0\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right)\;;\qquad \frac{15\times10^{-3}}{1\times10^{-4}} = \exp\left(\frac{(1.5)(96485)\eta}{RT}\right)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\eta = \frac{\ln(150)\,RT}{(1.5)(96485)}\;\;(\text{vs REF})
\eta = V - U\;;\qquad V_{SHE} = \eta + 0.115 + 0.222\ \text{V}

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 12 (Nernst)
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 26) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Nernst equation
For a half-reaction \sum_js_{ij}M_j = ne^- (s_{ij} = stoichiometric coefficient, n = e^- per mol of product):
\boxed{U_i - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ = \big(U_i^\circ - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ\big) - \frac{RT}{F}\left(\sum_j\frac{s_{ij}}{n}\ln c_{ij}^*\right)}
(both potentials referenced to SHE), with c_{ij}^* = c_{ij} for a solute and c_{ij}^* = P_{ij} for a gas.
Reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)
It is more convenient to reference a hydrogen electrode at pH ≠ 0.

↳ e.g. U_{cell} for an H₂ fuel cell / water electrolyzer does not depend on the H⁺ concentration (pH), but U_{red} and U_{ox} (i.e. the half-reactions) are both dependent on pH.
↳ If we reference a single half-reaction to SHE, it would appear that a large potential is required at pH > 0.

To avoid confusion, we employ an RHE, which is an SHE with a Nernstian correction for the pH shift:
\mathrm{H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2H^+ + 2e^-}\quad(\mathrm{H_2 - 2H^+ = 2e^-})
\text{Nernst: } U_{H_2/H^+} = \underbrace{\big(U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ\big)}_{0} - \frac{RT}{2F}\ln\left(\frac{P_{H_2}}{C_{H^+}^2}\right)\;;\qquad \text{pH} = -\log_{10}C_{H^+}
= \frac{RT}{F}\ln C_{H^+} = -\frac{RT}{F}\ln\big(10^{-\text{pH}}\big)\cdots
\qquad
\boxed{U_{H_2/H^+} = -0.0591\ \text{V vs RHE}}
(i.e. -0.0591 V per pH unit at 25 °C, relative to SHE)


                  
                  Open question in the notes 
                  
                

Is E_{OC} at equilibrium? i.e. is it the U_{eq} value?

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 13 (Transport)
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 27-29) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Spontaneity

(U_1\text{ vs SHE} - U_2\text{ vs SHE}) > 0? If < 0, take U_2 - U_1 → this will give a spontaneous (galvanic) cell. The reaction at the more negative potential proceeds in the oxidation direction.


→ The more negative the potential, the more likely oxidation is to occur.
→ The number of e^- involved does not matter to determine U_{cell} (since they are all normalized by the SHE).

Nernst, corrosion + Pourbaix diagrams
↳ They tell us about the stability/passivation of metal electrodes as a function of potential and pH.

Constructed with the Nernst equation.
Tell us how susceptible metals are to corrosion via H₂ or O₂.

E.g. P_{H_2} = 1 bar, P_{O_2} = 1 bar; U_{H_2/H^+} and U_{O_2/H_2O} as a function of pH:
\mathrm{H^+ + e^- \rightarrow \tfrac{1}{2}H_2}\;;\qquad \big(U_{H_2/H^+} - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ\big) = \underbrace{\big(U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ - U_{H_2/H^+}^\circ\big)}_{0} - \frac{RT}{F}\ln\left(\frac{P_{H_2}^{1/2}}{C_{H^+}}\right)
U_{H_2/H^+} = -0.0591\times\text{pH}\ \text{V vs SHE}\;;\qquad\text{similarly,}\quad U_{O_2/H_2O} = 1.23 - 0.0591\,\text{pH}\ \text{V vs SHE}
Sketch (Pourbaix-style): potential (V vs SHE) vs pH from 0 to 14 — the O₂/H₂O line falling from 1.23 V and the H₂/H⁺ line falling from 0 V; Cu/Cu²⁺ is a horizontal line at 0.337 V. Above the O₂ line → corrosion (yellow region); below Cu/Cu²⁺ and above H₂ → no corrosion (red hatched region).
Will a metal corrode?
\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}\;;\quad U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}} = \big(U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}}^\circ\text{ vs SHE}\big) - \frac{RT}{2F}\ln C_{Cu^{2+}}^{-1} = 0.337 + \frac{RT}{F}\ln C_{Cu^{2+}}^{1/2}\quad\leftarrow\;\text{not dependent on pH}
Stability:

\big(U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}} - U_{H_2/H^+}\big) > 0 → spontaneous ✓ — the H₂ couple is more negative (so it is the one oxidized) \therefore Cu does not corrode (via H⁺).
\big(U_{O_2/H_2O} - U_{Cu/Cu^{2+}}\big) > 0 → spontaneous ✓ — Cu is more negative (oxidation) \therefore Cu does corrode (via O₂).

Current density vs potential: what are the corrosion potential and corrosion rate?
Sketch (Evans diagram): \log|i| vs V vs SHE — the lines for \mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}, \mathrm{Fe^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Fe} / \mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-} (around −0.440 V) and \mathrm{Zn \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2e^-} (around −0.762 V). Where the rates of oxidation and reduction balance (one electrode process) gives the mixed potential; adding Zn gives a new mixed potential (below the potential at which H and Zn will oxidize).
Electrochemical transport
① Species can move via convection, diffusion and electrical migration:
\boxed{\vec{N}_j = \underbrace{-z_ju_jFc_j\nabla\phi}_{\text{migration}}\;\underbrace{-\,D_j\nabla c_j}_{\text{diffusion}}\;+\;\underbrace{c_j\vec{v}}_{\text{convection}}}
(u_j = ionic mobility, \nabla\phi = gradient of potential, \vec{v} = fluid velocity (Navier–Stokes).)

↳ Migration: how do things move in response to an electric field (-\nabla\phi)?

\phi represents the electrostatic potential
u_j describes the average velocity of the species when acted upon by a 1 N/mol force
z_jF → the charge per mole of species
\therefore\; \underbrace{(u_jFz_j\nabla\phi)}_{\text{cm/s}}\cdot\underbrace{c_j}_{\text{mol/cm}^3}; for neutral species, z_j = 0


↳ Diffusion: how do things move in response to a concentration driving force?
↳ Convection: how do things move in response to the bulk motion of the medium?

Valid for dilute solutions → D_j is constant and equal to D_j of j at infinite dilution ↳ no frictional forces on j besides the solvent (cf. molten salt).
② The flow of a charged species constitutes an electric current. ↳ The current in an electrolyte is due to the motion (flux) of charged particles:
\vec{i} = F\sum_jz_j\vec{N}_j\qquad(\vec{i} \text{ is a vector quantity})
③ Mass is conserved: Accumulation = in − out + generation − consumption
\frac{\partial c_j}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_j + R_j
(R_j = generation in homogeneous solution only — not electrode processes, i.e. R_j = 0 for no reaction in the bulk; electrode reactions will be boundary conditions.) Sketch: a control volume with fluxes N_{jx}, N_{jy}, N_{jz}. In 1D: \displaystyle\lim_{\Delta x\to0}\frac{N_{jx}|_x - N_{jx}|_{x+\Delta x}}{\Delta x} = -\frac{\partial N_j}{\partial x}.
④ Electroneutrality is imposed everywhere:
\sum_jz_jc_j = 0
These principles enable us to describe current flow in the electrolyte.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 14
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 30-31) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Current in an electrolyte
\boxed{\vec{i} = -F^2\nabla\phi\sum_jz_j^2u_jc_j - F\sum_jz_jD_j\nabla c_j + F\vec{v}\underbrace{\sum_jz_jc_j}_{0}}
— convection does not constitute a current (by electroneutrality).
For a well-mixed solution, \nabla c_j = 0 \Rightarrow \vec{i} = -F\nabla\phi\sum z_j^2u_jc_j; with \kappa = F^2\sum z_j^2u_jc_j:
\therefore\quad \boxed{\vec{i} = -\kappa\nabla\phi} \;\leftarrow\; \text{Ohm's law}
Sketch: fluid flowing from a region of high potential/high concentration to low potential/low concentration; a cation is carried by convection, diffusion and migration in the same direction, while an anion migrates against the flow.
Even in the case of migration only, ions move differently depending on chemical identity, concentration and charge → they carry different currents.
↳ We can characterize the fraction of current carried by a species as the transference number (i = individual species):
t_i\cdot i = -F^2z_i^2u_ic_i\nabla\phi\;\Rightarrow\; t_i = \frac{z_i^2u_ic_i}{\sum_jz_j^2u_jc_j}
Modelling reaction–convection–diffusion–migration
→ We use material balances that adhere to the concepts of mass and charge conservation:
\frac{\partial c_j}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_j + R_j
(R_j is often 0, but… precipitation, \mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightleftharpoons H_2O}, any buffer reaction with bicarbonate — any homogeneous reaction. The SEI is a faradaic process, actually (heterogeneous).)
\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_j = \nabla\cdot\big(-z_ju_jFc_j\nabla\phi - D_j\nabla c_j + c_j\vec{v}\big) = -\nabla\cdot\big(z_ju_jFc_j\nabla\phi + D_j\nabla c_j\big) + \nabla c_j\cdot\vec{v}
With Nernst–Einstein, u_j = D_j/RT:
\boxed{\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_j = -D_j\left(\frac{z_jF}{RT}\nabla\cdot(c_j\nabla\phi) + \nabla^2c_j\right) + \nabla c_j\cdot\vec{v}}

↳ We can write one of these equations for each species in our system (i.e. n equations for n species).
↳ But we have (n+1) variables, considering \phi.
↳ The final equation comes from electroneutrality ↳ this forces the electric field to take on whatever value satisfies this equation:

\frac{\partial}{\partial t}F\underbrace{\sum z_jc_j}_{0} = -\nabla\cdot F\underbrace{\sum z_j\vec{N}_j}_{\text{definition of current (flux of charged species)}}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \boxed{-\nabla\cdot\vec{i} = 0}
↳ Charge is conserved (the divergence is zero) → since charge is carried by physical particles (and these are conserved). Since \vec{i} = -\kappa\nabla\phi:
-\nabla\cdot\vec{i} = -\nabla\cdot(-\kappa\nabla\phi) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\nabla^2\phi = 0} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Laplace equation (valid for no concentration gradients)}
Boundary conditions
These n+1 equations (flux + electroneutrality) give a system of partial differential equations; we need BCs:
↳ BC at insulating surfaces: the normal component of flux is zero for all species:
\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_j = 0\;\;(n \text{ of these BCs + electroneutrality})\;;\qquad \vec{n}\cdot\vec{i} = 0
↳ BC at electrode surfaces: ★ Faraday’s law as flux ↳ the flux of species at the electrode is proportional to the current density:
\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_j = \frac{-s_j}{nF}i_n
where i_n is defined by B-V (or another relevant kinetic expression) ↓ with \eta at the electrode surface (we must account for the potential drop in the electrolyte formed by MT):
\eta = \underbrace{(V - \phi)}_{\substack{\text{applied } - \\ \text{electrolyte potential}}} - \underbrace{(U - \phi^\circ)}_{\substack{\text{electrode equilibrium potential};\\ \phi^\circ = \text{electrolyte potential at equilibrium } (i=0,\, \phi^\circ = 0)}}
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \boxed{\eta = V - \phi - U}
(V is user-defined; \phi is the variable to solve for in the PDE (\nabla^2\phi = 0 or other forms); U comes from thermodynamics.)
↳ i_0 will also depend on c_j^{surf} → these are also solved for at the surface.
Limiting cases for BCs

↳ Limiting current density: at large \eta, the reaction may be so fast that c_{ion} = 0 at the surface; in this case the current density at the electrode is defined completely by N_j.
↳ Chemically limited reaction rate: at slow reaction rates, c_j^{surf} = c_j^{bulk} and we can neglect concentration gradients ↳ our only variable is \phi, defined by \nabla^2\phi = 0.

★ And if the ohmic resistance to current flow is much larger than the charge-transfer resistance (e.g. a poorly conducting electrode), then V = \phi at the electrode surface.


↳ Slow charge-transfer rate: the charge-transfer resistance is much larger than the ohmic resistance in solution (e.g. a poorly conducting electrolyte), so we have a uniform current density, i_n = I/\text{area} at all positions.

Transport of a binary electrolyte
↳ \mathrm{M^+X^-} of a single salt species is present (migration is most important). E.g. Cu plating at an electrode where C_{Cu^{2+}} = 0 at the surface (fast reaction).
Sketch: concentration rising linearly from C_s = 0 at the electrode to C_b = C_{b,bulk} across the diffusion boundary layer (\delta \sim 10\ \mum) → Fick’s law:
N = -D\frac{(C_{Cu,bulk} - C_s)}{\delta}

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 15
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 32-37) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Non-Fickian transport
For \mathrm{M_{\nu_+}X_{\nu_-}} where z_+\nu_+ + z_-\nu_- = 0, with c = \dfrac{c_+}{\nu_+} = \dfrac{c_-}{\nu_-} (sketch: concentration rising linearly from the electrode at x = 0 to the edge of the boundary layer at x = \delta).
★ Start by writing the flux of each species:
\begin{aligned}
1)&\;\; \nabla\cdot\vec{N}_+ = \nabla\cdot\big(-z_+u_+Fc\nu_+\nabla\phi - D_+\nu_+\nabla c\big) + \nu_+\nabla c\cdot\vec{v} \qquad (c\nu_+ = \text{concentration of cation species}) \\
2)&\;\; \nabla\cdot\vec{N}_- = \nabla\cdot\big(-z_-u_-Fc\nu_-\nabla\phi - D_-\nu_-\nabla c\big) + \nu_-\nabla c\cdot\vec{v}
\end{aligned}
★ Material balances:
3)\;\; \nu_+\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_+ \Rightarrow \frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = -\frac{1}{\nu_+}(\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_+)\;;\qquad
4)\;\; \nu_-\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_- \Rightarrow \frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = -\frac{1}{\nu_-}(\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_-)
★ Subtract (3 − 4):
0 = (z_+u_+ - z_-u_-)\big(F\nabla\cdot(c\nabla\phi)\big) + (D_+ - D_-)\nabla^2c
\;\xrightarrow{\text{rearrange}}\;
\nabla\cdot(c\nabla\phi) = \frac{-(D_+ - D_-)}{F(z_+u_+ - z_-u_-)}\nabla^2c
★ Plug this into (either 3 or 4):
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\nabla^2c - \vec{v}\cdot\nabla c\;,\quad\text{where } D = \frac{z_+u_+D_- - z_-u_-D_+}{z_+u_+ - z_-u_-}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{Nernst–Einstein, } D_j = RTu_j}\;
\boxed{D = \frac{(z_+ - z_-)D_+D_-}{z_+D_+ - z_-D_-}}
At SS, \partial c/\partial t = 0; in 1D with \vec{v} = 0 (only diffusion and migration):
D\frac{d^2c}{dx^2} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; c = Ax + B\;;\quad\text{BCs: (1) } c = 0 \text{ at } x = 0;\;\; \text{(2) } c = c_{bulk} \text{ at } x = \delta
\qquad\boxed{c = \frac{c_{bulk}}{\delta}x}
\therefore\quad N_+ \text{ in the BL } (\vec{v} = 0) = -z_+\nu_+u_+Fc\frac{d\phi}{dx} - D_+\nu_+\underbrace{\frac{dc}{dx}}_{\text{we know this}}
(solve for d\phi/dx.) Since this is Cu plating, the anion does not play any role: N_- = 0:
\therefore\quad 0 = -z_-\nu_-u_-Fc\frac{d\phi}{dx} - D_-\nu_-\frac{dc}{dx}\quad\to\;\text{plug in for } \frac{d\phi}{dx} \text{ in } N_+
\boxed{N_+ = -\nu_+\left(\frac{z_-u_-D_+ - z_+u_+D_-}{z_-u_-}\right)\frac{dc}{dx}}
\qquad\text{For CuSO}_4,\; z_+ = 2,\; z_- = -2:\quad
\boxed{N_{Cu^{2+}} = -2D_{Cu^{2+}}\frac{c_{bulk,Cu^{2+}}}{\delta}}
↳ Exactly 2× the Fickian diffusion. Why? The concentration of anions also has to vary linearly in the BL even though their flux is 0, which imposes an electric field within which the Cu²⁺ ions migrate (i.e. the anions create an E-field such that Cu has 2× the flux).
From the transference number (with Nernst–Einstein):
t_+ = \frac{z_+^2u_+c_+}{\sum_jc_ju_jz_j^2} \;\xrightarrow{\text{binary electrolyte}}\; \frac{z_+D_+}{z_+D_+ - z_-D_-}\;;\qquad t_+ = \frac{z_+u_+}{z_+u_+ - z_-u_-}\;,\quad t_- = \frac{-z_-u_-}{z_+u_+ - z_-u_-}
Applying this with D = \dfrac{z_+u_+D_- - z_-u_-D_+}{z_+u_+ - z_-u_-}:
\frac{N_+}{\nu_+} = -\frac{dc}{dx}\left(\frac{z_-u_-D_+ - z_+u_+D_-}{z_-u_-}\right) = \frac{D(z_+u_+ - z_-u_-)}{z_-u_-}\frac{dc}{dx} = \frac{-D}{t_-}\frac{dc}{dx}
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{N_+}{\nu_+} = \frac{-D}{(1 - t_+)}\frac{dc}{dx}}
with t_- + t_+ = 1 (fractions of the total current). If t_+ is small, migration becomes unimportant!! ★

Often we want to add extra ions to the solution (called a supporting electrolyte):

↳ to increase the conductivity (good V);
↳ effect on migration → it decreases the electric field, which means migration is less important (it decreases the flux to the surface!).



Supporting electrolyte (ternary electrolyte)
↳ Add H₂SO₄, which completely dissociates to \mathrm{2H^+ + SO_4^{2-}}; Cu plating with CuSO₄ + H₂SO₄ at C_{Cu^{2+}} = 0 at the surface. Species: 1 = Cu²⁺, 2 = SO₄²⁻, 3 = H⁺. (Dilute solution: no ion–ion, just ion–solvent interactions.)
Assume: (1) SS; (2) \vec{v} = 0; (3) only Cu²⁺ reacts at the electrode (N_2 = N_3 = 0).
Flux of 2 and 3 (Nernst–Einstein: u \to D):
D\frac{dc_j}{dx} = -c_jz_j\frac{F}{RT}D\frac{d\phi}{dx} \;\Rightarrow\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{c_j}\frac{dc_j}{dx}}_{d\ln c_j/dx} = -\frac{z_jF}{RT}\frac{d\phi}{dx}
Integrate: \ln c_j = -\dfrac{z_jF}{RT}\phi + A; BC: at x = \delta, \phi = 0, c_j = c_{j,bulk} → A = \ln c_{j,bulk}:
c_j = c_{j,bulk}\exp\left[\frac{-z_jF}{RT}\phi\right]
↳ Apply electroneutrality to get c_1:
z_1c_1 = -\sum_{j=2}^{3}z_jc_j = -\sum_{j=2}^{3}z_jc_{j,bulk}\exp\left(\frac{-z_jF\phi}{RT}\right)
↳ Material balance for Cu: \dfrac{\partial c_1}{\partial t} = 0 = -\dfrac{\partial N_1}{\partial x} + \cancel{R_1} → N_1 = constant.
N_1 = -z_1\frac{D_1F}{RT}c_1\frac{d\phi}{dx} - D_1\frac{dc_1}{dx} \;\Rightarrow\; N_1 = D_1\frac{d\phi}{dx}\left(-z_1\frac{Fc_1}{RT} - \frac{dc_1}{d\phi}\right)
(from electroneutrality we saw c_1 = f(\phi), so \frac{dc_1}{dx} = \frac{dc_1}{d\phi}\frac{d\phi}{dx}.)
\int_{x=\delta}^{x}-\frac{N_1}{D_1}\,dx = \int_{\phi=0}^{\phi}\left(z_1\frac{Fc_1}{RT} + \frac{dc_1}{d\phi}\right)d\phi
\boxed{\frac{N_1(\delta - x)}{D_1} = \left(1 - \frac{z_2}{z_1}\right)c_{2,bulk}\exp\left(\frac{-z_2F\phi}{RT}\right) + \left(1 - \frac{z_3}{z_1}\right)c_{3,bulk}\exp\left(\frac{-z_3F\phi}{RT}\right) - c_{1,bulk} - c_{2,bulk} - c_{3,bulk}}
(using -\tfrac{z_2}{z_1}c_{2,bulk} - \tfrac{z_3}{z_1}c_{3,bulk} = c_{1,bulk}.) We only need to evaluate N_1 at one position (since it is a constant) and satisfy c_1 = 0 at x = 0:
c_1 = 0 = -\frac{1}{z_1}\left(z_2c_{2,bulk}\exp\left(\frac{-z_2F\phi}{RT}\right) + z_3c_{3,bulk}\exp\left(\frac{-z_3F\phi}{RT}\right)\right)
\;\Rightarrow\;
\phi = \frac{-RT}{F(z_2 - z_3)}\ln\left(\frac{-z_3c_{3,bulk}}{z_2c_{2,bulk}}\right)\;\;@\;x = 0
↳ Plug into the integrated N_1 expression at x = 0 to get N in terms of constants only. Define a useful parameter:
\gamma = \frac{-z_3c_{3,bulk}}{z_2c_{2,bulk}}\;;\qquad \phi_0 = \frac{-RT}{F(z_2 - z_3)}\ln\gamma
@\;x = 0:\quad \frac{N_1\delta}{D_1} = \left(1 - \frac{z_2}{z_1}\right)c_{2,bulk}\gamma^{z_2/(z_2 - z_3)} + \left(1 - \frac{z_3}{z_1}\right)c_{3,bulk}\gamma^{z_3/(z_2 - z_3)} - c_{1b} - c_{2b} - c_{3b}
\;\;\vdots
\frac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{1,b}} = \frac{-\frac{z_1}{z_2}\left[\left(1 - \frac{z_2}{z_1}\right)\gamma^{z_2/(z_2 - z_3)} - \frac{z_2}{z_3}\left(1 - \frac{z_3}{z_1}\right)\gamma^{1 + \frac{z_3}{z_2 - z_3}} + \frac{z_2}{z_1}(1 - \gamma) - 1 + \frac{z_2}{z_3}\gamma\right]}{(1 - \gamma)}
For our electrolyte (z_j):
\boxed{\frac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{1,b}} = \frac{\left(-2 - \gamma + 3\gamma^{2/3}\right)}{(1 - \gamma)}}\;;\qquad \gamma = \frac{-z_3c_{3,bulk}}{z_2c_{2,bulk}}

\gamma = 0 → reduces to the binary electrolyte ↳ \dfrac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{1b}} = -2.
\gamma \to 1 → “excess supporting electrolyte” (we have to apply L’Hôpital!) \Rightarrow \dfrac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{1b}} = -1 ↳ the expected result for diffusion only! (Migration is not important.) The main reason would be to increase the conductivity (improve the EE of the cell) ↓ you still want to keep the same kinetics by using the same electrolyte (but just reduce the ohmic resistance).

So generally, when is migration important?
↳ Solve our combined current-flux equation for \nabla\phi:
\vec{i} = -F\sum_j\big(z_j^2u_jFc_j\nabla\phi + z_jD_j\nabla c_j\big)\;\Rightarrow\; \nabla\phi = \frac{-1}{F\sum z_j^2u_jc_j}\left(\frac{\vec{i}}{F} + \sum z_jD_j\nabla c_j\right)
↳ Plug into the general flux expression for species k (p. 120; j → species, k → all other species): N_k = \dfrac{t_k}{z_kF}\big(\vec{i} + F\sum\dots\big), as t_k \to 0.


                  
                  Important
                  
                

★ When t_k \to 0, migration can be neglected (for the reacting species at the electrode).


Diffusion BL: \delta_{diff} = \delta_{mom}\,Sc^{-1/3}, with Sc = \nu/D_j (\delta_{mom} from Navier–Stokes).
Limiting cases for the governing equations
↳ Solving our transport equations can be cumbersome and require numerical techniques, but we can more easily determine transport behaviour in limiting cases that are often a good first approximation.
1. Uniform electrolyte composition (low current)
↳ When current is applied at the electrode, reactants are consumed, changing the composition (sketch: WE with a concentration boundary layer of thickness \delta, and a CE at distance L).
If i_{avg}/i_{lim} \ll 1, consider a uniform electrolyte (i_{lim} = the current at which c_{surf} = 0). ★ Even if i_{avg}/i_{lim} = 0.2, c_{surf} = 80\%\,c_{bulk}.

↳ If the composition is uniform, how many equations do we solve? Electroneutrality → to solve for the potential \phi in solution.
↳ As stated before, if \nabla c_j = 0 the potential is defined by the Laplace equation, \nabla^2\phi = 0.

In 1D, e.g. \dfrac{d^2\phi}{dx^2} = 0, subject to BCs at the electrodes:
BC 1 (WE at x = 0):
i_{avg} = -F\sum z_jN_j = -F\sum z_j\Big(z_ju_jFc_j\frac{d\phi}{dx} + \cancel{z_jD_j\nabla c_j} - \cancel{c_j\vec{v}}\Big) \;\Rightarrow\; i_{avg} = -\kappa\frac{d\phi}{dx}
Assume cathodic Tafel kinetics (often U gets dropped, assuming that the reference electrode is of the same composition as the WE):
-\kappa\frac{d\phi}{dx} = -i_0\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF(V - \phi - U)}{RT}\right) \;\Rightarrow\; -\kappa\frac{d\phi}{dx} = -i_0\exp\left(\frac{\alpha_cF(V - \phi)}{RT}\right)
BC 2 (CE): at x = L, \phi = 0. Integrating (×2) ⇒ \phi = Ax + B; applying the BCs:
\phi = \frac{i_{avg}}{\kappa}(L - x)\;,\quad\text{where } i_{avg} = -i_0\exp\left[\frac{-\alpha_cF\left(V - \frac{i_{avg}L}{\kappa}\right)}{RT}\right]
We can use \phi to tell us something about the resistances that are important for electrochemical performance. ↳ Using Ohm’s law, we can define:

Charge-transfer resistance (R_{ct}) → associated with the faradaic process at the electrode (★ the slope of the polarization curve: how much the current changes in response to a small change in overpotential):

R_{ct} = \left.\frac{\partial(V - \phi_0)}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}}\;;\qquad i_{avg} = -i_0\exp\left(\frac{-\alpha_cF(V - \phi)}{RT}\right)\;\Rightarrow\;(V - \phi) = \frac{RT}{\alpha_cF}\ln\left(\frac{i}{i_0}\right)

Ohmic resistance (solution resistance) at the electrode ↳ associated with charged species moving in the electrolyte:

R_\Omega = \left.\frac{\partial(\phi_0)}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}} = \frac{\partial}{\partial i}\left(\frac{i_{avg}}{\kappa}(L - x)\right) = \frac{L}{\kappa}
The ratio R_{ct}/R_\Omega → the current distribution.
2. Limiting current density (high current)
↳ c_{lim} = 0 at the electrode surface. ★ Assume t_{lim} \approx 0, \vec{v} = 0. At SS, \nabla^2c_{lim} = 0 subject to c_{lim} = 0 at x = 0 and c_{lim} = c_{bulk} at x = \delta:
\vec{n}\cdot\vec{N}_j = \frac{-s_j}{nF}i_{lim}\;\Rightarrow\; i_{lim} = \frac{nF}{-s_j}N_j\;\Rightarrow\; i_{lim} = \frac{nFD}{s_j}\left.\frac{dc_j}{dx}\right|_{x=0}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{i_{lim} = \frac{nFD_{lim}c_{bulk}}{\delta}}
In practice, we can compare this calculation to a measured i_{lim} (sketch: i vs E rising to a plateau at the measured i_{lim}).

                  Announcement 
                  
                

Exam 1: open book, 1 sheet of front-side notes, calculator.


Sketch: an electrode at x = 0 and the edge of the boundary layer at x = \delta.

The cation ⊕ moves toward the electrode by both diffusion and migration.
The anion ⊖ diffuses toward the electrode but migrates away from it. The migration term is there because we have imposed no flux of the anion at the electrode.

Since the anion is being pushed and pulled from both sides → its overall net flux is zero! Therefore, the E-field is such that the cation will have an extra migration term.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 39-40) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Recap
Ternary electrolyte:
\frac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{1,bulk}} = \frac{-2 - \gamma + 3\gamma^{2/3}}{1 - \gamma}\;;\qquad \gamma = \frac{-z_3c_{3,bulk}}{z_2c_{2,bulk}}

↳ \gamma = 0 → binary electrolyte ⇒ \dfrac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{bulk}} = -2
↳ \gamma = 1 → excess supporting electrolyte ⇒ \dfrac{N_1\delta}{D_1c_{bulk}} = -1 (when t_j \to 0, we neglect migration)

Limiting cases:

Uniform composition, i_{avg}/i_{lim} \ll 1 (corresponds to the maximum change in concentration in the BL): \nabla^2\phi = 0 \Rightarrow \phi = \dfrac{i_{avg}}{\kappa}(L - x).

→ Broke this down into charge-transfer + ohmic resistances; the R_{ct}/R_\Omega ratio would tell you what current regime you would be in:



R_{ct} = \left.\frac{\partial(V - \phi)}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}}\;;\qquad R_\Omega = \left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}}

↳ Limiting current density (c_{lim} = 0 at the surface): \nabla^2c_{lim} = 0 \Rightarrow c_{lim} = \dfrac{c_{bulk}}{\delta}x ↓ i_{lim} = \dfrac{nFD_{lim}}{s_{lim}}\dfrac{c_{bulk}}{\delta}.

When is a cell “ohmically limited”?
Using R_{ct} and R_\Omega (for uniform composition) → what cell length L would cause the current density to be “ohmically limited”?
With Tafel kinetics (the R_{ct} comes from differentiating the B-V i expression):
\frac{R_{ct}}{R_\Omega} = \frac{RT}{\alpha_cF|i_{avg}|}\left(\frac{\kappa}{L}\right)\;;\qquad\text{if } \frac{R_{ct}}{R_\Omega} \ll 1 \rightarrow \text{dominated by ohmic resistance}
Assume \kappa = 0.1\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}, i_0 = 0.1 mA/cm², \alpha_c = 0.5, at i_{avg} = 100 mA/cm² → L = 5 cm (the characteristic cell length; sketch: WE at x = 0, CE at x = L).
Linear kinetics
If we instead assume linear kinetics, how do V and \phi_0 vary with R_{ct}/R_\Omega?
\text{Linear: } i_{avg} = \frac{i_0F(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)}{RT}(V - \phi_0)\quad(\phi_0 = \text{potential at the electrode})\;;\qquad \phi_0 = \frac{i_{avg}L}{\kappa}
\left.\frac{\partial(V - \phi)}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}} = \frac{RT}{i_0F(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)} = R_{ct}\;;\qquad \left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}} = \frac{L}{\kappa} = R_\Omega
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{R_{ct}}{R_\Omega} = \frac{RT}{i_0F(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)}\left(\frac{\kappa}{L}\right)
— independent of i_{avg}. Plugging into \phi_0 = i_{avg}L/\kappa:
\phi_0 = \frac{i_0(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)FL}{RT\kappa}(V - \phi_0)\;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\phi_0}{(V - \phi_0)} = \frac{i_0(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)FL}{RT\kappa} = \frac{R_\Omega}{R_{ct}}
\boxed{\frac{\phi_0}{V} = \frac{1}{1 + W_a}}\;\;(\text{linear kinetics})\;;\qquad W_a = \frac{R_{ct}}{R_\Omega}
(the box in the notes reads \phi_0/V = 1/W_a with W_a = R_\Omega/R_{ct}; the form above follows from the line before it and matches the sketch)
Sketch: \phi_0/V vs R_{ct}/R_\Omega (log scale, 10^{-3} to 10^3) — \phi_0/V \to 1 when ohmically limited (small R_{ct}/R_\Omega) and → 0 when charge-transfer limited (an infinitely conductive electrolyte, or a high activation barrier for the reaction).
Limiting currents
\nabla^2c_{lim} = 0\;;\quad\text{BCs: at } x = 0,\; c_{lim} = 0;\;\; \text{at } x = \delta,\; c_{lim} = c_{bulk}
\qquad
c_{lim} = \frac{c_{bulk}}{\delta}x\;;\qquad i_{lim} = \frac{nFD_{lim}c_{bulk}}{s_{lim}\,\delta}
What will i be if c_{surf} \neq 0, assuming t_{lim} = 0, i.e. diffusion only?
\nabla^2c = 0\;;\quad\text{BC: at } x = 0,\; c = c_{surf};\;\; \text{at } x = \delta,\; c = c_{bulk}\;;\quad c = Ax + B
\qquad
\boxed{c = \frac{c_b - c_{surf}}{\delta}x + c_{surf}}
↳ Faraday’s law:
i = \frac{nFD_j}{-s_j}\left.\frac{dc_j}{dx}\right|_{x=0} = \frac{nFD_j}{-s_j}\left(\frac{c_{bulk} - c_{surf}}{\delta}\right)
If we measure i and then have \delta (from a BL analysis) ↳ then we can find c_{surf} → c_{surf} of H⁺ will give the local pH.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 18
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 41-42) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



(Aside: “Silent Spring”, Rachel Carson → “lucid” communication.)
Current distributions
The reaction rate is a key design parameter for any chemical reaction-engineering analysis, and we know that for non-electrochemical reactions it depends on c_j, T:
r_j = f(c_j, T, P)\quad\text{for non-electrochemical reactions}
In electrochemical systems, r = \dfrac{i}{nF}, and we know that i is additionally dependent on V and \phi:
i = f(c_j, T, P, V, \phi)
\therefore This can create spatial differences in reaction rate that we might not predict from classic reaction engineering (we have to solve PDEs for each finite element).
↳ We need some simplifications that arrive at approximations of real behaviour:

understand the scenarios that lead to specific regimes;
understand the governing equations + BCs within each regime;
generalities about current distributions, based on solutions to the governing equations.

Two dimensionless parameters:

\dfrac{i_{avg}}{i_{lim}} (spatial average, at each position) ⇒ describes the importance of concentration gradients.

↳ i_{avg}/i_{lim} \to 1 (MT-controlled limit) ↳ \nabla c is important.
↳ i_{avg}/i_{lim} \to 0 (uniform composition) ↳ \nabla c is not important.


W_a = \dfrac{R_{ct}}{R_\Omega} ⇒ describes the importance of charge transfer vs ohmic resistance.

↳ A different dependence on i, depending on the kinetic expression (Tafel or linear).



General case — decision tree
Governing equations:
N_j = -z_ju_jFc_j\nabla\phi - D_j\nabla c_j + \vec{v}c_j\;;\qquad \sum z_jc_j = 0
→ Solving this gives us the complete picture: the “tertiary current distribution”:

This occurs when \nabla c_j \neq 0 (i_{avg} \approx i_{lim}).
R_{ct} and R_\Omega are both important.
t_j \to 0 ⇒ convection–diffusion; with fast kinetics → i_{lim}.
t_j \neq 0 ⇒ the full governing equations (no simplifications).
W_a > 0.1.
MT BCs, typically.

↓ Can \nabla c_j be neglected? (i_{avg}/i_{lim} = ?)

No (i_{avg}/i_{lim} \sim 1) → can the electric field be neglected? (t_j = ?)

No (t_j > 0) → back to the full governing equations.
Yes (t_j \to 0) → governing equation: the convection–diffusion equation
\frac{\partial c_j}{\partial t} + \vec{v}\cdot\nabla c_j = D_j\nabla^2c_j
→ further considerations regarding convective transport: the Péclet number.


Yes (i_{avg}/i_{lim} \to 0) → governing equation (Laplace): \nabla^2\phi = 0 → should R_{ct} be considered? (W_a = ?)

Yes (W_a > 0.1) → secondary current distribution:

\nabla c_j = 0
Ohmic and charge-transfer resistances are both important (W_a > 0.1) ↳ (i\text{–}\eta)-type BCs [Tafel, linear, etc.] (kinetic BCs) ↳ always more uniform than primary.


No (W_a \to 0) → primary current distribution:

Occurs when \nabla c_j = 0 (uniform composition)
Ohmic resistance dominates
↳ Results in constant-potential BCs → linear BCs + governing equations, and a non-uniform current distribution (it has the maximum non-uniformity).





Regimes on a polarization curve
Sketch: a polarization curve with limiting-current plateaus — there is an i_{lim} for anodic and for cathodic (these two are different).

I → the low-current, kinetically controlled region.
II → secondary?
III → high kinetics (ohmically dominated), R_{ct} is small [primary].

(We don’t have enough information about R_\Omega to make the general claim.)

→ A large WE, or
→ an electrolyte solution with poor conductivity (\kappa\downarrow, R_\Omega\uparrow)

… are moving towards primary.
Large electrodes + high currents ↳ significant non-uniformity.

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 19
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 43-44) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Wagner number
↳ We can make good assumptions about uniformity:
W_a = \frac{R_{ct}}{R_\Omega}
Charge-transfer resistance (R_{ct}) → this is usually at the electrode (since that is where charge transfer is happening — the electrode is dealt with by B-V kinetics).

↳ The resistance to current flow due to charge-transfer kinetics at the electrodes (\eta = V - \phi_0 - U).
↳ Last chapter we said

R_{ct} = \left.\frac{\partial(V - \phi)}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}}\quad\text{or}\quad \left.\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}}\;\bigstar\qquad(i_{avg} = \text{average current over the entire electrode})

↳ Since it depends on kinetics → it will change with the given process:

Small overpotential (linear kinetics, i = i_0\frac{(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)F\eta}{RT}):
R_{ct} = \frac{RT}{(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)Fi_0}
Large overpotential (anodic Tafel kinetics, i = i_0\exp\left[\frac{\alpha_aF\eta}{RT}\right]):
R_{ct} = \left.\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial i}\right|_{i_{avg}} = \frac{RT}{\alpha_aF|i_{avg}|}\quad\to\;\text{does depend on } i_{avg}
★ Any other type of kinetics → solve for \eta = f(i) and differentiate, or get the slope of the polarization curve.



\uparrow kinetics → i_{avg}\uparrow → R_{ct}\downarrow → W_a \to 0 (primary).
Ohmic resistance (R_\Omega):

↳ The resistance to current flow due to the properties of the electrolyte and cell. For the 1D case:

R_\Omega = \frac{L}{\kappa} = \frac{\text{characteristic length}}{\text{conductivity}}
(we need to select the characteristic length carefully).

↳ Does not depend on kinetics.
↳ Depends on \kappa (type of electrolyte) and L (geometry).

Example: hemispherical electrode of radius r_0, with the counter electrode far away (r_c \gg r_0) — chosen since it becomes a 1D problem! If the composition is uniform:
\nabla^2\phi = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial\phi^2} = 0
\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial r}\right) = 0\;;\qquad \text{BCs: } \phi = V \text{ at } r = r_0;\;\; \phi = 0 \text{ at } r = \infty
\therefore\quad \frac{d^2\phi}{dr^2} + \frac{2}{r}\frac{d\phi}{dr} = 0\;\Rightarrow\; \phi = \frac{c_1}{r} + c_2 \;\xrightarrow{\text{BCs}}\; \boxed{\phi = \frac{r_0V}{r}}
i = -\kappa\left.\frac{d\phi}{dr}\right|_{r=r_0}\;(\nabla c = 0) \;\Rightarrow\; i_\Omega = \frac{V}{r_0}\kappa
(i_\Omega = the ohmically limited current, controlled by the potential and not by kinetics.)
R_\Omega = \frac{V}{i_\Omega}\;(\text{ignoring c.t.})\;\therefore\quad \boxed{R_\Omega = \frac{r_0}{\kappa}} \qquad (r_0 \text{ is the characteristic length})
Example: hemicylindrical electrode (r_{CE} = counter-electrode radius):
R_\Omega = \frac{r_0}{\kappa}\ln\left(\frac{r_{CE}}{r_0}\right)
↓ We need this for W_a ↓ we need W_a for the current distribution ↓ change the values of r_{CE} and r_0 to determine the R_\Omega dependence (what dominates).
Putting together R_{ct} and R_\Omega
W_{a,L} = \frac{R_{ct,L}}{R_\Omega} = \frac{RT\kappa}{(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)Fi_0\ell}\quad(\text{linear kinetics})\;;\qquad W_{a,T} = \frac{R_{ct,T}}{R_\Omega} = \dots
(the Tafel expression is left unfinished in the notes; \ell = characteristic length.)

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.title: Lecture 20
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 45-47) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Recap
W_a → tells us the uniformity of an electrochemical system (low W_a → primary current distribution):

↳ R_{ct} = \dfrac{\partial\eta}{\partial i} (depends on kinetics) → W_{a,L}, W_{a,T}
↳ R_\Omega = \dfrac{\partial\phi_0}{\partial i} (essentially characteristic length / conductivity)

Characteristics and solution of primary and secondary current distributions
↳ \nabla c_j = 0, W_a \to 0: the maximum non-uniformity in the current distribution.
↳ In practice, we get the governing equation and boundary conditions:
\boxed{\nabla^2\phi = 0\;;\qquad \text{BCs: at the WE surface } \phi = V;\;\; \text{at the CE } \phi = 0}
(\phi = 0 at the CE is an arbitrary constant value; \eta = V - \phi - U is where the reference matters.)
Example: the Hull cell
It has a specific geometry to allow experimental determination of current non-uniformity — determined to see the throwing power of an electrolyte, based on how much mass accumulates at the electrode at each distance.
Sketch: a trapezoidal cell — the CE on the top, the WE inclined at angle \theta along the bottom from x = 0 to x = L, with heights h, h' (h' = h + (k - k')), k = L/\tan\theta, k'(x) = x/\tan\theta.
For the primary current distribution, \nabla^2\phi = 0 (rectangular coordinates):
\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2} = 0\;;\qquad \text{BCs: } \phi = 0 \text{ at } y = h';\;\; \phi = V \text{ at } y = k\cdot k';\;\; \left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0} = \left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial x}\right|_{x=L} = 0
The last two are insulating BCs: \vec{i} = -\kappa\nabla\phi, and there is no i through an insulator ⇔ \partial\phi/\partial x = 0 (a symmetry condition).
Conformal-mapping solution (to solve a partial differential equation): the parameters are curve-fit by realizing the property of the primary current at a junction with an insulator. Sketch: an electrode meeting an insulator at angle \theta near r = 0:
\frac{i(r)}{i_{avg}} \propto r^{\left(\frac{\pi}{2\theta} - 1\right)}

If \theta > \pi/2 → i \to \infty (current flowing from everywhere)
\theta < \pi/2 → i \to 0 (current lines can’t flow into a narrow corner)
\theta = \pi/2 → i → finite

We get:
\boxed{\frac{i(x)}{i_{avg}} = \frac{\left(\frac{x}{L}\right)^a}{\left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)^b}\left(c - \frac{dK}{L}\right)}\qquad(a, b, c, d \text{ are constants})
(sketch: i(x)/i_{avg} vs x/L rising steeply toward x/L = 1 for \theta = 0.22\pi).
Secondary current distribution
\nabla c_j = 0; W_a > 0.1; always more uniform than primary; kinetics are no longer negligible (so \phi at the electrodes should include this).
\nabla^2\phi = 0\;;\qquad\text{BC: } i = f(V, \phi) \rightarrow \text{B-V kinetics (only describes the current normal to the electrode)}
↓ For uniform composition, \vec{i} = -\kappa\nabla\phi, so i = -\kappa\left.\dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0}.
↳ For linear kinetics: i = \dfrac{(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)i_0F}{RT}(V - \phi):
\boxed{\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y} = \frac{-(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)i_0F}{\kappa RT}(V - \phi)} \qquad\text{BC at the WE for the secondary current distribution (linear kinetics)}
↳ Tafel kinetics: (below).
Example: “line electrode”
Sketch: a WE from x = -L to x = L embedded in an insulating plane, with the CE far away (a hemisphere at infinity).
Secondary current distribution, linear kinetics: \nabla^2\phi = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial x^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial y^2} = 0.
BCs: at the CE (x^2 + y^2 = \infty), \phi = 0; at the WE, \dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial y} = \dfrac{i_0}{\kappa}\dfrac{(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)F}{RT}(V - \phi).
Non-dimensionalizing: let \bar{x} = x/L, \bar{y} = y/L, \bar{\phi} = \phi/V. Then \dfrac{\partial^2\bar{\phi}}{\partial\bar{x}^2} + \dfrac{\partial^2\bar{\phi}}{\partial\bar{y}^2} = 0, and at \bar{y} = 0:
\frac{\partial\bar{\phi}}{\partial\bar{y}} = -\underbrace{\frac{i_0(\alpha_a + \alpha_c)FL}{\kappa RT}}_{1/W_{a,L}}(1 - \bar{\phi})
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\frac{\partial\bar{\phi}}{\partial\bar{y}} = \frac{-(1 - \bar{\phi})}{W_{a,L}}}\quad\text{BC for linear kinetics}
↳ For Tafel kinetics:
\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial y} = \frac{-i_0}{\kappa}\exp\left[\frac{\alpha_aF(V - \phi)}{RT}\right]\;\;@\;y = 0
Non-dimensionalize using the term in the exponent, \bar{\phi} = \dfrac{\alpha_aF\phi}{RT}:
\frac{\partial\bar{\phi}}{\partial\bar{y}} = \frac{-i_0LF}{\kappa RT}\exp\left[\frac{\alpha_aFV}{RT} - \frac{\alpha_aF\phi}{RT}\right]
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{\partial\bar{\phi}}{\partial\bar{y}} = -A\exp\big[-\bar{\phi}\big]\;,\quad\text{where } A = \frac{i_0\alpha_aFL}{\kappa RT}\exp\left[\frac{\alpha_aFV}{RT}\right]}
The current distribution as W_a \to 0 (primary): sketch of i along the electrode for W_a = 4.2 (nearly flat) and W_a = 0.1 (rising sharply at the edge). As the electrode gets larger → greater non-uniformity; below W_a = 0.1 you are basically in the primary regime.
Using W_a to understand non-uniformity
↳ E.g. dendrite formation in batteries seriously limits the efficiency and development of new battery technology.

↳ Uncontrolled electrode deposition.
↳ A defect/asperity could create significant non-uniformity (sketch: an asperity of height h_a on the WE).

W_{a,T} = \frac{RT\kappa}{\alpha_cF|i_{avg}|\ell}\;,\quad \ell = h_a\;;\qquad\text{if } i_{avg} = -50\ \text{mA/cm}^2,\; \kappa = 0.1\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1},\; \alpha_c = 0.5

At W_a = 0.1: h_a = 1 cm ← this is high and unlikely to happen.
At W_a = 1: h_a = 1 mm.

Lecture 22
Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 51-54) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



Impact of electrode conductivity on the current distribution
So far we have shown that current non-uniformities arise from:

the electric field / geometry (primary, secondary);
MT effects during fast kinetics (sketch: a non-uniform diffusion layer \delta above an electrode).

We can also encounter current variations due to imperfect conductors (i.e. resistive substrates).
Current distribution in resistive substrates
↳ Encountered frequently during the metallization of Si chips.
Sketch: a WE (a thin film of thickness a) from x = 0 to x = L facing a CE, with the current collector connected only at x = 0. ★ Previously we set V = \phi at y = 0 (a 1D problem with a uniform current distribution).
Now, because the substrate is resistive, all current must flow through x = 0, so the potential of the metal is \phi_m = f(x) and
\eta = \phi_m - \phi_s\qquad(\phi_m = \text{potential of the metal},\; \phi_s = \text{potential in solution})
To solve, we assume \nabla c_j = 0; then
\nabla^2\phi_s = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\partial^2\phi_s}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2\phi_s}{\partial y^2} = 0
For the BCs, assume Tafel kinetics at the electrode:
i(x) = -\kappa\left.\frac{\partial\phi_s}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0} = -i_0\exp\left[\frac{-\alpha_cF}{RT}\underbrace{(\phi_m - \phi_s)}_{= f(x)}\right]
— we get \phi_m from a charge balance (sketch: a slice of the film from x to x + \Delta x with in-plane current i_m and current i_y(x) leaving into solution):
\text{In} - \text{out} + \text{gen} = \text{acc.}\;:\quad a\big[i_m(x) - i_m(x + \Delta x)\big] - i_y(x)\Delta x = 0
\;\Rightarrow\;
i_y(x) = \frac{\big(i_m|_x - i_m|_{x+\Delta x}\big)a}{\Delta x} \;\Rightarrow\; i_y(x) = -a\frac{di_m}{dx}
From Ohm’s law, i_y(x) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{R_s}\dfrac{d\phi_m}{dx}\right) (R_s = sheet resistance). Combining:
-a\frac{di_m}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{R_s}\frac{d\phi_m}{dx}\right)
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
\boxed{i_m = \frac{-1}{aR_s}\frac{d\phi_m}{dx} = -\sigma\frac{d\phi_m}{dx}}
(\sigma is analogous to \kappa, [=]\ \Omega^{-1}\text{cm}^{-1}.) BCs: at x = L, \dfrac{d\phi_m}{dx} = 0 (the gradient is zero perpendicular to the insulator position); at x = 0, \phi_m = V.
This can be solved numerically or analytically (limiting cases). It depends on
W_{a,T} = \frac{RT\kappa}{\alpha_cF|i_{avg}|L}\;;\qquad K_0 = \frac{\kappa L}{a\sigma}\quad(\text{ratio of electrolyte to substrate conductance})

If W_a/K_0 → large → more uniform.
K_0\downarrow, \sigma\uparrow (electrode conductivity goes up) → tends to be more uniform.

(sketch: current along the substrate — flat for large W_a, rising for low W_a (primary).)
Summary
1) Spatial variations of current on an electrode are caused by:

→ W_a = R_{ct}/R_\Omega \to 0 when R_\Omega is large, with i_{avg} \ll i_{lim}
→ MT conditions when i_{avg} \approx i_{lim}
→ Resistive electrodes (even when W_a > 0.1)

Uniform current:

Conductive electrolyte
Small electrodes
Uniform MT if i \sim i_{lim}
Conductive electrodes

Fluid flow to a rotating disk electrode (RDE)

→ Even under i_{lim} we have non-uniformity of current due to MT (a boundary-layer problem).
→ A rotating disk electrode provides a MT scenario where an exact solution to the fluid flow is obtained.

Sketch: a disk WE embedded in an insulating cylinder rotating at \Omega; fluid is drawn axially toward the disk and flung outward radially, with a thin BL above the disk (from r = 0 to r = r_0).
↳ The solution to the fluid flow reveals a momentum BL of thickness \sqrt{\nu/\Omega} (thicker than the diffusion BL) — not dependent on radial position.
↳ Based on this thickness, we can define a dimensionless axial variable \xi = \dfrac{z}{\sqrt{\nu/\Omega}}. Then we can define each velocity component in non-dimensional form as a function of \xi:

Radial: v_r = r\Omega F(\xi)
Angular: v_\theta = r\Omega G(\xi)
Axial: v_z = \sqrt{\nu\Omega}\,H(\xi)

No-slip condition at \xi = 0 ⇒ F = H = 0, G = 1 (whatever is at the surface keeps rotating with it).

↳ The axial velocity is not a function of radial position (uniform diffusion-layer thickness) → uniform current at i_{lim}.
↳ The radial velocity is outward (positive r) → negligible flux from large radial positions to smaller radial positions ↳ minimal edge effects.

These enable its use (very different from the earlier case).
Now solving for the current distribution:
↳ Assume the limiting current at the disk and t_i = 0 → the convection–diffusion equation:
v_z\left(\frac{\partial c}{\partial z}\right) = D\left(\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial z^2} + \cancel{\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial r^2}}\right)
(the diffusion layer is constant in the r-direction, even though we have flow in the r-direction → no concentration gradients in the r-direction.)
From the hydrodynamic analysis:
v_z = -az^2\left(\frac{\Omega^{3/2}}{\nu^{1/2}}\right)\;,\quad a = 0.51023\;(\text{fit parameter})
★ This is the 1-term Taylor expansion of v_z = \sqrt{\nu\Omega}\,H(\xi). ↓ Non-dimensionalize: \bar{z} = \left(\dfrac{\Omega^{1/2}}{\nu^{1/6}D^{1/3}}\right)z:
\therefore\quad \frac{\partial c}{\partial z} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial\bar{z}}\left(\frac{\Omega^{1/2}}{\nu^{1/6}D^{1/3}}\right)\;;\qquad \frac{\partial^2c}{\partial z^2} = \frac{\partial^2c}{\partial\bar{z}^2}\left(\frac{\Omega}{\nu^{1/3}D^{2/3}}\right)
(the notes write the exponents in the scaling factor slightly differently in places; the forms above are dimensionally consistent)
Plugging in:
\boxed{-a\bar{z}^2\frac{dc}{d\bar{z}} = \frac{d^2c}{d\bar{z}^2}}\;;\qquad\text{BCs: at } \bar{z} = 0,\; c = 0;\;\; \text{at } \bar{z} = \infty,\; c = c_\infty

Coursework/Electrochemistry/EChem_597/EC.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 55-60) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



RDE: solving the convection–diffusion equation
-a\bar{z}^2\frac{dc}{d\bar{z}} = \frac{d^2c}{d\bar{z}^2}\;,\qquad \bar{z} = \left(\frac{\Omega^{1/2}}{\nu^{1/6}D^{1/3}}\right)z\;;\qquad\text{BCs: at } \bar{z} = 0,\; c = 0;\;\; \text{at } \bar{z} = \infty,\; c = c_\infty
Let g = dc/d\bar{z}:
-a\bar{z}^2g = \frac{dg}{d\bar{z}} \;\Rightarrow\; -a\bar{z}^2\,d\bar{z} = \frac{1}{g}dg \;\Rightarrow\; -\frac{a\bar{z}^3}{3} = \ln g\cdots
\qquad
\frac{dc}{d\bar{z}} = g = c_1\exp\left(\frac{-a\bar{z}^3}{3}\right)
→ use gamma functions to solve for c ↓ add in the BCs:
c_\infty = c_1\left(\frac{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}{3^{2/3}a^{1/3}}\right) \;\Rightarrow\; c_1 = \frac{c_\infty3^{2/3}a^{1/3}}{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}
\qquad
\frac{dc}{d\bar{z}} = c_\infty\frac{3^{2/3}a^{1/3}}{\Gamma\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}\exp\left[\frac{-a\bar{z}^3}{3}\right]
At \bar{z} = 0: \left.\dfrac{dc}{d\bar{z}}\right|_{\bar{z}=0} = 0.62\,c_\infty, so
\boxed{\left.\frac{dc}{dz}\right|_{z=0} = \left(\frac{\Omega^{1/2}}{\nu^{1/6}D^{1/3}}\right)(0.62)\,c_\infty}
From Ch. 5, N = -D\left.\dfrac{dc}{dz}\right|_{z=0}:
N = -Dc_\infty\left(\frac{0.62\,\Omega^{1/2}}{D^{1/3}\nu^{1/6}}\right)
Normally, the flux at i_{lim} is N = -D\dfrac{c_\infty}{\delta} \therefore by similarity:
\delta = \left(\frac{0.62\,\Omega^{1/2}}{D^{1/3}\nu^{1/6}}\right)^{-1}
From Faraday’s law:
\boxed{\frac{s_{lim}i_{lim}}{nF} = \frac{Dc_\infty}{\delta} = 0.62\,D^{2/3}\nu^{-1/6}\Omega^{1/2}c_\infty} \qquad\textbf{Levich equation!}
If we can accurately vary \Omega (the rotation rate), we can understand species diffusion. Sketch: i_{lim} vs \Omega^{1/2} (\Omega in rad/s) is a line with
\text{slope} = 0.62\left(\frac{nFc_\infty}{s_{lim}}\right)\nu^{-1/6}D^{2/3}
— more spin, more convection, a smaller diffusion layer (higher c getting through → higher i_{lim}).


                  
                  Note
                  
                

We can also define a “Levich-type” equation for a non-limiting current, as long as the current distribution is uniform (W_a → large). (You just have to change the bounds of integration.) Then
\frac{s\,i_{avg}}{nF} = \frac{D(c_\infty - c_0)}{\delta} = 0.62\,D^{2/3}\nu^{-1/6}\Omega^{1/2}(c_\infty - c_0)


Koutecký–Levich analysis
Often, we have a charge-transfer resistance:

↳ This means the current has contributions from both MT and kinetics.
↳ To separate out kinetic and MT effects on the current, use “Koutecký–Levich” analysis.
↳ To understand kinetic effects, we generally define the current as a function of potential:

i = nFc_0K(V)\;;\qquad K(V) = K_0\exp\big(f(\eta)\big)
(c_0 = surface concentration; K(V) = potential-dependent rate constant.) We need an expression for c_0 in terms of i_{lim}:
\frac{s\,i_{avg}}{nF} = \frac{D(c_\infty - c_0)}{\delta} = \frac{Dc_\infty}{\delta} - \frac{Dc_0}{\delta} = i_{lim} - \frac{Dc_0}{\delta}\;(?)
\qquad
i = i_{lim}\left(\frac{c_\infty - c_0}{c_\infty}\right)
c_0 = c_\infty - \frac{i}{i_{lim}}c_\infty = c_\infty\left(1 - \frac{i}{i_{lim}}\right)
\qquad
\boxed{i = \underbrace{nFK(V)c_\infty}_{i_K}\left(1 - \frac{i}{\underbrace{i_{lim}}_{i_{MT}}}\right)}
(i_K = the kinetic contribution to the current; i_{lim} = i_{MT} = the mass-transport contribution to the current.)
i = i_K\left(1 - \frac{i}{i_{MT}}\right) \;\Rightarrow\; i = \frac{i_Ki_{MT}}{i_{MT} + i_K} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{\frac{1}{i} = \frac{1}{i_K} + \frac{1}{i_{MT}}} \qquad\textbf{Koutecký–Levich equation}
— like “summing up” resistors. Sketch: i vs \Omega^{1/2} — the curve bends from the i_{MT} line toward the plateau i_K.
If we tried to do a Levich analysis, D might not be accurate → we can plot \dfrac{1}{i} vs \Omega^{-1/2} (linearize the system): a line whose intercept is 1/i_K.
Primary current distribution for rotating disks
RDEs are typically used near i_{lim}, but not always (what about cases not near i_{lim}?).
↳ Does the rotation rate of the RDE affect a primary current analysis? No, because \nabla c_j = 0 for primary (convection and diffusion don’t matter; we just solve \nabla^2\phi).

The only difference is the geometry (solved by Newman analytically):

\frac{i(r)}{i_{avg}} = \frac{0.5}{\sqrt{1 - (r/r_0)^2}}\;;\qquad \text{at } z = 0,\; r > r_0 \Rightarrow \frac{\phi}{V} = 1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\tan^{-1}\sqrt{\left(\frac{r}{r_0}\right)^2 - 1}

The potential varies rapidly outside of the disk, close to the disk.
The position of the CE is determined by this sort of analysis ↓ if you are 3 disk radii away, you have already gone through 90% of the potential drop.
The potential drop in solution will affect the CE and RE? ↳ How? → That is why you have a compensation for a measured potential drop ↓ the Luggin capillary.

Rotating ring-disk electrode (RRDE)
↳ We can add a second WE co-planar with the disk to give added functionality to the well-defined hydrodynamics of the RDE (sketch: a disk WE1 surrounded by a ring WE2; species flow radially outward from the disk to the ring).
Most common application: “generator–collector” mode — R is converted to O at the disk, and O is swept to the ring where it is converted back to R → we can get exactly how much (partial) current is going toward the desired reaction.

Demo: RDE

Au disk (WE)
Hg/HgSO₄ RE (0.62 V vs SHE)
Pt wire CE
0.1 M K₂SO₄ (+ H₂SO₄) → pH ≈ 4

Relevant reactions:
① Hydrogen evolution reaction (HER)
\mathrm{2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2}\;;\qquad U^\circ = 0 \text{ vs SHE at pH } 0\;;\quad U = 0\text{ V vs RHE}
(RHE has a built-in pH correction — it shifts with the pH of the solution.) At pH ≈ 4 the electrolyte is proton-limited; HER still occurs when we run out of protons, via
\mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 + 2OH^-}\;;\qquad U^\circ = -0.828\text{ V vs SHE at pH } 14\;;\quad U = 0\text{ V vs RHE}
② Oxygen reduction reaction (since we are not purging with Ar, O₂ will also react at the electrode):
\mathrm{O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2H_2O}\;;\qquad U^\circ = 1.23\text{ V vs SHE at pH } 0\;;\quad U = 1.23\text{ V vs RHE}
\mathrm{O_2 + 2H_2O + 4e^- \rightarrow 4OH^-}\;;\qquad U^\circ = 0.401\text{ V vs SHE at pH } 14\;;\quad U = 1.23\text{ V vs RHE}
Nernst:
V_{applied} = V_{RHE} - V_{RE} - (0.0591\text{ V}\times\text{pH})\;;\qquad V_{applied} = 0 - 0.62 - 0.0591(4) = -0.856\text{ V vs RE}

At 0 V vs RHE, \eta_{HER} = V_{applied} - U = 0 — we are giving it no “extra” potential (i.e. no reaction should be driven).
\eta_{ORR} = -1.23 V → a very large driving force for this to happen, so at V_{applied} = 0 it will be dominating.

We want the current density on the CE to be very small (thus a high surface area).
CV → a linear change between two vertices.
Sketch of the measured polarization curve: going negative, an ORR plateau (the overpotential for ORR is high here), then HER beyond −0.856 V, then water HER at the most negative potentials. We need to go to a lower potential to have overpotential for HER (but ORR is still happening as well!).

The diffusion coefficient tells you the spacing between the plateaus (resulting in different slopes).
An oscillation in the trace is due to the potentiostat switching its current range (since it is on Auto).

Rotating ring-disk electrode
Sketch: a disk (WE₁) surrounded by a ring (WE₂).
→ “Generator–collector” mode

↳ A redox species is generated at the disk, and that species does not exist in the bulk electrolyte.
↳ The ring potential is held such that the generated species’ concentration is zero at the ring surface. (If not known, we need to do a sweep and measure i to see where/what could be possible.)

For c_{ring} = 0, the MT equations are solved to yield i_{ring} as a function of i_{disk}:
i_{ring} = \frac{nF}{s}D\int_{r_2}^{r_3}\left.\frac{\partial c}{\partial y}\right|_{y=0}r\,dr
The solution provides:
\boxed{i_{ring} = -N_c\,i_{disk}}
N_c = collection efficiency (the fraction of species generated at the disk that reacts at the ring) — only a function of r_1, r_2, r_3 ↳ not a function of \Omega, D, c_\infty.
How to maximize N_c? A small r_2 and a large (r_3 - r_2) — a small gap and a large ring [since you want to collect all the species formed on the disk, which are moving outwards].
→ “Detection mode”

↳ Instead of the generated species reacting at the ring, the average concentration of the species at the ring induces a change in the ring’s equilibrium potential.
↳ This can be useful to detect surface pH changes if the ring is a potentiometric pH sensor.
↳ The hydrodynamics are the same, but now we are not reacting on the ring:

\boxed{(c_{ring} - c_\infty) = N_D(c_{disk} - c_\infty)}
N_D = detection efficiency (the fraction of species generated at the disk detected as a surface concentration at the ring) ↳ only depends on r_1, r_2, r_3.
Maximizing N_D? A small ring — we don’t want to “average” out the measurement.

HW0 pt 2



Fundamental techniques

Chronoamperometry (CA)
Chronopotentiometry (CP)
Polarization curves (LSV, CV)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)

→ CA: chronoamperometry
Chrono → time, amp → current: the changing current (while holding the potential constant).
The time-dependent concentration profile can be solved with MT concepts. E.g. assume:

double-layer current negligible (since it takes time/charge for the double layer to form);
no forced convection;
t_j \to 0

→ diffusion-controlled.
Mass balance:
\frac{\partial c_j}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_j + \cancel{R_j}\;;\qquad \vec{N}_j = \cancel{\text{migration}} + \text{diff.} + \cancel{\text{convection}}
(this may not always be valid — e.g. steady-state voltammetry; application of current will usually result in gradients and “flow” ↳ harder to reach steady state in these larger electrodes.)
\text{PDE:}\quad \boxed{\frac{\partial c_j}{\partial t} = D\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial x^2}}\;;\qquad\text{BCs: at } t = 0,\; c = c_\infty;\;\; \text{at } x \to \infty,\; c = c_\infty;\;\; \text{at } [t > 0, x = 0],\; c = 0 \;\leftarrow\; \text{limiting current}
Combination of variables or a Laplace transform to solve the PDE:
\frac{c(x,t)}{c_\infty} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^{x/\sqrt{4Dt}}\exp\big[-y^2\big]\,dy = \text{erf}\left[\frac{x}{2(Dt)^{1/2}}\right]
From the concentration profile we get the flux, and then the current (i). Flux at x = 0:
\left.\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0} = \left.\frac{2c_\infty}{\sqrt{\pi}}\exp\left[\frac{-x^2}{4Dt}\right]\frac{1}{\sqrt{4Dt}}\right|_{x=0} = \frac{c_\infty}{\sqrt{\pi Dt}}
\qquad
-N_x = D\left.\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}\right|_{x=0} = \frac{Dc_\infty}{\sqrt{\pi Dt}}
\boxed{i(t) = \frac{nF}{s}\frac{Dc_\infty}{\sqrt{\pi Dt}}} \;\leftarrow\;\textbf{Cottrell equation}


                  
                  Notes 
                  
                


As t\uparrow, i\downarrow (depletion of the reacting species near the surface) → since we are only considering diffusion, the species close to the electrode react, depleting this layer more and more.
As t \to 0, i \to \infty ↳ an infinite driving force (the potentiostat usually has current limits that will artificially cap the current).
★ According to c(x,t) ↳ the diffusion BL (defined as the x at which c = c_\infty) grows with t.



CP: chronopotentiometry
Vary the potential with time (at constant current) — the same system as before.
\text{Material balance:}\quad \frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial x^2}\;;\qquad \text{at } t = 0,\; c = c_\infty;\;\; \text{at } x \to \infty,\; c = c_\infty;\;\; \text{at } x = 0,\, t > 0:\; i = \frac{nF}{s}D\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}\;[\text{flux BC}; i \text{ constant!}]

★ Will this result in c_{lim} = 0 at all t > 0? ↳ No: initially c_{lim} > 0; at some time c_{lim} will get depleted at the electrode.
★ What happens after c_{lim} \to 0 when applying a constant current (the concentration of our limiting species goes to zero)? ↳ Since we are applying a constant current and all the species have been depleted ↓ a secondary reaction will turn on, which may cause an abrupt change in potential — something else has to make up the current (pass charges).

The time at which c_{lim} \to 0 is given by the solution to the PDE with a constant-flux BC — the Sand equation (for semi-infinite geometry):
\boxed{\tau = \frac{\pi D}{4}\left(\frac{c_\infty nF}{s_{lim}\,i}\right)^2}
Polarization curves (LSV/CV)
→ A polarization curve (I vs V) can be obtained by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) (apply a linearly changing potential function and measure the current; sketch: V rising linearly from V_i with t).
This measurement is affected by the ohmic drop in solution (solution resistance) ↳ the potential gradient in solution resulting from current flow between the WE and CE:
\eta = \underbrace{(V - U_{ref})}_{\text{RE potential}} - (U - U_{ref}) - \underbrace{\Delta\phi_\Omega}_{\text{ohmic drop}}
↳ We can estimate the value of \Delta\phi_\Omega at an RE far away from a disk electrode for a primary current distribution (r_0 = WE radius):
\Delta\phi_\Omega = \frac{\pi r_0}{4\kappa}i_{avg}
— the ohmic drop depends on electrode size and electrolyte conductivity [proportional to the current].
↳ LSVs for reversible reactions, with only one half of the redox couple in solution. E.g. \mathrm{O + ne^- \rightleftharpoons R} with equilibrium potential U: if the solution contains O but no R, and we apply an LSV (sketches: V ramping from V_i through U; surface c_O decaying from c_\infty while c_R rises).
How does i vs V look? We get a peak (non-SS) that results from an increasing flux followed by a decreasing concentration (a non-SS process): the current is ~0 from V_i until near U (the equilibrium potential), where species start to react; the increasing overpotential then drives diffusion, the reactant is rapidly depleted, which shuts off i, giving a peak i_p before approaching i_{lim}.
For V(t) = V_i + \nu t (\nu = scan rate, V/s; no species O initially in the system):
\boxed{i_p = -0.4463\,(nF)^{3/2}\left(\frac{D_0}{RT}\right)^{1/2}c_\infty\,\nu^{1/2}}
— for semi-infinite geometry (like a disk electrode) and diffusion only. The height changes but not the peak position (as you sweep faster).
Often we want to reverse the potential sweep to create a cyclic voltammogram (CV) (sketch: a triangular V(t) waveform, and the resulting duck-shaped i–V loop — an “upside-down CV” in this convention — with forward reduction peak and reverse peak around U; some reduction still occurs after the vertex). We don’t get back to i = 0 at V_i, because we do have species that can be reduced. The peak separation is \sim60 mV for a reversible process \left[\frac{2.303RT}{F}\right] (it comes from the math).
These techniques have complex math analysis due to the time response, but we can simplify some of these techniques by using “ultramicroelectrodes” (UME):
↳ electrodes of \sim10\ \mum → they establish SS in electrochemical synthesis at much shorter time scales than standard electrodes. Sketch: a sigmoidal i–V curve from V_i through U to V_1 — no peaks! (SS voltammetry).
