Question 1
Steady-state, non-isothermal catalyst pellet; first-order reaction:
\nabla^2u = \phi^2u\exp\left\{\frac{\gamma\beta(1 - u)}{1 + \beta(1 - u)}\right\}\quad 0 < \rho < 1\;;\qquad \nabla^2 = \frac{1}{\rho^q}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\rho^q\frac{d}{d\rho}\right)
(i)
u_N = 1 + (1 - \rho^2)\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}\alpha_n^{(N)}P_n(\rho^2)\;\Rightarrow\;u_1 = 1 + (1 - \rho^2)(\alpha_0P_0(\rho^2))\;,\quad P_0(\rho^2) = 1\;\therefore\;u_1 = 1 + (1 - \rho^2)\alpha_0 = 1 + \alpha_0 - \alpha_0\rho^2
The Jacobi-type polynomial:
P_1(\rho^2) = \sum_{k=0}^{1}(-1)^k\frac{(n!)}{(n - k)!}\frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}q + \frac{3}{2} + n + k\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}q + \frac{1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}q + \frac{3}{2} + n\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{1}{2}q + \frac{1}{2} + k\right)}\rho^{2k} = 1 - \frac{\Gamma\left(\frac{q}{2} + \frac{7}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{q}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{q}{2} + \frac{5}{2}\right)\Gamma\left(\frac{q}{2} + \frac{3}{2}\right)}\rho^2
We know \Gamma(x) = (x - 1)!, so (cancelling factorials)
P_1(\rho^2) = 1 - \frac{q + 5}{(q + 1)}\rho^2
From the question: collocation for an N-point is the root of the (N + 1)th basis function. Root of P_1(\rho^2) = 1 - \frac{(q + 5)}{(q + 1)}\rho^2 = 0:
\rho^2 = \frac{(q + 1)}{(q + 5)}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\rho^* = \left[\frac{(q + 1)}{(q + 5)}\right]^{1/2}}
(ii)
\eta = \frac{(q + 1)}{\phi^2}\left.\frac{du}{d\rho}\right|_{\rho=1}\;;\qquad \frac{du_1}{d\rho} = -2\alpha_0\rho\;\Rightarrow\;\left.\frac{du_1}{d\rho}\right|_{\rho=1} = -2\alpha_0
Solving for \alpha_0: u_1 = 1 + (1 - \rho^2)\alpha_0; @ \rho = \rho^* ⇒ u_1 = U:
\alpha_0 = \frac{(U - 1)}{(1 - \rho^{*2})} = \frac{(U - 1)}{\left[1 - \frac{(q + 1)}{(q + 5)}\right]} = \frac{(U - 1)(q + 5)}{4}
\;\therefore\;\eta = \frac{(q + 1)}{\phi^2}(-2)\frac{(U - 1)(q + 5)}{4}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\eta = \frac{(q + 1)(q + 5)(1 - U)}{2\phi^2}}
(iii) From the transport equation:
\nabla^2u_1 = \frac{1}{\rho^q}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(\rho^q\frac{d}{d\rho}[1 + (1 - \rho^2)\alpha_0]\right) = \frac{1}{\rho^q}\frac{d}{d\rho}\left(-2\rho^{(q+1)}\alpha_0\right) = (-2\alpha_0)(q + 1) = \frac{(1 - U)(q + 5)(q + 1)}{2}
@ \rho = \rho^*, u_1 = u = U:
\boxed{\frac{(1 - U)(q + 5)(q + 1)}{2} = \phi^2U\exp\left\{\frac{\gamma\beta(1 - U)}{1 + \beta(1 - U)}\right\}}
(iv) q = 1:
(1 - U)(6) = \phi^2U\exp\left\{\frac{\gamma\beta(1 - U)}{1 + \beta(1 - U)}\right\}\;\Rightarrow\;U\text{ as } f(\gamma, \beta, \phi^2)
\eta @ q = 1: \eta = \dfrac{6(1 - U)}{\phi^2} ⇒ \eta\phi^2 = 6(1 - U); \dfrac{d(\eta\phi^2)}{d\phi} = -6\dfrac{dU}{d\phi}.
} Using Python, for given \gamma, \beta values we can solve for \eta as a function of \phi ↓ this can be plotted for various initial guesses for the implicit function of U ↓ \underline{\phi} & \bar{\phi} represent the Thiele values for which multiplicity may appear ↓ numerically it is shown in the graph:
\underline{\phi} = 0.3\;;\qquad \bar{\phi} = 0.6\qquad\text{for } \gamma = 4,\;\beta = 10\quad(\text{see Python file attached})
Solving for the criteria: if the solution is not unique, \underline{u} \le u \le \bar{u} everywhere in \Omega. By letting f(u) = u\exp\left\{\frac{\gamma\beta(1 - u)}{1 + \beta(1 - u)}\right\}:
\nabla^2\bar{u} = -\phi^2f(\bar{u})\text{ in }\Omega,\;\bar{u} = 1\text{ on }\partial\Omega\;;\qquad \nabla^2\underline{u} = -\phi^2f(\underline{u})\text{ in }\Omega,\;\underline{u} = 1\text{ on }\partial\Omega
\int_\Omega[(\underline{u} - 1)\nabla^2\bar{u} - (\bar{u} - 1)\nabla^2\underline{u}]\,dV = -\phi^2\int_\Omega[(\underline{u} - 1)f(\bar{u}) - (\bar{u} - 1)f(\underline{u})]\,dV
With F(u) = \dfrac{f(u)}{(u - 1)}:
\boxed{-\phi^2\int_\Omega[(\underline{u} - 1)(\bar{u} - 1)]\,(F(\bar{u}) - F(\underline{u}))\,dV = 0}
A sufficient condition for uniqueness regardless of the \phi^2 value is that F(u) has to be monotonic in the range 0 < u < 1 (additionally, this equation is a requirement for multiplicity):
\therefore\;\frac{dF}{du} < 0\;,\quad 0 \le u \le 1\;;\qquad \frac{dF}{du} = \frac{d}{du}\left(\frac{f(u)}{(u - 1)}\right) = \frac{f'(u)(u - 1) - f(u)}{(u - 1)^2}
Using Wolfram Alpha for f'(u) and cancelling the common exponential:
\frac{[-(\gamma + 2)\beta u + \beta^2(u - 1)^2 + 2\beta + 1](u - 1)}{(1 - \beta(u - 1))^2} - u < 0
\;\Rightarrow\;
[-(\gamma + 2)\beta u + \beta^2(u - 1)^2 + 2\beta + 1](u - 1) - u(1 - \beta(u - 1))^2 < 0
↓ Expanding, this can be solved to get the condition for the inequality relating \beta, \gamma, u, using the roots of the cubic, to be less than 0.

Question 1
CSTR; \mathrm{B} + \sigma\mathrm{S} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B} + \cdots (B = biomass; \sigma = mass of substrate); K_s = Michaelis constant; \mu = max. specific growth.
(i) Steady states? Desirable steady states? Inequality involving the operating parameters \theta and s_f?
Assuming perfectly mixed, the CSTR design equation:
\frac{d(Vc_j)}{dt} = q_{in}c_{jf} - q_{out}c_j + V\sum_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{ij}r_i\;\xrightarrow{\text{constant }V}\;V\frac{dc_j}{dt} = q_{in}c_{jf} - q_{out}c_j + Vr_B
Mass equation for B (no b coming in):
V\frac{db}{dt} = -q_{out}b + V\left(\frac{\mu sb}{K_s + s}\right)\;;\qquad b = \frac{us_f}{\sigma},\; s = vs_f,\; t = \frac{\tau}{\mu},\; K_s = \kappa s_f
With q = V/\theta (V = total volume, \theta = average residence time):
\boxed{\frac{du}{d\tau} = -\frac{1}{(\mu\theta)}u + \left(\frac{v\cdot u}{\kappa + v}\right)}
Mass equation for S (r_B = -r_s/\sigma):
V\frac{ds}{dt} = q_{in}s_f - q_{out}s + Vr_s\;;\qquad\text{for a CSTR } q_{in} = q_{out} = \frac{V}{\theta}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\frac{dv}{d\tau} = \frac{1}{(\mu\theta)}(1 - v) - \left(\frac{v\cdot u}{\kappa + v}\right)}
@ SS: \dfrac{dv}{d\tau} = \dfrac{du}{d\tau} = 0 = F(u, v).


                  
                  Condition I: v = 1, u = 0
                  
                

→ No biomass formation, just substrate feed going in and out unreacted ↳ undesirable.


Condition II: \dfrac{du}{d\tau} = -\dfrac{u}{\mu\theta} + \dfrac{vu}{\kappa + v} = 0. Solving for v:
\frac{v}{\kappa + v} = \frac{1}{\mu\theta}\;\Rightarrow\;v(\mu\theta - 1) = \kappa\;\Rightarrow\;v = \frac{\kappa}{\mu\theta - 1}
Plugging v into \frac{(1 - v)}{\mu\theta} - \frac{vu}{\kappa + v} = 0 and solving for u:
u = \frac{(1 - v)(\kappa + v)}{v\mu\theta} = \cdots = \frac{(\kappa + 1) - \theta\mu}{(1 - \theta\mu)}


                  
                  Condition II 
                  
                

(u^*, v^*) = \left[\frac{(\kappa + 1) - \theta\mu}{(1 - \theta\mu)},\;\frac{\kappa}{(\mu\theta - 1)}\right]
↳ This state is desirable.


Inequality for operation: u > 0 ⇒ \dfrac{(\kappa + 1) - \theta\mu}{(1 - \theta\mu)} > 0.
(b) Evaluating stability: F = \dfrac{du}{d\tau}, G = \dfrac{dv}{d\tau} vs. (u, v). Jacobian matrix:
J = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial F}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial F}{\partial v} \\ \frac{\partial G}{\partial u} & \frac{\partial G}{\partial v}\end{pmatrix}_{(u^*, v^*)}\;;\quad
\frac{\partial F}{\partial u} = -\frac{1}{\mu\theta} + \frac{v}{(\kappa + v)}\;;\quad \frac{\partial F}{\partial v} = \frac{(\kappa + v)u - vu}{(\kappa + v)^2}\;;\quad \frac{\partial G}{\partial u} = -\frac{v}{\kappa + v}\;;\quad \frac{\partial G}{\partial v} = -\frac{1}{\mu\theta} - \frac{(\kappa + v)u - vu}{(\kappa + v)^2}
Plugging in the steady-state values we can obtain the determinant (\Delta) and trace (\tau). For stability: \tau^2 - 4\Delta < 0, \Delta \neq 0 and \tau^2 \neq 4\Delta & \Delta < 0 [?].
J_1 = \begin{pmatrix}-\frac{1}{\mu\theta} + \frac{1}{(\kappa + 1)} & \frac{\kappa}{(\kappa + 1)^2} \\ \frac{-1}{(\kappa + 1)} & -\frac{1}{\mu\theta}\end{pmatrix}\;;\qquad
J_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \frac{1}{(\mu\theta)^2} \\ -\frac{1}{\mu\theta} & -\frac{1}{\mu\theta}\left(\frac{2 + \kappa - 2\theta\mu}{1 - \theta\mu}\right)\end{pmatrix}
\det(J_1) = \frac{1}{(\mu\theta)^2} - \frac{1}{\mu\theta(\kappa + 1)} + \frac{\kappa}{(\kappa + 1)^3}\;;\qquad \det(J_2) = \frac{1}{(\mu\theta)^3} > 0
\tau_{J_1} = -\frac{2}{\mu\theta} + \frac{1}{(\kappa + 1)}\;;\qquad \tau_{J_2} = -\frac{1}{\mu\theta}\left(\frac{2 + \kappa - 2\theta\mu}{(1 - \mu\theta)}\right)
(iii) Oscillations can exist when there are complex values for the eigenvalues of the Jacobian.
(A side calculation on the page sets up the CSTR energy balance \frac{d\eta}{d\tau} = -\eta - \beta(\eta - \eta_c) + B\,Da\,R(\xi, \eta), adiabatic (\beta = 0), with T - T_f = \frac{(-\Delta H_R)X}{\sum\theta_ic_{pi}}, and the rate ratio \frac{r(c,T)}{r(c_f,T_f)} = \frac{sb}{(K_s + s)}\frac{(K_s + s_f)}{s_fb_f} with conversion X = \frac{N_j^0 - N_j}{\alpha_j}; it is not continued.)
Question 2
PBR, axial dispersion model; no reaction; tracer experiment. (sketch: an axis with the fore-section (D^-) for x < 0, the packed section (D) for 0 < x < l, and the aft-section (D^+) for x > l.)
(i) & (ii) From class notes, each section has a general equation:
D^-\frac{\partial^2c^-}{\partial x^2} - v_x\frac{\partial c^-}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial c^-}{\partial t}\;;\qquad c^- = \frac{u^-Q}{Al}\;,\quad \frac{\tau Al}{q} = t\;,\quad x = \xi l\;,\quad v_x = \frac{Pe\,D^-}{l}
↓ (substituting and simplifying, with Pe = \frac{lv}{D} = \frac{lq}{DA}):
\boxed{\frac{\partial^2u^-}{\partial\xi^2} - Pe^-\frac{\partial u^-}{\partial\xi} = Pe^-\frac{\partial u^-}{\partial\tau}}
\qquad\text{Similarly,}\qquad
\boxed{\begin{aligned}\frac{\partial^2u^+}{\partial\xi^2} - Pe^+\frac{\partial u^+}{\partial\xi} &= Pe^+\frac{\partial u^+}{\partial\tau} \\ \frac{\partial^2u}{\partial\xi^2} - Pe\frac{\partial u}{\partial\xi} &= Pe\frac{\partial u}{\partial\tau}\end{aligned}}
Boundary conditions (2 BCs & 1 IC):

@ t = 0 and x = 0: c^- = \frac{Q}{Al}\delta(x) + c ⇒ @ \tau = 0, \xi = 0: u = u^- = \delta(\xi)
@ x = l: c = c^+
@ x = -\infty: c^- = 0 ⇒ @ \xi = -\infty, u^- = 0
@ x = +\infty: c^+ = 0 ⇒ @ \xi = +\infty, u^+ = 0

(iii) Laplace transform (of the dimensionless residence time):
\bar{f}(s) = \int_0^\infty f(t)e^{-st}dt\;;\qquad \mathcal{L}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial\tau}\right) = s\bar{u}(s) - u(0)\;,\quad\text{where } u^-(0) = \delta(\xi),\; u^+(0) = 0,\; u(0) = \delta(\xi)
\mathcal{L}\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial\xi}\right) = \frac{\partial\bar{u}(\xi, s)}{\partial\xi}
⇒ Turning the PDE into ODEs:
\frac{d^2\bar{u}^-}{d\xi^2} - Pe^-\frac{d\bar{u}^-}{d\xi} - Pe^-s\bar{u}^- = 0\;;\qquad \frac{d^2\bar{u}}{d\xi^2} - Pe\frac{d\bar{u}}{d\xi} - Pe\,s\bar{u} = Pe\,\delta(\xi)\quad(\text{for } + \text{ \& normal } u)
↳ This can be solved numerically.

2A \xrightarrow{k}\text{Products}\quad(\text{occurring only in the drops of the dispersed phase});\qquad\text{dispersed-phase mixing; second order; liq–liq dispersion}
Continuous CSTR; \theta = \dfrac{\omega N_0V}{q}.
(i)
\mu_n(\tau) = \int_0^1x^n\phi(x, \tau)\,dx\quad(\phi = \text{dimensionless population density})\;;\qquad \mu_0(\tau) = \int_0^1x^0\phi(x, \tau)\,dx = \int_0^1\phi(x, \tau)\,dx = 1
(ii) Steady-state reactor, CSTR population balance:
\cancelto{0\,(SS)}{\frac{\partial n(c, t)}{\partial t}} + \frac{\partial[\dot{c}n]}{\partial c} = \underbrace{h^+ - h^-}_{\text{coalescence – redispersion}} + [\text{In}] - [\text{Out}]\;;\qquad h^- = \omega n\;,\quad h^+ = 2\omega\iint n(c_1, t)\,n(c_2, t)\,dc_1\,dc_2\;,\quad \dot{c} = -r(c) = -kc^2
\frac{\partial[\dot{c}n]}{\partial c} = \omega\iint_{c_1 + c_2 = c}n(c_1, t)\,n(c_2, t)\,dc_1\,dc_2 + \frac{q}{V}(\delta(c - c_0)) - \left(\frac{qn}{V}\right) - \cdots
Multiplying by \dfrac{x^rc_0}{\omega N_0}, taking the integral (\int_0^1) and non-dimensionalizing based on class notes (n \rightarrow \phi, x^n\phi \rightarrow \mu_n):

[In] term: \displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{qc_0}{VN_0\omega}\delta(x - x_0)\,dx = \frac{q}{\omega VN_0}\int_0^1\delta(x - x_0)\,dx = \frac{1}{\theta}
[Out] term: \displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{x^rc_0}{N_0\omega}\frac{qn}{V}dx = \frac{q}{\omega VN_0}\int_0^1x^r\left(\frac{c_0n}{N_0}\right)dx = \frac{1}{\theta}(\mu_n)
h^+ term (using the binomial theorem): \displaystyle\frac{x^rc_0}{N_0}\iint n_{c_1}n_{c_2}\,dc_1\,dc_2 = \frac{1}{2^n}\sum_{r=0}^{n}\frac{n!}{(n - r)!\,r!}\int_0^1x^{n-r}\phi\,dx\int_0^1x^r\phi\,dx
h^- term: \displaystyle\int_0^1x^n\phi\,dx
\dfrac{\partial[-kc^2n]}{\partial c}: \dfrac{\partial(-kc^2n)}{\partial(c_0x)} = \cdots = \dfrac{kc_0n}{\omega N_0}\displaystyle\int_0^1x^{n+1}\phi\,dx

Combining:
\frac{kc_0n}{\omega N_0}\int_0^1x^{n+1}\phi\,dx = \underbrace{\frac{q}{\omega N_0V}\left(1 - \int_0^1x^n\phi\,dx\right)}_{\text{In – out}} - \int_0^1x^n\phi\,dx + 2^{-n}\sum_{r=0}^{n}\frac{n!}{(n - r)!\,r!}\int_0^1x^{n-r}\phi\,dx\int_0^1x^r\phi\,dx
\boxed{\kappa n\,\mu_{n+1} = \frac{1}{\theta}(1 - \mu_n) - \mu_n + 2^{-n}\sum_{r=0}^{n}\frac{n!}{(n - r)!\,r!}\mu_{n-r}\mu_r}
(iii) n = 1:
\kappa\mu_2 = \frac{1}{\theta}(1 - \mu_1) - \mu_1 + 2^{-1}\left(\frac{1!}{1!\,0!}\mu_1\mu_0 + \frac{1!}{1!\,0!}\mu_0\mu_1\right) = \frac{1}{\theta}(1 - \mu_1) - \cancel{\mu_1} + \frac{1}{2}(2\cancel{\mu_1})\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\mu_2 = \frac{1}{\kappa\theta}(1 - \mu_1)}
(iv) \mu_{n+1} \rightarrow 0 for large n; \theta \gg 1. Since \mu_n = \int_0^1x^n\phi(x, \tau)\,dx and, as n \to \infty, x^n \to 0 (since x is a non-dimensional value between 0 & 1):
\therefore\;\mu_n \to 0\text{ as } n \to \infty
(v) \kappa = \{0.1, 1, 10\}. Have to solve for \mu_1; \mu_2 = \frac{1}{\kappa\theta}(1 - \mu_1) ↳ have to iteratively solve until large n values, where \mu_n for large n is equal to 0:
\mu_0 = 1\;,\quad \mu_1 = f(\mu_2)\;,\quad \mu_2 = f(\mu_3)\;,\quad \dots\;,\quad \mu_{10} = 0

\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = \mathbf{K}\mathbf{x}\;;\qquad \mathbf{K} = \begin{bmatrix}k_{11} & k_{12} & \cdots & k_{1n} \\ \vdots & \ddots & & \\ k_{n1} & & & k_{nn}\end{bmatrix}\;;\qquad k_{ii} = -\sum_{j}^{n}k_{ji}
\mathbf{K}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\;;\qquad k_{ij}x_j^* = k_{ji}x_i^*\;\to\;\text{principle of microscopic reversibility}
\sqrt{\mathbf{D}} = \begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{x_1^*} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \sqrt{x_2^*} & \\ 0 & & \sqrt{x_n^*}\end{bmatrix}\;;\qquad (\sqrt{\mathbf{D}})^{-1}\mathbf{K}(\sqrt{\mathbf{D}}) = \tilde{\mathbf{K}}
(Similarity: \mathbf{B}^{-1}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{C} → A & C have the same eigenvalues, since \mathbf{B}^{-1}(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I})\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{C} - \lambda\mathbf{I} ⇒ |\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}| = |\mathbf{C} - \lambda\mathbf{I}| = 0.)
\mathbf{z}^T\mathbf{K}\mathbf{z} \le 0\;;\qquad \mathbf{z}_j\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{z}_k = 0\;(j \neq k)\;;\qquad \boxed{\mathbf{x} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\alpha_j\mathbf{z}_j}\;,\quad \mathbf{z}_0 = \mathbf{x}^*
(\sqrt{\mathbf{D}})^{-1}\mathbf{K}(\sqrt{\mathbf{D}}\mathbf{z}_j) = \tilde{\mathbf{K}}\tilde{\mathbf{z}}_j, given \mathbf{z}_j\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{z}_k = 0. We can find \alpha_j:
\boxed{\alpha_j = \frac{\mathbf{z}_j\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{z}_j\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{z}_j}}\;;\qquad \mathbf{x}_0 = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(\mathbf{x}_0\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{z}_k)}{(\mathbf{z}_k\mathbf{D}^{-1}\mathbf{z}_k)}\mathbf{z}_ke^{\lambda t}
Parameter estimation in nonlinear kinetics
Determining kinetic parameters: r → rate; \xi → extent; k → rate constants, \mathbf{k} = [k_1, k_2, \dots, k_p] → p parameters.
\frac{d\xi}{dt} = r(\xi, \mathbf{k})\;;\quad \xi(0) = 0\;\to\;\text{ODE representing the temporal evolution of }\xi
\{\hat{\xi}_i\}_{i=1}^{N}:\quad \min_{\mathbf{k}\in\mathbb{R}^p}\sum_{i=1}^{N}|\xi(t_i, \mathbf{k}) - \hat{\xi}_i|^2\quad(\text{prediction vs. measured})
Bellman’s elegant quasi-linearization approach (mth → (m + 1)st iterate). Redefining the variables:
\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n\end{bmatrix};\quad n = p + 1;\quad x_1 = \xi,\; x_2 = k_1, \dots, x_n = k_p\;;\qquad f_1(\mathbf{x}) = r(\xi, \mathbf{k}),\; f_2(\mathbf{x}) = 0, \dots \Rightarrow \mathbf{f}
→ \dfrac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) → new ODE. Linearize this, with the Jacobian (derivative w.r.t. each variable) \mathbf{J}^{(m)} \equiv \nabla\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(m)}):
\frac{d\mathbf{x}^{(m+1)}}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(m)}) + (\nabla\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(m)}))(\mathbf{x}^{(m+1)} - \mathbf{x}^{(m)})

↳ Particular soln: \dfrac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}^{(m)}) + \mathbf{J}^{(m)}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{x}^{(m)}); \mathbf{p}(0) = 0
↳ Homogeneous soln: \dfrac{d\mathbf{h}^j}{dt} = \mathbf{J}^{(m)}\mathbf{h}^{(j)}; \mathbf{h}^j(0) = \mathbf{e}^j \equiv [0 \cdots 1 \; 0 \cdots 0]^T

\therefore\;\mathbf{x}^{(m+1)}(t) = \mathbf{p}(t) + \sum_{j=1}^{n}x_j(0)\,\mathbf{h}^j(t)\;;\qquad p\text{ unknowns } \{x_j(0)\}
Minimize the first component → extent of reaction:
\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[p_1(t_i) - \sum_{j=2}^{n}x_j(0)h_1^j(t_i) - \hat{\xi}_i\right]^2\;\to\;\text{iterate until satisfactory convergence}

\mathbf{A}_{(n\times n)} = \sum_j^n\lambda_j\mathbf{P}_j\;;\qquad \mathbf{P}_j = \frac{\text{adj}(\lambda_j\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A})}{\prod_{r=1, r\neq j}^{n}(\lambda_j - \lambda_r)}\;\to\;\text{projection matrix}\quad(\mathbf{P}_j^2 = \mathbf{P}_j;\;\mathbf{P}_i\mathbf{P}_j = 0,\; i \neq j)
Let \mathbf{w}_1^T, \mathbf{w}_2^T, \dots, \mathbf{w}_n^T be the row eigenvectors of \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n the column eigenvectors of \mathbf{A}:

v = \tilde{v} + y (perturbation) ↳ we want to see if … Linearized problem (an initial boundary-value problem):

Given an IVP V(\rho):

Q1
\mathrm{2A_1 + 3A_2 \rightarrow 2A_3}\;;\qquad \mathrm{A_1 + A_2 + A_3 \rightarrow 3P}\qquad(\text{no residual amount of } A_1, A_2 \text{ \& } A_3)
(First attempt: A_1 + \frac{3}{2}A_2 \rightarrow A_3; A_1 + A_2 + (A_1 + \frac{3}{2}A_2) \rightarrow 3P ⇒ 2A_1 + \frac{5}{2}A_2 \rightarrow 3P, so \frac{A_1}{A_2} = \frac{2}{5/2} = \frac{4}{5}.)
2A_1 + 3A_2 - 2A_3 = 0\;;\qquad A_1 + A_2 + A_3 - P = 0\;\Rightarrow\;\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & -2 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}
Solution: dN_j = \alpha_j\,dX (X → extent of reaction) } for 1 reaction; X = \frac{N_f - N_i}{\alpha}.
\Delta N_1 = N_{1f} - N_{1i} = -2X_1 - X_2\;;\quad \Delta N_2 = -3X_1 - X_2\;;\quad \Delta N_3 = 2X_1 - X_2\;;\quad \Delta N_4 = 3X_2
\Delta\mathbf{N} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}:\quad \Delta\begin{bmatrix}N_1 \\ N_2 \\ N_3 \\ N_4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}X_1 \\ X_2\end{bmatrix}\;;\qquad \mathbf{A}^T = \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf{A}^T is a wide matrix (max rank = 2) → has a null space: \mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{z} = 0. So \Delta\mathbf{N}^T\mathbf{z} = 0 → must also have a non-trivial solution, \mathbf{z} = [z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4]^T:
\begin{aligned}
-2z_1 - 3z_2 + 2z_3 + 0z_4 &= 0 \\
-z_1 - z_2 - z_3 + 3z_4 &= 0
\end{aligned}
\;\Rightarrow\; -z_2 + 4z_3 - 6z_4 = 0\;;\quad (+)\;-2z_1 - 5z_2 + 6z_4 = 0\,[?]
Q2
2A \rightarrow B; isothermal, ideal gas. (sketch: a bubble starting at depth H_0 at t = 0, rising at velocity u_B, containing n_0.)
→ Bubble volume at time t.
(a) Production of gas → rate r = k[A]^2; V = \dfrac{NRT}{P}.
Pressure balance: P = \rho gh_0; P = \rho g(u_Bt) → \boxed{(H_0 - u_Bt)\rho g + P_a = P}
Mass balance:
dN_j = \alpha_j\,dX\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{dN_j}{dt} = \alpha_j\frac{dX}{dt} = \alpha_jV\cdot r\;;\qquad r = k[A]^2
\frac{dN_A}{dt} = -2V(t)\cdot r\;,\quad V = \frac{NRT}{P}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\frac{dN_A}{dt} = -2\frac{NRT}{P}r}
— with P from the pressure balance, giving dN/dt and V(t).
Q3
(sketch: a pore of length l and diameter 2a, from x = 0 to x = L.) \hat{V}_{max} = max. area-specific reaction rate; a pore-diffusion problem.
(i) Shell balance:
\boxed{D\frac{d^2c}{dx^2} + \frac{P}{A}\hat{r}(c) = 0}\;;\qquad\text{BC: @ } x = 0,\; c = c_s\;;\quad @\; x = l,\;\frac{dc}{dx} = 0\;;\qquad \frac{P}{A} = \frac{l\cdot2\pi a}{\pi a^2}\cdots = \frac{2l}{a}\,[?]
R(u) = \frac{\hat{r}(c)}{\hat{r}(c_s)} = \frac{\frac{\hat{V}_{max}c}{K + c}}{\frac{\hat{V}_{max}c_s}{K + c_s}} = \frac{c}{c_s}\frac{(K + c_s)}{(K + c)} = \frac{u\left(\frac{K}{c_s} + 1\right)}{\left(\frac{K}{c_s} + u\right)} = \frac{u(K' + 1)}{(K' + u)}\;;\qquad \hat{r}(c) = R(u)\,\hat{r}(c_s)
\frac{Dc_s}{l^2}\frac{d^2u}{d\rho^2} = -\hat{r}(c)\cdot\frac{2l}{a}\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{d^2u}{d\rho^2} = -\left(\frac{2l^2\hat{r}(c_s)}{aDc_s}\right)R(u)\cdot l\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{d^2u}{d\rho^2} = -\phi^2R(u)\,l

Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 70-71)

Titled “Phase mixing r” in the original (11 April 2023).
Dispersed-phase mixing: coalescence & break-up occur.
Cell mass model
\frac{\partial n(m, t)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial m}[\dot{m}n] = \underbrace{-\Gamma(m, s)n(m, t)}_{\text{change in no. density (due to division)}} + 2\int_m^\infty\Gamma(m', s)\,p(m|m', s)\,n(m', t)\,dm'\;;\qquad \int_0^{m'}p(m|m', s)\,dm = 1

These two events are the same → p(m|m', s) = p(m' - m|m', s); \int_0^{m'}m\,p(m|m', s)\,dm = \frac{1}{2}m'.
Cell division does not change the overall mass.

Total no. of cells → N(t) = \int_0^\infty n(m, t)\,dm:
\frac{dN}{dt} + \Big[\dot{M}(m, s)\,n(m, t)\,dm\Big]_0^\infty = -\int_0^\infty\Gamma(m, s)n(m, t)\,dm + 2\int_0^\infty dm\int_m^\infty dm'\,\Gamma(m', s)\,p(m|m', s)\,n(m', t)
\frac{dN}{dt} = -\int_0^\infty\Gamma(m, s)n(m, t)\,dm + 2\int_0^\infty dm'\int_0^{m'}dm\,\Gamma(m', s)\,n(m', t)\,p(m|m', s) = \int_0^\infty\Gamma(m, s)\,n(m, t)\,dm
Aggregation:
\frac{\partial n(x, t)}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^xa(x - y, y)\,n(x - y, t)\,n(y, t)\,dy - \int_0^\infty a(x, y)\,n(x, t)\,n(y, t)\,dy
\frac{dN}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^\infty dx\int a(x - y, y)\,n(x - y, t)\,n(y, t)\,dy - \int_0^\infty dx\int_0^\infty dy\,a(x, y)\,n(x, t)\,n(y, t) = \cdots = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^\infty dy\int_0^\infty dx\,a(x, y)\,n(y, t)\,n(x, t)\quad(x - y = u)
Transcriber’s note: combining the two terms gives dN/dt = -\frac{1}{2}\iint a(x, y)\,n(x, t)\,n(y, t)\,dx\,dy (aggregation reduces the number); the sign is as written.
General form: n(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}, t) \Rightarrow \dfrac{\partial n}{\partial t} + \nabla_x\cdot\dot{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) + \nabla_r\cdot\dot{\mathbf{R}}n.
Monte Carlo simulations: if you know the distribution → you can generate random variables to model that distribution.
Precipitation reaction
Occurs because the system wants to reach equilibrium:

→ The solubility product is exceeded (leads to supersaturation)
→ Mixing of two liquids giving rise to chemical reactions between ionic species

} You have to play with …
1D model; l (characteristic length), t (how long the crystal is grown). (sketch: an NH₃ feed F_{NH_3} bubbling into a stirred tank.)
\mathrm{NH_{3(aq)} \overset{K_b}{\rightleftharpoons} NH_4^+ + OH^-}\;;\qquad K_b = \frac{[\mathrm{NH_4^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}]}{[\mathrm{NH_3^{aq}}]}
\mathrm{M^{\alpha+}} + \alpha\,\mathrm{OH^-} \rightarrow \underbrace{\mathrm{M(OH)_\alpha}}_{\text{precipitate}}\quad[\text{precipitation reaction}]\;;\qquad K_s = [\mathrm{M^{\alpha+}}]^*[\mathrm{OH^-}]^{*\alpha}\quad(* = \text{equilibrium})
K_s ↳ solubility product; supersaturation ↳ \Lambda = [\mathrm{M}]c^\alpha [?].
K_w = 10^{-14} = [\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = [\mathrm{H^+}]c = K_w\quad(\text{ionic product of water})
Principle of electroneutrality: the anion A⁻ remains at its original level of [\mathrm{M}]_0 (since it does not participate in the reaction).

Precipitate particles are consuming OH⁻.
Have to donate OH⁻ to maintain K_w.

\dot{L} → rate of growth of particle; M → precipitate.

Coursework/Reaction_Engineering_and_Cata.title: Reactions 660: Chemical reaction engineering
Coursework/Reaction_Engineering_and_Cata.content:
Handwritten class notes from Reactions 660 (Spring 2023), exported from OneNote and transcribed into Markdown and LaTeX. Each note shows the typed version first. The original handwritten pages are in a collapsible box at the top, with a link to open just those pages as a PDF.

All original pages (PDF, 24 MB)

Lectures

Lecture Biomass · 2023-03-28 — Lecture on biomass — cybernetic and hybrid cybernetic models, elementary modes and linear programming (FBA), and the cell population balance equation with growth, division and daughter-cell distributions; dissolution processes.
Lecture notes · 2023-01-16 — Section divider page for the Reactions 660 lecture notes (no content on this page).
Lecture population balances · 2023-04-04 — Lecture on population balances — steady continuous extraction in a well-stirred vessel (drop age, size and breakage generations), Monte Carlo/Markov chains, and the aggregation (coalescence) model.
Lecture 01 · 2023-01-14 — Lecture 1 — extent of reaction and reaction rate, and deriving the species balance for a variable-volume batch reactor in terms of concentration and intensive extent.
Lecture 02 · 2023-01-17 — Lecture 2 — the species continuity equation, material vs local derivatives, heterogeneous reactions at surfaces and consuming solid surfaces, and mass-action / de Donder kinetics for batch reactors with forward and reverse orders.
Lecture MT2 review · 2023-04-18 — Midterm 2 review — the effectiveness factor as the link between local and actual reaction rates, the coarse-grain model, the axial dispersion equation, and an introduction to optimizing chemical reactors.
Lecture 03 · 2023-01-19 — Lecture 3 — slides only (an attached PowerPoint file; no handwritten notes on this page).
Lecture 04 · 2023-01-24 — Lecture 4 — intrinsic kinetics in catalysis (active centres, chemisorption, surface reaction and desorption, poisoning and thermal deactivation) and lumping in kinetic systems (PONA).
Lecture 07 · 2023-01-31 — Lecture 7 — first-order reaction networks (Wei–Prater): microscopic reversibility, symmetrization and eigenvector expansion; parameter estimation by Bellman’s quasi-linearization; and the start of single-pore transport analysis.
Lecture 08 · 2023-02-02 — Lecture 8 — the matrix effectiveness factor for a single pore with first-order reaction networks, Sylvester’s expansion with projection matrices and biorthogonality, and how diffusion limitations distort the apparent activation energy.
Lecture 09 · 2023-02-07 — Lecture 9 — setting up a regular perturbation expansion in the Thiele modulus for diffusion–reaction in a catalyst (∇²u = φ²u).

Homework

HWs · 2023-01-16 — Section divider page for the Reactions 660 homework sets (no content on this page).
HW 01 · 2023-01-14 — Homework 1 — linearly independent reaction sets and their uniqueness via the rank of the stoichiometric matrix (isomerizations, the Leblanc soda process, propane pyrolysis), and the minimum number of balance equations for multiple reactions in a variable-volume batch reactor.
HW 02 · 2023-01-16 — Homework 2 — phase-transfer catalysis (Q⁺X⁻ shuttling A⁻ between aqueous and organic phases): dimensionless balances for BX, QA, QX, the catalyst and A⁻ in a well-stirred two-phase batch reactor.
HW 03 · 2023-01-31 — Homework 3 — Michaelis–Menten kinetics with product inhibition, the Hill expression for ligand binding, and scale invariance of rate expressions leading to power-law forms with non-integer orders.
HW 04 · 2023-02-07 — Homework 4 — the matrix Thiele modulus and effectiveness matrix for xylene isomerization in a catalyst pore via projection matrices, and selectivity to para-xylene.
HW 05 · 2023-02-13 — Homework 5 — maximum of a substrate-inhibited rate law, dimensionless rate for a plate catalyst pellet, numerical effectiveness factors for non-linear kinetics (η > 1), and regular perturbation of the first-order effectiveness factor.
HW 06 · 2023-02-16 — Homework 6 — Maxwell–Stefan diffusion through a film to a non-porous catalyst surface for A₁ + A₂ → 2A₃, effectiveness factor, non-dimensional linear system, matrix-exponential solution, eigenvalues and projection matrices, and Sylvester’s theorem.
HW 07 · 2023-02-27 — Homework 7 — shell-progressive (“shrinking core”) catalyst poisoning with external mass transfer, diffusion through the poisoned shell and reaction at the core boundary in series, and diffusion–reaction in a pellet with an inactive poisoned shell.
HW 08 · 2023-03-06 — Homework 8 — a non-isothermal first-order reaction in a plate catalyst with only external heat-transfer resistance: the concentration profile, the coupled temperature equation (ν − 1) = βψ tanh ψ, the effectiveness factor, and its limits.
HW 09 · 2023-03-20 — Homework 9 — one-point orthogonal collocation for a non-isothermal first-order catalyst pellet (Weisz–Hicks form), the collocation point and effectiveness factor, the multiplicity window in Thiele modulus, and a sufficient condition for uniqueness.
HW 11 · 2023-03-27 — Homework 11 — steady states and their stability for a chemostat (CSTR) growing biomass on a substrate with Monod kinetics, and the axial-dispersion model of a packed bed with fore/aft sections for a tracer pulse, via the Laplace transform.
HW 12 · 2023-04-18 — Homework 12 — cybernetic modelling of diauxic microbial growth on two substrates: elementary modes, PSSH on growth precursors, enzyme balances, cybernetic optimality laws (u, v), and the substrate and biomass balances.
HW 13 · 2023-04-25 — Homework 13 — a second-order reaction in the drops of a liquid–liquid dispersion in a CSTR: the population balance with coalescence–redispersion, its moment equations, the first-moment result, and the moment closure for large n.

Other notes

Lecture · 2023-02-21 — Lecture (21 Feb) — linear stability of non-isothermal steady states in a catalyst pellet via the linearized eigenvalue problem, and the Sturm comparison theorem for detecting instability.
Phase mixing r · 2023-04-11 — Lecture on dispersed-phase mixing — the cell mass model with division, the aggregation population balance and total number, Monte Carlo simulation, and precipitation reactions (solubility product, supersaturation, electroneutrality).
A_Bhadouria_HW11 · 2023-04-11 — Homework 11 (submitted version), Question 1 — absorption of two gases reacting reversibly in the liquid, using the surface-renewal concept: a lumped conserved concentration, its erf profile, the combined flux and the Danckwerts average rate √(Ds)(c₀ − cᵢ).
Past exam 2021 · 2023-02-22 — Practice on the 2021 exam — reaction invariants from the null space of the stoichiometric matrix, a reacting gas bubble rising through a liquid column, and the dimensionless pore-diffusion problem with Michaelis–Menten-type kinetics.
Notes 2023-04-27 · 2023-04-27 — Notes (27 April 2023) — phase balances for a dispersed/continuous two-phase reactor, why population balances describe phase mixing better, the coalescence number density in concentration space, and closed-book review of reaction invariants (Fredholm alternative).

Coursework/Reaction_Engineering_and_Cata.title: Reaction engineering and catalysis
Coursework/Reaction_Engineering_and_Cata.content:
Chemical reactor design and energy balances, reaction kinetics and mechanisms, and heterogeneous catalysis and its characterization. Each course links to one page per lecture or homework set. Cheat sheets and review notes are typed versions of exam sheets, with the original scans in a collapsible box at the top of each page.
Courses

CHE 666: Catalysis · 18 notes — Characterization of heterogeneous catalysts — IR, UV-vis and Raman spectroscopy, XRD and XAS, temperature-programmed methods, solid-state NMR, chemisorption and porosimetry — plus mechanism-based kinetics and DFT/d-band theory.
Reactions 660: Chemical reaction engineering · 29 notes — Reaction stoichiometry and species balances, intrinsic catalytic kinetics, reaction networks and effectiveness factors for diffusion–reaction in pores, pellet stability, biochemical and population-balance models, and reactor optimization.

Cheat sheets and review notes

CBE 142 Cheat Sheet — Cheat sheets and review notes for CBE 142 (chemical kinetics and reactor design) — design equations and stoichiometric tables, equilibrium conversion, energy balances for every reactor type, multiple steady states, selectivity and yield, Langmuir–Hinshelwood kinetics, porous-catalyst diffusion and effectiveness factors, and the final crib sheet.
CBE 142 Crib Sheet — Two-page crib sheet for CBE 142 (chemical kinetics and reactor design) — energy balances for batch, semi-batch, CSTR, PFR and PBR reactors, X–T and G–R graphs and multiple steady states, then midterm material on reactor design equations, pressure drop (Ergun), membrane reactors, porous catalysts, effectiveness factors, Thiele modulus and the Weisz–Prater criterion.
PFR and PBR Energy Balances — One-page summary of non-isothermal reactor energy balances — PFR and PBR temperature profiles with heat exchange (co- and counter-current coolant), adiabatic conversion–temperature relations, Arrhenius and van ‘t Hoff temperature dependence, and selectivity and yield.

Qualifying exam
Written report (due Sept. 15):

Summary
Intro
Research objective
Literature review & theory
Research plan
Materials & methods
Preliminary results
Plan for next 12 months

Oral report (due Oct. break!):

20 min (uninterrupted)
No back-up slide
30 min of questions → general engineering knowledge; → details about methods

Research hypothesis (problem definition)

↳ Do not be vague
↳ Define the rationale (why do you think that happens? — your expectation)
↳ Should be testable
↳ Justification of why you think you could do/falsify



                  
                  Become skeptical! → Why? How? 
                  
                

Hypothesis vs. problem definition.
Evaluation: current state-of-the-art in field

Defend underlying basis (why are you doing what you are doing)
Impact of the proposed work: Why is this important to other ChemEs? Why should people care? How does your work fit in? → read review papers to gain better understanding
Preliminary results & mastery of key research techniques:

↳ point out the limitations of your approach/idea → and what you are going to do to deal with it
↳ design of experiment
↳ independence
↳ why & how (the machine works & what the results mean?)
↳ does the data prove or disprove the initially-proposed hypothesis


Potential of the project for tangible product generation

↳ trajectory (research plan)
↳ can change direction / report failure
↳ careful analysis of why things went wrong


Communication ability:

↳ explain to other ChemEs
↳ graph → clear, easily readable
↳ animations
↳ enthusiastic voice



Grading
3 faculty; grading: 2 “not passing” on 2 same fields → fail.

Written: 95% pass rate
Oral: 75% pass rate for first time

Full-page feedback; retake with 3 new faculty.

M^R(T, P) \equiv M(T, P) - M^{IG}(T, P)
\frac{G^R(T, P)}{RT} = \int_0^P\frac{Z(T, P) - 1}{P}\,dP\;;\qquad \frac{S^R}{R} = -\int_0^P\frac{(Z - 1)}{P}\,dP - T\int_0^P\left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}\right)_P\frac{dP}{P}\;;\qquad \frac{H^R}{RT} = -T\int_0^P\left(\frac{\partial Z}{\partial T}\right)_P\frac{dP}{P}
\frac{S^R}{R} = \frac{(S^R)^0}{R} + \omega\frac{(S^R)^1}{R}\;;\qquad G_i^R = G_i - G_i^{IG} = RT\ln\frac{f_i}{P}\;;\qquad \ln\phi_i = \int_0^P\frac{(Z - 1)}{P}\,dP
\Delta H = \Delta H^R + \Delta H^{IG}\;;\quad \Delta H^{IG} = \int_{T_1}^{T_2}c_p(T)\,dT\;;\quad \Delta H^R = H_2^R - H_1^R\;;\qquad S_2 - S_1 = S_2^R + (S_2^{IG} - S_1^{IG}) - S_1^R
Equilibrium
G^\alpha = G^\beta\;;\qquad \frac{dP^{sat}}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H^{\alpha\beta}}{T\Delta V^{\alpha\beta}}\;;\qquad \ln\left(\frac{P_2^{sat}}{P_1^{sat}}\right) = -\frac{\Delta H^{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)\;;\qquad \mu^\alpha = \mu^\beta
VLE (pure species)
G_i^l = \Gamma_i(T) + RT\ln f_i^l\;;\qquad G_i^v = \Gamma_i(T) + RT\ln f_i^v\;;\qquad G_i^v - G_i^l = RT\ln\frac{f_i^v}{f_i^l}
\phi_i^v = \phi_i^l = \phi_i^{sat}\;;\qquad f_i = y_iP\;;\qquad \phi^{sat} = \frac{f^{sat}}{P^{sat}}\;;\qquad \hat{\phi} = \frac{\hat{f}_i}{y_iP}\;;\qquad \ln\phi_i = \int_0^P\frac{(Z - 1)}{P}\,dP
\phi < 1: attractive forces dominate.
Species in a solution
\hat{f}_i^\alpha = \hat{f}_i^\beta = \cdots = \hat{f}_i^\pi\;;\qquad \bar{G}^R = RT\ln\phi_i\;;\qquad M = (1 - x)M^l + xM^v
Quality: x = mole fraction of vapor; \hat{\phi} = \dfrac{\hat{f}_i}{y_iP}.
Partial molar properties
d(nG) = (nV)\,dP - (nS)\,dT + \sum_i\mu_i\,dn_i\;;\qquad \mu_i^\alpha = \mu_i^\beta
M = \sum x_i\bar{M}_i\;,\quad \sum x_i\,d\bar{M}_i = 0\;\Big\}\quad \bar{M}_1 = M + x_2\frac{dM}{dx_1}\;;\quad \bar{M}_2 = M - x_1\frac{dM}{dx_1}\;;\quad \frac{dM}{dx_1} = \bar{M}_1 - \bar{M}_2
Ideal gas
\frac{RT}{P^T} = x_i\left(\frac{RT}{P_1^*}\right) + x_j\left(\frac{RT}{P_2^*}\right)\;;\qquad [V = x_1\bar{V}_1 + x_2\bar{V}_2]
G_i^{IG} = \Gamma_i(T) + RT\ln P\;;\qquad \mu_i^{IG} = \bar{G}_i^{IG} = RT\ln(y_iP) + \Gamma(T)\;;\qquad g - g_i^0 = \mu_i - \mu_i^0 = RT\ln\left[\frac{P}{P_0}\right] = \int_{P_{low}}^P\bar{V}\,dP
\bar{H}^{IG} = H_i^{IG} = \sum y_iH_i^{IG}\;;\qquad S^{IG} = \sum y_iS_i^{IG} - R\sum y_i\ln y_i\;;\qquad G^{IG} = \sum y_iG_i^{IG} + RT\sum y_i\ln y_i
Joule–Thomson (\Delta H = 0, W_s = 0):
\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_H = \mu_{JT} = \frac{1}{c_p}\left(V - T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P\right)
Amagat’s law: a straight line connecting V_1 & V_2; V = \sum_i^C x_iV_{i,pure}. (sketch: V vs. x_1 — the real curve bows above the straight “Amagat’s” line joining V_1 and V_2.)
(worked sketch: water added to a beaker of total initial moles at 7 mol% to reach V^t = 100 mL at 15 mol%, with n^t = \frac{V^t}{V(x_1)} split into n_1 and n_2 (in final) — “whole point is to find total moles in initial solution”: n_{initial}^{total}\cdot V(x_1) = volume [mol · mL/mol = mL].)
S_2 - S_1 = S_2^R + (S_2^{IG} - S_1^{IG}) - S_1^R\;;\qquad S^E = \Delta S^{mix} + \underbrace{R\sum x_i\ln x_i}_{\Delta S^{id} = -\ldots}
Page 2
Thermodynamic square (sketch: a 3×3 mnemonic grid with G, P, H along the top, T and S in the middle row and A, V, U along the bottom.)
dU = T\,dS - P\,dV\;;\quad dH = T\,dS + V\,dP\;;\quad dA = -P\,dV - S\,dT\;;\quad dG = V\,dP - S\,dT
\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial V}\right)_S = -\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial S}\right)_V\;;\quad \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial T}\right)_V = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T\;;\quad \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_S = \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\right)_P\;;\quad \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P
\gamma = \frac{c_p}{c_v}\;;\qquad PV^\gamma = P^{1-\gamma}T^\gamma = TV^{\gamma-1} = \text{constant}\;;\qquad \Delta H = \int_{T_1}^{T_2}c_p\,dT\;;\quad \Delta U = \int_{T_1}^{T_2}c_v\,dT
c_p = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right)_PT = \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial T}\right)_P\;;\qquad c_v = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right)_VT = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V\;\rightarrow\;\Delta S = c_p\ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)
\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_T\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial P}\right)_V = -1\;;\qquad \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial P}\right)_T = \frac{1}{\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_T}\;;\qquad c_p = c_v + R\;(\text{ideal gas})
\left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0 [?]. Air: 79% N₂, 21% O₂.
\Delta U = Q + W\;;\qquad W = -\int P\,dV\quad(W > 0\text{ in compression — done on the system})
dS^t = \frac{\delta Q_{rev}}{T}\;;\qquad \Delta S_{univ} = \Delta S_{sys}^t + \Delta S_{surr}\quad(\Delta S_{univ} = 0\text{ for a reversible process})
Energy balance:
\Delta H + \frac{\Delta u^2}{2} + g\Delta z = Q + W_s\quad(\text{open, S.S.})\;;\qquad \frac{d(mU)_{cv}}{dt} + \Delta\left[\left(H + \frac{1}{2}u^2 + zg\right)\dot{m}\right] = \dot{Q} + \dot{W}\quad(\text{transient})
Cycles
Carnot engine. (sketch: P–V diagram between T_H and T_C, states ①–④ with two adiabats (Q = 0), Q_H absorbed on the top isotherm and Q_C rejected on the bottom.)
W = Q_H - Q_C\;;\qquad \eta = \frac{W_{net}}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{Q_C}{Q_H} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}

Q = 0: \Delta U = -W; \ln\frac{V_a}{V_b} = -\ln\frac{V_d}{V_c}.
\Delta U = 0: \frac{Q_H}{Q_C} = \frac{T_H\ln(V_b/V_a)}{T_C\ln(V_c/V_d)}; \frac{Q_H}{Q_C} = \frac{T_H}{T_C}.
\Delta S_{surr} = -\frac{q_H}{T_H} - \frac{q_C}{T_C} = 0.

(sketches: the Carnot cycle as a rectangle on T–S and on \ln P–H axes.)
Heat pump / Rankine. (sketches: Rankine cycle on T–S and \ln P–H diagrams with the two-phase dome; flowsheet ① pump → boiler (Q_H) → ② turbine (W_s) → ③ sat. v → condenser (Q_C) → ④ sat. l; P–V diagrams of the cycle and its reverse.)
\eta = \frac{\text{Desired output}}{\text{Price you have to pay}} = \frac{W_{net}}{Q_H} = \frac{H_3 - H_2}{H_2 - H_1}
Vapor-compression refrigeration. (sketches: T–S and \ln P–H diagrams; flowsheet ① boiler (evaporator, Q_C) → ② sat. v → compressor (W_s) → ③ condenser (Q_H) → ④ sat. l → throttle.)
Tons of refrigeration (power rating) = \dot{Q}_C;
\dot{m} = \frac{\text{Power}}{Q_C} = \frac{\dot{Q}_C}{Q_C}\;;\qquad \text{COP} = \frac{Q_C}{W_{net}} = \frac{H_2 - H_1}{H_3 - H_2}
\eta^{thermal} = \eta_{ideal\ cycle}^{thermal}\cdot\eta_{turbine}^{mech}\;;\qquad 1\,°\mathrm{F} = 460\text{ Rankine}\,[?]

Turbine (expansion): \eta = \frac{W_{actual}}{W_{ideal}}
Pump (compression): \eta = \frac{W_{ideal}}{W_{actual}}

(sketch: engine — Q_H from T_H into the device, work out, Q_C to T_C; heat pump — work in, Q_C from T_C, Q_H to T_H.)
Carnot refrigerator (replacing the throttle w/ a turbine): (sketches on P–V, T–S and \ln P–H axes, states ①–④ run in reverse.)
\text{COP} = \frac{T_C}{T_H - T_C}
Energy balance, heat exchanger: (sketch: two streams ①→② and ③→④.) \dot{m}_1(H_2 - H_1) = \dot{m}_2(H_4 - H_3).
Transcriber’s note: “1 F = 460 Rankine” is as written; the usual relation is T(°\mathrm{R}) = T(°\mathrm{F}) + 459.67.
Page 3
Equations of state — T_r = T/T_c, P_r = P/P_c.

Van der Waals: P = \dfrac{RT}{V_m - b} - \dfrac{a}{V_m^2}; a = \dfrac{27}{64}\dfrac{(RT_c)^2}{P_c}; b = RT_c/8P_c
Redlich–Kwong: P = \dfrac{RT}{V_m - b} - \dfrac{a}{V_m(V_m + b)}; a = \dfrac{\Psi\alpha R^2T_c^2}{P_c}, b = \dfrac{\Omega RT_c}{P_c} (\Psi & \Omega are EOS constants); \alpha = T_r^{-1/2}
2nd virial: Z = Z^0 + \omega Z'; Z^0 = 1 + B^0\frac{P_r}{T_r}; Z' = B'\frac{P_r}{T_r}; Z = 1 + \frac{BP}{RT} = 1 + BP_r [?]; B^0 = 0.083 - \frac{0.422}{T_r^{1.6}}; B' = 0.139 - \frac{0.172}{T_r^{4.2}}

Random — Mollier (H–S) → isobars, H(S, P):

dH = T\,dS + V\,dP \Rightarrow dH = T\,dS \Rightarrow \left(\frac{\partial H}{\partial S}\right)_P = T; \left(\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial S^2}\right)_P = \left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial S}\right)_P; \left.\frac{\partial T}{\partial S}\right|_P = \frac{T}{c_p} \Rightarrow \left(\frac{\partial^2H}{\partial S^2}\right)_P = \frac{T}{c_p}
U(T, V) \Rightarrow dU = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_TdV + \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_VdT; \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = T\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial V}\right)_T - P\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial V}\right) (@ const T); dU = T\,dS - P\,dV → dV
S(T, P): dS = \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right)_PdT + \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_TdP; \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial T}\right)_P = \frac{c_p}{T}; \left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial P}\right)_T = -\left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_P = -\frac{R}{P} ∴ \ln\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = \frac{R}{c_p}\ln\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)
S(T, V) (left blank)

VLE

Lewis–Randall: \hat{f}^L = x_if_{i,pure}; \hat{f}^V = x_if_{i,pure}
\gamma_i = \dfrac{\hat{f}^l}{\hat{f}^{Id}} = \dfrac{\hat{f}^l}{x_if_i^0}; Henry’s law: y_iP = x_iH (x \approx 1 [?]); Raoult’s law: y_iP = x_iP_i^{sat}
→ Comparing the same species in a VLE mixture, \hat{f}^V = \hat{f}^L:

\hat{\phi}y_iP = \gamma_ix_i\phi_i^{sat}P_i^{sat}\exp\left[\frac{V_i^L(P - P_i^{sat})}{RT}\right]

Ideal gas + ideal solution (@ low P): \phi^{sat} = \gamma = \mathcal{P} = 1; y_iP = x_iP_i^{sat} (Raoult’s law)
Ideal gas + non-ideal solution (@ low P): \phi^{sat} = 1, \mathcal{P} = 1; y_iP = \gamma_ix_iP_i^{sat} (modified Raoult’s law)
Non-ideal gas + non-ideal liquid (moderate P): \mathcal{P} = 1; \hat{\phi}_iy_iP = \gamma_ix_i\phi_i^{sat}P_i^{sat}

\hat{\phi}^V = \frac{\hat{f}^V}{y_iP}\;;\qquad \phi^L = \frac{\hat{f}^L}{x_iP}\;;\qquad \ln\phi^{sat} = \frac{B_{11}P^{sat}}{RT}\;;\qquad \ln\hat{\phi}_i^V = \frac{P(B_{11} + y_2^2\delta_{12})}{RT}\;;\quad \delta_{12} = 2B_{12} - B_{11} - B_{22}
→ Consistency (Gibbs–Duhem): \sum x_i\ln\gamma_i = 0; x_1\left(\frac{\partial\ln\gamma_1}{\partial x_1}\right) + x_2\left(\frac{\partial\ln\gamma_2}{\partial x_1}\right) = 0.
Transcriber’s note: the Gibbs–Duhem consistency condition is usually \sum x_i\,d\ln\gamma_i = 0; the first form is as written.
Mixing

Van der Waals mixing rule: a_{mix} = \left(\sum_iy_ia_i^{1/2}\right)^2 [?], b_{mix} = \sum_iy_ib_i } use in the van der Waals EOS
2nd virial (Pitzer): B_{ij} = \frac{RT_{c,ij}}{P_{c,ij}}(B^0 + \omega_{ij}B'); \omega_{ij} = \frac{\omega_i + \omega_j}{2}; P_{c,ij} = \frac{Z_{c,ij}RT_{c,ij}}{V_{c,ij}}; T_{c,ij} = (T_{c,i}T_{c,j})^{1/2}(1 - k_{ij}); Z_{c,ij} = \frac{Z_{c,i} + Z_{c,j}}{2}; V_{c,ij} = \left(\frac{V_{c,i}^{1/3} + V_{c,j}^{1/3}}{2}\right)^3; B_{overall} = y_1^2B_{11} + 2y_1y_2B_{12} + y_2^2B_{22}
1-parameter Margules: \dfrac{G^E}{RTx_1x_2} = A
2-parameter Margules: \dfrac{G^E}{RTx_1x_2} = A_{21}x_1 + A_{12}x_2, with G^E/RT = x_1\ln\gamma_1 + x_2\ln\gamma_2; \lim_{x_2\to1}\frac{G^E}{x_1x_2RT} = \ln\gamma_1^\infty = A_{21} [?]

\ln\gamma_1 = x_2^2\left[A_{12} + 2(A_{21} - A_{12})x_1\right]\;;\qquad \ln\gamma_2 = x_1^2\left[A_{21} + 2(A_{12} - A_{21})x_2\right]

Van Laar: \ln\gamma_1 = A_{12}\left(\dfrac{A_{21}x_2}{A_{12}x_1 + A_{21}x_2}\right)^2; \ln\gamma_2 = A_{21}\left(\dfrac{A_{12}x_1}{A_{12}x_1 + A_{21}x_2}\right)^2

Excess properties
M^E = \Delta M - \Delta M^{id}\;;\qquad H^E = \Delta H^{mix}\;;\quad \Delta H^{id} = \Delta V^{id} = 0\;;\quad V^E = \Delta V^{mix}
-\frac{H^E}{RT^2} = \frac{\partial}{\partial T}\left(\frac{G^E}{RT}\right)\bigg|_{P,x}\;;\qquad G^E = \sum x_i\bar{G}_i^E = RT\sum x_i\ln\gamma_i\;;\qquad \Delta G^{id} = RT\sum x_i\ln x_i
\bar{G}_i^E = \bar{G}_i - \bar{G}_i^{Id} = RT\ln\gamma_i\;;\qquad \Delta G_{mix} = g - \sum x_ig_i\;;\quad \Delta G_{mix}^{Id} = RT\sum x_i\ln x_i\;;\qquad g = \sum x_ig_i + \underbrace{RT\sum x_i\ln x_i}_{\text{ideal}} + g^E
\bar{H}_1^E = H^E + x_2\,dH^E/dx_1\;;\qquad \bar{H}_2^E = H^E - x_1\,dH^E/dx_1\;;\qquad \frac{\gamma_a}{\gamma_b} = \frac{P_b^{sat}}{P_a^{sat}}
S^E = \Delta S^{mix} + R\sum x_i\ln x_i.
Reaction equilibrium
K(T) = \exp\left(-\frac{\Delta G^\circ(T)}{RT}\right)\;;\qquad K(T) = K_yK_\phi\left(\frac{P}{1\text{ bar}}\right)^{\Delta\nu}\;;\qquad K_y = \frac{y_C^c}{y_A^ay_B^b}\;;\qquad K(T) = \prod\left(\hat{f}_i/f_i^\circ\right)^{\nu_i}
\frac{dn_i}{\nu_i} = d\xi\;;\qquad \frac{dG}{d\xi} = \sum\mu_i\nu_i = 0\;(@\,\text{VLE})\;;\qquad n_f = n_i + \nu_i\xi
\frac{d\ln K}{dT} = \frac{\Delta H}{RT^2} \Rightarrow \ln\left(\frac{K_2}{K_1}\right) = -\frac{\Delta H_{rxn}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)

Q1. Effusion of gas through a small hole
f(\vec{v})\,d\vec{v} = probability of a given molecule having a velocity vector between \vec{v} and \vec{v} + d\vec{v}.
f(\vec{v}) = f(|\vec{v}|) = f(v^2)\;;\qquad \iiint f(\vec{v})\,d^3\vec{v} = 1\;;\qquad f(v^2) = C\,e^{-av^2},\; a > 0\;(\text{Maxwell distribution})
\langle v_x\rangle = \bar{v}_x = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_xf_x(v_x^2)\,dv_x\;;\qquad \langle v_x^2\rangle = \overline{v_x^2} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}v_x^2f_x(v_x^2)\,dv_x\;;\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(v^2)\,dv = 1
Solving this in spherical coordinates gives
\langle v\rangle = \bar{v} = 4\pi\int_0^\infty v\,f(v^2)\,v^2\,dv\;;\qquad \langle v^2\rangle = \overline{v^2} = 4\pi\int_0^\infty \cdots
The number of molecules crossing the hole per unit time with speed v is \bar{v}f_E(\bar{v})\,d\bar{v}:
\langle v_E\rangle = \frac{\int_0^\infty\bar{v}f_E(\bar{v})\,d\bar{v}}{\int_0^\infty f_E(\bar{v})\,d\bar{v}}
↓ solving this integral using f_E(\bar{v})\,d\bar{v} = \left(\dfrac{m}{2\pi kT}\right)^{1/2}e^{-m\bar{v}^2/2kT}\,d\bar{v} from the Maxwell–Boltzmann dist. & some math…
Similarly,
\langle v_E^2\rangle = \frac{\int_0^\infty\bar{v}^2f_E(\bar{v})\,dv}{\int_0^\infty f_E(\bar{v})\,d\bar{v}} \;\to\; \text{this should yield } 2kT
Q2. Maxwell–Boltzmann for a 2D gas (v_x and v_y directions)
Probability of speed for a 2D ideal gas between \bar{v} and \bar{v} + d\bar{v}:
f_{2D}(\bar{v})\,d^2\bar{v} = \int_0^{2\pi}f(v_x, v_y)\,d^2v\;;\qquad f(v_x, v_y) = \frac{m}{2\pi kT}e^{-m(v_x^2 + v_y^2)/2kT}\;(\text{Boltzmann dist.})\;;\qquad v^2 = v_x^2 + v_y^2\;(\text{ideal gas})
Q6. Random walk in 3D
N → total number of steps during the walk.
(a) \langle R\rangle (average length), \langle R^2\rangle vs. N.
(b)
P(R) = 4\pi R^2\left(\frac{3}{2\pi N}\right)^{3/2}\exp\left(\frac{-3R^2}{2N}\right)
— the probability density that the random walk has an end-to-end distance equal to R. What happens as N \to large?

Final project → catalysis (adsorption mechanism, kMC).

Convention: capital letters → extensive (depend on the amount of substance).
Postulate I (Duhem’s) → n species; n + 2 variables for bulk properties.
Macro vs. micro ↳ average behaviour over length & time scales.

Kinetic theory of gases

Dilute (ig. limit)
Non-interacting hard spheres
Neutral atoms
Polarizability of atom (induced dipole)

(sketch: the pair potential u(r) vs r — a steep 1/r^{12} repulsive wall and an attractive well going as 1/r^6, derived from Schrödinger’s eq.)
f = -\frac{\partial u}{\partial r}\quad(\text{force between two atoms})

Coulomb’s law is still at play, but these are averaged (so no two particles…).
The zero point (u(r) = 0) gives r = \sigma as the effective size — the 6-12 Lennard-Jones potential: a very good model for noble gases (Xe, Ar, Kr).
Gas → 10\sigma separation; liquid → 1\sigma separation.

N = nN_A (# of molecules from # of moles); V → extensive volume.
\rho = \frac{N}{V}\;(\text{no. density})\;;\qquad k = \frac{R}{N_A} = 1.38\times10^{-23}\ \text{J/K}\;;\qquad \boxed{\rho = \frac{N}{V} = \frac{P}{kT}}

Elastic collisions

KE is distributed independently and in an equal manner } principle of equipartition (KE scaling as v^2 or p^2)

g(v_x^2) = \alpha\,e^{-av_x^2}\;;\qquad \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_x(v_x^2)\,dv_x = 1

In a liquid, molecules are “always colliding”; gases have a mean free path (the distance between each collision).
Probability of collisions + no. of particles incident for a cross-sectional area ↓ gives the survival equation ↓
l = \frac{1}{\pi\sigma^2\rho}
Effusion: gas leaks through a very small hole of diameter much smaller than the mean free path.
(sketch: a hole of diameter d in a wall.) When l \ll d, molecules will undergo various collisions, and this is where the "PV" term comes in when forcing gas/liquid through an orifice } the idea of viscous stresses.
Effusion is when the collision has already occurred and the gas just passes through.
Viscous stresses arise from net transport of momentum via gases moving at different speeds & colliding with other particles/molecules.

Classical mechanics } know precise knowledge of positions, velocities, momentum; model the future evolution of the system.
Macro thermo } N \sim 10^{23} particles; 6N degrees of freedom.

We usually have information about the “macroscopic state” of a system (V, E, T, etc.) ↳ how do we get the micro-state, i.e. the particular values of all 6N dofs?
↓ Construct an ensemble of the system → the average behaviour of a collection of identical N-particle systems distributed over a range of different possible states.
(sketch: one N, V, E box ⇒ copies of the N, V, E box at t = t_0, t_1, t_2, \dots — Q = \sum ensembles (total ensembles).) They are not smaller systems or control volumes ↓ more so representing the entire system & its time evolution with identical systems at different times (or initial conditions).
Each ensemble has N particles whose dynamic behaviour is given by Hamilton’s equations of motion — a set of first-order differential equations that describe how a system evolves through phase space (q_i, p_i) (H = total energy of system):
\dot{q}_i = \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial p_i}\;;\qquad \dot{p}_i = -\frac{\partial H_i}{\partial q_i}
↓ A point in phase space represents the complete state of the system (position & momentum) → as time progresses this point traces a path called a trajectory. (sketch: flow lines in the p–q plane; f(p, q, t) = density in phase space.)
\Omega = \int_{E \le H \le E + \delta E}dp\,dq \;\to\; \text{the volume of phase space whose energy lies between } E \text{ and } E + \delta E
↳ just a pure number quantum-mechanically → the no. of microstates for a given E.


                  
                  TL;DR 
                  
                


Each ensemble can be represented by a single point in 6N-dimensional space (3N position & 3N momentum).
Those ensembles are clubbed together in a phase-space density? Thus this cloud/collection of ensembles can be modelled like an incompressible flow.
This way we can use ensemble averages, since if you wait long enough a single system will visit every part of the phase space allowed by its energy ↓ in a way, the time evolution is just modelled as taking place already to give all the possible states → then you are just sampling from it. (This is the ergodic hypothesis → Boltzmann 1871.)



\boxed{S = -k\sum_\nu P_\nu\ln(P_\nu)}





















Microcanonical ensemble — (N, V, E) constantCanonical ensemble — (N, V, T) constant (energy can change)Describes an isolated system (no exchange with the environment).All microstates are not equally likely (since E is not constant): the probability of finding the system in microstate i with energy E_i is given by the Boltzmann distribution — specifically, lower energies are favoured. (sketch: system N, V inside a bath N_b, V_b.)Principle of equal a-priori probability → every accessible microstate \Omega is equally likely to be occupied: P_i = 1/\Omega if E_i = E, else 0.Probability of finding the system in any microstate \nu: P_\nu = \Omega_b(E_b)/\Omega(E), with E_b + E_\nu = E ↓ math & Taylor expansion ↓ P_\nu = e^{-\beta E_\nu}/\sum_\nu e^{-\beta E_\nu}S = k_B\ln\Omega(N, V, E)The denominator is the partition function (Q or Z): the sum of the probabilities of all possible microstates equals 1, and it has information about all the system’s energy levels — later used to bridge between micro and macro.
In the thermodynamic limit, both ensembles become equivalent.
A = -kT\ln Q\;;\qquad U = \langle E\rangle = -\left.\frac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial\beta}\right|_{N,V} = kT^2\left.\frac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial T}\right|_{N,V}
P = k_BT\left.\frac{\partial\ln Z}{\partial V}\right|_{N,T}\;;\qquad S = \frac{U - A}{T} = k_B\ln Q + k_BT\left.\frac{\partial\ln Q}{\partial T}\right|_{N,V}
For non-interacting, independent particles the Hamiltonian, and hence the energy microstates, are separable ↓ therefore we can assign
Q = \sum_\nu e^{-\beta E_\nu} = q_aq_bq_c\cdots\;,\qquad q_i = \sum_{\nu_i}e^{-\beta\varepsilon_{\nu_i}}\ (\text{molecular partition function}),\; q_i = q_i(V, T)\;;\qquad H = H_{trans} + H_{elec} + H_{nucl}

Coursework/Thermodynamics/CHE_611/index.title: CHE 611: Thermodynamics
Coursework/Thermodynamics/CHE_611/index.content:
Handwritten class notes from CHE 611 (Spring 2026), exported from OneNote and transcribed into Markdown and LaTeX. Each note shows the typed version first. The original handwritten pages are in a collapsible box at the top, with a link to open just those pages as a PDF.

All original pages (PDF, 4 MB)

Lectures

Lecture 01-12 Thermo syllabus · 2026-01-12 — Course start — final project idea, notation conventions, Duhem’s postulate, macro vs micro descriptions, and the kinetic theory of gases with the Lennard-Jones potential and number density.
Lecture 01-14 · 2026-01-14 — Kinetic-theory assumptions, the Maxwell velocity distribution and its normalization, molecular flux at equilibrium, force as change in momentum, and kT as the thermal energy scale.
Lecture 01-16 · 2026-01-16 — Pressure on container walls from kinetic theory, experimental confirmation of the Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution, and why the atmosphere holds more N₂ than H₂.
Lecture 01-21 · 2026-01-21 — Mean free path from the collision probability, effusion through holes smaller than the mean free path versus viscous flow, and the molecular origin of viscous stresses.

Homework

HW 01 · 2026-02-06 — Homework 1 notes — effusion of gas through a small hole using the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, the 2D Maxwell–Boltzmann speed distribution, and a 3D random walk end-to-end distance distribution.

Other notes

Review · 2026-02-20 — Review sheet — from macro thermodynamics to ensembles, phase space and Hamilton’s equations, the ergodic hypothesis, microcanonical vs canonical ensembles, the partition function and the thermodynamic quantities derived from it.
Week, 2nd Feb · 2026-02-02 — A simple lattice model of rubber elasticity, the fundamental equation for an elastic band, Ω as a phase-space volume and the uncertainty principle, the ideal-gas Ω, and the canonical (N, V, T) ensemble.
Week of 9th Feb · 2026-02-09 — Molecular partition functions, the third law, decoupled energy levels and the de Broglie wavelength, thermodynamic properties from Q, heat capacity as energy fluctuations, equipartition, the rotational partition function, and potential energy surfaces.
Week, 26th Jan · 2026-01-26 — Lagrangian and Hamiltonian descriptions of microstates, phase space, conservative and isolated systems, the microcanonical ensemble, Liouville’s theorem, the ergodic hypothesis, and Boltzmann’s entropy formula.

Macroscopic momentum balance: \sum F = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\iiint_{CV}\rho\mathbf{v}\,dV + \rho\iint\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{n})_\perp\,dA ↳ (using average vel. & \beta) \sum F = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\iiint_{CV}\rho\mathbf{v}\,dV + \sum_{CS}\rho\langle v^2\rangle A\mathbf{n}_\perp = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\iiint_{CV}\rho\mathbf{v}\,dV + \sum_{CS}\dot{m}\langle v\rangle\beta\mathbf{n}_\perp; \beta = \frac{\langle v^2\rangle}{\langle v\rangle^2}
Cauchy (micro momentum) or force balance:

x: \frac{\partial(\rho v_x)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial(v_x\rho v_x)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(v_x\rho v_y)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(v_x\rho v_z)}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\tau_{yx}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\tau_{zx}}{\partial z} + \rho g_x
y: \frac{\partial(\rho v_y)}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial(v_y\rho v_x)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial(v_y\rho v_y)}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial(v_y\rho v_z)}{\partial z} = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\tau_{xy}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\tau_{yy}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\tau_{zy}}{\partial z} + \rho g_y
z: similar (\tau_{xz}, \tau_{yz}, \tau_{zz})



Page 4 — sample problems
Reducing bend (sketch: flow enters at P_1, v_1 along x and leaves at P_2, v_2 at angle \theta below the x-axis; wall shear \tau along the bend; weight mg.)
(\text{RHS})\;\sum F = \sum_{CS}\dot{m}\langle v\rangle\beta\mathbf{n}_\perp = \dot{m}_1\langle v_1\rangle\beta_1(-\mathbf{e}_x) + \dot{m}_2\langle v_2\rangle\beta_2(\cos\theta\,\mathbf{e}_x - \sin\theta\,\mathbf{e}_y)
(\text{LHS})\;\sum F = P_1A_1\mathbf{e}_x - P_2A_2(\cos\theta\,\mathbf{e}_x - \sin\theta\,\mathbf{e}_y) - m_Fg\,\mathbf{e}_y + \underbrace{\left(-\iint P\,\mathbf{n}_\perp\,dA + \iint_{CS}\boldsymbol{\tau}\cdot\mathbf{n}_\perp\,dA\right)}_{F_{wf}}
Resolving:

x: (F_{fw})_x = P_1A_1 - P_2A_2\cos\theta - \dot{m}_1\langle v_1\rangle\beta_1 + \dot{m}_2\langle v_2\rangle\beta_2\cos\theta
y: F_{fw} = +P_2A_2\sin\theta - m_Fg - \dot{m}_2\langle v_2\rangle\beta_2\sin\theta (only dependent on v_2, and as v_2\uparrow, F_y increases)

Forces on a bolt (sketch: a pipe ending in a bolted nozzle; free body of the nozzle with P_1A_1 in, P_2A_2 out, bolt forces and atmospheric pressure.)

Finding v_2: \rho\langle v_1\rangle A_1 = \rho\langle v_2\rangle A_2 → \langle v_1\rangle = \frac{\langle v_2\rangle A_2}{A_1}
\sum F = \cancel{\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\int_{CV}\rho\mathbf{v}\,dV} + \sum_{CS}\beta\dot{m}\langle v\rangle\mathbf{n}_\perp, with \dot{m} = \rho\langle v\rangle A:

\sum F = \rho v_1^2A_1(-\mathbf{e}_x) + \rho v_2^2A_2(\mathbf{e}_x)\;;\qquad \sum F_x = (F_B)_x + P_1A_1 - P_aA_2 - P_a(A_3 + A_4) = (F_B)_x + P_1A_1 - P_a(A_2 + A_3 + A_4)
(F_B)_x + (P_1 - P_a)A_1 = \rho v_1^2A + \rho v_2^2A_2\;;\qquad (P_a)_x = P_a\cos\theta
(sketch: the nozzle end with the inlet area A_1 split into A_2, A_3, A_4.)
Manometer (sketch: tanks A and B joined by a U-tube with liquid height difference h and reference pressure P_0.)

Always have a reference.
Make sure the correct densities of the two liquids are taken (they may be different).
(P_A - P_0) = -\rho gh; (P_B - P_0) = -\rho gd_2 (subtract).

Submerged gate (sketch: a tank of depth h with a circular gate.) h(\theta) = h - r\cos\alpha + r\cos\theta; F_y = \underbrace{(\rho gh(\theta))}_{P}\cdot A.
Torque (i) (sketch: a disk of radius R with a tangential force F_R; a conical gap with dl = \frac{dr}{\sin\theta}.)
i = r\times F_R = rF_r = \int_0^{D/2}rF_r\;;\qquad dF_R = \tau\cdot dA = \mu\frac{(v_2 - v_1)}{h}\,dA\;;\qquad dF_R = \frac{\mu\omega r\,dA}{h}\;\rightarrow\;F_R\text{ exerted on a slide}
Film shell (sketch: a falling film element of length L, width W, thickness \Delta x, with convective fluxes v_z(\rho v_z)|_{z=0}, v_z(\rho v_z)|_{z=L} and v_z(\rho v_y)|_{y=W} — “this is the normal term”.) Force balance on faces LW, W\Delta x, L\Delta x (6 terms + gravity & pressure):
F_z = \left[v_z\rho v_z|_{z=L}\right]W\Delta x\;(6\text{ terms})\;;\qquad \left[\tau_{xz}|_{x+\Delta x} - \tau_{xz}|_x\right]WL

Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 1-24) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF


























Cheat sheets and review notes for CBE 150B, mass transfer and separation processes (UC Berkeley). 24 handwritten pages: pages 1–4 are the full-size draft of the final exam sheet, pages 5–9 the compact final sheet, and the rest midterm cheat sheets and review notes.
Pages 1–4 — full-size draft of the final sheet
These pages carry the same formulas as the compact final sheet on pages 5–6 (drying, thermodynamics, flash, absorption and stripping, binary and multicomponent distillation), written larger. Only the items that do not also appear on pages 5–6 are transcribed here; see the scans for the rest.

Drying: T(°\mathrm{R}) = T(°\mathrm{F}) + 459.67; heat-transfer coefficients h = 0.0204G^{0.8} [J/m²·s·K] (parallel flow), G = \rho v [kg/m²·h]; h = 1.17G^{0.37} (perp. flow).
Distillation energy balance: V = \bar{V} + V_F (partially vaporized); (L + D) = V_B\cdot B + V_F; D(R + 1) = V_B\cdot B + V_F; Q_R = Q_R - V_F; Q_R = Q_R\left(1 - \frac{V_F}{Q_R}\right) = Q_R\left(1 - \frac{V_F}{D(R + 1)}\right) (V_F/F for the flash).
Cost plot: (sketch: cost vs. R — capital cost falls from R_{min}, operating cost rises, total minimum at \left(\frac{R}{R_{min}}\right)_{opt} = 1.3.)
Assumptions for stripper/absorber: (1) constant L, V; (2) no air dissolved in L or L evaporated in air; (3) ideal gas for air.
Stage (count the reboiler as 0); tray (count the reboiler as 1); partial reboiler → 1st stage is R; partial condenser → last stage is R [?].
Membrane separation (new formulas):

Porous — gas: N_i = \frac{D_{e_i}C_m}{P\,l_m}(P_{i_0} - P_{i_L}); C_m = \frac{\rho}{RT}; D_{e_i} = \frac{\varepsilon}{\tau}\left[\frac{1}{\frac{1}{D_i} + \frac{1}{D_{K_i}}}\right]; permeance \Rightarrow P_{m_i} = \frac{D_{e_i}C_m}{P}
Porous — liquid: N_i = \frac{D_{e_i}}{l_m}(C_{i_0} - C_{i_L}); D_{e_i} = \frac{\varepsilon D_iK_{r_i}}{\tau}; K_{r_i} = \left[1 - \frac{d_{m_i}}{d_p}\right]^4; permeance: \frac{\varepsilon D_iK_{r_i}}{\tau}
Non-porous — gas: N_i = \frac{H_iD_i}{l_m}(P_{i_0} - P_{i_L}); H_i = \frac{C_{i0}}{P_{i0}} = \frac{C_{iL}}{P_{iL}}; P_{m_i} = H_iD_i
Non-porous — liquid: N_i = \frac{D_i}{l_m}(C_{i0} - C_{iL}) = \frac{K_iD_i}{l_m}(C_{i0}' - C_{iL}'); K_i = \frac{C_{i0}}{C_{i0}'} = \frac{C_{iL}}{C_{iL}'}; P_{m_i} = K_iD_i


Multicomponent distillation: Fenske (N_{min}) → Underwood (R_{min}) → Gilliland (real N & R); Underwood class I (all components distribute) or class II (only LK & HK distribute). \alpha = y_i/x_i; ↑\alpha means it’s more volatile (lower Teq).

Page 5 — compact final sheet (1)
Drying
\underbrace{H}_{\text{absolute humidity}} = \frac{P_A}{P_t - P_A}\left(\frac{18.02}{28.97}\right)\;;\qquad RH = (100)\frac{P_{H_2O}}{P_{H_2O}^{sat}}\;;\qquad \frac{H - \tilde{H}_s}{T - T_s} = \frac{-c_p}{\lambda_{H_2O}}\;\Big\}\;\text{energy needed to achieve a certain level of drying}
\underbrace{c_p = 1.005 + 1.88H}_{\text{humid heat}}\;;\qquad \tilde{H}_s = c_p(T - T_{ref}) + H\lambda_{H_2O}\;(H\text{ absolute})\;;\qquad C = \rho/MW\;;\qquad \%H = 100H/H_s
V_H = \left[2.83\times10^{-3} + (4.56\times10^{-3})H\right]T\;\left[=\right]\frac{\mathrm{m^3}}{\mathrm{kg\,DA}}\;;\qquad V_H = \left[0.0252 + (0.0405)H\right]T\;\left[=\right]\frac{\mathrm{ft^3}}{\mathrm{lb_m\,DA}}\;;\qquad T = 459.67 + °\mathrm{F}
Free moisture and diffusion in the slab:
X_t = \frac{W_{total} - W_{dry}}{W_{dry}}\;;\qquad \frac{dX}{dt} = D_t\frac{\partial^2X}{\partial y^2}\;;\quad\text{BC: (1) }X(y, t = 0) = X_c\;;\;(2)\;X(y = y_1, t) = 0\;;\;(3)\;\frac{\partial X}{\partial y}\bigg|_{y=0} = 0
\frac{X(t)}{X_c} = \frac{8}{\pi^2}\exp\left(-D_t\left(\frac{\pi}{2y_1}\right)^2t\right)
Rate of drying: R = -\frac{W_{dry}}{A}\frac{dX}{dt} = \frac{q}{\Delta H_{vap}}; q = k(T - T_w); X = X_t - X_e (critical free moisture). (sketch: drying rate R vs. X — a falling-rate segment up to X_c, then a constant-rate (unbound water) plateau.) h = 0.0204G^{0.8} (parallel flow), G = \rho v; h = 1.17G^{0.37} (perp. flow).
Time to dry:

t = \dfrac{W_{dry}}{A\left(\frac{k(T - T_w)}{\lambda_{H_2O}}\right)}(X_c - X_f) } const. rate (MT limited), with k the MT coefficient
t = \dfrac{4y_1^2}{\pi^2D_t}\ln\left(\dfrac{8X_c}{\pi^2X_f}\right) } changing rate (diff. limited); D_t = diffusivity of H₂O in the slab (sketch: a slab of half-thickness y_1 and area A.)

Thermodynamics
\text{EB} = \sum_{out}(nh + Q + W_s) - \sum_{in}(ns + \tfrac{Q}{T_s}) = 0\;[?]\;;\qquad T_s = \text{coolant/heatant }T\;;\quad T_0 = \text{surrounding }T
\eta = \frac{W}{Q_{in}} = 1 - \frac{T_{out}}{T_{in}}\;;\qquad \eta = \frac{W_{min}}{LW + W_{min}}\;;\qquad \text{Entropy balance: }\sum_{out}\left(ns + \frac{Q}{T_s}\right) - \sum_{in}\left(ns + \frac{Q}{T_s}\right) = \Delta S_{irr}
\text{Availability balance: }\sum_{in}\left[nb + Q\left(1 - \frac{T_0}{T_s}\right) + W_s\right] - \sum_{out}\left[nb + Q\left(1 - \frac{T_0}{T_s}\right) + W_s\right] = LW = T\Delta S_{irr}
\Delta S_{univ} \geq 0; LW = lost work; W_{min} = \sum_{out}nb - \sum_{in}nb; f_{iV} = f_{iL}; b = h - T_0s; G = H - TS;
W_{min} + LW = \sum_{in}Q_{in}\left(1 - \frac{T_0}{T_{in}}\right) - \sum_{out}Q_{out}\left(1 - \frac{T_0}{T_{out}}\right) + W_{s,in} - W_{s,out}
\phi_iy_iP = x_i\gamma_iP_i^{sat}\;;\qquad K = \frac{y_i}{x_i} = \frac{\gamma_i\phi_L}{\phi_V} = \frac{\gamma_iP_i^{sat}}{\phi_iP} \approx \frac{P_i^{sat}}{P}\;;\qquad \alpha_{AB} = \frac{K_A}{K_B} = \frac{P_A^{sat}}{P_B^{sat}}\;,\;\alpha_{AB} > 1\text{ (easy separation)}
Gibbs: F = C - P + 2; \mathcal{V} = cP + 2 (internal vars T, P); \mathcal{E} = P + C(P - 1); \sum x_i = 1, \sum y_i = 1, K_i = \frac{y_i}{x_i}; F = \mathcal{V} - \mathcal{E}. System: \mathcal{V} = \mathcal{V}_{int} + (C + P + 4); \mathcal{E} = \mathcal{E}_{int} + (C + 1); F = \mathcal{V} - \mathcal{E} = C + 5.
Flash: F = C + 5; \mathcal{E} = 3C + 10 (3C = \{z_i, x_i, y_i\}; 10 = \{3T, 3P, F, V, L, Q\}); \mathcal{E} = 2C + 5 (2 vars undefined, C + 3 defined in feed). (sketch: a flash drum — feed z_i, F at T_F, P_F; vapor y_i, T_V, P_V, V; liquid x_i, T_L, P_L, L; duty Q.)

T_V, P_V ⇒ isothermal; V/F = 0, P_L ⇒ bubble point; V/F = 1, P_V ⇒ dew point; T_L, V/F = 0 ⇒ bubble-point pressure; T_V, V/F = 1 ⇒ dew-point pressure; Q = 0, P_V ⇒ adiabatic flash; Q, P_V ⇒ non-adiabatic flash; V/F, P_V ⇒ percent vap. flash

P_{bubble}(\Psi = 0) = \sum z_iP_i^{sat}\;(z_i = x_i)\;;\qquad P_{dew}(\Psi = 1) = 1\Big/\sum\left(\frac{z_i}{P_i^{sat}}\right)\;(z_i = y_i)\;;\qquad P_i^{sat} = \exp\left(A - \frac{B}{T + C}\right)
\sum_{i=1}^{C}\frac{z_i(1 - K_i)}{1 + \Psi(K_i - 1)} = 0\;(\text{Rachford–Rice})\;;\qquad \frac{\Psi - 1}{\Psi}x_A + \frac{1}{\Psi}z_A = y_A\;;\qquad \Psi = \frac{V}{F}
Page 6 — compact final sheet (2)
Absorption & stripping
Absorber (g → liq); stripper (liq → g). (sketches: an absorber with clean liquid x_0, L' in at the top (stage 1) and dirty gas V', y_{N+1} in at the bottom (stage N); a stripper with dirty liquid x_{N+1}, L' in at the top (stage N) and clean gas y_0, V' in at the bottom (stage 1).)
X_n = \frac{x_n}{1 - x_n}\;;\qquad Y_n = \frac{y_N}{1 - y_N}\;;\qquad A = \frac{1}{S}\;;\qquad X_0L' + Y_{n+1}G' = X_nL' + Y_1G'
\phi_A = \frac{v_1}{v_{N+1}} = \frac{y_1V'}{y_{N+1}V'}\;;\quad A_e = \frac{L}{VK}\;;\quad \phi_A = \frac{A_e - 1}{A_e^{n+1} - 1}\;;\quad \text{opt. }A_e = 1.4\;;\qquad \phi_S = \frac{l_1}{l_{N+1}} = \frac{xL'}{x_{N+1}L'}\;;\quad S_e = \frac{VK}{L}\;(\text{stripping factor})\;;\quad \phi_S = \frac{S_e - 1}{S_e^{n+1} - 1}
\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)_{min} = \frac{(Y_{N+1} - Y_1)}{\left[\frac{Y_{N+1}}{Y_{N+1}(K_n - 1)} + K_n\right] - X_0}\;;\qquad \left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)_{opt} = 1.5\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)_{min}
\text{Op. line: }Y_{n+1} = X_n\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right) + Y_1 - X_0\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)\;(\text{absorber})\;;\qquad X_n = X_{n+1}\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right) + Y_0 - X_1\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)\;(\text{stripper})
(sketches: Y vs. X — for the absorber the operating line (slope m = L'/G', from top to bottom) lies above the equilibrium line; for the stripper it lies below.)
Packed bed: k_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^Lk_x\,dx; Length = H_{OG}\cdot N_{OG};
\frac{k_xa}{C_tD_{AB}} = \frac{k_La}{D_{AB}} = Sh = \alpha\left(\frac{L}{\mu_L}\right)^{1-n}\left(\frac{\mu_L}{\rho D_{AB}}\right)^{0.5}\;;\qquad \frac{1}{K_GC_g} = \frac{1}{k_gC_g} + \frac{K}{k_LC_L}\;;\qquad \frac{1}{K_La} = \frac{1}{k_La} + \frac{1}{Kk_ga}
N_A = k_G(P_{A,i} - P_A) = K_G(P_A^* - P_A) = k_L(C_A - C_{A,i}) = K_L(C_A - C^*)\;;\qquad N_A = k_y(y_{A,i} - y_A) = K_y(y_A^* - y_A) = k_x(x_A - x_{A,i}) = K_x(x_A - x_A^*)
a = area/volume. (sketches: P^* vs. C with the bulk, interface and equilibrium points; concentration profiles on either side of the gas–liquid interface.)

































Driving forceH_{OG} [m]Driving forceH_{OL}(y - y^*)V/K_yaS(x - x^*)L/K_xaS(p - p^*)V/K_GaPS(c^* - c)L/[K_La(\rho/M_L)S](Y - Y^*)V'/K_YaS(X - x)L'/(K_XaS)
N_{OG} = \frac{\ln\left[\left(\frac{A - 1}{A}\right)\left(\frac{y_{in} - Kx_{in}}{y_{out} - Kx_{in}}\right) + \frac{1}{A}\right]}{\left(\frac{A - 1}{A}\right)}
Assumptions: (1) const. L, V; (2) no air dissolved in L or L evap. in air; (3) ideal gas for air. Minimum stripping rate: V_{min} = \frac{L}{K_n}\cdot(fraction of solute stripped).
Binary distillation
(sketch: a column with feed F, z_F at stage f; total condenser returning L and taking distillate D, x_D; partial reboiler returning \bar{V} and taking bottoms B, x_B.)
R = \frac{L}{D}\;(\text{reflux ratio})\;;\qquad V_B = \frac{\bar{V}}{B}\;(\text{reboiler ratio})\;;\qquad \text{opt. }R = 1.3R_{min}\,[?]
Quality: (sketches of the feed stage for each case.)



















q > 1q = 1q = L_F/Fq = 0q < 0subcooled liq. (V < \bar{V}, \bar{L} = L + F)sat. liq. (V = \bar{V})partially vap. (V = \bar{V} + V_F, \bar{L} = L + L_F)sat. vapor (V = \bar{V} + F, \bar{L} = L)superheated vapor (V > \bar{V} + F, \bar{L} < L)
(sketch: McCabe–Thiele y–x diagram with the rectifying line y = \left(\frac{R}{R + 1}\right)x + \left(\frac{1}{R + 1}\right)x_D, the stripping line y = \left(\frac{V_B + 1}{V_B}\right)x - \frac{1}{V_B}x_B and the q-line y = \left(\frac{q}{q - 1}\right)x - \frac{z_F}{(q - 1)}; R_{min} = m/(1 - m) from the pinch.)

→ Total reboiler/reflux (R \to \infty \Rightarrow N_{min}) ↳ least capex, highest opex. (sketch: stages stepped between the equilibrium curve and the diagonal.)
McCabe–Thiele assumptions: no heat loss, const. P, binary mixture, c_p\Delta T & \Delta H_{mix} are negligible, components have equal & const. latent heat.
→ Murphree efficiency (how close it reaches eq.): E_M = \dfrac{y_N - y_{N+1}}{y_N^* - y_{N+1}} (sketch: one stage on the y–x diagram.)
→ Overall efficiency: E_o = \dfrac{N_{theoretical}}{N_{actual}} = 50.3(\alpha_{AB}\mu_{liq})^{-0.226} (sketch: E_o falling with \alpha_{AB}\mu_L from 0.1 to 10.)
→ Plate efficiency (specific to each stage): E_o \propto \left(K_LM_L\frac{\mu_L}{\rho_L}\right)^{-1} — K_L eq. const., M_L MW of liq., \mu_L visc. of liq., \rho_L density of liq. (sketch: E_o vs. 0.1–10².)

EB on distillation:
Fh_F + Q_R = Dh_D + Bh_B + Q_C + \cancel{Q_{loss}}\;;\qquad \text{Condenser: }Q_C = \underbrace{D(R + 1)}_{V}\Delta H^{vap}\;;\qquad \text{Reboiler: }Q_R = \underbrace{BV_B}_{\bar{V}}\Delta H^{vap}
V = \bar{V} + V_F\;(\text{partial vaporized})\;;\quad (L + D) = V_BB + V_F\;;\quad D(R + 1) = V_BB + V_F\;;\quad Q_R = Q_R - V_F\;;\quad Q_R = Q_R\left(1 - \frac{V_F}{Q_R}\right) = Q_R\left(1 - \frac{V_F}{D(R + 1)}\right)
Multicomponent distillation

Specify splits (LK, HK)
Estimate splits of non-key components
Determine column pressure & type of condenser (dew point & bubble point)
Flash the feed @ column pressure (adiabatic flash)
Calculate N_{min} (Fenske)
Calculate splits of non-key
Calculate (R_\infty)_{min} (Underwood)
Calculate N, R (Gilliland)
Calculate feed location (Kirkbride)
Condenser & reboiler duties

Class I → narrow-boiling-range mixture, low degree of separation.
5) Fenske (i = LK, j = HK):
N_{min} = \frac{\log\left\{\frac{(x_{i,D})}{(x_{i,B})}\frac{(x_{j,B})}{(x_{j,D})}\right\}}{\log\alpha_{ij}} = \frac{\log\left\{\frac{d_i}{d_j}\frac{b_j}{b_i}\right\}}{\log\alpha_m}\;;\qquad \alpha_m = \left[(\alpha_{ij})_N(\alpha_{ij})_1\right]^{1/2}
6) Non-key dist. (sanity check), with d_r, b_r → HK (reference):
b_i = \frac{f_i}{1 + \left(\frac{d_r}{b_r}\right)(\alpha_{i,r})^{N_{min}}}\;;\qquad d_i = \frac{f_i\left(\frac{d_r}{b_r}\right)(\alpha_{i,r})^{N_{min}}}{1 + (d_r/b_r)(\alpha_{i,r})^{N_{min}}}
7) Underwood

↳ Class I:

\frac{(L_\infty)_{min}}{F} = \frac{\left(\frac{L_F}{F}\right)\left[\frac{Dx_{LK,D}}{L_Fx_{LK,F}} - (\alpha_{LK,HK})_F\frac{Dx_{HK,D}}{L_Fx_{HK,F}}\right]}{(\alpha_{LK,HK})_F - 1}\;;\qquad (R_\infty)_{min} = \frac{(L_\infty)_{min}}{D}
Non-key components: 0 < \left(\frac{Dx_{i,D}}{Fx_{i,F}}\right) < 1;
\frac{Dx_{i,D}}{L_Fx_{i,F}} = \left[\frac{(\alpha_{i,HK})_F - 1}{(\alpha_{LK,HK})_F - 1}\right]\left(\frac{Dx_{LK,D}}{L_Fx_{LK,F}}\right) + \left[\frac{(\alpha_{LK,HK})_F - (\alpha_{i,HK})_F}{(\alpha_{LK,HK}) - 1}\right]\left(\frac{Dx_{HK,D}}{L_Fx_{HK,F}}\right)

↳ Class II (only LK & HK distribute), solving for \alpha_{HK} < \theta < \alpha_{LK}:

\sum_{i=1}^{C}\frac{(\alpha_{i,HK})z_{i,F}}{(\alpha_{i,HK}) - \theta} = 1 - q\;;\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{C}\frac{(\alpha_{i,HK})x_{i,D}}{(\alpha_{i,HK}) - \theta} = 1 + (R_\infty)_{min} = \frac{(V_\infty)_{min}}{D}
8) Gilliland:
\frac{N - N_{min}}{(N + 1)} = 1 - \exp\left[\frac{(1 + 54.4x)}{(11 + 117.2x)}\frac{(x - 1)}{x^{0.5}}\right]\;;\qquad x = \frac{R - R_{min}}{(R + 1)}
9) Kirkbride:
\frac{N_R}{N_S} = \left[\frac{(z_{HK,F})}{(z_{LK,F})}\left(\frac{x_{LK,B}}{x_{HK,D}}\right)^2\frac{B}{D}\right]^{0.206}\;;\qquad N = N_S + N_R
Page 7 — compact final sheet (3): membranes and LLE
Membranes
(sketch: a membrane module — feed F in, retentate (R) out along the top, permeate (P) through the membrane.)
