X_0L' + Y_{n+1}G' = X_nL' + Y_1G'
\text{Absorber: }Y_{n+1} = X_n\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right) + Y_1 - X_0\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)\;;\qquad \text{Stripp.: }Y_n = X_{n+1}\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right) + Y_0 - X_1\left(\frac{L'}{G'}\right)\;;\qquad L'_{min} = \frac{G'(Y_{n+1} - Y_1)}{\left[\frac{Y_{n+1}}{Y_{n+1}(K_n - 1)} + K_n\right] - X_0}
Using the solute-free method, we can construct Y vs. X graphs. (sketches: absorber — the operating line from the top (X_0) to the bottom above the equilibrium curve Y = f(K, X), with the L_{min} line touching the curve; stripper — stages stepped between the operating line and the equilibrium line.)
Packed column separator
→ For continuous separation (no stages). (sketch: a packed column with packing.) H_{OG} = height of effective plates; N_{OG}.
S = K_ya(y_1 - y^*) = K_xa(x^* - x_b)\;;\qquad L = \text{length of column} = \text{height}\times\text{effective number}\;\rightarrow\;L = H_{OG}\cdot N_{OG}
H_{OG} = \frac{G'}{K_ga\,S}\;;\qquad A = \frac{L'}{k_{eq}G'}\;;\qquad A = \frac{1}{S}\;;\qquad N_{OG} = \frac{\ln\left[\left(\frac{A - 1}{A}\right)\left(\frac{y_{in} - K_{eq}x_{in}}{y_{out} - K_{eq}x_{in}}\right) + \frac{1}{A}\right]}{\left(\frac{A - 1}{A}\right)}
Mass transport (local MT coeff.): \frac{k_xa}{C_{tot}D_{AB}} = \frac{k_La}{D_{AB}} = Sh = \alpha\left(\frac{L}{\mu_L}\right)^{1-n}\left(\frac{\mu_L}{\rho D_{AB}}\right)^{0.5} (L = length of column); average MT coeff. k_L = \frac{1}{L}\int_0^Lk_x\,dx.
Binary distillation
R = \frac{L}{D}; V_B = \frac{\bar{V}}{B}; q = \frac{\bar{L} - L}{F} (how vaporized the feed is); R \to \infty (total reflux).
Page 17 — “Heating & Mixing Sh*t”
Absorption/stripping — two ways to solve this:

(a) Graphical: McCabe–Thiele (any VLE)
(b) Analytical: Kremser (assume dilute-solution VLE) ↳ Henry’s law & constant L/V

(a) Graphical (sketch: an absorber — inlet solvent L_0, x_0 at the top (stage 1), vapor V_1, y_1 out; inlet gas V_{N+1}, y_{N+1} at the bottom (stage N), liquid L_N, x_N out; around stage n: L_{n-1}, x_{n-1} down and V_n, y_n up above; L_n, x_n and V_{n+1}, y_{n+1} below.)

Overall material balance (@ the ends): y_{N+1}V_{N+1} + x_0L_0 = y_1V_1 + x_NL_N
Balance from 1 \to n stages (n = stages from the top ≠ N, the total no. of stages): y_{n+1}V_{n+1} + x_0L_0 = y_1V_1 + x_nL_n
Rearranging this equation:

y_{n+1} = \frac{y_1V_1 + x_nL_n - x_0L_0}{V_{n+1}} = y_1\frac{V_1}{V_{n+1}} + x_n\frac{L_n}{V_{n+1}} - x_0\frac{L_0}{V_{n+1}}\;\Rightarrow\;y_{n+1} = \underbrace{\left(\frac{L_n}{V_{n+1}}\right)}_{\text{gradient}}x_n + \underbrace{\left(y_1 - \frac{L_0}{V_{n+1}}x_0\right)}_{\text{intercept}}\;\rightarrow\;\text{this becomes the operating line}
VLE & \frac{L}{V} is constant (ideal stages): y_N = \left(\frac{L}{V}\right)x_N + \left(y_1 - \frac{L}{V}x_0\right).
Small technicality: we define y_A = \frac{\text{moles of solute A (in gas)}}{\text{total moles of gas mixture}}. However, the gas is in two different mixtures ∴ y_A = \frac{\text{A in gas}}{[\text{moles of carrier gas} + \text{mole of solute B}]} ∴ y_1 = Y_1 = \frac{y_A}{1 - y_A}. Similarly, X_1 = \frac{y_B}{1 - y_B}.
Therefore the final equations we get:
Y_{N+1} = \left(\frac{L}{V}\right)X_N + \left(Y_1 - \frac{L}{V}X_0\right)
Steps: (1) draw the eq. line from Henry’s law; (2) draw the operating line (Y_{N+1}, X_1, \frac{L}{V}, X_N are known).
Page 18 — liquid–liquid extraction
(sketch: a mixer–separator — carrier/feed and solvent in; raffinate and extract out.)

→ The “carrier” carries the “solute”; → this is what you need to extract (the solute from the carrier).
The raffinate carries the unwanted carrier/feed (and some small amounts of remaining solute).
The extract carries the desired solute and some amount of carrier that might have slightly dissolved.

(sketch: a ternary diagram with solute B at the top, solvent C at the bottom left, carrier/feed A at the bottom right.)
Finding M graphically: F + S = M = E + R (F, S, M lie on the same line; M, E, R lie on the same line — “sht going in = sht coming out”).
Pages 19–21 — “Gaurav: The legend” (diffusion cases)
\nabla\cdot\vec{N}_A + \frac{\partial C_A}{\partial t} - R_A = 0
→ Make sure to use this correctly according to the different coordinates (divergence of a vector is a scalar).
Fick’s law (c is constant): \vec{J}_A = -D_{AB}\nabla C_A; \vec{N}_A = \vec{J}_A + \underbrace{c_i\vec{V}}_{\text{convection}}.
Different cases:

First-order homogeneous rxn (C_A = f(z) + Cartesian + SS + any BCs; 2nd-order ODE, linear): D_{AB}\frac{d^2C_A}{dz^2} - k_1C_A = 0; C_A(z) = C_1\cosh\left(z\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{D_{AB}}}\right) + C_2\sinh\left(z\sqrt{\frac{k_1}{D_{AB}}}\right). (sketch: A diffusing (v = 0) toward a reaction plane; C_{A0} = C_A^{bulk}.)
Semi-infinite diffusion (partial diff. eq.): \frac{\partial\theta}{\partial t} = D_{AB}\frac{\partial^2\theta}{\partial z^2}; \theta = C_A - C_{A0}; \theta(z, t = 0) = 0; \theta(z = 0, t) = C_{As} - C_{A0}; semi-infinite → \theta(z = \infty, t) = 0.

\text{Solution: }\frac{C_{A,s} - C_A(z, t)}{C_{A,s} - C_{A0}} = \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{z}{2\sqrt{D_{AB}t}}\right)\;;\qquad \mathrm{erf}(x) = \int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx
Transcriber’s note: erf is written here with limits 0 to ∞ and no 2/\sqrt{\pi} prefactor; the definition on page 10 (\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^z) is the standard one.
Check: when t \to \infty, \mathrm{erf}(0) = 0, C_{A,s} = C_A(z, t) → everything diffuses. When \mathrm{erf}(z) = 1, z is very big: C_{A,s} - C_A(z, t) = C_{A,s} - C_{A0}, C_A(z, t) = C_{A0} (makes sense!). (sketches: C_A vs. z profiles spreading with t; erf rising to 1.)

Falling film (sketch: a film of thickness δ flowing down, velocity profile v_x, inlet conc. C_{A0}.)

\vec{N}_{A,x} = C_Av_x\;(\text{ignore diffusion})\;;\quad \vec{N}_{A,y} = -D_{AB}\frac{\partial C_A}{\partial y}\;(\text{only diffusion})\;\Big\}\;v\frac{\partial C_A}{\partial x} = D_{AB}\frac{\partial^2C_A}{\partial\xi^2}\;;\qquad \nabla\cdot N_A = \frac{dN_{A,x}}{dx} + \frac{dN_{A,y}}{dy}
BCs: C_A(x = 0, \xi) = 0; C_A(x, \xi = 0) = C_{A,0}; * C_A(x, \xi = \infty) = 0 ⇒ C_A(x, y) = C_{A0}\left(1 - \mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{y - \delta}{\sqrt{\frac{4D_{AB}x}{v_x}}}\right)\right).
It appears as semi-infinite as the convection in x is much faster than the diffusion in y ↓ the δ is infinite in a way (x dimension the same as t).
(sketch: a tube of length L connecting outside air to an inert box, with A = O₂ diffusing in against convection.) D_{AB}\frac{\partial^2c}{\partial z^2} - v\frac{\partial c}{\partial z} = 0 (diff. = convection).

Glovebox: N_A = -D_{AB}\frac{dC_A}{dz} + C_AV → solution: C_A = C_{A0}\left(\frac{\exp(vz/D_{AB}) - 1}{\exp(vL/D_{AB}) - 1}\right)
Finite slab (sketch: a slab at C_{A0} with surfaces at C_{A,s}, from z = 0 to L; profiles flattening with time.)

\frac{\partial C_A}{\partial t} = D_{AB}\frac{\partial^2C_A}{\partial z^2}\;;\quad Y = \frac{C_{As} - C_A}{C_{As} - C_{A0}}\;;\quad Y(z, t = 0) = 1\;;\;Y(z = 0, t) = 0\;;\;{}^*Y(z = L, t) = 0
Y(z, t) = \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}\sin\left(\frac{n\pi z}{L}\right)\exp\left(-\left(\frac{n\pi}{2}\right)^2\left(\frac{4D_{AB}t}{L^2}\right)\right)\;\;\hookrightarrow \text{ Sturm–Liouville theorem}
Stagnant-film [?] diffusion (sketch: a tube of liquid with gas flowing across the top; flux N_A upward in y.) Constant flux: N_A = -D_{AB}\frac{\partial C_A}{\partial y} — linear profile. PSS → liquid height does not change ↓ conc. only depends on the VLE partial pressure. (sketches: two concentration profiles — the steeper one has the higher flux.) But we are looking at a snapshot of flux in space: both fluxes at these heights are the same ↓ that’s why the flux is constant (although changing w/ time).
Page 22 — non-dimensional numbers and two-phase transfer
\nu = kinematic viscosity.

Re = \frac{\rho vD}{\mu} = \frac{vD}{\nu} = \frac{\text{inertial}}{\text{viscous}}
Sc = Pr_m = \frac{\nu}{D_{AB}} = \frac{\text{diff. momentum transfer}}{\text{diff. mass transfer}}
Le = \frac{k}{\rho c_pD_{AB}} = \frac{\text{thermal diffusion}}{\text{mass diffusion}} (k = thermal conductivity)
Sh = Nu_m = \frac{k_cL}{D_{AB}} = \frac{\text{convective mass T}}{\text{diffusive MT}} (at an interface)
Pe_c = \frac{v_\infty L}{D_{AB}} = Re\,Pr = \frac{\text{convective mass T}}{\text{diffusive mass T}} (in the same phase)
Da = \frac{kL}{D_{AB}} = \frac{\text{1st-order rate}}{\text{diffusive MT}}
K_n = \frac{\lambda}{d_{pore}} = \frac{\text{diffusion (normal)}}{\text{Knudsen diffusion}}

2 phases (sketch: gas | liquid with the interface i and partial pressure P_A dropping toward the interface.)
N_{A,g\to L} = k_G(P_A - P_{A_i}) = k_L(C_{A_L,i} - C_{A_L})
Liquid transfer coefficient (how fast can stuff move in liquid) ↓ resistance \left(\frac{1}{k_L}, \frac{1}{k_G}\right); high k_L, low resistance (things can move faster).
(sketch: P_A vs. C_{AL} — the equilibrium curve, the bulk point (C_{A,L}^{bulk}, P_{A,L}^{bulk}) (“physical point”), a line of slope -k_L/k_G to the interface, and p^*, C_{AL}^*; “if you take the bulk conc. ↳ what will be the pressure @ equil.“)
N_{A,G\to L} = K_G(P_A - P_A^*) = K_L(C_A^* - C_{AL})\;;\qquad \frac{1}{K_G} = \frac{1}{k_G} + \frac{H}{k_L}\;;\qquad \frac{1}{K_L} = \frac{1}{Hk_G} + \frac{1}{k_L}
Page 23 — “Chem 150B” fluxes

\bar{V} → molar average velocity = \frac{\sum(c_i\bar{v}_i)}{\sum c_i}; \bar{v} → mass average velocity = \frac{\sum(\rho\bar{v}_i)}{\sum\rho_i}; \bar{v}_i → absolute velocity
Molar flux N_i = c_i\bar{v}_i; molar diffusion \bar{J} = c_i\bar{v}_{D_i} = -D_{AB}\nabla c_i; mass diffusion \bar{j} = -D\rho\nabla w_i (w = \frac{\rho_i}{\rho})
Mass flux n_i = \rho_i\bar{v}_i; J_i = -D_{AB}c\nabla y_i (y_i = \frac{c_i}{\sum c})
\boxed{\bar{N}_i = \bar{J}_i + c_i\bar{V}}

For a binary mixture:
(\text{i})\quad \bar{N}_A = -cD_{AB}\nabla y_A + y_A(\bar{N}_A + \bar{N}_B)\;;\quad \bar{N}_B = -cD_{BA}\nabla y_B + y_B(\bar{N}_A + \bar{N}_B)\;;\quad \bar{n}_A = \underbrace{-\rho D_{AB}\nabla w_A}_{\text{diffusive term}} + \underbrace{w_A(\bar{n}_A + \bar{n}_B)}_{\text{convective term}}
Mass balance: we know \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + (\nabla\cdot\rho\bar{v}) = 0 ∴ \boxed{\frac{\partial\rho_i}{\partial t} + \bar{\nabla}\cdot n_i = r_i}; \boxed{\frac{\partial c_i}{\partial t} + \bar{\nabla}\cdot\bar{N}_i = R_i} … (ii)
We can combine equations (i) & (ii) for a binary system to get:
\underbrace{-D_{AB}\nabla^2C_A}_{\text{diffusion}} + \underbrace{\bar{V}\cdot\nabla C_A}_{\text{convection}} + \underbrace{\partial C_A/\partial t}_{\text{non-steady}} - \underbrace{R_A}_{\text{chemical reaction}} = 0
Page 24 — “Hella Diffusion”
D_{AB} = \frac{-J_A}{\nabla C_A} [cm²/s]; D_{AB} \propto T, P^{-1}, composition. Gas ≈ 10^{-2}–10^{-1}; liq ≈ 10^{-6}–10^{-5}; sol ≈ 10^{-10}–10^{-6}. There are various models describing the diffusion of various species in various phases.
Gases (kinetic theory)

Ideal gas: D_{AA^*} = \frac{1}{3}\lambda u; \lambda = \frac{kT}{\sqrt{2}\pi\sigma_A^2P}; u = \sqrt{\frac{8kNT}{\pi M_A}}
Hirschfelder (non-reacting, low P, non-polar): D_{AB} = \frac{0.001858T^{3/2}\left(\frac{1}{M_A} + \frac{1}{M_B}\right)^{1/2}}{P\sigma_{AB}^2\Omega_D}
Fuller (when σ & ε are not available): D_{AB} = \frac{0.001T^{1.75}\left(\frac{1}{M_A} + \frac{1}{M_B}\right)^{1/2}}{P\left[(\sum v_i)_A^{1/3} + (\sum v_i)_B^{1/3}\right]^2}

Liquid

Stokes–Einstein: D_{AB} = \frac{kT}{6\pi r_A\mu_B}
Wilke & Chang: \frac{D_{AB}\mu_B}{T} = \frac{7.4\times10^{-8}(\Phi_BM_B)^{1/2}}{V_A^{0.6}}; V_A = 0.285V_c^{1.048} (if V_A not available)
Scheibel: \frac{D_{AB}\mu_B}{T} = \frac{K}{V_A^{1/3}} (analytical)

Pore diffusivity — diffusion of gas molecules through small pores: K_n = \frac{\lambda}{d_{pore}}; 0.1 < K_n < 1 (moderate), K_n > 1 (important), K_n > 10 (dominate). K_n \propto P (as more collisions with pore walls) [?] (K_n does not work for liquids as λ is very small).
\underbrace{\frac{1}{D_{Ae}}}_{\text{effective diffusion (within the pore)}} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{D_{AB}}}_{\text{molecular diffusion}} + \frac{1}{D_{KA}}
} “Series” competition of Knudsen & molecular (in a dilute mixture) ⇓ straight, cylindrical pores.
Transcriber’s note: since \lambda \propto 1/P, the Knudsen number falls as pressure rises (K_n \propto P^{-1}); "K_n \propto P" is as written.

Problem 6.39 (29 October 2023)
(sketch: flow up a channel inclined at ψ, with axes \hat{e}_x along the flow and \hat{e}_z normal to it, and a dashed control volume.)
\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} = -\rho g_z \Rightarrow P = -\rho g_zz + f(x)\;;\qquad \frac{dP}{dx} = \frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{df}{dx} \Rightarrow f(x) = \frac{\Delta P}{L}x + c_1
P = -\rho g_zz + \frac{\Delta P}{L}x + c_1\;;\qquad \text{BC} \rightarrow P(z, x) = P(0, 0) = P_0 \Rightarrow c_1 = P_0\;\therefore\;\boxed{P = -\rho g_zz + \frac{\Delta P}{L} + P_0}
Transcriber’s note: the boxed result drops the x multiplying ΔP/L; as written.
Radial continuity:
\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(\rho rv_r)}{\partial r} = 0 \xrightarrow{\text{incomp. \checkmark }} \rho\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rv_r) = 0\quad\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rv_r) \neq \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r}\right) \xrightarrow{\text{integrate once}} rv_r = c_1 \Rightarrow \boxed{v_r = \frac{c_1}{r}}\;;\qquad Q = \langle v\rangle\cdot A

Problem 7.10 — radial flow between parallel plates (6 November 2023)
(sketch: fluid fed down a central tube spreading radially between two parallel plates, with a parabolic v_r profile across the gap; z up, r outward.) Unknowns P(r), v_r(r, z).


Continuity: v_r = \frac{f(z)}{r} (f = arbitrary function of z, which we don’t know!)


Navier–Stokes, r-component:


\rho\left(v_r\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r}\right) = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial r} + \mu\frac{\partial^2v_r}{\partial z^2}
Although v_r is changing w/ r (as you go further away to the periphery), we can assume this process is slow enough that only the variation in v_r in the z-direction dominates } this is the “slow” or developed flow assumption. We have said \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r} \approx 0 but that does not mean v_r \neq f(r).
Now we have \frac{\partial P}{\partial r} = \mu\frac{\partial^2v_r}{\partial z^2} ↓ cannot solve this expression as of yet since v_r is f(r, z), so cannot take the integral of both sides! However, substitute v_r = \frac{1}{r}f(z):
\frac{dP}{dr} = \mu\frac{1}{r}\frac{d^2f}{dz^2} \Rightarrow r\frac{dP}{dr} = \mu\frac{d^2f}{dz^2} = \lambda
Now separation of variables is possible! (since f is only a function of z & P only of r) — λ is the common parameter.

r\frac{dP}{dr} = \lambda → BCs ✓ → solve for λ here (which we can plug in at the end)
\frac{d^2f}{dz^2} = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} → BCs ✓ → solve for f → get v_r

Check Q1 of the exam 2 review session!

Derivation (29 September 2023)
\nabla = \left(\hat{e}_r\frac{\partial}{\partial r} + \frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} + \hat{e}_z\frac{\partial}{\partial z}\right)\;;\qquad \underline{v} = (v_r\hat{e}_r + v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta + v_z\hat{e}_z)\;;\qquad \underline{\underline{\tau}} = \nabla\underline{v} + (\nabla\underline{v})^T = \begin{pmatrix}\tau_{rr} & \tau_{r\theta} & \tau_{rz} \\ & \tau_{\theta\theta} & \tau_{\theta z} \\ & & \tau_{zz}\end{pmatrix}
\nabla\underline{v} → this is a dyadic product but w/ the del operator:
(\nabla\underline{v})^T = \begin{pmatrix}\hat{e}_r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(v_r\hat{e}_r) & \hat{e}_r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta) & \hat{e}_r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(v_z\hat{e}_z) \\ \frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(v_r\hat{e}_r) & \frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta) & \frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(v_z\hat{e}_z) \\ \hat{e}_z\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(v_r\hat{e}_r) & \hat{e}_z\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta) & \hat{e}_z\frac{\partial}{\partial z}(v_z\hat{e}_z)\end{pmatrix}
Unit-vector derivatives: \frac{\partial\hat{e}_r}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial\hat{e}_\theta}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial\hat{e}_z}{\partial r} = 0; \frac{\partial\hat{e}_r}{\partial\theta} = \hat{e}_\theta; \frac{\partial\hat{e}_\theta}{\partial\theta} = -\hat{e}_r.

\hat{e}_r\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(v_r\hat{e}_r)\right] = \hat{e}_r\left[\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r}\hat{e}_r\right] + v_r\cancel{\frac{\partial\hat{e}_r}{\partial r}} = \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r}\hat{e}_r\hat{e}_r
\frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta) = \frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\left[\hat{e}_\theta\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial\theta} + v_\theta\frac{\partial\hat{e}_\theta}{\partial\theta}\right] = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial\theta}\hat{e}_\theta\hat{e}_\theta - \frac{1}{r}v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta\hat{e}_r; and \hat{e}_r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(v_\theta\hat{e}_\theta) = \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r}\hat{e}_\theta\hat{e}_r
\frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(v_r\hat{e}_r) = \frac{\hat{e}_\theta}{r}\left[\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial\theta}\hat{e}_r + v_r\frac{\partial\hat{e}_r}{\partial\theta}\right] = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial\theta}\hat{e}_r\hat{e}_\theta + \frac{v_r}{r}\hat{e}_\theta\hat{e}_\theta

(\nabla\underline{v})^T = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r} & \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r} & \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial\theta} - \frac{v_\theta}{r} & \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial\theta} + \frac{v_r}{r} & \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial\theta} \\ \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial z} & \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial z} & \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z}\end{pmatrix}
\underline{\underline{\tau}} = \nabla\underline{v} + (\nabla\underline{v})^T (the transposed matrix added to it):
\boxed{\underline{\underline{\tau}} = \begin{pmatrix}2\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r} & \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial\theta} - \frac{v_\theta}{r} & \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ & 2\left(\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial\theta} + \frac{v_r}{r}\right) & \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial\theta} + \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial z} \\ & & 2\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z}\end{pmatrix}_{r\theta z}}\quad(\text{symmetric; times }\mu\text{ for a Newtonian fluid})

Inclined plane derivation (21 September 2023)
(sketch: a fluid element \Delta x\Delta y\Delta z on a plane inclined at β, with gravity resolved into g\cos\beta and g\sin\beta; the textbook figure of the element on the incline is pasted beside it.)
\underline{f} = \iint_A(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\,dS\;;\qquad (\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\big|_{top} = (1\ 0\ 0)\begin{pmatrix}\tau_{xx} - p & \tau_{xy} & \tau_{xz} \\ \vdots & & \vdots\end{pmatrix} = (\tau_{xx} - p\;\;\tau_{xy}\;\;\tau_{xz})\quad(1\times3\cdot3\times3)
\sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{f} = 0 = \underline{f}_{gravity} + \sum_{k=1}^{6}\underline{f}_{k^{th}\text{ side}}\quad\to\text{force balance on a fluid element}
\sum\underline{f} = \begin{pmatrix}-\rho g\sin\beta \\ 0 \\ \rho g\cos\beta\end{pmatrix}\Delta x\Delta y\Delta z + \left[\Delta y\Delta z\begin{pmatrix}\tau_{xx} - p \\ \tau_{xy} \\ \tau_{xz}\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}\Bigg|_{x+\Delta x} - \Delta y\Delta z\begin{pmatrix}\tau_{xx} - p \\ \tau_{xy} \\ \tau_{xz}\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}\Bigg|_x + \cdots\right]
(also: the dyadic \nabla\underline{v} as a 3×1 times 1×3 product, giving the 3×3 matrix of \frac{\partial v_j}{\partial x_i}.)
Split into each x, y, z component & take limits:
x:\quad 0 = -\rho g\sin\theta + \left(\frac{\tau_{xx}|_{x+\Delta x} - \tau_{xx}|_x}{\Delta x}\right) - \left(\frac{p|_{x+\Delta x} - p}{\Delta x}\right) + \left(\frac{\tau_{yx}|_{y+\Delta y} - \tau_{yx}|_y}{\Delta y}\right) + \left(\frac{\tau_{zx}|_{z+\Delta z} - \tau_{zx}|_z}{\Delta z}\right)
\text{Limit:}\quad\boxed{x:\;0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \left[\frac{\partial\tau_{xx}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\tau_{yx}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\tau_{zx}}{\partial z}\right] - \rho g\sin\beta}\quad\text{x-component momentum balance! [4.357, 4.358, 4.359]}
↓ But our goal is to find the velocity profile! ↳ Need to use an equation which now relates τ & v → Newtonian constitutive equation \underline{\underline{\tau}} = \mu(\nabla\underline{v} + (\nabla\underline{v})^T), with \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z(x)):
\underline{\underline{\tau}} = \mu\begin{pmatrix}2\frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial z} \\ \cdots & 2\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y} & \cdots \\ \cdots & \cdots & 2\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z}\end{pmatrix}_{xyz} \Rightarrow \underline{\underline{\tau}} = \mu\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & \frac{dv_z}{dx} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{dv_z}{dx} & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}\;;\qquad \tau_{xz} = \tau_{zx} = \mu\frac{dv_z}{dx}
↓ Substitute in the balance to arrive at simplified forms } there will be only 1 direction where velocity would remain for unidirectional flows! (Pg 380, 381, 382.)
\boxed{z:\;0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial z} + \mu\frac{d^2v_z}{dx^2} + \rho g\cos\beta}
↓ Solve for v_z w/ BCs: @ x = 0 [v_z = 0]; @ x = H, \tau_{xz} = 0 = \mu\frac{dv_z}{dx}:
\boxed{v_z(x) = \frac{\rho g\cos\beta}{\mu}\left[Hx - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]}
Transcriber’s note: the x-balance writes “sin θ” in one place where β (the incline angle) is meant.

FL Lab 2 (29 September 2023)
Title: turbulent flow in a pipe. Goal: determine the friction factor for turbulent flow over a range of flow rates.
Theory — Reynolds number: Re = \frac{\rho\langle v\rangle D}{\mu} (⟨v⟩ = fluid average velocity; D = pipe diameter (ID); μ = viscosity); Re > 4000 (turbulent flow).
(Darcy) friction factor (f_D): twists, turns, pipe flow → frictional losses → can become important in many industrial applications so important to study! ↳ Empirically determined correlations exist:

Blasius: f_D = 0.316Re^{-0.25}
Colebrook: \frac{1}{f_D^{1/2}} = -2\log\left(\frac{\varepsilon/D}{3.7} + \frac{2.51}{Re f_D^{1/2}}\right) (ε = surface roughness)

} f_D is non-dimensional! P.S. f → Fanning friction factor, f = \frac{1}{4}f_D } same concept but developed by different scientists so off by a factor!
Darcy–Weisbach equation — relates head loss due to friction:
\boxed{\frac{\Delta p}{L} = f_D\cdot\frac{\rho\langle v\rangle^2}{2D}} = f_D\left(\frac{\rho\langle v\rangle D}{\mu}\right)\frac{\langle v\rangle\mu}{2D^2} = \frac{f_D\langle v\rangle\mu}{2D^2}(Re)
Experiment: + flow water at a specific Q → record variables in order to calculate Re (⟨v⟩, D, ρ, μ) → calculate f & compare Darcy vs. (Colebrook & Blasius). Fluid properties: water ✓; pipe specs: given ✓.
(figure 1: process flow diagram for turbulent flow in a pipe — cold water in past a pressure indicator (PI), through a rotameter (vary the Q) and a valve, up the test section with a differential pressure gauge DP-1 across it, and out. Annotations: DP-1 reads in units of mA ↓ need to get to psi (pressure)! ↓ calibration curves! (sketch: Q vs. DP-1, a straight line).)

→ RTT on fluid flow in pipe to evaluate \sum_{cv}\underline{f} → \sum_{cv}\underline{f} balance (pressures + shear stress). (sketch: a pipe section with P_1 on the inlet face, P_2 on the outlet, \underline{v} = v_x\hat{e}_x.)

\sum_{\text{on fluid}}\underline{F} = \frac{d\underline{P}}{dt} + \iint_{CS}\rho(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\underline{v}\,dS\;\xrightarrow{@\,SS\text{ \& CS as opening \& exit}}\;\sum_{\text{on fluid}}\underline{F} = \text{Term 1} + \text{Term 2} = 0
If ΣF = 0, the pressures must be balanced w/ shear stress to give net force = 0: P_1A - P_2A - \tau(\text{surface area}) ↓ rearrange to give the τ & Δp relation.

Similar analysis (sketch: an inclined pipe) — redo ① analysis; now account for gravity as a force in the force balance.

FL4 lab guide — pump characteristic curves (7 November 2023)
Theory & background
The theory section repeats the recitation derivation in Week of 7th Nov: pumps and centrifugal pumps, ΔE = Q + W, the energy balance on a CV, the SS macro energy balance \Delta E_p + \Delta E_k + \Delta H = Q_{in,cv} - W_{s,by\,cv}, the mechanical energy balance \frac{\Delta p}{\rho} + \frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2\alpha} + g\Delta z + F = -\frac{W_{s,by}}{m}, pump efficiency \eta = \frac{-W_{s,by}/m - F}{-W_{s,by}/m}, brake horsepower bhp = -W_{s,by}, and the head form below.
\boxed{\left(\frac{P_d}{\rho g} + \frac{\langle v\rangle_d^2}{2g} + z_d\right) - \left(\frac{P_s}{\rho g} + \frac{\langle v\rangle_s^2}{2g} + z_s\right) = \eta\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{mg}\right)}\;;\qquad \underbrace{(H_d - H_s)}_{\text{head loss}} = \eta\left(-\frac{\text{bhp}}{mg}\right)

This form is useful when we know the efficiency of the pump already (since that takes into account friction losses).

(sketch: head loss (ft) vs. Q (capacity, related to ⟨v⟩!) — curves at fixed RPM; gives info about η & bhp.) Pumping ability of a CP: + shaft rotational speed (RPM); + shape of vanes; + flow path.
Carrying out the lab
Characterize relationships b/w discharge flow rate, net head, bhp, efficiency in a CP ↳ vary Q (via rotameter) ↳ measure pressure loss → calculate head loss (H_{loss} or H_{net} = H_d - H_s) ↳ non-dimensionalize variables & then plot them!
Lab calculations, discussions & variables
H_{net} = \text{head loss} = \frac{P_{out} - P_{in}}{\rho g} + \frac{\langle v\rangle_{out}^2 - \langle v\rangle_{in}^2}{2g\alpha} + \Delta z + \frac{F}{g}\;;\qquad F_{piping} = \sum_{j,\,\text{straight pipe}}\left[4f_j\frac{L_j}{D_j}\frac{\langle v\rangle_j^2}{2}\right] + \sum_{i,\,\text{fittings}}\left[n_iK_{f,i}\frac{\langle v\rangle_i^2}{2}\right]\;[9.358]
where f is the friction factor given for steady turbulent flow in smooth pipes [9.361].
Non-dimensional variables (n = rotational speed (on pump label); D = impeller diameter (handout)):
C_H = \frac{gH_{net}}{n^2D^2}\;;\qquad C_Q = \frac{Q}{nD^3}\;;\qquad C_P = \frac{\text{bhp}}{\rho n^3D^5}\;;\qquad \eta = \frac{C_HC_Q}{C_P}

Plot the characteristic pump curves (for water & CMC solution): C_H vs. C_Q; C_P vs. C_Q; η vs. C_Q. * Can use multiple graphs or one graph w/ a secondary axis ↓ be creative w/ your data graphs to allow readers to understand.
Discuss the trends! → Why are they like that? Does it make sense? How do these compare w/ a real pump curve (reference other sources)?
Error analysis! ↳ What is the error associated w/ all the variables H_{net}, C_H, C_P, C_Q, η? ↳ Are they high/low? ↳ Can they account for the deviations seen in the trends (if any?)? ↳ What are the sources of error in the experiment?

Good luck!

Gravity on an incline. (sketch: a slope at θ with g vertical; the angle between g and the slope normal is θ since 90 + (90 − θ) + x = 180 ⇒ x = θ; SOH CAH TOA, \sin\theta = \frac{\text{opp}}{g}.) With x along the slope and z normal to it:

Transcriber’s note: which component carries sin vs. cos depends on how θ and the axes are drawn; as written.
Q1 — film flowing down the outside of a vertical rod
(sketch: a vertical rod of radius R with a film flowing down its outside; z downward, r outward.) \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z); \underline{g} = (0, 0, g_z). Effect of gravity & pressure? Assumptions: + Newtonian fluid.
Mass: \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = 0. Stokes:
\mu\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) + \rho g_z = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) = -\frac{\rho g_z}{\mu}r \Rightarrow r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = -\frac{\rho g_z}{\mu}\frac{r^2}{2} + c_1 \Rightarrow v_z = -\frac{\rho g_z}{2\mu}\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\right) + c_1\ln r + c_2

Problem clarification (27 October 2023)
\boxed{\underline{F} = \iint(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\Big|_{@surface}dA}

\underline{F} = force on a surface of area given by dA [force on a surface (by the fluid flow) is positive]
\hat{n} = normal to surface
\underline{\underline{\Pi}} = total stress tensor, contains information about the stress at a point in a fluid

∴ (1) Bounds on the integral must define the area of the surface (not the fluid!). (2) The integral is evaluated @ the surface coordinates (i.e. the Jacobian will be at a specific coordinate).
E.g. force on wire. (sketch: a wire of radius κR along z inside a tube of radius R, pulled at V; normal \hat{e}_r on the wire surface.)
\underline{F} = \iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\big|_{@surface}dS; the surface is the entire wire/small cylinder, where 0 < \theta < 2\pi, 0 < z < L:
\therefore\;\underline{F} = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}\left[\hat{e}_r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}-p & 0 & \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ 0 & -p & 0 \\ \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} & 0 & -p\end{pmatrix}r\right]_{@r=\kappa R}d\theta\,dz = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}\begin{pmatrix}-p \\ 0 \\ \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\end{pmatrix}_{r\theta z}\Bigg|_{@r=\kappa R}\kappa R\,d\theta\,dz
= \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}\left(-p\hat{e}_r + \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\hat{e}_z\right)\Big|_{@r=\kappa R}\kappa R\,d\theta\,dz = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}(-p\hat{e}_r)\big|_{@r=\kappa R}\kappa R\,d\theta\,dz + \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}\mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\Big|_{@r=\kappa R}\hat{e}_z\,\kappa R\,d\theta\,dz
v_z = V\left[\frac{\ln(r/R)}{\ln(\kappa)}\right] → solved from previous parts; \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = \frac{V}{\ln\kappa}\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)\cdot\frac{1}{R} = \frac{V}{\ln\kappa}\frac{1}{r} ↳ @ r = κR → \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = \frac{V}{\ln\kappa}\left(\frac{1}{\kappa R}\right) \neq f(r, \theta, z).
\therefore\;(\kappa RL)\int_0^{2\pi}(-p\hat{e}_r)\big|_{@r=\kappa R}d\theta + L\int_0^{2\pi}\left(\frac{\mu V}{\ln\kappa}\cdot\frac{1}{\cancel{\kappa R}}\cdot\cancel{\kappa R}\right)\hat{e}_z\,d\theta
\hat{e}_r → unit vector but has some θ dependence ↳ express in θ units: \hat{e}_r = \cos\theta\,\hat{e}_x + \sin\theta\,\hat{e}_y:
= (\kappa RL)\int_0^{2\pi}-p_{\kappa R}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta \\ \sin\theta \\ 0\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}d\theta + \frac{\mu VL}{\ln\kappa}(2\pi)\hat{e}_z
\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta = 0 (entire term goes to zero!); \hat{e}_z independent of θ direction:
\boxed{\underline{F} = \frac{\mu VL}{\ln\kappa}(2\pi)\hat{e}_z = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ \frac{\mu VL}{\ln\kappa}(2\pi)\end{pmatrix}_{r\theta z}}\quad\to\text{always a vector!}
Physically: + longer the wire, larger the force required to yank it out; + faster the V, more force exerted on the wire surface } makes sense!
Transcriber’s note: since κ < 1, ln κ < 0, so this force on the wire points in −z (the fluid resists the wire’s motion).

Coursework/Transport_and_Separations/CHE.content:
Original handwritten notes (PDF p. 1-17) 
                  
                

Open these pages as a PDF



TA recitation notes for CHE 377, Fall 2023. Pages 1–17 cover a short note on drag coefficients (28 Aug), the week 3 divider, and four copies of the 9/5 recitation worksheet: the draft (pp. 3–5), the “master” (pp. 6–9), the copy annotated live in class (pp. 10–13) and the 9/7 repeat (pp. 14–17). The worksheet is transcribed once below, followed by the worked problems from the annotated copies.
Drag coefficient (28 August 2023)
(sketches: a flat disk of diameter D and thickness H edge-on to the flow — characteristic area H·D; the same disk face-on — characteristic area \pi\frac{D^2}{4}.)
If the disk was very small w/ a much larger H (i.e. a cylinder) ↓ then the characteristic area of circumference would make the most sense — characteristic area \pi D\cdot H. } Either way, providing a C_D w/ the reference area taken for calculation is the convention.
Recitation 09/05 — concept review (typed and handwritten)
Surface tension (typed)

Now we are dealing with interactions b/w two fluids at their interface (e.g. bubbles)
Phase boundary = “free surface” of the flow
Surface tension is a fluid property (like density and viscosity; denoted by σ) and is a result of unbalanced molecular forces at a surface
Force is tangent to the surface and normal to the boundary
The downward force on surface particles is not balanced by an upward force of fluid on the other side of the interface; the net effect is that the free surface behaves like a thin massless film under tension.

Reynolds transport theorem (typed)


Has different forms depending on the frame of reference we are in.


We could apply balance laws on each fluid element (box) → but have to deal with awkward shapes.


We can define a control volume — an arbitrary shape region that is fixed within the flow and sees fluid coming and going out. (figure: fluid elements deforming as they move through a channel, top view at t = 0, t_1, t_2.)


Extensive property: depends on the amount of matter in a sample, Ψ. Intensive property: independent of the size of sample, \psi = \frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial m} (m = mass).


Total material volume corresponding to a mass w/ the property ψ is written as \Psi = \iiint_{V(t)}\rho\,\psi\,dV (an arbitrary material volume).


Frames of reference: material volume vs. control volume. (sketches: a material blob followed along a path x_1 \to x_2 \to x_3, labelled D/Dt; a fixed control volume at position x with streamlines passing through it.)

Material volume: flux of a property across a material volume is 0 ↳ i.e. a volume whose boundaries are moving w/ time. Rate of change of a fluid property is given by \left[\frac{D}{Dt}\right].
Control volume: fixed x-position; there is a non-zero flux. Rate of change of a fluid property is given by \left[\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\right].

\boxed{\frac{D}{Dt}[FP] = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}[FP] + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla(FP)}\qquad(FP = \text{fluid property};\; \underline{v} = \text{velocity of fluid})
We know \Psi = \iiint_{V(t)}\rho\psi\,dV → this is w/ respect to the material frame of reference ↳ however, the volume is changing, so we cannot evaluate (as we don’t know the limits of integration) ↳ but we know we can go from the material to the control frame of reference via the green equation: \frac{D\Psi}{Dt} = \frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial t} + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla\Psi = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left[\iiint_{V_0}\cdots\right].
Material coordinates vs. control volume coordinates (master copy):
\frac{D\Psi}{Dt} = \int_{V_a(t)}\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}\rho\,dV + \int_{A_a(t)}\psi\rho\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n}\,dA_a\quad(\text{general form — can be applied to a particular fluid property such as mass, energy, momentum})
\text{Reynolds transport theorem (momentum balance on CV):}\quad \sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{f} = \frac{d\mathbf{P}}{dt} + \iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\rho\underline{v}\,dS\qquad(3.137)
(annotations: Σf = force; P = momentum; CS = control surface.)
Momentum balance

Momentum (p) = mass (m) · velocity (v): \underline{p} = m\underline{v}; mass = (density)·volume, m = \rho V → \underline{p} = (\rho V)\underline{v} (the m^3 term = m^2\cdot m → area · length).
Rate of momentum change: momentum per unit time. “Dividing” by time: \underline{p} = (\rho\cdot\text{Area}\cdot l)\underline{v} ≈ \frac{\underline{p}}{\Delta t} = \rho\cdot\text{Area}\cdot\frac{l}{\Delta t}\cdot\underline{v}, with \frac{l}{\Delta t} = v. That is why the momentum balance has two velocity terms!

(figure 5.2: fluid flow through a control volume — streamlines at time t crossing a surface element dA with normal n at angle θ to v.) We care about fluid velocity in the direction of the normal to the surface.
→ Volume of fluid passed through cross-section A (sketch: a slanted cylinder of base A, height unknown, with v at angle θ to \hat{n}): V_{cylinder} = A\cdot\text{Height}; height = \Delta x\cos\theta (SOH CAH TOA) ∴ V_{cylinder} = A\,\Delta x\cos\theta;
\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta t} = A\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\cos\theta = A\,v\cos\theta\;;\qquad \hat{n}\cdot\underline{v} = |\hat{n}||\underline{v}|\cos\theta = v\cos\theta
\text{Volumetric flow rate through A: }\;Q = v\cos\theta\,A = \boxed{(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})A}\;;\qquad \text{mass flow: }\;\dot{m} = \rho Q = \boxed{\rho(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})A}
\text{Momentum flow of liquid through A: }\;d\underline{p} = \dot{m}\underline{v} = \boxed{\rho(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})A\,\underline{v}}
↳ Now we choose an arbitrary area → taking a differential area & integrating the momentum quantity over the entire control surface:
\boxed{\text{Net momentum change from CV: }\;\iint_S\underline{v}\rho(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\,dA}\;\Rightarrow\;(\text{In} - \text{out}) = \text{change}\quad(\text{efflux; surface; area})
In − out (+gen − cons) = acc. (with gen, cons and acc. = 0 here).
Problems
Problem 3.14: a uniform flow \underline{v} = U\hat{e}_z of an incompressible fluid of density ρ passes through a volume that is in the shape of a half sphere of radius R. The outwardly pointing unit normal of the flat surface of the half sphere is \hat{n} = -\hat{e}_z. What is the mass flow rate through the hemispherical surface of this volume? Show that you can obtain the correct answer by integrating the formal expression for Q (Equation 3.87). (annotation: mass balance — accumulation = 0.)
Problem 3.15: what is the flow of momentum through the hemispherical surface described in Problem 14?
(sketch: uniform flow \underline{v} = U\hat{e}_z approaching a hemisphere; on the flat face \hat{n} = -\hat{e}_z, on the curved face \hat{n} = \hat{e}_r (spherical coordinates).)
\frac{d\underline{p}}{dt} = \iint_A\rho\underline{v}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\,dS = \rho\underline{v}\iint_A(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\,dS\quad(\text{\rho  constant, }\underline{v}\text{ uniform})
With \hat{n} = \hat{e}_r: (\hat{e}_r\cdot U\hat{e}_z) — unit basis conversion (representation of spherical in Cartesian):
\hat{e}_r = \sin\theta\cos\phi\,\hat{e}_x + \sin\theta\sin\phi\,\hat{e}_y + \cos\theta\,\hat{e}_z\;;\qquad \begin{pmatrix}\sin\theta\cos\phi \\ \sin\theta\sin\phi \\ \cos\theta\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ U\end{pmatrix}_{xyz} = U\cos\theta
\frac{d\underline{p}}{dt} = \rho\underline{v}\iint_AU\cos\theta\,dS\;;\qquad \text{Jacobian} \rightarrow R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi\;(\text{full sphere: }0 < r < \infty,\;0 < \phi < 2\pi,\;0 < \theta < \pi)
\frac{\Delta\underline{p}}{\Delta t} = \rho U\hat{e}_z\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}U\cos\theta(R^2\sin\theta)\,d\theta\,d\phi\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\text{change in }\underline{p} = \int d\phi\int\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta}\;\rightarrow\;\text{solve for HW}\;(u\text{-sub / int. by parts})
(hemisphere limits 0 < \theta < \frac{\pi}{2}, 0 < \phi < 2\pi.)
Problem 3.21: the y-component of a velocity field in flow through a slit (Cartesian coordinates) is given here. What is the average value of the velocity? 2H is the gap between the plates. At what location is the velocity a maximum? The units on velocity and A are m/s and the units of x and H are m.
\underline{v} = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ v_y(x) \\ 0\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}\;;\qquad v_y(x) = A\left(1 - \frac{(x - H)^2}{H^2}\right)
(sketch: flow in y between plates at x = 0 and x = 2H, parabolic profile with its maximum at x = H; v_y(0) = v_y(2H) = 0; v depends only on x, flow only in the y direction.)
\text{Average of }f(z) = \langle f\rangle = \frac{\int_{z_{min}}^{z_{max}}f(z)\,dz}{(z_{max} - z_{min})}\;(3.41)\;\left(\frac{\text{total}}{\#}\right)\;;\qquad \langle v_y\rangle = \frac{\int_0^{2H}v_y(x)\,dx}{2H - 0} = \frac{A}{2H}\int_0^{2H}\left(1 - \frac{(x - H)^2}{H^2}\right)dx \Rightarrow \boxed{\langle v_y\rangle = \frac{2}{3}A}
Maximum velocity: \frac{dv_y}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}\left[A\left(1 - \frac{(x - H)^2}{H^2}\right)\right] = 0 (where the max is) ⇒ \boxed{x = H}, \boxed{v_y(x = H) = A}.
Problem 3.31: for the Cartesian coordinate system shown in Figure 3.38, what is a unit vector in the direction of gravity? What is the component of gravity in the flow direction? (figure 3.38: water flowing down an incline at angle δ from the vertical, z along the flow, y normal to the plate; air above.)
(working: \underline{f} = m\underline{g}; gravity drawn vertically down with the z axis at angle δ to it and y at 90° − δ; \underline{g} = (\ \cdot\ ,\ \cdot\ ,\ \cdot\ )_{xyz} — the z entry is the component in the flow direction; SOH CAH TOA.) (The unit vector is left for the students; it is \hat{g} = -\sin\delta\,\hat{e}_y + \cos\delta\,\hat{e}_z [?] from the sketch, so the flow-direction component is g\cos\delta.)

At a point P the stress has normal and shear parts } collected in the tensor:

\underline{\underline{\Pi}} = \begin{pmatrix}\tau_{xx} & \tau_{xy} & \tau_{xz} \\ \tau_{yx} & \tau_{yy} & \tau_{yz} \\ \tau_{zx} & \tau_{zy} & \tau_{zz}\end{pmatrix}\quad(\text{diagonal: normal stress})

p_a = \rho_Agh_2 + \rho_Cgh_1 + p_1\;;\qquad p_b = \rho_Bgh_3 + \rho_Dg(h_1 + h_2 - h_3) + p_2

Pre-lab assignment
→ How can we go from measurable quantities to determine μ?
F_D = 3\pi\mu Dv. (sketch: a sphere with F_B and F_D up, F_g down, z upward.) At terminal velocity, ΔF = 0:
F_B + F_D = F_g\;;\qquad F_g = mg = (\rho_{ball}V)g\;;\qquad F_B = \rho_{liq}Vg = m_{liq}g

F_B: Archimedes — upward force related to the volume of water displaced (equal to the volume of the submerged object).
F_D: Stokes’ law.

→ Write viscosity as a function of \rho_{liq} & \rho_{ball}?
[(\rho_lV)g] + [3\pi\mu Dv] = (\rho_{ball}V)g\;\Rightarrow\;\mu = \frac{(\rho_lVg - \rho_{ball}Vg)}{3\pi Dv}\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\mu = \frac{(\rho_l - \rho_s)Vg}{3\pi Dv}}
(annotations: \rho_l given, \rho_{ball} from measured mass and volume (\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3), D measured, v measured/varied.)

Interesting analysis: μ varying w/ v; μ varying w/ D; v varying w/ D.

TA recitation worksheet for CHE 377, week of 25 September 2023.
Viscosity and stress
\text{Viscosity }(\mu) = \frac{\text{shear stress}}{\text{rate of shear strain}} \sim \text{rate of deformation}
Shear stress: + accounts for intermolecular forces during fluid motion; + requires magnitude, direction & orientation.
(figure 7.7: shear strain in the xy plane — a square element at t deforming into a parallelogram at t + Δt.) Deformation occurring in two directions due to fluid flow:
-\frac{d\delta_{xy}}{dt} = \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial x}\;(\text{deformation})\;;\qquad \text{shear stress} = (\text{viscosity})(\text{rate of shear strain}) = \mu\left(-\frac{d\delta}{dt}\right)\;\left(\frac{dv}{dy}\text{ or }\dot{\gamma}\right)
(figure: the stress vectors a, b, c on three faces of an element around a point P.) Similar analysis on each plane (xy, yz, xz) } for stress at a point P in fluid motion, + normal stresses → gives 9 elements to describe all forces at a point in a fluid (moving or stationary).
\boxed{\tau_{xy} = \tau_{yx} = \mu\left(\frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial x}\right)\;;\quad \tau_{yz} = \tau_{zy} = \mu\left(\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial y}\right)\;;\quad \tau_{zx} = \tau_{xz} = \mu\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial z}\right)}\quad\text{laminar flow \checkmark }
\tau_{ij} = \tau_{ji} } always true (angular momentum conservation).
Normal stress: \sigma = \tau_{ii} (based on Hooke’s law):
\boxed{\sigma_{xx} = \mu\left(2\frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} - \frac{2}{3}(\nabla\cdot\underline{v})\right) - p\;;\quad \sigma_{yy} = \mu\left(2\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y} - \frac{2}{3}(\nabla\cdot\underline{v})\right) - p\;;\quad \sigma_{zz} = \mu\left(2\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} - \frac{2}{3}(\nabla\cdot\underline{v})\right) - p}\quad\text{Newtonian fluid}
Fluid stress:

Isotropic [same magnitude of stress exerted on any surface & stress acts ~ normal stress] → independent of surface orientation & always normal to any surface: \underline{\underline{\Pi}} = -p\underline{\underline{I}}.
Anisotropic (shear stress → different values of stress on different surfaces) } \underline{\underline{\tau}} → symmetric; 6 components.

\boxed{\underline{\underline{\Pi}} = \underline{\underline{\tau}} - p\underline{\underline{I}}}
(figure 4.52 “Tension stress tensor in flow”: molecular contact stress; symmetric, i.e. \tilde{\Pi}_{ik} = \tilde{\Pi}_{ki}, \tilde{\tau}_{pm} = \tilde{\tau}_{mp}; \tilde{\Pi}_{jn} is stress on a j-surface in the n-direction; infinitesimal surface \underline{f} = \Delta A\,\hat{n}\cdot\tilde{\Pi}; finite surface \underline{f} = \iint_S[\hat{n}\cdot\tilde{\Pi}]\,dS; \tilde{\Pi} = \tilde{\tau} - pI, i.e. the diagonal entries are \tilde{\tau}_{ii} - p. “The stress tensor in matrix form can be used to calculate the tension on a surface in a flow.“)
Manometer review
Pascal’s principle: pressure exerted on a confined liquid is transmitted equally to every part of the liquid & to the walls of the container } idea of incompressibility ↓ applicable to confined fluids at rest.
Manometer → device to accurately measure pressure differences.
\text{Momentum balance (RTT)} \rightarrow \frac{dp}{dz} = -\rho g \rightarrow \boxed{p(z) = -\rho gz + p_0}
Pressure in a stationary fluid at elevation z (upward), i.e. only dependent on the vertical height! (Not shape.) Pressures at the same elevation (of the same fluid) are equal.
Problems
Problem 4.16: a manometer is configured as shown in Figure 4.67. A heavy fluid (Fluid B) has been placed in the bottom of the manometer. A light fluid (Fluid A) has been added to the left side only. The left side of the manometer has been connected to a process stream in which water (25 °C, Fluid C) is flowing, while the right side of the manometer is open to the atmosphere (Fluid D). (figure 4.67: a U-tube with fluid C above fluid A on the left, B in the bend and D (air) on the right.)
Problem 5.35: we solved the incline problem using a coordinate system that sits on the solid surface (Figure 5.12). Here, choose instead to solve the same problem with a coordinate system in which the coordinate position x = 0 is located at the free surface (i.e., the top of the film) (Figure 5.42). What is the gravity acceleration vector in this coordinate system? What are the flow boundary conditions? Are there any advantages or disadvantages to this choice of coordinate system? Discuss your observations.

Annotations on the balances

The continuity equation is the mass balance; the Cauchy equation is the momentum balance, which becomes Navier–Stokes for an incompressible Newtonian fluid.

Problem 6.43 / 6.49 worked in class
Assumptions marked on the figure: (1) coordinates — cylindrical, θ from 0 to 2π; (2) \underline{v} = f(z) only through v_z = f(r); \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z(r)), \underline{g} = (g_r, g_\theta, 0); v_r = v_\theta = 0; \frac{\partial}{\partial\theta} = 0.
Navier–Stokes, struck out term by term (red zeros on the pasted equations):

r-direction → \boxed{\frac{\partial P}{\partial r} = 0} (with \rho g_r)
θ-direction → \boxed{\frac{\partial P}{\partial\theta} = 0} (with \rho g_\theta)
z-direction (continuity gives \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = 0, so \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(0) = 0): 0 = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} + \mu\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)

For 6.49, P = P(z): \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} \approx \frac{\Delta P}{\Delta z} = \boxed{\frac{\Delta P}{L}}, with P(z_0) = P_0, P(z_L) = P_L: \frac{P_L - P_0}{(z_L - z_0)} = \frac{\Delta P}{L}.
For 6.43 (no pressure variation):
0 = \mu\left[\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)\right] \Rightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) = 0 \Rightarrow r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = c_1 \Rightarrow \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = \frac{c_1}{r} \Rightarrow \boxed{v_z = c_1\ln r + c_2}
BCs (2 eqs, 2 unknowns → c₁ & c₂):

@ r = κR, v_z = V: \boxed{V = c_1\ln\kappa R + c_2}
@ r = R, v_z = 0: \boxed{0 = c_1\ln R + c_2}

Subtracting: V = c_1(\ln\kappa R - \ln R) ⇒ c_1 = \frac{V}{(\ln\kappa R - \ln R)} = \frac{V}{\ln\kappa}, since (\ln\kappa R - \ln R) = \ln\frac{\kappa R}{R}.
Transcriber’s note: the denominator is written “ln κR − R” in one place; it is \ln\kappa R - \ln R = \ln\kappa.
Flow rate: Q = \iint_S\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v}\,dS = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_{\kappa R}^Rv_z\,r\,dr\,d\theta → \int x\ln x\,dx by parts.
Force on the wall/wire: (sketch: the wire at r = κR moving to the right.) \underline{F} = \iint(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\,dS at r = \kappa R with \underline{\underline{\Pi}} = -p\underline{\underline{I}} + \underline{\underline{\tau}}; in the pasted τ matrix only \tau_{rz} = \tau_{zr} = \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} survives (since v_z = f(r), v_\theta = v_r = 0), so \hat{e}_r\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}} gives a vector (\,\cdot\,)_{r\theta z} and F_r = \iint\cdots dr\,d\theta.
Problem 6.52 annotations: Navier ✗, Cauchy ✓ — for the power-law fluid start from the Cauchy equation with \underline{\underline{\tau}} = \eta(\dot{\gamma})\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}}.

TA recitation notes for CHE 377, week of 23 October 2023.
Macro control-volume balance vs. microscopic balance
“Macro” control volume balance:
0 = \frac{dm}{dt} + \iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\rho\,dS\;;\qquad \sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{f} = \frac{d(m\underline{v})_{CV}}{dt} + \iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\rho\underline{v}\,dS
Macro → micro: arbitrary CV; express terms as integrals; Leibniz rule & divergence theorem.
Microscopic balance (ρ = density; v = velocity; p = pressure; g = gravity):
\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla\rho = -\rho(\nabla\cdot\underline{v})\;;\qquad \rho\left(\frac{\partial\underline{v}}{\partial t} + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla\underline{v}\right) = -\nabla p + \nabla\cdot\underline{\underline{\tau}} + \rho\underline{g}

Macro: choosing a CV (can be arbitrary) ↓ writing out equations specific to that CV ↳ have to rewrite & recalculate if the CV is changed.
Micro: already written for an arbitrary, microscopic CV ↳ applicable to any problem ✓ ↳ just need to change boundary conditions & get velocity & pressure profiles!

Problems 6.43 and 6.49 — axial annular drag, wire coating
Problem 6.43: an incompressible Newtonian fluid fills the annular gap between a cylindrical wire of radius κR and an outer shell of inner radius R (Figure 6.22). The wire is pulled to the right at speed V. There is no pressure variation throughout the apparatus. Calculate the steady state velocity profile, the flow rate, and the force on the wire. This geometry occurs in wire-coating. (The printed answer is scribbled out.)
Problem 6.49: repeat Problem 43 with an imposed pressure gradient −Δp/L in the flow direction. Calculate the velocity field only.
(figure: the wire drawn through the bath, entrance and exit at P_o, cross-section with the annular velocity profile. Annotations: flow in z ✓; gradient in r ✓; symmetric around θ ✓. The Navier–Stokes equations in cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z components) are pasted beside the problem.)
6.43: no pressure variation; \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z)_{r\theta z}; \underline{g} = (g_r, g_\theta, 0)_{r\theta z}. (sketch: the annulus between κR and R.)
Mass balance / continuity equation (SS, incompressible):
\cancel{\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}} + \cancel{\underline{v}\cdot\nabla\rho} = -\rho(\nabla\cdot\underline{v}) \Rightarrow (\nabla\cdot\underline{v}) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial(r\cancel{v_r})}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial\cancel{v_\theta}}{\partial\theta} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = 0 \Rightarrow \boxed{\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = 0}
Start w/ Navier–Stokes:

r-direction: 0 = \rho g_r
θ-direction: 0 = \rho g_\theta
z-direction: \rho\left(v_z\cancel{\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z}}\right) = \mu\left[\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) + \cancel{\frac{\partial^2v_z}{\partial z^2}}\right] ⇒ \mu\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left[r\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right] = 0 } solve for the velocity profile

Boundary conditions (always have to be about the variable you need to solve in the PDE! — its value or its derivative’s value): @ r = \kappa R, v_z = V; @ r = R, v_z = 0.
Flow rate: (sketch: \underline{v} = v_z\hat{e}_z through a disk with normal \hat{e}_z.)
Q = \iint_S\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v}\,dS = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_{\kappa R}^Rv_z\,r\,dr\,d\theta
↳ \int x\ln x\,dx — integration by parts: \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du (from \int d(uv) = \int v\,du + \int u\,dv); choose u = \ln x (easier to calculate the derivative of!), du = \frac{1}{x}dx; dv = x\,dx, v = \frac{x^2}{2}:
\int x\ln x\,dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\ln x - \int\frac{x}{2}\,dx
Force on wall?
\underline{F} = \iint(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\Big|_{r=\kappa R}dS\;;\qquad \underline{\underline{\Pi}} = -p\underline{\underline{I}} + \underline{\underline{\tau}}\;;\qquad \hat{n} = \hat{e}_r
(the Newtonian τ in cylindrical coordinates is pasted beside it.)
\underline{F} = \iint\hat{e}_r\cdot\begin{pmatrix}-p & 0 & \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ 0 & -p & 0 \\ \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} & 0 & -p\end{pmatrix}_{r\theta z}(r)\,dr\,d\theta\quad(r = \kappa R\text{ constant})
Transcriber’s note: on the surface r = κR the area element is \kappa R\,d\theta\,dz, not r\,dr\,d\theta; as written.
(6.49) Pressure variation (heading only).
Problems 6.44 and 6.52 — upward pressure-driven pipe flow
Problem 6.44: calculate the velocity profile and flow rate for pressure-driven flow of an incompressible, Newtonian liquid in a vertical pipe of radius R. The pressure at the bottom entrance to the tube is P_0; at a point a distance L upward the pressure is P_L. Assume that the flow is well developed and at steady state. Do not neglect gravity. (HW problem.)
Problem 6.52: repeat problem 6.44 with a power-law, generalized Newtonian fluid with parameters m and n.
(sketch: a vertical pipe with z upward; \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z); \underline{g} = (0, 0, g_z).)
Power law: non-Newtonian behavior. Start from the Cauchy balance:
\rho\left(\frac{\partial\underline{v}}{\partial t} + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla\underline{v}\right) = -\nabla p + \nabla\cdot\underline{\underline{\tau}} + \rho\underline{g}\;;\qquad \underline{\underline{\tau}} = \eta(\dot{\gamma})\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}} = \eta(\dot{\gamma})[\nabla\underline{v} + (\nabla\underline{v})^T]
where \dot{\gamma} = |\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}}| = +\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}(\text{sum of squares of each term})}, and \eta(\dot{\gamma}) = m\dot{\gamma}^{n-1} } power law.
\therefore\;\underline{\underline{\tau}} = m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\tau_{rr} & \tau_{r\theta} & \tau_{rz} \\ \tau_{\theta r} & \tau_{\theta\theta} & \tau_{\theta z} \\ \tau_{zr} & \tau_{z\theta} & \tau_{zz}\end{pmatrix}\quad(\text{only }\tau_{rz}, \tau_{zr}\text{ survive})
Momentum equation: the left side is (0, 0, 0)_{r\theta z}; \nabla p = \left(\frac{\partial p}{\partial r}, \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial p}{\partial\theta}, \frac{\partial p}{\partial z}\right); and (using the divergence of a tensor in cylindrical coordinates, with most terms struck out)
\nabla\cdot\underline{\underline{\tau}} = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial\tau_{zr}}{\partial z} \\ 0 \\ \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(r\tau_{rz})\end{pmatrix}
\tau_{rz} = \tau_{zr} = m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) = \frac{(-1)}{(-1)}m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) = \frac{m}{(-1)}\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^1\;\Rightarrow\;\boxed{\tau_{zr} = -m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^n}

The copy of the week of 27 November 2023 recitation annotated in class. The shared derivations (macroscopic mass, momentum and energy balances and the problem statements) are not repeated; the in-class work is below.
Annotations on the balances: large-scale info is the practical side; flow profiles come from Navier–Stokes as \underline{v}(r, \theta, z). (\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v}) = |\hat{n}||\underline{v}|\cos\theta — θ = 0 at an outlet (cos = 1) and θ = 180° at an inlet (cos θ < 0). \langle v\rangle^2 \neq \langle v^2\rangle, since \langle v\rangle^2 = \left(\frac{\iint v\,dS}{\iint dS}\right)^2 while \langle v^2\rangle = \frac{\iint v^2\,dS}{\iint dS}. Inlet/outlet forces: \underline{f} = (\text{pressure})\cdot A, i.e. \underline{f}_{in} = -P_1A_1, \underline{f}_{out} = P_2A_2. α ≈ 0.98 [?]. Dividing the MEB by g gives every term as a head [=] length (H_d, h_f, h_p, …), with F \to 4f\frac{L}{D}\frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2} [?] and the “closed form” f = \frac{A}{\sqrt{f}} [?].
Problem 1.21 — Venturi meter (α = β = 1; 0 to 200 gpm)
(sketch: the control volume between ① (area A₁, pressure P₁, inlet normal \hat{n}_1) and ② (A₂, P₂, outlet normal \hat{n}_2).)
① Velocity relationship — mass balance:
\cancel{\frac{dm}{dt}} + \rho_1A_1\cos\theta_1\langle v_1\rangle + \rho_2A_2\cos\theta_2\langle v_2\rangle = 0 \Rightarrow \rho_1A_1(-1)\langle v_1\rangle + \rho_2A_2(1)\langle v_2\rangle = 0
\rho_1A_1\langle v_1\rangle = \rho_2A_2\langle v_2\rangle \Rightarrow \boxed{Q_1 = Q_2}\;(\rho_1 = \rho_2) \Rightarrow \frac{\pi D_1^2}{4}\langle v_1\rangle = \frac{\pi D_2^2}{4}\langle v_2\rangle \Rightarrow \langle v_1\rangle = \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^2\langle v_2\rangle
② Pressure drop (MEB) — no Δz, no friction, no shaft work, α = 1:
\frac{\Delta p}{\rho} + \frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2} = 0\;(\text{out} - \text{in}) \Rightarrow \frac{P_2 - P_1}{\rho} = -\frac{(\langle v_2\rangle^2 - \langle v_1\rangle^2)}{2} \Rightarrow \frac{P_1 - P_2}{\rho} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\langle v_2\rangle^2 - \left[\left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^2\langle v_2\rangle\right]^2\right)
\boxed{-\Delta p = \frac{\rho\langle v_2\rangle^2}{2}\left(1 - \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^4\right)}\;;\qquad \text{pressure drop} = -\Delta p = -(P_2 - P_1)\;(\text{"neg."})\;;\quad \langle v_2\rangle = \frac{Q}{A_2}
Transcriber’s note: the last line is written v_2 = Q/A_1; at the throat it is Q/A_2.
Problem 1.23 — siphon
(figure annotations: ① at the liquid surface where h = 0 and v ≈ 0; the hose entry 1.5 ft down; ② at the hose exit, level with the bottom of the 4.0 ft stand, with P_1 = P_2 (both atmospheric); the liquid height is h(t) while draining; the pressure inside the tank is P = \rho gh.)
① Exit velocity — mechanical energy balance, no shaft work, no friction, α = 1 (turbulent):
\frac{\cancel{(P_2 - P_1)}}{\rho} + \frac{v_2^2 - \cancel{v_1^2}}{2} + g(z_2 - z_1) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{v_2^2}{2} = -g(z_2 - z_1) \Rightarrow \boxed{v_2 = \sqrt{2g(z_1 - z_2)}}\;(z_1 - z_2 = 5.5\text{ ft})
② Max height: find the height @ P = P_{vap} (sketch: the siphon from ① over the top point ⓐ, where P_a = P_{vap}, down to ②):
\frac{P_2 - P_a}{\rho} + \frac{\cancel{v_2^2 - v_a^2}}{2\alpha} + g(+h) = 0\;;\qquad P_{vap} = 12.3\text{ psia},\;P_{atm} = 14.69\text{ psia}
↓ solve for h. (The numeric value is not written out.) Figure 1.16 is annotated with the flow direction in the working siphon and the vapor bubble forming at the top.

Additions on the 27 November copy

Macro vs. micro: the dot product \underline{a}\cdot\underline{b} = |\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\cos\theta turns (\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v}) into v(\hat{n}\cdot\hat{e}_v) = v\cos\theta; from Q and the ID you get ⟨v⟩ at each port.
F = \frac{dP}{dt} = \frac{d(mv)}{dt}; \langle v^2\rangle = \frac{\iint v^2\,dS}{A_i}; β = 1 (turbulent), β = 0.75 (laminar).
Inlet/outlet pressure forces: \underline{f}_{in} = -P_1A_1\hat{n}_{A_1}, \underline{f}_{out} = -P_2A_2\hat{n}_{A_2}.
On the Venturi sketch, −Δp increases as the flow accelerates from v_1, D_1 into the throat v_2, D_2; the mass balance gives the velocity relationship.

Week of 5 December
Problem 3.42: an incompressible fluid enters a converging bend flowing at a steady flow rate of Q gpm (Figure 3.42). The bend makes a 20° turn and has a circular cross-section all along its length. At the inlet to the bend the radius of the conduit is R₁ and at the exit the radius is a smaller value, R₂. What is the average velocity of the fluid entering the conduit in terms of these variables? What is the average velocity of the fluid exiting the conduit?
Recipe: (1) draw diagram; (2) set up the info (w/ the coordinates); (3) knowns, unknowns → how can you solve?
(sketch: the bend from inlet area A₁ (normal −x) with flow Q along x, turning 20° up to the outlet A₂ with velocity v_2.)
Q_1 = Q_2 ✓; Q ✓, R ✓ → area:
\langle v_1\rangle = \frac{Q}{A_1} = \frac{Q}{\pi R_1^2}\;;\qquad \langle v_2\rangle = \frac{Q}{\pi R_2^2}
For the momentum terms \rho\cos\theta\langle v\rangle^2\hat{e}_v: \hat{e}_{v_1} = \begin{pmatrix}-1 \\ 0\end{pmatrix}_{xy} [?]; \hat{e}_{v_2} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta \\ \sin\theta\end{pmatrix}_{xy} (sketch: v_2 resolved at 20° — cos along x, sin along y; SOH CAH TOA).
Transcriber’s note: the inlet velocity points along +x; the (−1, 0) vector is the inlet’s outward normal. As written.
Problem 6.41 — combined backward pressure and forward drag of a Newtonian fluid in a slit. Calculate the velocity profile for the flow shown in Figure 6.21. The flow is steady flow of an incompressible, Newtonian fluid between two wide plates. The flow is driven forward by the motion of the top plate (the top plate moves in the x-direction at speed V), and the flow is opposed by the pressure, which is slightly higher at the exit, P_L, than at the entrance, P₀; P_L > P₀. You may neglect the effect of gravity. Use the coordinate system given in Figure 6.21. (figure 6.21: plates of length L, width W, gap H; top plate moving at V; entrance P_0, exit P_L. Annotations: dt → 0, P, Navier ✓.)
① Mass balance (Cartesian x, y): \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} + \cancel{\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y}} + \cancel{\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z}} = 0; \underline{v} = (v_x(y), 0, 0), v_y = v_z = 0 ⇒ \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} = 0 (developed flow) ✓. (sketch: v_x rising from 0 at the bottom plate to V at the top.) (The continuity equations in rectangular, cylindrical and spherical coordinates are pasted beside it, with the Cartesian Navier–Stokes equations.)
② Navier–Stokes:

x: 0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} + \mu\frac{\partial^2v_x}{\partial y^2}
y: 0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y}; z: 0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial z} } P is not changing w/ y & z, P \neq f(y, z)

\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \mu\frac{\partial^2v_x}{\partial y^2} = \lambda\quad(\text{p has no y dependence; }v_x\text{ has no x dependence}) \Rightarrow \frac{\partial p}{\partial x} = \lambda\;;\qquad \frac{\partial^2v_x}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}
BCs: @ y = 0, v_x = 0; @ y = h, v_x = V; @ x = 0, P = P₀; @ x = L, P = P_L.
1st order (pressure): \frac{dP}{dx} = \lambda ⇒ P = \lambda x + C; @ x = 0, C = P_0 ⇒ P = \lambda x + P_0; @ x = L, P_L = \lambda L + P_0 ⇒ \boxed{\lambda = \frac{P_L - P_0}{L}}.
2nd order (velocity): \frac{\partial^2v_x}{\partial y^2} = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} ⇒ (integrate 1) \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y} = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}y + c_1 ⇒ (integrate 2) v_x = \frac{\lambda}{2\mu}y^2 + c_1y + c_2; @ y = 0, v_x = 0 → c_2 = 0; @ y = h, v_x = V → V = \frac{\lambda}{2\mu}h^2 + c_1h → c_1 = \left(V - \frac{\lambda h^2}{2\mu}\right)\frac{1}{h} = \left(\frac{V}{h} - \frac{\lambda h}{2\mu}\right):
\boxed{v_x = \frac{\lambda}{2\mu}y^2 + \left(\frac{V}{h} - \frac{\lambda h}{2\mu}\right)y}\quad\rightarrow\;\text{input }\lambda
Maximum velocity? @ max v, \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial y} = 0:
\frac{\lambda}{\mu}y + \left(\frac{V}{h} - \frac{\lambda h}{2\mu}\right) = 0 \Rightarrow y = \left(\frac{\lambda h}{2\mu} - \frac{V}{h}\right)\cdot\frac{\mu}{\lambda} \Rightarrow \boxed{y = \frac{h}{2} - \frac{V\mu}{\lambda h}} \neq h
(sketch: the velocity profile between the plates — the drag-driven linear part plus the backward pressure-driven parabola, with P_0 on the left and P_L on the right.)
Transcriber’s note: the boxed y_{max} is written with “Vμ/λh” partly circled; it follows from the line above.
Problem 9.19: what is the direction and magnitude of the force needed to support the 90° expanding pipe bend shown in Figure 9.47? The water flow is steady and turbulent, and the cross-section of the inlet of the pipe bend is \pi R_1^2 and the cross-section of the outlet of the bend is \pi R_2^2, where R₂ > R₁. Evaluate your answer for R₁ = 0.545 in and R₂ = 0.834 in and various values of flow parameters.
(sketch: flow Q entering downward at ⟨v₁⟩ through radius R₁, turning 90° to exit horizontally at ⟨v₂⟩ through area A₂; x to the right, y up.)
(1) Macro; (2) force → momentum; velocity → mass (Q_1 = Q_2 → ⟨v₂⟩, A ✓).
\cancel{\frac{d\underline{P}}{dt}} + \frac{\rho_1A_1\cos\theta\langle v_1\rangle^2}{\beta}\hat{e}_{v_1} + \frac{\rho_2A_2\cos\theta\langle v_2\rangle^2}{\beta}\hat{e}_{v_2} = \sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{f} = \underline{f}_{in} + \underline{f}_{out} + \underline{f}_g + \underline{f}_w
with \underline{f}_g = (0, -M_{cv}g, 0)_{xyz} [?]; \underline{f} = \iint_S(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})_{@surface}dS, \underline{\underline{\Pi}} = -p\underline{\underline{I}} + \cancel{\underline{\underline{\tau}}}, so \underline{f}_{in} = -P_1A_1\hat{n}_1 and \underline{f}_{out} = -P_2A_2\hat{n}_2; the support force is \underline{f}_w (with its reaction on the bend).

TA recitation notes for CHE 377, “week of 27th Nov.” (page dated 14 November 2023).
Shift in perspective: flow profiles (microscopic look) to large-scale info → total force on wall; → overall flow rate; → total work performed by a pump/turbine/mixer.
Macroscopic mass balance
\text{Mass balance on a CV:}\quad\frac{dm_{cv}}{dt} + \iint_{CS}\rho(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\,dS = 0
→ Multiple inlets & outlets; → constant density: \sum\rho_i\iint_{A_i}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\,dS, with \underline{v} = v\hat{e}_v (magnitude; “velocity” direction or unit vector [constant @ each inlet/outlet]):
\sum\rho_i\iint_{A_i}v\cos\theta\,dS = \sum\rho_i\cos\theta\iint_{A_i}v\,dS\;;\qquad \langle v\rangle = \frac{\iint_{A_i}v\,dS}{\iint_{A_i}dS} = \frac{1}{A_i}\iint_{A_i}v\,dS\;\therefore\;\iint_{A_i}v\,dS = \langle v\rangle A_i
\boxed{\frac{dm_{cv}}{dt} + \sum_{i=1}^{\#\text{streams}}\left[\rho A\cos\theta\langle v\rangle\right] = 0}
\theta_i = angle b/w \hat{n}_i & \hat{v}_i (will carry the negative sign depending on inlet & outlet).
Macroscopic momentum balance
\frac{d\underline{P}}{dt} + \iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\rho\underline{v}\,dS = \sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{f}\;;\qquad \sum\rho_i\cos\theta\,\hat{v}\iint v^2\,dS = \sum_{i=1}^{\#\text{streams}}\rho A\cos\theta\langle v^2\rangle\hat{v}\;(\text{somewhat hard to compute})
\beta = \frac{\langle v\rangle^2}{\langle v^2\rangle}; β = 1 (turbulent); β = 0.75 (laminar).
\boxed{\frac{d\underline{P}}{dt} + \sum_{i=1}^{\#}\left[\frac{\rho A\cos\theta\langle v\rangle^2}{\beta}\hat{v}\right] = \sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{f}}\quad(\hat{v} = \text{unit vector!})
\sum\underline{f} = \underline{f}_g + \underline{f}_{inlet} + \underline{f}_{outlet} + \underline{f}_{walls}, with \underline{f}_g = m\underline{g} and the inlet/outlet forces \iint[\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}}]\,dS = \iint\hat{n}\cdot[-p\underline{\underline{I}} + \underline{\underline{\tau}}]\,dS = \underbrace{\iint-p\hat{n}\,dS}_{\text{pressure dominates!}} + \cancel{\iint\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\tau}}\,dS} (viscous terms accounted for in \underline{f}_{wall}!).
Macroscopic energy balance
\frac{dE}{dt} + \iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\rho\hat{E}\,dS = Q_{in} - W_{by}\;;\qquad \alpha = \frac{\langle v\rangle^2}{\langle v^3\rangle}\;;\;\alpha \approx 1\;(\text{turbulent})
→ open sys.; → E = E_K + E_P + U; → constant velocity across inlet/outlet; → \hat{H} = \hat{U} + P\hat{V}; → flow work/shaft work; → no phase change; → SS, single input/single output; → ΔT ≈ 0, no reaction:
\boxed{\frac{\Delta p}{\rho} + \frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2\alpha} + g\Delta z + F = -\frac{W_{s,by}}{m}}
Problems
Problem 1.21: a Venturi meter with a 1.00 in diameter throat is to be installed into a 2 in line (Schedule 40 piping, smooth) with water flowing at 25 °C. If the flow is turbulent, and the range of expected flow rates is 0–200 gpm, what is the expected range of pressure drop in the Venturi meter? You may neglect friction.
(figure: flow is directed through a gently tapering tube; pressure is measured before the contraction (1) and at the throat (2); the relationship between the measured pressures and the fluid velocity may be deduced from the MEB with the macroscopic mass balance.) 2″ Schedule 40 pipe: ID = 2.067″ (pg. 772 [Ex. 9.5]).

Velocity relationships (v_1 vs. v_2)?

Problem 1.23: a gasoline tank is connected to a 25 ft hose (ID = 1.50 cm) as shown in Figure 1.49. The ambient temperature is 38 °C. What is the maximum height of the barrier over which the gasoline may be siphoned? You may neglect frictional losses. Note the following physical property data: density of gasoline = 5.6 lb_m/gal, vapor pressure at 38 °C is 12.3 psia.
(figure: the tank on a 4.0 ft stand with 1.5 ft of liquid, the hose over a barrier of height h into a can below; redrawn with the liquid surface 1.5 ft above the hose entry, 5.5 ft total drop and exit velocity v_2.)

What is the exit velocity?
Max height: fluid will stop flowing when suction breaks (i.e. gas/air is introduced somehow) ↳ this can happen when the pressure equals vapor pressure (to “boil” the liquid).

Siphon flow: you treat the fluid as a continuum (no breaks) (free to choose the pressure that is the most convenient) ↓ as the liquid level is falling (the pressure @ bottom will be changing) ↳ hard to use that. (figure 1.16: formation of a vapor gap in a siphon with increasing height — p > p_v^* functions normally; p = p_v^* fluid boils; p \leq p_v^* fluid breaks, siphon fails.)
Problem 1.24: a water tank is connected to a 100 ft hose (ID = 1.50 cm) as shown in the top of Figure 1.50. The height h is 1.8 m. Calculate the average velocity of water in the hose. Do not neglect friction; you may assume turbulent flow. (figure 1.50: tank (1) with liquid h above the hose outlet (2); below, the same with the hose rising over a hump of height H.)

Turbulent flow drawn as eddies in a pipe (sketch: v_z in, swirling green eddies inside, v_z out); “time dependent and 3D” ⇒ the governing equations stay PDEs.
Pressure drop (F_{drag}) vs. flow-rate (Q) relationships are what the empirical correlations supply. (sketch: a vertical pipe with the wall force \underline{F} resolved into F_{drag} along the axis.)

Turbulent flow in smooth pipes — worked setup. (sketch: a pipe with P_0 = 65 psi at the inlet, P_L = 0 at the outlet, Q = ?; \Delta p_2 = P_L - P_0 = 65 - \Delta p_1 [?].) Like y = ax + b, the Prandtl correlation is solved iteratively:
Iterative solver for \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = g(f) = 4\log[Re\sqrt{f}] - 0.4:

guess f ✓
compute g(f) = 4\log[Re\sqrt{f}] - 0.4 ✓
new f: \sqrt{f} = \frac{1}{g(f)} ⇒ f_{new} = \frac{1}{(g(f))^2}
confirm/compare f w/ f_{new} (and iterate)

In Algorithm 1, \langle v\rangle = \frac{Q}{A_c}; steps 1–5 loop through the friction factor, and step 8 gives Q_{new}, which feeds back into step 1. The “LHS” form gives f(\langle v\rangle) directly from Δp.

Open these pages as a PDF



TA recitation notes for CHE 377, week of 30 October 2023.
Realistic & practical flow
Turbulent flow: can use the same equations (microscopic balances) ↳ however, flow is no longer unidirectional & SS } time dependent and 3D (v_\theta, v_r \neq 0) ↓ cannot solve for the velocity profile! Use experiments to fill in the gaps! → empirical correlations — pressure drop (F_{drag}) vs. flow rate (Q) relationships.
Fluid force on a surface S:
\underline{F} = \iint_S[\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}}]\big|_{@surface}dS
This force is being exerted by the fluid on the surface ↓ this is the cause of pressure drop in pipe flow!! \underline{F} ⇒ total force; F_{drag} = F_z (i.e. the z-th component of force). (sketch: a vertical pipe with z downward and the wall normal -\hat{e}_r pointing into the fluid.)
\therefore\;F_{drag} = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}\hat{e}_z\cdot\left(-\hat{e}_r\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}}\big|_R\right)R\,d\theta\,dz \xrightarrow{\text{non-dimensionalize}} \boxed{F_{drag} = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}-\mu\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} + \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial z}\right)\bigg|_RR\,d\theta\,dz}
(fluid drag in turbulent flow on a pipe surface of unit normal -\hat{e}_r.)
Practice questions
Laminar flow in a pipe (unidirectional, SS) } continuity + Navier → BC → v profile. \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z)_{r\theta z}; \underline{g} = (0, 0, g)_{r\theta z}; p = p(z). (sketch: a vertical pipe with z downward.)

Pressure profile: p(z) = -\left(\frac{P_0 - P_L}{L}\right)z + P_0
Velocity profile: v_z(r) = \frac{(P_0 - P_L + \rho gL)R^2}{4\mu L}\left[1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right]
Q = \langle v\rangle\pi R^2 = \frac{\pi(P_0 - P_L)R^4}{8\mu L}; \langle v\rangle = \frac{(P_0 - P_L)R^2}{8\mu L}

\underline{\underline{\Pi}}(r, z) = -p\underline{\underline{I}} + \underline{\underline{\tau}} = -p\underline{\underline{I}} + \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \mu\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}_{r\theta z} = \begin{pmatrix}-p(z) & 0 & (P_L - P_0)\frac{r}{2L} \\ 0 & -p(z) & 0 \\ (P_L - P_0)\frac{r}{2L} & 0 & -p(z)\end{pmatrix}
→ Neglect gravity:
v_z(r) = \frac{(P_0 - P_L)R^2}{4\mu L}\cdot\frac{2}{2}\left[1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right] \Rightarrow v_z(r) = 2\langle v\rangle\left[1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right]\;;\qquad \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = -\frac{4\langle v\rangle}{R^2}r
F_{drag} = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}-\mu\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} + \cancel{\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial z}}\right)\bigg|_RR\,d\theta\,dz = \int_0^L\int_0^{2\pi}-\mu\left(-\frac{4\langle v\rangle r}{R^2}\right)\bigg|_RR\,d\theta\,dz = (4\mu\langle v\rangle)(2\pi L) = 4\mu\,2\pi L\cdot\frac{(P_0 - P_L)R^2}{8\mu L}
\boxed{F_{drag} = \pi R^2(P_0 - P_L)}
Turbulent flow in smooth pipes
\text{Prandtl correlation (7.156):}\quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = 4\log\left[Re\sqrt{f}\right] - 0.4\;(\text{smooth pipes})\;;\qquad Re = \frac{\rho\langle v\rangle D}{\mu}\;;\qquad f = \frac{\Delta pD}{2L\rho\langle v\rangle^2}\;(\text{pipe friction factor from experiments})
Substituting f into Re\sqrt{f} eliminates ⟨v⟩:
4\log\left[\frac{\rho\langle v\rangle D}{\mu}\sqrt{\frac{\Delta pD}{2L\rho\langle v\rangle^2}}\right] - 0.4 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} \Rightarrow 4\log\left[\frac{\rho D}{\mu}\sqrt{\frac{\Delta pD}{2L\rho}}\right] - 0.4 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} \Rightarrow \underbrace{4\log\left[\sqrt{\frac{\rho\Delta pD^3}{2L\mu^2}}\right] - 0.4}_{\text{"LHS"}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}}
Algorithm 1:

Guess Q_{guess} (will give ⟨v⟩)
Find Re
Find f_1 (Prandtl correlation)
Find \Delta p_1 (friction factor)
Calculate \Delta p_2 = known value − \Delta p_1
Solve for “LHS” (given \Delta p_2) → gives f_2 → ⟨v⟩ (using the friction factor)
Solve for Q_{calc} [Q_{calc} = \langle v\rangle\pi R^2]
Compare this to step 1 Q_{guess} → if close then stop ↳ else iterate

Turbulent flow in connected smooth pipes
Example 7.9: a 40-foot section of 1.0-inch ID piping branches into two pipes of the same diameter, one of which is 60.0 feet long and one of which is 85.0 feet long (Figure 7.23). The main pipe is connected to the municipal water supply, which supplies a constant water pressure of 62 psig at the pipe entrance. What are the flow rates through the two pipe exits? What is the pressure at the splitting point? Assume smooth pipes. (figure: p_1 = 62 psig, Q = Q_1 + Q_2 through 40 ft to the split at p_2; 60 ft to p_3 = 0 psig (Q_1 = ?) and 85 ft to p_4 = 0 psig (Q_2 = ?).)
\Delta p_2 = P_2 - P_3 = P_2 - P_4.

Guess \Delta p_2 (“LHS”) → find f (friction factor) → ⟨v⟩ → Q_1, Q_2
Total Q (Q_1 + Q_2 = Q) → now use Algorithm 1! (until step 5) ↳ \Delta p_1 = p_1 - p_2
(\Delta p_2)_{calc} = 62 - \Delta p_1
Iterate until (\Delta p_2)_{calc} \approx (\Delta p_2)_{guess}

(1) Since we don’t know Q ↳ we first need to solve for Q_1 & Q_2 by guessing a \Delta p_2 value. (2) Once we know Q → then focus on the small initial 40 ft pipe and calculate the \Delta p_2 value independently ↓ see if it matches? ↳ if not we iterate!
Turbulent flow in connected rough pipes
\text{Colebrook correlation:}\quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = \underbrace{-4\log\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{D} + \frac{4.67}{Re\sqrt{f}}\right) + 2.28}_{g(f)}
With f = \frac{\Delta pD}{2L\rho\langle v\rangle^2} and Re = \frac{\rho\langle v\rangle D}{\mu}:
\frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = \underbrace{-4\log\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{D} + \frac{4.67}{\left(\sqrt{\frac{\rho\Delta pD^3}{2L\mu^2}}\right)}\right) + 2.28}_{\text{"LHS" (when we only know pressure drop \& no average velocity)}}
Problem 7.16: for steady pipe flow, repeat the branched-piping example, Example 7.9, for pipes with roughness ε = 0.005.

The copy of the week of 7 November 2023 recitation annotated in class. The shared derivation (energy balance → MEB → pump efficiency, bhp and head) is not repeated; the additions are below.
Pump annotations: suction (inlet, E_s) and discharge (outlet, E_d) labelled on the pump sketch, with the pump “adding energy” between them; out − in = \eta\cdot\text{bhp}. Laminar vs. turbulent profiles are sketched beside α. On the head-loss vs. Q curves, points A, B, C mark operating points at fixed RPM. Measured in the lab:
\Delta H = \text{head loss} = \frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} + \Delta z + \frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2g}
(sketch: the pump rig with the pressure-sensor (PS) taps on the suction and discharge lines, and Q set by the rotameter.)
Problem 8.30 — potential flow around a sphere. Inviscid → μ = 0 → shear stress = 0:
\rho\left(\frac{\partial\underline{v}}{\partial t} + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla\underline{v}\right) = \cancel{\mu\nabla^2\underline{v}} + \rho\underline{g} - \nabla P\quad(\text{dynamic pressure }\mathcal{P})\;;\qquad \underline{\underline{\tau}} = 0\;;\qquad \underline{\underline{\Pi}} = -p\underline{\underline{I}} + \cancel{\underline{\underline{\tau}}}
(sketch: streamlines around a sphere — potential flow follows the body and closes behind it, vs. separation and eddies in real flow; “Addison cycle” [?] is written beside it.)
Interface conditions: at the interface between fluid 1 (μ₁) and fluid 2 (μ₂), \tau_1 = \tau_2; between air (μ ≈ 0) and fluid 1, \tau_{@interface} = 0.
Problem 8.40 — drag on a thin plate. (sketch: the plate, 0.52 m long in the flow direction and 6.3 m wide, with v_{bulk} = v_\infty; \underline{F} = \iint(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}})\,dS; v ∝ x₁.) The velocity profile f'(\zeta) is a PDE solution with non-dimensional x_1; no slip at the plate → the flow changes → \underline{v}(x_1, x_2).
Units check on \tau_w = 0.332\mu v_\infty\left(\frac{\rho v_\infty}{\mu x_1}\right)^{1/2}:
\left(\frac{\tau_w}{0.332}\right)^2 = \mu v_\infty^2\left(\frac{\rho v_\infty}{x_1}\right) [=] \frac{\mu v_\infty^3\rho}{x_1} [=] \frac{\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m\,s}}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{m^3}}{\mathrm{s^3}}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m^3}}}{\mathrm{m}} = \frac{\mathrm{kg^2}}{\mathrm{m^2s^4}}\;;\qquad \text{Pa} = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{m^2}} = \frac{\mathrm{kg\cdot m}}{\mathrm{m^2s^2}} = \frac{\mathrm{kg}}{\mathrm{m\,s^2}}
so \tau^2 [=] Pa² ✓. Stress = \frac{F}{A} ⇒ \boxed{F = \tau_w\cdot A}.
Transcriber’s note: τ_w varies with x₁, so the plate force is \int_0^L\tau_w(x_1)W\,dx_1, which is twice \tau_w(L)\cdot A; “F = τ_w·A” is as written.
