TA recitation notes for CHE 377, week of 7 November 2023.
Pump characteristic curves
Pumps → mechanical devices that allow for fluid transportation via pipes (Section 9.2.4.1) ↳ centrifugal pumps are a common type → transfer rotational energy (from an electric motor) to fluid movement. (figure: a centrifugal pump — flow in at the eye, vanes inside the housing, flow out.)

Working principle is energy balance! Electric energy → shaft work (by pump to fluid) → affects speed, pressure & other fluid characteristics.
Pump manufacturers need to characterize a pump → pump operation under various conditions [pump curves!].

\Delta E = Q + W\quad(\Delta E = \text{total energy of system};\;Q = \text{heat from environment to the system via boundary};\;W = \text{work done on system by environment})
Energy balance on CV:
\underbrace{\frac{dE_{cv}}{dt}}_{\text{closed system}} + \underbrace{\iint_{CS}(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v})\rho\hat{E}\,dS}_{\text{open system (mass flow in \& out)}} = Q_{in,cv} - W_{by,cv}\qquad[E_{cv} = U + E_K + E_P]
↓ some assumptions:
\Delta E_p + \Delta E_k + \Delta U = Q_{in,cv} - W_{by,cv}
where W_{by,cv} = shaft work (W_s, work performed by the fluid due to moving parts) + flow work (W_f, work done by the fluid as it enters & leaves the system; W_f = F\cdot d = (P\cdot A)\cdot d). With H = U + PV:
\text{SS macro energy balance:}\quad\boxed{\Delta E_p + \Delta E_k + \Delta H = Q_{in,cv} - W_{s,by\,cv}}
↓ single in, single out, incompressible fluid:
m\left(\frac{\langle v\rangle_2^2}{2} - \frac{\langle v\rangle_1^2}{2}\right) + mg(z_2 - z_1) + m\left(\hat{U}_2 - \hat{U}_1 + \frac{P_2}{\rho} - \frac{P_1}{\rho}\right) = Q_{in,cv} - W_{s,by\,cv}
↓ temp constant, no phase changes/chemical reaction, negligible heat transfer:
\text{Mechanical energy balance (MEB):}\quad\boxed{\frac{\Delta p}{\rho} + \frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2\alpha} + g\Delta z + F = -\frac{W_{s,by}}{m}}
(ρ = density; ⟨v⟩ = average velocity; α = 1 (turbulent flow); F = friction term [ΔU − Q].)
(sketch: a pump with suction point (s) on the inlet and discharge point (d) on the outlet.) Pump can add energy via: + increase velocity of fluid; + create pressure differential; + pump can change fluid height (raise its potential energy).
\eta = \text{pump efficiency} = \frac{(\text{useful energy})}{(\text{total energy})} = \frac{\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{m} - F\right)}{\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{m}\right)}\quad(\text{useful energy = energy converted to work, rather than friction})
Pump brake horsepower: bhp = -W_{s,by} (total work delivered by pump). Dividing by g:
\therefore\;\frac{\Delta p}{\rho g} + \frac{\Delta\langle v\rangle^2}{2\alpha g} + \Delta z = \eta\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{m}\right) = \eta\cdot(\text{bhp})
\boxed{\underbrace{\left(\frac{P_d}{\rho g} + \frac{\langle v\rangle_d^2}{2g} + z_d\right)}_{\text{discharge head }(H_d)\;[=]\text{ length}} - \underbrace{\left(\frac{P_s}{\rho g} + \frac{\langle v\rangle_s^2}{2g} + z_s\right)}_{\text{suction head }(H_s)\;[=]\text{ length}} = \eta\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{mg}\right)}
\underbrace{(H_d - H_s)}_{\text{head loss}} = \eta\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{mg}\right) = \eta\left(-\frac{\text{bhp}}{mg}\right)
(sketch: head loss (ft) vs. Q (capacity, related to ⟨v⟩!) — falling curves, one for each fixed RPM; gives info about η & bhp.) Pumping ability of a CP: + shaft rotational speed (RPM); + shape of vanes; + flow path.
Transcriber’s note: dividing the MEB by g gives \eta\left(-\frac{W_{s,by}}{mg}\right); the first line after “dividing by g” omits the g, as written.
Lab: characterize relationships b/w discharge flow rate, net head, bhp, efficiency in a CP ↳ vary Q (via rotameter) ↳ measure pressure loss → calculate head loss (H_{loss} or H_{net} = H_d - H_s) ↳ non-dimensionalize variables & then plot them!
Problems
Problem 8.30: calculate the extra stress tensor \underline{\underline{\tilde{\tau}}} for potential flow around a sphere of an inviscid, Newtonian fluid. Calculate the total stress tensor \underline{\underline{\tilde{\Pi}}}. Comment on what is obtained.
Problem 8.40: what is the force (i.e., drag) on a thin plate given the following conditions? The fluid is water, the plate is 0.52 m long and 6.3 m wide, and the free-stream velocity is 1.3\times10^{-2} m/s.
Boundary layer flow: ∇·v = 0 + Navier–Stokes } v varying w/ two dimensions → (assumptions) → velocity profile for laminar flow past a flat plate:
\frac{v_1}{v_\infty} = f'(\zeta) = 1 - (0.5434)\log\left[1 + (68.3)10^{-0.6247\zeta}\right]
↓ \underline{F} = \iint[\hat{n}\cdot\underline{\underline{\Pi}}]_{@surface}dS; drag is the force component in the flow direction:
\tau_w = 0.332\mu v_\infty\left(\frac{\rho v_\infty}{\mu x_1}\right)^{1/2}
(figure: the boundary layer growing along a flat plate from the leading edge, with uniform v_\infty outside and the profile inside thickness b.)

Exam review sessions I ran as TA for CHE 377 (Fall 2023). The 33 pages contain each session’s worksheet several times (prepared copy and in-class copies, pages 3–4, 10–13 and 17–28 repeat earlier pages with annotations); each problem is transcribed once from its cleanest worked copy.
Review session MT1 (20 September 2023)
Reynolds transport theorem
\frac{D\Psi}{Dt} = \underbrace{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\iiint\rho\psi\,dV\right)}_{\text{accumulation}} + \underbrace{\iint\rho\psi(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA}_{\text{efflux (in - out)}}\;;\qquad \psi = \frac{d\Psi}{dm}\;(\text{intensive}; \Psi\text{ extensive})\;;\qquad \Psi = \{m, \underline{P}, E\}
(D/Dt = material derivative.)
Mass balance (continuity equation): Ψ = m; \psi = \frac{dm}{dm} = 1:
\cancel{\frac{Dm}{Dt}} = \underbrace{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\iiint_{CV}\rho\,dV\right)}_{\text{rate of accumulation of mass w/n CV (@ SS = 0)}} + \underbrace{\iint_{CS}\rho(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA}_{\text{net outward flow of mass across the CS, "efflux"}}
Efflux > 0 (net mass going out); < 0 (net mass going in); = 0 (mass w/n CV is constant) ↓ evaluate at all control surfaces of the chosen control volume. For incompressible flow ρ = constant ∴ for SS, incompressible flow through a CV: \iint_{CS}\rho(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA = \cancel{\frac{dm}{dt}} = 0.
(figure: a tank with inlet ① (A_1, v_1, inward-pointing normal) and outlet ② (A_2, v_2).) @ SS, incompressible:
\rho\iint_{A_1}(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA + \rho\iint_{A_2}(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA = 0 \Rightarrow \rho(-v_1)\iint_{A_1}dA + \rho v_2\iint_{A_2}dA = 0 \Rightarrow \boxed{\rho v_1A_1 = \rho v_2A_2}
↑ Irrespective of the flow inside the control volume! (Would work anytime for constant velocity!)
Momentum balance: \Psi = m\underline{v}; \psi = \frac{d(m\underline{v})}{dm} = \underline{v}\cancel{\frac{dm}{dm}} + m\cancel{\frac{d\underline{v}}{dm}} = \underline{v}. RTT becomes:
\frac{D(m\underline{v})}{Dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\iiint_{CV}\rho\underline{v}\,dV\right) + \iint_{CS}\rho\underline{v}(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA\;;\qquad \text{Newton's second law: }\sum\underline{F} = \frac{D(m\underline{v})}{Dt}
\therefore\;\underbrace{\sum\underline{F}}_{\text{sum of forces acting on CV, i.e. on the fluid}} = \underbrace{\frac{d}{dt}\left(\iiint_{CV}\rho\underline{v}\,dV\right)}_{\text{rate of acc. of momentum w/n CV}} + \underbrace{\iint_{CS}\rho\underline{v}(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA}_{\text{net rate of momentum efflux from CV}}
@ SS, Cartesian coord.: \sum F_x = \iint\rho v_x(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA; \sum F_y = \iint\rho v_y(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA; \sum F_z = \iint\rho v_z(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\,dA.

Force balance: (sketch: \hat{n}_1 = -\hat{e}_x at the inlet, \hat{n}_2 at the outlet; \underline{v}_2 = a\hat{e}_x + b(\hat{e}_y) with \cos\theta = \frac{a}{v_2}, \sin\theta = \frac{b}{v_2}, so \underline{v}_2 = v_2\cos\theta\,\hat{e}_x - v_2\sin\theta\,\hat{e}_y.)

Since the entire system is stationary → net forces are zero: \underline{F}_{ext} - \sum\underline{F} = 0. Taking the control volume as the entire object:

(figure: fluid between a stationary wall at x = 0 and a wall at x = L moving up at v_0; y up.)



Cartesian coordinate system (xyz); + gravity ✓; + Newtonian, incomp. ✓; + pressure? → closed system so most likely present.


\underline{v} = (0, -v_y, 0)_{xyz} [?]; v_y = f(x) (wide/infinite wall, i.e. symmetric in z direction); \underline{g} = (0, -g, 0)_{xyz}

→ Mass balance: 0 = \nabla\cdot\underline{v} (SS, incomp.): \cancel{\frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x}} + \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y} + \cancel{\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z}} = 0 ∴ \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y} = 0 [developed flow].
→ EOM: \rho\left(\cancel{\frac{\partial\underline{v}}{\partial t}} + \underline{v}\cdot\nabla\underline{v}\right) = -\nabla p + \mu\nabla^2\underline{v} + \rho\underline{g}:

x: 0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}
y: 0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial y} + \mu\left(\frac{\partial^2v_y}{\partial x^2}\right) + \rho g_y; g_y = -g
z: 0 = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial z}

No pressure gradients in x & z direction; P = f(y); \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{dP}{dy} = constant:
\therefore\;\underbrace{\frac{1}{\mu}\left(\frac{dP}{dy} - \rho g\right)}_{\text{not a function of }x!\;= \lambda} = \frac{\partial^2v_y}{\partial x^2} \Rightarrow \frac{\partial v_y}{\partial x} = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}x + c_1 \Rightarrow v_y = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}\frac{x^2}{2} + c_1x + c_2
BCs: @ x = 0, v_y = 0 → c_2 = 0; @ x = L, v_y = v_0 → \left(v_0 - \frac{\lambda}{\mu}\frac{L^2}{2}\right)\frac{1}{L} = c_1, c_1 = \frac{v_0}{L} - \frac{\lambda L}{2\mu}:
\boxed{v_y = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}\frac{x^2}{2} + \left(\frac{v_0}{L} - \frac{\lambda L}{2\mu}\right)x}\quad\text{Sketch it out!}

Practice 2 — Problems 6.44 & 6.52: upward pressure-driven flow in a tube, non-Newtonian fluid (power law); incompressible; SS
Problem 6.44: calculate the velocity profile and flow rate for pressure-driven flow of an incompressible, Newtonian liquid in a vertical pipe of radius R. The pressure at the bottom entrance to the tube is P₀; at a point a distance L upward the pressure is P_L. Assume that the flow is well developed and at steady state. Do not neglect gravity. Problem 6.52: repeat problem 6.44 with a power-law, generalized Newtonian fluid with parameters m and n.
(sketch: a vertical tube of radius R from z = 0 (P = P_0) to z = L (P = P_L).) \underline{v} = (0, 0, v_z)_{r\theta z}; \underline{g} = (0, 0, -g)_{r\theta z}; flow profile? pressure profile? cylindrical coordinates.
→ Mass balance: \nabla\cdot\underline{v} = 0 (incomp., SS): \cancel{\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}} + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(\rho r\cancel{v_r}) + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(\rho\cancel{v_\theta}) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\rho v_z) = 0 ⇒ \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = 0.
→ Non-Newtonian flow → cannot use Navier–Stokes! (only incompressible flow) — Table B.6: cylindrical coordinates of the Cauchy momentum balance. \underline{\underline{\tau}} = \eta(\dot{\gamma})\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}} (μ for Newtonian); \underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}} = (\nabla\underline{v} + (\nabla\underline{v})^T); \eta(\dot{\gamma}) = m\dot{\gamma}^{n-1}. Equation B.8-2 (Newtonian constitutive equation) gives the components of \underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}}; only \tau_{rz} = \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} (times η) survives:
\dot{\gamma} = \|\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}}\| = \left\|\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\right\| = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}(\text{sum of squares of each term in }\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}})} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^2\right]} = \left|\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right|
As r↑, v_z↓ (closer to the wall): \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} < 0 \rightarrow -\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} > 0 ∴ \dot{\gamma} = -\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}.
\underline{\underline{\tau}} = m\dot{\gamma}^{n-1}\underline{\underline{\dot{\gamma}}} = m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 & \partial v_z/\partial r \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \cdot & 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\;\therefore\;\tau_{rz} = m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right) \neq f(\theta, z)
Only \tau_{rz} exists (due to flow direction), which is a function of r (and not z!):

r-direction: 0 = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial r}; θ-direction: 0 = -\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial P}{\partial\theta} } P has no θ & r dependence: -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} = -\frac{dP}{dz}
z-direction: 0 = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} + \left(\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(r\tau_{rz})\right) + \underbrace{\rho g_z}_{-\rho g}

\therefore\;\underbrace{\frac{dP}{dz} + \rho g}_{\neq f(r)} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{r}\frac{d}{dr}(r\tau_{rz})}_{\neq f(z)} = \lambda\quad\to\text{solve them separately!}

\frac{dP}{dz} + \rho g = \lambda ⇒ P = (\lambda - \rho g)z + c_1; @ z = 0, P = P₀ → c_1 = P_0; @ z = L, P = P_L → (P_L - P_0) = (\lambda - \rho g)L ⇒ \lambda = \frac{P_L - P_0}{L} + \rho g
\frac{d}{dr}(r\tau_{rz}) = \lambda r ⇒ \tau_{rz} = \frac{\lambda r}{2} + \frac{c_1}{r}; @ r = 0, \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r} = 0, \tau_{rz} = 0 } c_1 = 0 ⇒ \tau_{rz} = \frac{\lambda r}{2}
With \tau_{rz} = m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^{n-1}\left(\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)\cdot\frac{(-1)}{(-1)} = -m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^n: \frac{\lambda r}{2} = -m\left(-\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial r}\right)^n ⇒ -\frac{dv_z}{dr} = \left(\frac{-\lambda}{2m}\right)^{1/n}r^{1/n} ⇒ v_z = -\left(\frac{-\lambda}{2m}\right)^{1/n}\frac{r^{1/n+1}}{(\frac{1}{n} + 1)} + c_1
@ r = R, v_z = 0 } c_1 = \left(-\frac{\lambda}{2m}\right)^{1/n}\frac{R^{(1/n+1)}}{(\frac{1}{n} + 1)}

\therefore\;\boxed{v_z = \left(-\frac{\lambda}{2m}\right)^{1/n}\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{n} + 1)}\left(R^{\frac{1}{n}+1} - r^{\frac{1}{n}+1}\right)}

Question 1
A liquid with a given viscosity (mew) enters and leaves the above bend as shown. Solve the following questions. (figure: a bend with inlet a (radius R_a, flow up, \underline{v}_a = \langle v\rangle_a\hat{e}_y, normal \hat{n}_a down) and outlet b (radius R_b, flow out down-left at 18° from vertical, \underline{v}_b = \langle v\rangle_b\hat{e}_{v_b}, normal \hat{n}_b).)
(a) Using Reynolds transport theorem, solve for the overall force on the fluid.
\text{RTT:}\quad\frac{d\underline{P}}{dt} + \iint_{CS}\rho(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\underline{v}\,dS = \sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{F}
Taking the fluid inside the pipe as the CV: there is flow through surface A and surface B.
Inlet: \underline{v}_a = (0, \langle v\rangle, 0)_{xyz}; \hat{n}_a = -\hat{e}_y = (0, -1, 0)_{xyz}:
\iint_{inlet}\rho\underline{v}_a(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v}_a)\,dS = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{R_a}\rho(\langle v\rangle_a\hat{e}_y)\left[\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ \langle v\rangle_a \\ 0\end{pmatrix}\right]r\,dr\,d\theta = (\rho\langle v\rangle_a\hat{e}_y)(-\langle v\rangle_a)\iint r\,dr\,d\theta = (-\rho\langle v\rangle_a^2\pi R_a^2)\hat{e}_y
Outlet: \hat{n}_b = \hat{e}_{v_b} = (-\sin\theta, -\cos\theta, 0)_{xyz}; \underline{v}_b = \langle v\rangle_b(-\sin\theta, -\cos\theta, 0)_{xyz}:
\iint_{outlet}\rho\underline{v}_b(\hat{n}\cdot\underline{v}_b)\,dS = \rho(\langle v\rangle_b\hat{e}_{v_b})\left[\langle v\rangle_b\sin^2\theta + \langle v\rangle_b\cos^2\theta + 0\right]\iint r\,dr\,d\theta = \rho\langle v\rangle_b^2\pi R_b^2\hat{e}_{v_b} = [\rho\langle v\rangle_b^2\pi R_b^2]\begin{pmatrix}-\sin\theta \\ -\cos\theta \\ 0\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}
Overall RTT @ steady state:
\sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{F} = \iint_{CS}\rho(\underline{v}\cdot\hat{n})\underline{v}\,dS = \boxed{\begin{pmatrix}-\rho\langle v\rangle_b^2\pi R_b^2\sin\theta \\ -\rho\langle v\rangle_a^2\pi R_a^2 - \rho\langle v\rangle_b^2\pi R_b^2\cos\theta \\ 0\end{pmatrix}_{xyz}}
(b) Using macroscopic momentum balance, solve for the overall force on the fluid (@ SS):
\sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{F} = \cancel{\frac{d\underline{P}}{dt}} + \sum_{i=1}^{\#}\left[\frac{\rho A\cos\theta\langle v\rangle^2}{\beta}\hat{v}\right] = \frac{\rho A\cos\theta\langle v\rangle^2}{\beta}\hat{v}\Big|_{inlet} + \frac{\rho A\cos\theta\langle v\rangle^2}{\beta}\hat{v}\Big|_{outlet}
(inlet: \theta_a = 180° between \hat{n} and \hat{v}; outlet: \theta_b = 0°.)
\Rightarrow \sum\underline{F} = \frac{\rho\pi R_a^2(-1)\langle v\rangle_a^2}{\beta}\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{pmatrix} + \frac{\rho\pi R_b^2(1)\langle v\rangle_b^2}{\beta}\begin{pmatrix}-\sin\theta \\ -\cos\theta \\ 0\end{pmatrix}\;;\qquad \text{for turbulent flow: }\beta = 1
\boxed{\sum_{\text{on CV}}\underline{F} = \begin{bmatrix}-\rho\pi R_b^2\langle v\rangle_b^2\sin\theta \\ -\rho\pi R_a^2\langle v\rangle_a^2 - \rho\pi R_b^2\langle v\rangle_b^2\cos\theta \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}
(c) Are your force expressions in (a) and (b) different from each other? Why or why not? No! Because RTT & MMB are the one & same → macroscopic look @ CV ↳ using either to arrive at the expression is valid!
Question 2
Consider two concentric disks which are fixed to stay in place. There is an inflow of an incompressible fluid through a hole in the top plate. The flow is driven by a pressure drop, \Delta p = p(r = aR) - p(r = R), between the inlet at r = aR (a ≪ 1) and the outlet at r = R. (figure: the disks of radius R with the inlet hole of radius aR; front view with plates at z = h and z = −h, flow in from the top and out radially.) The following figure shows the front view of the apparatus above. Consider the cylindrical coordinate system to be positioned in the center.
You can make the following assumptions: (1) the outflow is homogeneous along the circumference; (2) the flow is fully developed and at steady-state; (3) the fluid is incompressible; (4) the outlet is at atmospheric pressure p_{atm}; (5) the effects due to flow around the corner at the inlet can be neglected (a ≪ 1). The pressure at that point is unperturbed by the flow around the corner.
(a) (10 points) Write down the kinematics for this problem by stating physically reasonable assumptions. (i) Which velocity components are non-zero? (ii) Which coordinates (i.e. r, θ, z) do the non-zero velocity component(s) depend on?
Kinematics refer to velocity profiles: (i) \underline{v} = (v_r, v_\theta, v_z); v_\theta = v_z = 0; only v_r is non-zero. (ii) v_r(r, \cancel{\theta}, z) (symmetric).
(b) (20 points) Use the local form of the balance of mass to determine the radial component of the velocity profile in terms of an integration constant.
\nabla\cdot\underline{v} = 0\;(@\,SS,\text{ incompressible}):\quad \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(\rho rv_r) + \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}(\rho\cancel{v_\theta}) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(\rho\cancel{v_z}) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial r}(\rho rv_r) = 0 \xrightarrow{\text{integrate once}} \boxed{v_r = \frac{c_1}{r}}
c_1 has to be a function of z (c_1(z)) (since we know v_r(r, z) & c_1 is a constant w.r.t. variable r).
Transcriber’s note: the intermediate line reads "rv_r = 0"; it should be rv_r = c_1.
(c) (50 points) Use the Navier–Stokes equations to find the velocity profile. Start by simplifying them by using your results from (a) and (b). When solving the resulting differential equation, state and apply appropriate boundary conditions. In order to be able to find an analytical solution, neglect the nonlinear term (\rho C^2/r^3, where C is your integration constant from (b)). Express your final answer in terms of Δp, μ, a, R, h, z, r.
(the cylindrical Navier–Stokes equations are pasted beside it with the vanishing terms struck out.)

r-direction: \rho\left(v_r\frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r}\right) = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial r} + \mu\left[\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}(rv_r)\right) + \frac{\partial^2v_r}{\partial z^2}\right]
θ-direction: -\frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial P}{\partial\theta} = 0
z-direction: -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} + \rho g_z = 0

From part (b): v_r = \frac{c_1(z)}{r}; \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r} = -\frac{c_1(z)}{r^2}; \frac{\partial}{\partial r}(r\cdot v_r) = \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\cancel{r}\frac{c_1(z)}{\cancel{r}}\right) = 0 (not a function of r!). r-direction:
\rho\left(\frac{c_1(z)}{r}\cdot\left(-\frac{c_1(z)}{r^2}\right)\right) = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial r} + \mu\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}\left(\frac{c_1(z)}{r}\right) \Rightarrow \underbrace{\rho\left(-\frac{c_1^2(z)}{r^3}\right)}_{\text{can neglect as per question}} = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial r} + \frac{\mu}{r}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(c_1(z)) \Rightarrow \frac{\partial P}{\partial r} = \frac{\mu}{r}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(c_1(z))
Transcriber’s note: the term written -\partial P/\partial r on the right becomes +\partial P/\partial r in the last line once the nonlinear term is dropped (sign as written).
From the other dimensions: P = f(r, z); -\frac{\partial P}{\partial z} + \rho g_z = 0 ⇒ \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} = \rho g_z ⇒ P = \rho g_zz + c_2(r) ↳ we would need BCs for P in z to solve for c_2(r). BCs for P: @ r = aR, P = P(r = aR) = P_{in}; @ r = R, P = P(r = R) = P_{out}.
Integrating both sides w.r.t. r:
\int_{aR}^R\frac{\partial P}{\partial r}dr = \int_{aR}^R\frac{\mu}{r}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(c_1(z))\,dr \Rightarrow P(r, z)\Big|_{aR}^R = \mu\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(c_1(z))\ln r\Big|_{aR}^R
\Delta p = P(r = R) - P(r = aR) @ any z:
\Delta p = \mu\frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}(c_1(z))\ln\left(\frac{R}{aR}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{\partial^2}{\partial z^2}c_1(z) = \frac{\Delta p}{\mu}\cdot\left(\ln\left(\frac{R}{aR}\right)\right)^{-1} = \lambda \xrightarrow{\text{integrating twice w.r.t. }z} c_1(z) = \lambda\frac{z^2}{2} + A_1z + A_2
\boxed{v_r = \frac{c_1(z)}{r} = \frac{\lambda z^2}{2r} + \frac{A_1z}{r} + \frac{A_2}{r}}
Transcriber’s note: the problem statement defines \Delta p = p(aR) - p(R), the opposite sign of the working’s \Delta p = P(R) - P(aR); the final sign follows the working.
BCs: @ z = h, v_r = 0 ⇒ 0 = \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\lambda h^2}{2} + A_1h + A_2\right); @ z = −h, v_r = 0 ⇒ 0 = \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\lambda h^2}{2} + A_1(-h) + A_2\right). 2 eq; 2 unknowns: 2A_2 = -\lambda h^2 ⇒ A_2 = -\frac{\lambda h^2}{2}; A_1 = 0:
\therefore\;v_r(r, z) = \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\lambda z^2}{2} - \frac{\lambda h^2}{2}\right) = \frac{\lambda h^2}{2r}\left(\left(\frac{z}{h}\right)^2 - 1\right)\;;\qquad \lambda = \frac{\Delta p}{\mu}\left(\ln\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)\right)^{-1} = \frac{\Delta p}{-\mu(\ln a)}
\boxed{v_r(r, z) = \frac{\Delta ph^2}{2\mu r(\ln a)}\left(1 - \left(\frac{z}{h}\right)^2\right)}

Coursework/Transport_and_Separations/CHE.title: CHE 377: Momentum transfer (TA notes)
Coursework/Transport_and_Separations/CHE.content:
Notes I wrote as a teaching assistant for CHE 377 (Fall 2023), exported from OneNote and transcribed into Markdown and LaTeX. They are split into recitations, office-hour (OH) notes and exam reviews. Each note shows the typed version first, with the original pages in a collapsible box at the top and a link to open just those pages as a PDF.

Recitations (PDF) · Office hours (PDF) · Reviews (PDF)

Lectures

Lecture 09-26 · 2023-09-25 — Recitation 9/26 as annotated in class — review of the stress tensor, viscosity and static-fluid problems (shear and normal stresses on a fluid element, incompressibility, Π split into normal and shear parts), the manometer review, and a worked solution of the two-fluid manometer pressure difference.

Other notes

Derivation · 2023-09-21 — Office-hours derivation of film flow down an inclined plane — the force balance on a fluid element with the stress tensor, the x-component momentum balance, the Newtonian constitutive equation, and the velocity profile v_z(x) = (ρg cos β/μ)(Hx − x²/2).
Problem Clarification · 2023-10-27 — Office-hours clarification on computing the force on a surface from the total stress tensor — integration bounds over the surface, evaluating at the surface coordinates, and the wire-coating example giving F = (2πμVL/ln κ) ê_z because the pressure term integrates to zero around the wire.
Drag coefficient · 2023-08-28 — Recitation notes (weeks 2–3) — characteristic areas for drag coefficients, then the Reynolds transport theorem worksheet (material vs. control volume, D/Dt, momentum flux through a surface) with worked problems on momentum flow through a hemisphere, average and maximum velocity in a slit, and gravity components on an incline.
Derivation (2) · 2023-09-29 — Office-hours derivation of the Newtonian stress tensor in cylindrical coordinates — ∇v as a dyadic product with the del operator, derivatives of the unit vectors, the transpose (∇v)ᵀ, and the resulting symmetric τ components.
FL Lab2 · 2023-09-29 — Office-hours overview of Fundamental Lab 2, turbulent flow in a pipe — Reynolds number, Darcy friction factor (Blasius and Colebrook correlations, Fanning f = f_D/4), the Darcy–Weisbach equation, the experimental setup with a differential pressure gauge and rotameter, and pre-lab hints for a force balance relating wall shear stress to Δp.
Week 03 · 2023-09-04 — Office-hours sketch of spherical coordinates — the polar angle θ from z and azimuth φ in the xy plane, with the full-sphere limits 0 < φ < 2π, 0 < θ < π.
FL4 Lab Guide · 2023-11-07 — Lab guide for Fundamental Lab 4, centrifugal pump characteristic curves — theory from the energy balance to the MEB, pump efficiency and brake horsepower, discharge and suction heads, the lab procedure, net head with piping and fitting friction, the dimensionless pump coefficients C_H, C_Q, C_P and η, and what to plot, discuss and include in the error analysis.
Week 04 · 2023-09-11 — Section divider page for the week 4 recitations (no content on this page).
6.39 · 2023-10-29 — Office-hours help on Problem 6.39 — the pressure field in inclined flow, P = −ρg_z z + (ΔP/L)x + P₀, from integrating ∂P/∂z and matching ∂P/∂x, and integrating radial continuity to get v_r = c₁/r.
L6 Surface Tension, Reynolds Transport Theorem · 2023-09-04 — Office-hours worked example for lecture 6 (surface tension and the Reynolds transport theorem) — the momentum RTT for steady flow through a 90° bend with uniform inlet and outlet velocities, giving ΣF = −ρv₁²A₁ê_i − ρv₂²A₂ê_k.
7.10 · 2023-11-06 — Office-hours help on Problem 7.10, radial flow between parallel plates — continuity gives v_r = f(z)/r, the slow (developed) flow assumption drops the inertial term, and separation of variables r dP/dr = μ f″ = λ splits the problem.
Week of 7th Nov · 2023-11-07 — Recitation for the week of 7 November — centrifugal pump characteristic curves from the energy balance on a control volume (macro energy balance, mechanical energy balance, pump efficiency, brake horsepower, discharge and suction head), the pump lab, and boundary-layer drag on a flat plate.
Week of 7th Nov (2) · 2023-11-07 — In-class copy of the week-of-7-November recitation — pump-curve annotations (head loss from Δp/ρg, Δz and Δ⟨v⟩² across suction and discharge), inviscid potential flow around a sphere (τ = 0, Π = −pI), interface stress conditions, and the flat-plate drag force F = τ_w·A with a units check.
Week of 7th Nov (3) · 2023-11-07 — Second in-class copy of the week-of-7-November recitation — the pump energy balance traced as a PFD, a head-loss example lifting water 30 m from a river, the inviscid-flow argument via the Re → ∞ limit and dynamic pressure, and the flat-plate drag geometry with the boundary-layer edge at v = 0.99 v∞.
Recitation 09 12 · 2023-09-11 — Recitation 9/12 as annotated in class — the Stokes’-law viscosity lab and pre-lab force balance, plus a worked setup of the truncated-cone control volume (counting surfaces, normals, the ê_θ transformation and the mass-flow integral over the cone side).
Recitation 09 12 (master) · 2023-09-11 — Recitation 9/12 worksheet (master) — Fundamental Lab 1 on fluid viscosity by Stokes’ law (drag on a falling sphere, lab logistics and report structure, pre-lab derivation of μ from a terminal-velocity force balance), then problems on a truncated-cone control volume, an average velocity in cylindrical coordinates and gravity in wire coating.
Recitation 09 12 (master) (2) · 2023-09-11 — A second copy of the 9/12 recitation master (Stokes’-law viscosity lab and pre-lab, truncated-cone, average-velocity and wire-coating problems), with extra sketches of the spherical unit vectors around the cone’s control surfaces.
Week of 23rd · 2023-10-23 — Recitation for the week of 23 October — macroscopic control-volume vs. microscopic balances (continuity and Cauchy/Navier–Stokes), axial annular drag in wire coating with and without a pressure gradient (velocity profile, flow rate by integration by parts, force on the wire), and upward pressure-driven pipe flow of a power-law fluid.
Week of 23rd (2) · 2023-10-23 — In-class copy of the week-of-23-October recitation — simplifying the cylindrical Navier–Stokes equations term by term for wire-coating flow, the pressure gradient Δp/L for Problem 6.49, solving for v_z = c₁ ln r + c₂ with the wire and shell boundary conditions, and setting up the force on the wire.
Week of 23rd (3) · 2023-10-23 — Second in-class copy of the week-of-23-October recitation — a four-step recipe for flow problems (characterize the flow, continuity, Navier–Stokes, BCs), the wire-coating solution with ∂P/∂z = ΔP/L, and the setup for Problem 6.49 with a pressure gradient.
Week 25th Sept · 2023-09-25 — Recitation worksheet for the week of 25 September — viscosity as shear stress over rate of shear strain, the Newtonian constitutive equations for shear and normal stresses, isotropic vs. anisotropic stress and the total stress tensor Π = τ − pI, a manometer review (Pascal’s principle, hydrostatic pressure), and problems on a two-fluid manometer and an incline-film coordinate system.
Week 25th Sept (2) · 2023-09-25 — A clean second copy of the week-of-25-September recitation worksheet (viscosity, Newtonian stresses, the stress tensor, manometer review, and the manometer and incline-film problems).
Week of 27th Nov · 2023-11-14 — Recitation for the week of 27 November — the shift from flow profiles to large-scale quantities, macroscopic mass, momentum and energy balances (stream sums with β and α), and problems on a Venturi meter, the maximum siphon height before the liquid boils, and tank-and-hose flow with friction.
Week of 27th Nov (2) · 2023-11-14 — In-class copy of the week-of-27-November recitation — worked Venturi-meter pressure drop from the mass balance and MEB (−Δp = ρ⟨v₂⟩²/2 · [1 − (D₂/D₁)⁴]), the siphon exit velocity v₂ = √(2g(z₁ − z₂)), and the maximum siphon height where the pressure reaches the vapor pressure.
Week of 27th Nov (3) · 2023-11-14 — A second in-class copy of the 27 November recitation, then the final recitation (week of 5 December) — velocities in a converging 20° bend, combined pressure-driven and drag (Couette–Poiseuille) flow in a slit solved from Navier–Stokes with the location of maximum velocity, and the macroscopic momentum balance for the force to support a 90° expanding pipe bend.
Week of 31st · 2023-10-30 — Recitation for the week of 30 October — why turbulent flow needs empirical correlations, the fluid drag force on a pipe wall, laminar pipe flow (pressure and velocity profiles, Q, Π and F_drag = πR²(P₀ − P_L)), and turbulent flow in smooth, branched and rough pipes with the Prandtl and Colebrook correlations and iterative algorithms.
Week of 31st (2) · 2023-10-30 — In-class copy of the week-of-30-October recitation — turbulent eddies, the drag force on the pipe wall, and annotations on the friction-factor algorithms, including an iterative fixed-point solver for the Prandtl correlation and a worked numeric setup (P₀ = 65 psi, P_L = 0).
Week of 31st (3) · 2023-10-30 — Second in-class copy of the week-of-30-October recitation — turbulence as a 3D PDE needing CFD or Darcy friction correlations, a series-pipe example (1-in and ½-in pipes from 60 psig to 0 psig) worked with Algorithm 1, and notes on the branched-pipe flow split.
CHE_377_Reviews — Exam review sessions for CHE 377 — MT1 (Reynolds transport theorem, mass and momentum balances, force on a pipe bend), an OH review of two-layer incline flow, the exam 2 algorithm with falling-film and power-law pipe-flow problems, MT3 boundary layers with sailboat and roof-wind problems, and the final review (pipe-bend force by RTT vs. macroscopic balance, radial flow between disks).
Notes 2023-10-23 · 2023-10-23 — Office-hours notes (23 October) — resolving gravity on an incline, falling-film flow outside a vertical rod (velocity profile with a zero-shear free surface), and setting up flow down an inclined plane with continuity, Navier–Stokes and boundary conditions.
Notes 2023-11-28 · 2023-11-28 — Office-hours worked problems (28 November) — turbulent drag on both sides of a flat plate from C_D = 0.031/Re^(1/7), and a pipe-bend problem using the mass balance, the MEB for the inlet pressure, the outlet direction at 40°, and the momentum balance.

Coursework/Transport_and_Separations/ind.title: Transport phenomena and separations
Coursework/Transport_and_Separations/ind.content:
Momentum, heat and mass transfer, boundary layers, and separation processes such as drying, distillation and absorption. Each course links to one page per lecture or homework set. Cheat sheets and review notes are typed versions of exam sheets, with the original scans in a collapsible box at the top of each page.
Courses

CHE 377: Momentum transfer (TA notes) · 32 notes — Teaching-assistant notes for Purdue CHE 377, momentum transfer — recitation worksheets, office-hour derivations and exam reviews on fluid statics, the Reynolds transport theorem, viscosity and Stokes flow, Navier–Stokes solutions, boundary layers, drag and pipe flow.

Cheat sheets and review notes

CBE 150A Cheat Sheet — Exam cheat sheets for CBE 150A (fluid mechanics and heat transfer) — macroscopic mass, momentum and energy balances, Bernoulli, viscosity and power-law fluids, boundary-layer scaling, conduction resistances, lumped and fin models, separation of variables, and worked force-balance sample problems.
CBE 150B Cheat Sheet — Cheat sheets and review notes for CBE 150B (mass transfer and separations) — drying and psychrometry, separation thermodynamics, flash, absorption and stripping (Kremser), packed columns, binary and multicomponent distillation (McCabe–Thiele, Fenske–Underwood–Gilliland–Kirkbride), membranes, liquid–liquid extraction, and diffusion and mass-transfer correlations.
Mass Transfer Notes — Notes on solid-state diffusivity and convective mass transfer — the Arrhenius diffusivity, the mass-transfer coefficient, Schmidt and Sherwood numbers, and the laminar flat-plate (Blasius) results for local and average Sherwood numbers.

Coursework/index.title: Coursework
Coursework/index.content:
Class notes, homework and exam cheat sheets from undergraduate (UC Berkeley) and graduate (Purdue) coursework, sorted under the broader areas of chemical engineering. Everything is transcribed from handwritten pages into searchable text and equations. The original pages are kept in a collapsible box on every note, so typos in the transcription can be checked against the handwriting.
Topics

Chemistry · 2 cheat sheets — General, inorganic and organic chemistry: atomic structure, bonding, periodic trends, and acids and bases.
Computational and data methods · 2 courses, 1 cheat sheet — Numerical methods for PDEs and computational fluid dynamics, density functional theory, and statistics for data science.
Electrochemistry · 1 course, 2 cheat sheets — Electrochemical thermodynamics, electrode kinetics, transport in electrolytes and electrochemical engineering.
Materials and solid-state science · 3 cheat sheets — Crystal structures, semiconductors and solid-state physics, and materials processing for microelectronics.
Process control · 1 cheat sheet — Feedback control of chemical processes: transfer functions, block diagrams and controller tuning.
Reaction engineering and catalysis · 2 courses, 3 cheat sheets — Chemical reactor design and energy balances, reaction kinetics and mechanisms, and heterogeneous catalysis and its characterization.
Research methods · 1 course — Graduate research skills: literature searching, forming and testing hypotheses, and the qualifying exam.
Thermodynamics · 1 course, 1 cheat sheet — Classical and molecular thermodynamics: equations of state, phase and chemical equilibrium, and solution thermodynamics.
Transport phenomena and separations · 1 course, 3 cheat sheets — Momentum, heat and mass transfer, boundary layers, and separation processes such as drying, distillation and absorption.

index.title: Ashutosh Bhadouria
index.content:
hello, there! my name is Ashutosh (Ashu), and I am a PhD candidate at Purdue University in the field of chemical engineering.
hailing from Rajasthan, India, I have been fortunate enough to travel across the globe and experience a myriad range of cultures. I began my schooling in Kota, moved to Pune, followed by a short stint in Mumbai before finishing high school in Istanbul, Turkey. I carry an inquisitive attitude and take pleasure in small and beautiful things that life offers. When not busy suffering through grad school, I enjoy spending time with my friends, playing badminton, and catching up with science fiction movies/shows.
thank you for taking the time to visit this website, and stay tuned for regular (or maybe not-so-regular updates) in the near future…cheers!

“Sometimes, it’s better to bunk a class and enjoy with friends, because now, when I look back, marks never make me laugh, but memories do.” — Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (Aerospace Engineer and Former President of India)
